--[p337]-- Postexposure bake (PEB) was carried out at a temperature of $9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C } .$ , and the development was carried out using aqueous 0.26 N tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH) at a temperature of $2 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C } .$ A resolution of 25-nm hp without pattern collapse and, in addition, partially resolved 20-nm hp at an exposure dose of $3 6 \mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ were obtained.
--[p336]-- 9.3.2 POLYPHENOLS
The polyphenols represent one of the most studied families of compounds proposed as components of molecular resists. This may be due to the popularity of phenolic resins such as novolac and poly(hydroxyl) styrene derivatives as the main components of polymeric resists used at 248-nm and longer wavelength, lithography. The molecular compounds investigated have diverse structures, and it is difficult to propose a generic structure representing them all.
--[p336]-- Positive-tone molecular resists were tested using both 248 nm and e-beam exposures with the molecule of Fig. 9A. The Nikon NSR-1505 EX-1 stepper used for 248-nm exposure has a numerical aperture of 0.42, which limits its resolution to 300 nm. Patterns down to this size (300-nm line/ spaces) were resolved. Materials were also tested using a 40-kV e-beam tool under process conditions similar to those used in the 248-nm exposure.
--[p337]-- 150-nm line/spaces and 120-nm isolated lines were resolved at doses of $4 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ A tetrahydropyran group was also used as a low-energy deprotection group in the same molecule (Fig. 9A), and the measured sensitivity was an order of magnitude higher than that of the corresponding molecule protected with t-BOC in similar conditions.
--[p336]-- Typical examples are shown in Figs. 9A and B, which refer to materials proposed by the Ober group.<sup>30</sup> In the specific work, phenolic molecules were protected with acid-sensitive t-BOC in various degrees of introduction and evaluated. For the molecule shown in Fig. 9B, the $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ ranged from 7.1 to $6 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for substitution with 1e4 t-BOC groups, respectively. Images were produced using photoacid generator (PAG) to catalyze deprotection chemistry.
--[p337]-- Phenolic molecules were also investigated<sup>31</sup> in 2004 and, more recently,<sup>32,33</sup> in 2009 and 2010 by researchers of Tokyo Ohka Kogyo. Typical structures are shown in Fig. 10. The lithographic performance of the resist samples was evaluated by e-beam lithography. A 50-kV e-beam writing system was utilized for exposure.

===== [p213-213] The chemistry and application of nonchemically amplified (non-CA) chain-scission resists > 6.3.4 POLYESTERS AND POLYCARBONATES (8块) =====
--[p213]-- Nuclear magnetic resonance analysis of the soluble polymer allowed identification of phenol-type chain-end structures, with a G-value for formation of 0.7.
Inspired by these observations, Yu et al.<sup>12,81,98,99</sup> prepared a series of aliphatic polycarbonates with cyclic ring structures within the main chain to increase the glass transition temperature and ultimately etch resistance.
--[p213]-- 6.3.4 POLYESTERS AND POLYCARBONATES
In recent years, the radiation chemistry of linear aliphatic polyesters, such as the polyalkanoates and the copolymers of lactic and glycolic acids, have attracted significant interest as a result of their widespread use as biomedical materials. These polymers undergo net chain scission on exposure to high-energy photons.
--[p213]-- Similarly, Babanalbandi et al.<sup>93</sup> reported values of the G-value for radical formation at 77K for poly(Llactic acid) (L-PLA) and poly(D,L-lactic acid) (D,L-PLA) as 2.0 and 2.4, respectively. They also reported G(S) 2.3 and G(X) 0.0 for D,L-PLA, G(S) 2.4 and G(X) 0.28 for L-PLA. So in summary, the polyesters have similar or superior sensitivity compared with PMMA but that incorporation of longer aliphatic side chains leads to measurable yields of cross-linking reactions.
--[p213]-- The ester main chains contained linear, cyclic, bicyclic, tricylic, or polycyclic (adamantyl) rings, and the glass temperature increased with the weight of the ring structure. The polymers achieved reasonable sensitivity to EUV photons $( \mathrm { E } _ { 0 }$ of the order 50 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>) despite their low absorbance at these wavelengths.
--[p213]-- For example, Carswell-Pomerantz et al.<sup>91,92</sup> examined in detail the g-radiation chemistry of copolymers of hydroxybutyrate and hydroxyvalerate.
--[p213]-- The low-temperature radical yields were of the order of 1.7, independent of copolymer composition.<sup>91</sup> The yields of chain scission on irradiation at room temperatures range from G(S)  2.2 up to 3.4 for higher hydroxyvalerate content; however, small yields of cross-linking reactions were noted with the inclusion of the longer-branched comonomer.
--[p213]-- It was suggested<sup>98</sup> that increasing absorbance through inclusion of high cross-section elements or small molecule absorbers could result in sensitivities approaching 10 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>.
--[p213]-- There have been few reports of the high-energy degradation chemistry of polycarbonates and none to our knowledge of aliphatic polycarbonates. The common engineering polymer bis-A polycarbonate undergoes chain scission during irradiation in vacuum, evidence of the high sensitivity of the carbonate group to degradation.<sup>94,95</sup> A later study by Babanalbandi et al.<sup>96,97</sup> provided a measure of G(R) 0.5 at 77K.

===== [p159-160] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.3.2 RLS TRADEOFF (10块) =====
--[p159]-- The distance the acid molecules travel during PEB or “resist blur” determines the minimum feature size that can be resolved using the resist or its resolution. Upon development, the distribution of the deprotection within the resist gives rise to the LER in the resist (Fig. 9C).
Based on this briefly explained mechanism, the following conclusions can be made:
--[p160]-- • For a lower absorbed dose (i.e., a more sensitive resist), fewer acid molecules are released upon exposure, and thus, deprotection will not occur uniformly in the entire resist leading to high LER. The LER is said to be dominated by photon shot noise.
• To decrease LER, a longer PEB can be used to deprotect more labile groups and to expand the acid diffusion range leading to smoothening of the pattern, but at the expense of resolution.
--[p160]-- This result is commonly known as the Resolution, LER, and Sensitivity tradeoff, which has been observed and studied in detail by several researchers.<sup>52e57</sup> The LER values in a typical CAR have been found to be inversely proportional to the square root of the exposure dose.<sup>53,56</sup> Hence, increasing exposure dose decreases the LER, until a certain minimum value (3e4 nm), as determined by the molecular size and high-order interaction of the polymer chains within the CAR.
--[p159]-- Upon exposure, some photons interact with the resist leading to acid being generated inside the bulk of the exposed part of the resist, at random locations (Fig. 9A). The number of acid molecules released per one photon absorbed by the system is called the resist’s quantum yield. During the PEB, the acid molecules diffuse within the resist film deprotecting more labile groups (Fig. 9B).
--[p160]-- It should be noted, though, that the acid generators have been found to decompose during prolonged exposures, setting a limit on the minimum LER in CARs requiring high exposure doses.<sup>58</sup>
To compare different resist materials to each other several figures of merit for the interdependence of the acid blur, LER and sensitivity have been formulated.
--[p160]-- High-resolution patterning with low LER requires lots of acid release during exposure and minimal diffusion of acid during PEB, hence higher dose, that is, lower sensitivity.
Therefore, it is a challenging task to achieve low sensitivity, low LER, and high resolution at the same time in CARs.
--[p160]-- For a rigorous treatment of this relationship, blur or effective diffusion length, exposure latitude, image quality of the exposure setup etc. need to be carefully determined. However, the relationship of the three constituents can be generalized in the following simple form<sup>59</sup>:
$$
\mathbf { B l u r } ^ { 3 } \times \mathbf { L E R } ^ { 2 } \times \mathbf { D o s e } = \mathbf { C o n s t a n t }\tag{11}
$$
--[p160]-- As all the parameters for determining the Z-factor can be extracted from scanning electron micrographs of the exposed resist material using suitable image analysis software, the Z-factor has found popularity as a quick means of comparing the performance of different resists to each other with a single parameter. However, it should be noted that the Z-factor does not take into account the imaging performance of the exposure tool and the quality of the illumination.
Therefore, the Z-factor is best suited for comparing results achieved using the same or very similar exposure setups.
--[p160]-- Wallow et al.<sup>59</sup> have proposed a further simplified model where the experimental measurement for resist blur is substituted by the limiting minimum resolution of the material:
$$
{ \mathrm { H a l f ~ p i t c h } } ^ { 3 } \times { \mathrm { L E R } } ^ { 2 } \times { \mathrm { S e n s i t i v i t y } } = Z\tag{12}
$$
where Z is a constant called the Z-factor. In this context, sensitivity is determined as the dose-to-size (the dose where the anticipated feature sizes are achieved).
--[p159]-- 4.3.2 RLS TRADEOFF
Chemically amplified resists (CAR) have thus far successfully met the scaling requirements of the semiconductor industry. However, to meet the performance targets set for future nodes, significant further improvements in resolution, LER, and sensitivity need to be achieved. Optimization of all three parameters simultaneously is challenging, since these parameters show an inherent tradeoff relationship between each other.
Consider a CAR that is exposed to high-energy photons.

===== [p371-372] Mainstreaming inorganic metal-oxide resists for high-resolution lithography > 10.3 HIGH-Z NANOCLUSTER PATTERNING (6块) =====
--[p372]-- Then, we will detail historical lithographic progress in high Z oxo-hydroxo materials, which has culminated in commercial development of tin-oxide EUV photoresists that overcome HafSOx solution and film instabilities.
--[p371]-- 10.3 HIGH-Z NANOCLUSTER PATTERNING
While high-resolution is achievable with HSQ, its sensitivity is too low for manufacturing. The need for both high resolution and high sensitivity, particularly for EUV applications, led to research on new high-Z oxo-hydroxo cluster photoresists represented by HafSOx and ZircSOx. Their performancedcomprising high resolution, low line-edge roughness, high sensitivity, and high etch resistanced have motivated renewed and widespread interest in inorganic resists.
--[p371]-- Such atomic smoothness is a key requirement for high-performance EUV resists, and it stimulated thinking about how to translate the observed smoothness to the sidewall of a lithographic pattern. Consequently, a vision was advanced to synthesize and pattern nanostructures from clusters directly on the wafer.
In the following sections, we detail our understanding of the solution chemistry, the film formation processes, and exposure mechanisms in the HafSOx and ZircSOx systems.
--[p371]-- initially demonstrated that oxo-hydroxo nanocluster solutions comprised a unique platform for spin-on high-quality dielectric films.<sup>57</sup> Hafnium and zirconium sulfate clusters and films, commonly known as HafSOx and ZircSOx, respectively, were among those initially studied.<sup>58</sup> Because most spin-coated cluster films resist crystallization, they consistently show atomically smooth surfaces (Fig. 8).
--[p371]-- $\mathrm { H f } _ { 4 }$ and $\mathrm { Z r } _ { 4 }$ clusters bound by peroxide and sulfate ligands dominate solution speciation. Peroxide and sulfate act as “L” ligands in Fig. 2, both enhancing solution cluster stability and solubility. As described in Section 10.3.3, the materials develop as negative-tone resists in TMAH. In development, peroxide promotes dissolution of unexposed regions, while sulfate ion exchange with eOH from TMAH promotes additional condensation and insolubility.
--[p371]-- Furthermore, peroxide plays an additional role as a radiation-sensitive ligand, gating crosslinking and condensation reactions in exposed areas.
High-Z oxo-hydroxo materials research began during the mid 2000s, when Oregon State University and Hewlett Packard researchers were investigating them for printed electronics. This work not only laid the foundation for both oxide thinfilm transistor backplanes in displays<sup>56</sup> but also led to high-Z nanocluster patterning work. Keszler et al.

===== [p192-193] EUV lithography patterning challenges > 5<sub>.</sub>2 EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET RESIST STOCHASTICS 5<sub>.</sub>2<sub>.</sub>1 MULTIVARIATE POISSON PROPAGATION MODEL (10块) =====
--[p193]-- The second diffusion process is going from the acid image to the deprotection image dominated by the acid blur. Noting that cascaded diffusion processes can be modeled as the convolution of the individual processes which ends up strongly dominated by the largest term, we can largely ignore the smaller terms focusing on the dominant diffusion term which for a CA resist will be the acid diffusion. From Fig.
--[p193]-- Also explicit in the model are a series of nonstochastic terms including absorptivity, diffusion lengths, and reaction rates. We note that these terms could also readily be converted to stochastic terms if desired.
Key parameters in this model are the diffusion processes that serve to smooth out the input stochastic terms. The first diffusion process is the electron blur that causes a spread from the absorbed photon image.
--[p193]-- The model can be summarized by stating that the various input RVs have been propagated through the process and combined to yield the final output RV that can be used to assess patterned variability. Depending on the input aerial image, the variability can take the form of line-edge roughness (LER), line-width roughness (LWR), contact critical dimension uniformity, tip-to-tip variations, among others.
--[p192]-- Examples of stochastic materials’ parameters of concern are photoacid generators, quenchers, protecting groups, generated acids, and so on. To predict the stochastic limits of a material process, stochastic resist models are needed as opposed to the traditional mean field models that work only based on average parameters. An example of such a model is the Multivariate Poisson Propagation Model (MPPM).<sup>18e22</sup>
--[p193]-- 6, it is also evident that the spatial frequency content in the deprotection image and the developed image is set by these diffusion processes and thus the LER power spectral density (PSD) serves as an excellent metric for this key model parameter.
Fig. 7 shows the measured PSD for three different resists, two (A and B) being CA and the third (C) not. The correlation length measured from the PSD serves as a measure of the dominant diffusion term, which can then be used in the MPPM model.
--[p192]-- Recall that under higher energy EUV radiation, a single photon absorption event can yield multiple acids on average, but the exact number will be an RV. The next step in the model is the reaction diffusion process where the acid distribution reacts with the quencher (RV4) and the protecting groups (RV5).
--[p192]-- 5<sub>.</sub>2 EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET RESIST STOCHASTICS 5<sub>.</sub>2<sub>.</sub>1 MULTIVARIATE POISSON PROPAGATION MODEL
As we approach the atomic scale for patterning, stochastics driven by simple counting statistics begin to dominate variability concerns. This issue is most commonly discussed from the perspective of photon shot noise, but in fact is more fundamentally applicable to also incorporate photoresist material components.
--[p192]-- In the MPPM model, counting statistics theory is used to determine the local nanoscale density of all key material, reaction, and exposure components. Fig. 6 pictorially depicts the flow of the model for the case of a chemically amplified (CA) resist (described elsewhere in this book). The model starts with a given aerial image that represents the infinite time averaged photon distribution.
--[p192]-- Finally, applying a develop model, which in the current implementation of the MPPM is simply a fractional threshold develop relative to RV5, we end up with the final output RV representing the dissolved fraction. We note that, a more complicated stochastic dissolution model<sup>23e25</sup> c ould also be applied.
--[p192]-- The first random variable (RV1) appears at the absorption step where we now end up with a Poisson distribution of absorbed photons per pixel based on the input dose, pixel volume, and material absorptivity. The next step is release of acid, which is determined by the counting statistics of local photoacid generator (PAG) density (RV2) and the counting statistics of the acid yield (RV3).

===== [p202-205] The chemistry and application of nonchemically amplified (non-CA) chain-scission resists > 6.1 INTRODUCTION (18块) =====
--[p204]-- We proposed that the yield of fragmentation reactions is proportional to the scission yield on exposure to 92 eV EUV photons. The measure of the sensitivity adopted is the ratio of the intensity of the parent ion signal to the total ion count (relative molecular ion intensity (RMI), a parameter which decreases with increasing sensitivity to bond cleavage). The results of screening a very large number of small molecules are shown in Fig. 2.
--[p202]-- This polymer and other subsequent nonchemically amplified (non-CA) resists have almost exclusively been positive-tone resists displaying an increase in solubility on exposure. Before the advent of chemical amplification, the focus of much of the research in the field was on increasing the yield of scission reactions per absorbed photon.
--[p205]-- The results further allowed construction of a quantitative structure-property relations model-relating structure to sensitivity to EUV photons.<sup>12</sup>
--[p202]-- 6.1 INTRODUCTION
The very first photoresists for deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography, appearing in the early 1970s, were based on poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA).<sup>1</sup> PMMA undergoes chain scission on exposure to high-energy photons, and the resultant decrease in molecular weight provides the contrast necessary for selective dissolution of the exposed material.
--[p204]-- Importantly a number of groups, including our own,<sup>12</sup> have established that a strong relationship exists between the relative yields on absorption of high-energy gamma photons and lower energy radiation. Typical values of G-values for chain scission (G(S)) for materials discussed here range from less than unity to, in unusual circumstances, 10.
--[p203]-- Over the past decade, reduction in LER has become a significant challenge for the industry and despite tremendous efforts remains one of the main barriers to successful introduction of sub-20-nm patterning. Therefore, in recognition of the need to achieve smoother features, the industry is contemplating acceptance of slower resist materials; a number of non-CA resist platforms may therefore re-emerge as viable resist materials for future lithographic nodes.
--[p202]-- However, these efforts ultimately only led to incremental increase in sensitivity of the non-CA resists and the disruptive technology of chemical amplification meant that interest in this class of materials declined abruptly.
In recent years, focus has again turned to non-CA resists, driven by the observation of superior pattern fidelity compared with chemically amplified resists. This is quantitatively described by the reduced line-edge roughness (LER) of non-CA resists.<sup>2,3</sup> In Fig.
--[p204]-- Work in the field of non-CA chain-scission resists builds upon decades of studies of the effects of ionizing radiation on polymeric systems. A very detailed understanding has been built of the relationship between polymer structure and the response to incident photons.<sup>6e11</sup> In that field, the yield of chemical reactions is defined as the radiochemical G-value or the number of chemical events occurring for every 16 aJ (100 eV) of absorbed energy.
--[p204]-- The yield of these reactions determines in many instances the sensitivity of the resist. Subsequent reactions such as depolymerization steps, discussed in the next section, are also critically important for non-CA resists; however, the relative sensitivities to bond cleavage remain worthy of consideration when designing non-CA systems.
--[p204]-- Two-component resists usually comprise a matrix material, for example, a phenolic resin, and a photosensitizer such as a naphthoquinone derivative. In this chapter, we consider primarily positive-tone one-component resists, specifically chain-scission resists; interested readers are referred to the excellent summary by Willson<sup>5</sup> for discussion of the other classes of non-CA resists.
--[p204]-- As acknowledged previously, we rely on the accumulated knowledge of several generations of researchers in the field of radiation chemistry to guide our design; however, these studies usually report the yields of end products, not of the primary events.
--[p204]-- Low values of RMI identify candidate structures including esters, carbonates, and sulfones,

--[p204]-- Recently, we developed a simple approach to quantifying the susceptibility of certain molecules to undergo bond cleavage reactions, which is especially applicable to gauging sensitivity to EUV photons.<sup>12</sup> The approach consists of measuring the degradation of small organic molecules under electron impact in a standard mass spectrometer with an electron ionization source operating at 70 eV.
--[p204]-- developed can be categorized on the basis of their response to incident photons and on the number of active components within the resist. Willson describes a “resist hierarchy,” with the principal level of taxonomy describing whether the polymer undergoes positive or negative changes in solubility. Both positive- and negative-tone resists can be either one-component or two-component resists.
--[p203]-- Non-CA resists have been developed over almost five decades, and so a range of ingenious approaches have been adopted to produce a change in solubility of the resist polymer on exposure. As described by Willson,<sup>5</sup> the range of materials
--[p204]-- Since the average dissociation energy of a carbonecarbon bond is of the order of 350 kJ/mol (3.6 eV), it is hoped that the yield of primary degradation products may approach values exceeding 20, however, even on achieving these yields, non-CA resists will be significantly slower than the best performing chemically amplified competitors.
The primary events resulting from interaction with high-energy photons result in cleavage of side-chain or main-chain bonds.

--[p67]-- Another approach that seems to be more successful is the addition of surfactant to the developer or rinse liquid to reduce the surface tension with less impact on contact angle.<sup>514,515</sup> Other alternative developers and rinses have been investigated such as perfluorohexane, which has low surface tension<sup>516</sup> and even supercritical carbon dioxide, which has no surface tension.<sup>517e522</sup> Another interesting approach was the use of tetra-butylammonium hydroxide as the developer instead of the standard TMAH.<sup>523e526</sup> It generally improved pattern collapse performance in several resists, but there is no clarity on whether it reduced swelling<sup>527</sup> or increased the contact angle<sup>528</sup> or both.
--[p68]-- Although the patterned resist is chemically different than the unpatterned areas, there is usually not sufficient selectivity between regions to allow direct etching because each region generally has the same atoms. One way to overcome this issue is to use a process known as surface or top-surface imaging of the resists.<sup>540,541</sup> This typically involves deposition of a silicon containing species onto the patterned resist before any development steps.
--[p68]-- Common approaches to increase adhesion include optimizing wafer pretreatment<sup>529</sup> or by using different organic ULs.<sup>530e533</sup> Another novel method was developed that used small molecule organic functionalized silanes which could covalently cross-link the resist to the wafer.<sup>534,535</sup> The one end of the molecule will covalently react with silica surfaces to covalently attach to the wafer, while the other end was functionalized with a vinyl ether which could react with OH groups commonly found on resist. The cross-link of the vinyl ether can form an acetal group, which can be cleaved by photoacid to allow clean development of the resist in the exposed regions.
--[p68]-- They are often more effective the narrower the resist sidewalls get because the surface-to-volume ratio of the resists increases.
Since pattern collapse occurs during the drying process after rinsing, one possible solution is to not develop the resist in a liquid process, but instead selectively remove or maintain the patterned areas in the resist using a plasma etching process. This approach is called dry development.
--[p70]-- The drastic change in material properties that comes with increasing surface-to-volume ratios in polymer structures is and will continue to be a challenge to continued feature shrinking.
--[p68]-- The chemical changes brought about by patterning means the silylating agent selectively deposits in one region. Subsequent oxygen plasma etching is therefore region selective because the silicon containing areas form an etch stop consisting of silicon dioxide.
--[p67]-- This is phenomenologically similar to other observed forms of thin film buckling behavior to relieve stress.<sup>509</sup> The ultimate mode that causes pattern collapse can change depending on a large number of resist parameters such as mechanical properties, pattern geometry, and surface chemistry after development.
There have been multiple strategies investigated to improve pattern collapse performance, each designed to improve one or more of the modes of failure described earlier.
--[p66]-- High aspect ratio features tend to collapse because the stress is much higher than in lower aspect ratio features. The stress that is put on the line can cause pattern collapse (i.e., mechanical failure of the resist line) generally through one of several different failure modes.<sup>501</sup>

--[p68]-- There have also been studies to help mitigate pattern collapse by improving the adhesion of the resist to the substrate of UL.
--[p67]-- If the capillary forces exceed the adhesion forces (also described as van der Waals forces), then the resist line will detach from the substrate and fail.<sup>506,507</sup> Improving the adhesion of the resist to the substrate improves this mode of failure. One final mode of pattern collapse that is important, but not directly related to the capillary pressure is swelling induced failure of the resist line.
--[p65]-- 1.6.4 PATTERN COLLAPSE
Many additional challenges are encountered as resist feature sizes shrink below 100 nm. Some of these challenges were not present at larger features sizes but become apparent because the physicochemical properties of the resists actually change at these length scales due to so-called confinement effects. Other challenges were already present at larger feature sizes, but can no longer be easily corrected.
--[p67]-- A resist line can swell by imbibing developer during development.<sup>508</sup> Because the pattern is constrained at the substrate, it relieves stress by buckling into a pseudoregular pattern that looks similar to a cosine wave during the rinse process.
--[p66]-- The parameters are the surface tension $( \gamma )$ of the rinse liquid, the contact angle (q) of the rinse liquid on the photoresist, and the space width to the next feature on either side of the resist line $( S _ { 1 }$ and $S _ { 2 } )$ .<sup>498</sup> If the space on one side $( S _ { 2 } )$ is much larger than the space on the other side $( S _ { 1 } )$ , then Eq. (14) can be simplified to Eq. (15).
--[p66]-- Because the pressure difference is proportional to inverse $\mathbf { S } _ { 1 }$ , the pressure gets bigger as the space gets smaller, which is one reason why pattern collapse appears to be a bigger issue as pitches reduce. If the space on either side of the resist line is exactly the same $( \mathsf { i . e . , } S _ { 1 } = S _ { 2 } )$ , then there should theoretically be no pressure differential as in Eq. (14).
--[p67]-- However, many times changing one parameter positively can change the other parameter negatively such that they offset one another. For example, using isopropanol for the rinse liquid instead of water can reduce the surface tension to onethird its original value, but can cause a decrease in contact angle that leads to a three to four times increase in the cos q term.
--[p70]-- 25, which shows the normalized polymer modulus as a function of film thickness determined by film buckling measurements.<sup>509,549</sup> The free surface of a polymer film is a region of enhanced mobility with very different properties than the bulk polymer. The modulus of the polymers decreases with decreasing film thickness because the surface layer becomes a larger and larger component of the total film thickness.
--[p68]-- The patterned resist is essentially turned into a continuous film. Now the film can be plasma etched and the silicon containing regions are selectively left behind while the pure resist regions are removed. This approach has shown promising results at even sub-15-nm EUV patterns.<sup>548</sup>
Pattern collapse becomes a bigger problem as feature sizes shrink because the capillary forces increase as the resist space decreases.
--[p66]-- Although it is apparent that a pressure differential can be created on the resist lines during the drying process, there are several different potential ways in which this pressure can cause collapse. The pressure differential wants to mechanically deform the resist line. At the top of the resist, the line can bend due to the applied force but the bottom of the resist line is fixed to the substrate and cannot bend.
--[p67]-- There are also some reports that suggest LER significantly increases as resist thickness decreases, so that can be a trade-off as well.<sup>512,513</sup>
Other methods to improve pattern collapse include those that have attempted to reduce the surface tension or increase the contact angle of the final rinse liquid to nearly 90 degrees because those changes reduce the critical stress as shown in Eq. (16).
--[p68]-- Dry development of the exposed or unexposed region provides the final relief pattern.<sup>542,543</sup> Another more recent approach that has garnered much attention is the so-called dry development rinse process, which uses a Dry Development Rinse Material.<sup>544e547</sup> This process is the same as conventional resist processing up until the rinse after the standard development.

--[p68]-- Another interesting approach to improve pattern collapse that has been developed is the use of a reactive rinse, which is an aqueous solution containing reactive species that is used to rinse the resist after development.<sup>536</sup> The resist sidewall often contains sites such as phenols or carboxylic acids, which can react with components in the rinse to form esters or amides.
--[p67]-- One mode of pattern collapse failure is elastic failure where the top of the beam bends so far that the elastic restoring force of the resist line cannot overcome the pressure force and so the pattern fails.<sup>502e504</sup> The magnitude of the displacement is inversely proportional to the elastic modulus of the resist, so increasing the resist modulus reduces the displacement and this mode of failure.
--[p66]-- Pattern collapse occurs because there is a capillary pressure exerted on the resist lines as the final rinse liquid is being dried. The drying is usually done using forced nitrogen or by spinning the wafer until it dries. While this capillary pressure should occur regardless of the type of liquid, the magnitude of the pressure will be different depending on the type of liquid and the geometry of the pattern.
The capillary pressure difference $( \Delta P )$ experienced by a resist line during drying can be described by Eqs. (14) and (15).
--[p68]-- Instead of rinsing with a neutral liquid or even with a rinse with small molecule reactive species, this rinse has a dissolved silicon containing polymer which thoroughly deposits in the spaces between resist walls created during development. Now when the rinse is dried off, there is no collapse because all the capillaries that were created by the resist spaces are filled and so there is no capillary force experienced by the resist.
--[p70]-- A significant drop in the glass transition temperature of polymer thin films is also observed below 40 nm as the higher mobility, lower $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ surface layer becomes a larger proportion of the total film thickness very similarly to the drop in modulus.<sup>550e555</sup> Large drops in diffusivity and water uptake are also seen as films drop in thickness below 40 nm.<sup>556</sup> The limit where the resist polymer structure will be entirely surface chains is rapidly approaching and is likely on the order of 5e10-nm feature size. In this regime, polymer properties will be so different from conventional bulk properties that the material may no longer behave suitably for use as a resist.
--[p68]-- Monofunctional species can change the surface chemistry of the resist to increase the contact angle and thus improve collapse. By using difunctional and other multifunctional species, not only is the contact angle modified, bu the modulus of the resist sidewall, it is more resistance to bending and thus can accommodate greater stress before collapsing.
--[p67]-- The most commonly used method is to simply make the resist thinner.<sup>510,511</sup> This approach works because it lowers the H in Eq. (16) which reduces critical stress on the resist. Reducing the resist thickness to improve collapse comes with the trade-off of reduced etch mask, so more sophisticated pattern stacks are required for robust pattern transfer from the resist into the UL.
--[p65]-- There has also been expanded interest in using organic solvents for development such as n-butyl acetate or methyl isobutyl ketone among others with rinses of an alcohol such as isopropanol (IPA). Some of the inorganic resists such as HSQ use even more uncommon development routines such as heated or cooled development or salt-added base development.<sup>492e497</sup>

Both experiments show a drop in properties at similar surface-to-volume ratios.
The top of the resist line also plays a role but it is a relatively small amount of the total surface area.
--[p65]-- Some issues that were occasional nuisances become potentially limiting of future improvements. Pattern collapse is an issue that continues to become a greater challenge the smaller the features shrink.
Practically all resists are developed by immersion or spraying with a liquid development solvent, which selectively dissolves parts of the resist to form patterns.
--[p67]-- Another mode of failure has been called elastoplastic failure.<sup>505</sup> This occurs in polymers, which show a yield stress at high strains. The line will begin to bend elastically at low strains related to modulus until the stress on the line exceeds the yield stress and it will then plastically deform which is a collapse failure. Increasing the resist yield stress improves this mode of failure. Another important mode of failure is adhesion failure.
--[p66]-- Unfortunately, experimental patterns are not always so ideal (for instance LER) and so pattern collapse still frequently occurs because small variations in space width or drying rates on either side of the line can induce sufficient pressure differential for collapse.

===== [p412-414] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.5.2.2 Homolytic cleavage of the tinecarbon bond (8块) =====
--[p412]-- Tin<sub>e</sub>carbon bonds are relatively weak (w50 kcal/mol), and tin forms extremely stable radicals, therefore, it is conceivable that EUV exposure could cause homolysis.<sup>78</sup> If homolysis occurs, we predict that stabilizing or destabilizing the organic radical should result in a change in the photosensitivity of the cluster. Fig. 34 shows a series of organic groups with the associated CeH bond dissociation energy.
--[p414]-- This method, however, was found to be too harsh for phenyltin trichloride, resulting in an insoluble white solid which was thought to be tin(IV) oxide (due to hydrolysis of the phenyletin bond). Several hydrolysis methods were subsequently attempted, and hydrolysis of the organotin trichloride using ammonium hydroxide proved the most successful route (Fig. 35B). The reaction product is a soluble polymeric material, which had similar size to the Sn-12 cluster by GPC.
--[p412]-- The bond dissociation energy of the CeH bond should directly correlate with the relative radical stability of the organic group. The goal of this study was to synthesize a series of Sn-12 clusters containing alkyl groups with varied radical stabilities and to then test these clusters for sensitivity and imaging.
--[p412]-- 11.5.2.2 Homolytic cleavage of the tinecarbon bond
A second possible reaction that could occur during exposure is homolytic cleavage of the tin<sub>e</sub>carbon bond.
--[p414]-- Due to the poor image quality, it was difficult to accurately measure linewidths for the imaged patterns and so the dose approximately at E<sub>SIZE</sub> was used. Fig. 37 shows the CeH bond energy versus dose curve for clusters 57 through 59.<sup>77</sup> The dose of these clusters appears to correlate directly with CeH bond energy which supports the mechanism of tinecarbon bond homolysis.
--[p414]-- Sn-12 clusters have been synthesized by either the dehydration of butylstannoic acid,<sup>57</sup> or the controlled hydration of butyltin trichloride,<sup>73</sup> butyltin trialkoxide,<sup>49</sup> or butyltin trialkynide.<sup>56</sup> Since butylstannoic acid is generally made by rapid hydrolysis of butyltin trichloride, our starting material targets were alkyltin trichlorides.<sup>73</sup> Allyltin trichloride was synthesized through a previously published route, phenyl and butyltin trichlorides were purchased.<sup>79</sup>
Initial attempts to synthesize the Sn-12 clusters involved converting the organotin trichloride to the organostannoic acid, followed by dehydration to make the cluster (Fig. 35A).
--[p414]-- All attempts to crystallize the clusters were unsuccessful, and so the uncrystallized products were lithographically evaluated. The predicted structures (allyl (57), butyl (58) and phenyl (59)) are shown in Table 2.
Clusters 57 through 59 were coated on Si wafers and evaluated lithographically (Fig. 36). Clusters 57 and 58 showed poor image quality, likely attributed to impurities.

===== [p368-370] Mainstreaming inorganic metal-oxide resists for high-resolution lithography > 10.2.3 HSQ DEVELOPMENT MECHANISM (14块) =====
--[p369]-- Silicon oxygen bonds can potentially break during development in base, and this will be enhanced in base with added salts. Similar to what happens in quartz, cations from the salt coordinate with lone-pair electrons on oxygen. These cations act as Lewis acids, increasing the electrophilic character of the silicon reaction thereby weakening the SieO bond. The SieO bond can be broken and reduce the networking of the material, further increasing solubility.
--[p369]-- Harry et al.<sup>49</sup> and Strobel et al.<sup>50s</sup> were able to develop HSQ electrochemically in NaCl solutions indicating that it was leaky to charge, even in 100-nm films.
Note that in these studies, all (except Lee et al. who baked the HSQ at $9 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ the HSQ was vacuum dried as a means to increase the crosslink differential between the exposed and unexposed material. Thus, the unexposed material was not well networked.
--[p369]-- The difference between a solvation based development mechanism and one that etches the material was demonstrated using organic solvent for HSQ development.<sup>52</sup> Organic developers can only solvate the material such that whole chains of HSQ are removed. HSQ was found to develop in methyl isobutyl ketone and xylene(s). However, as mentioned previously, stronger aqueous developers can attack an SieO bond in the SieOeSi network. In the presence of base, SiOe and SiOH are formed.
--[p370]-- They studied various developers, NaOH, TMAH, KOH, and LiOH with and without added salts of LiCl, KCl, NaCl, and tetramethylammonium chloride. They noted that in solution, ion exchange between the salt and hydroxide depends on the cations involved. For example, lithium does not readily dissociate from its cation. This makes developers with LiOH or added LiCl salts weaker than the others studied.
--[p370]-- Three factors are at play: the solvated and nonsolvated cation radii; HSQ density as a function of exposure dose; and the electrostatic double layer all play a role. They found that a mixture of TMAH and NaCl gave the highest contrast, slightly better than NaOH and NaCl mixtures at the same normality. Kim et al.
--[p370]-- They also related contrast difference between developers to the difference in the solvated and nonsolvated ionic radii of the cations. They considered the possibility of multiple dissolution mechanisms as indicated by the change of development rate with time (Fig. 7). Moreover, they discussed the dissolution rates based on whether the developer attacked only from the surface of the exposed material or was able to penetrate into the matrix.
--[p370]-- Consequently, the density should be much lower than the material exposed by e-beam. For instance, the refractive index of e-beam-cured HSQ, generally indicative of density, was found to be higher than even $4 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ baked HSQ, at the same relative SieH concentration.<sup>30</sup> This will change penetration of ions into the matrix and affect development.
Along these lines, Kim et al.<sup>51</sup> went on to discuss possible development mechanisms in more detail.
--[p368]-- 10.2.3 HSQ DEVELOPMENT MECHANISM
HSQ is generally developed in aqueous base. Namatsu et al.<sup>1</sup> initially demonstrated development in 2.38% TMAH and 20% KOH (by weight). TMAH at 2.38% is a weaker developer, and hence, HSQ patterns can be realized with less exposure dose. However, higher resolution and better reproducibility are found by strengthening the developer.
--[p368]-- This is accomplished by increasing concentration,<sup>18,46</sup> heating,<sup>29,46e48</sup> or adding salt to the base.<sup>15</sup> The highest resolutions have been achieved using a mixture of concentrated base and salt, a high-contrast development process first discovered by Yang et al.<sup>15</sup> In addition, electrochemical development in NaCl also yielded high resolution.<sup>49,50</sup> Improved resolution and reproducibility in these cases always comes at the expense of sensitivity.
--[p369]-- These can reversibly react to form the original bond or be solvated and contribute to dissolution.
The role of HSQ density, ion size, and surface charge in the salt developer mechanism is an important question. Lee et al.<sup>53</sup> noticed that in 25% TMAH developer, the development stopped after a certain time. They restarted the development with a brief dip in hydrofluoric acid (HF) followed by further development.
--[p370]-- speculated on the mechanism of increased contrast with the TMAH/NaCl developer: TMAH at the surface of highly exposed, higher density material helps block OH- penetration into the matrix, slowing down the development. While at the same time, lower dose materials are more easily penetrated by sodium cations, enhancing SieO bond breakage (as per Fig. 6). Yan et al.<sup>55</sup> confirmed that this developer had higher contrast. Contrast was increased further by heating the developer solution.
--[p369]-- Nam et al.,<sup>54</sup> like Kim et al.,<sup>51</sup> noticed that with mixed NaOH/NaCl developer, there were multiple development rate regimes. That is, the development would start at one rate, slow down, and start again at a faster rate (Fig. 7). This suggests that multiple development mechanisms are at play. In addition, Nam et al.<sup>54</sup> saw that development in NaOH was more isotropic than with a NaOH/NaCl mixture.
--[p370]-- Yang et al.<sup>13</sup> noted, however, that contrast in large features does not necessarily indicate higher resolution in smaller features due to confinement affects.
--[p368]-- The development of HSQ in base with and without added salts was discussed by Kim et al.<sup>51</sup> and is shown schematically in Fig. 6. In base, nucleophilic hydroxide ions attack electropositive silicon ions. Attack on a hydrogenated silicon leads to deprotonation and release of H . The newly formed SieOH bond can be deprotonated to form water and a sodium silicate. After dehydrogenation of HSQ, it can be solvated by aqueous base.

--[p65]-- Evaluating novel resist designs has also been relatively slow because of the limited availability of experimental tools such as the microexposure tool at Lawrence Berkeley National Lab and the interferometric tool at the Paul Scherrer Institute. Comparing results from one tool to the next is also difficult due to the fact that they have very different aerial image profiles compared to each other and compared to commercial EUV tools.
--[p63]-- While there are many reports of EUV resists which can obtain resolutions below 20-nm and with sensitivity below $2 0 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } .$ , there are very few which can obtain sub-20-nm resolution with sensitivity of $1 0 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ or below and likewise few reports of sub-20-nm resolution with sensitivity of $1 5 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ or below.
--[p63]-- Given that a trade-off exists, it is difficult to directly compare overall performance of one resist to another if two of the three parameters are different. A mathematical relation between these three parameters based on theoretical arguments and experimental observations has been developed as shown in Eq. (13).<sup>482</sup> The parameter Z has been treated as a resist material constant for a particular CAR design.
--[p63]-- The LWR metric has been even more of a challenge as 3s LWR has generally been reported to be 3e 4 nm for top-performing resists and more commonly reported as 4 nm and greater.<sup>484</sup> This is more than 2e3 times the ITRS recommendation for sub-20-nm resolution. Some reports of EUV patterning of metal oxide resists have shown LER as low as 2 nm, but at very low sensitivity of $7 0 + \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ 485
--[p65]-- Although champion CAR resolution at EUV improved rapidly in the first few years that exposure tools were made accessible, it has slowed considerably since 2010.<sup>486</sup> The best reported resolution in CARs has generally improved by no more than 1e2 nm per year and is flat some years, currently around 13e15-nm half-pitch.<sup>444,464,487</sup> Resolution has shown some slow improvements over the last several years, but it has generally come at the cost of increased dose-to-size and LWR improvement has been roughly flat.
--[p65]-- These results are seen in the fact that there appears to have been no substantial improvement in the Z values of champion resists since 2012.<sup>488</sup> It is also interesting to note that as the sensitivity in metal oxide resists has been improved and resolution in conventional CARs has been improved at the cost of sensitivity, their RLS performance has grown surprisingly similar to one another, each reporting resolution of 13e14 nm at a sensitivity of 35e45 mJ/ cm<sup>2</sup>.<sup>464,489</sup> This has occurred even though the materials have very different physical properties and patterning mechanisms, which demonstrates how difficult the RLS trade-off is to overcome.
--[p65]-- EUV resist design appears to have entered a time where continued development will be increasingly difficult, but critical for the implementation of EUV lithography at a commercial scale.
--[p65]-- Many resists tend to perform much better in terms of resolution and other properties on tools with relatively high aerial image contrast such as the interferometer at PSI compared to the lower aerial image contrast often found in conventionally illuminated tools near the resolution limit.<sup>490,491</sup> This has made it difficult to determine the practical performance limits for many resists as might be seen in high volume EUV manufacturing.
--[p64]-- http://hdl.handle.net/1853/39601.

Reproduced from Lawson RA, 2011. Molecular resists for advanced lithography e design, synthesis, characterization, and simulation [Ph.D. dissertation]. Atlanta, GA: Georgia Institute of Technology. http://hdL handle net/1853/39601
--[p62]-- This trade-off between resolution, LER, and sensitivity has been termed the RLS trade-off or the trilateral challenge (or more ominously the triangle of death).<sup>480</sup> The RLS trade-off states that there is a trade-off between RLS, such that any two of these performance parameters can be improved but only at the expense of the third parameter.<sup>481</sup> For example, reducing acid diffusion improves resolution but at the cost of sensitivity and LER might get better or worse depending on how far diffusion is restricted and overall PAG loading. Nonchemically amplified systems are some of the best performing in terms of resolution and LER, but generally have sensitivities 1e2 orders of magnitude higher than CARs, or worse.
--[p63]-- The International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS) sets the goal for EUV resist metrics to less than 20-nm half-pitch resolution, $5 { - } 2 0 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ sensitivity, and LWR equal to or less than 8% of the CD.
--[p62]-- 1.6.3 RESOLUTION, LINE EDGE ROUGHNESS, AND SENSITIVITY TRADE-OFF
Discussing the issues associated with acid diffusion and methods of controlling diffusion, it is clear that there generally exists a trade-off between sensitivity and resolution because methods to improve resolution generally reduce the spatial efficiency of each individual acid, which means higher catalyst concentration (i.e., dose) is required to pattern.
--[p63]-- Even if improving the resist design leads to an improved (smaller) $Z ,$ the resist is still restricted by the RLS trade-off because it is ultimately a result of the physics of lithography. This can be graphically demonstrated by Fig. 22 where the area of the triangle represents $Z ,$ and the smaller triangle is an improved resist design. Although this type of figure is good for conceptually understanding the trade-off, Eq.
--[p63]-- (13) suggests that the trade-off in many parameters is actually more drastic because of the powers on the parameters. This is more clearly seen in Fig. 23, which was made using Eq. (13) and reasonable experimental values of Z. As any one parameter is strongly minimized, the other parameters begin to climb quite rapidly.
Given the challenge of the RLS trade-off, how well are current resist materials performing?
--[p63]-- Other similar parameters such as $\mathrm { K _ { L U P } }$ have also been developed.<sup>483</sup>
$$
{ \mathrm { R e s o l u t i o n } } ^ { 3 } \times { \mathrm { L E R } } ^ { 2 } \times { \mathrm { S e n s i t i v i t y } } \approx Z\tag{1.13}
$$
Increasing base quencher levels generally maintains Z and simply moves RLS up or down depending on the level of addition. Changing the resist structure in more fundamental ways such as by increasing the PAG loading can potentially improve Z.
--[p62]-- Further experimental and simulation work has shown that this trade-off actually exists not only between resolution and sensitivity, but also between both of these parameters and LER (or LWR).

--[p30]-- Like many of the lithographic figures of merit, adjectives attached to the term resolution can be nonobvious; the most common example is the term high resolution. --[p34]-- The higher contrast resist still produces reasonable patterns when the aerial image is poor, but the low contrast resist produces very poor patterns and does not even completely clear at this dose (Fig. 10D). Increasing the dose to fully clear the low contrast resist in this case would actually lead to significant top loss. Good contrast in the resist can accommodate a wider range of exposure conditions.
--[p32]-- Contrast curves are made by exposing a resist coated wafer in multiple different locations with a different dose at each location, developing the exposed wafer, and measuring the remaining pattern thickness in each location. The remaining thickness is often normalized by the resist thickness before development. The contrast curve is the plot of normalized remaining thickness (NRT) versus dose and contrast is effectively the slope of this plot.
--[p35]-- Mathematical modeling of the exposure, resist chemistry change, and development process are important techniques for the semiconductor industry. Full discussion of these models and techniques are outside the scope of this review due to the complexity and often proprietary nature of these models. However, some simple resist exposure models are still widely used when evaluating resists and will be discussed.
--[p31]-- LWR is an increasing concern for future generations of devices because the gate width is rapidly approaching the scale of resist LWR which appears to be limited to 2e3 nm at a minimum.
Resist contrast is a measure of the photoresist’s conversion of the aerial image (i.e., the spatial distribution of energy) during exposure into a spatial distribution of resist material in the final physical relief image.
--[p29]-- These three metrics are the outcome of the patterning process and are the most commonly measured and reported; however, there is a large list of other parameters that are informative regarding resist fundamentals and patterning capability. Some of these parameters include contrast, exposure latitude, Dill C parameter, Z factor, and dissolution rate, among others. This section discusses many of the metrics and parameters in more detail.
--[p30]-- 130e132 Other techniques have also been used including scatterometry and AFM measurements.<sup>133</sup> Resolution is not purely controlled by the resist’s capabilities, but is a complex function of the resist properties, tool and conditions used to expose the resist, thermal and development conditions, aspect ratio of the final structures, adhesion to the substrate, among many other conditions.
--[p29]-- The goal of the lithographer, and especially those who work on resists, is to improve each of these metrics by optimizing the resist formulation and patterning process. There are three critically important resist metrics that must be considered: resolution, sensitivity, and line roughness, which is typically measured as line edge roughness (LER) or linewidth roughness (LWR).
--[p32]-- These parameters are used to calculate contrast in Eq. (2), and $E _ { 0 }$ is a direct measure of sensitivity. For a negative-tone resist, both $E _ { 0 }$ and $E _ { 1 }$ can be calculated and used similarly in Eq. (2), but sensitivity is also sometimes characterized by a parameter that can be called $E _ { 5 0 }$ as shown in Fig. 8B, which is the dose where NRT crosses 0.5 or 50% of the original film thickness.
--[p34]-- Exposure latitude will increase with increasing NILS and the magnitude of the increase is affected by resist contrast (higher contrast means larger improvements in exposure latitude with increasing NILS).<sup>158</sup> NILS is also important because it has been found that increasing NILS in an exposure system will lead to improved LER in the resist, although this improvement reaches a plateau at higher NILS.<sup>159</sup>
--[p31]-- LER is the root-mean-square deviation of the line edge profile shape from the straight line or plane, and it is almost always reported as the 3s value, where s is the standard deviation in line edge.<sup>139</sup> LWR is similarly the RMS deviation of the linewidth from the average CD and is also reported as the 3 value.<sup>140</sup> These two parameters are graphically illustrated in Fig. 7.
LWR and LER have been found to be related in many resists by the relation that LWR is equal to the square root of two times LER.
--[p34]-- The interplay between NILS and resist contrast are also important because they can be related to the resist feature’s exposure latitude.<sup>156</sup> Exposure latitude describes the change in resulting linewidth for a given change in exposure dose and is most often defined as the range of exposure energies that keeps the linewidth within specified limits. 24 These limits are often defined as 10% of the nominal feature size.
--[p32]-- (4), where I(x) is the aerial image intensity at a lateral position x. ILS is used rather than simply the slope of the aerial image because it normalizes out changes in dose as shown on the right hand side of Eq. (4). By multiplying ILS by the linewidth w, the normalized ILS (NILS) is obtained and is shown in Eq. (5). As NILS increases, the aerial image quality increases. This is illustrated in Fig.
--[p29]-- 1.4 CHARACTERIZATION AND FIGURES OF MERIT FOR RESISTS
Before specific resist chemistry and materials are considered, it is helpful to examine the general parameters for which any resist would be evaluated regardless of chemistry or exposure tool. The success of a lithographic process is usually measured against certain figures of merit or performance metrics.
--[p30]-- Thus, it is difficult to attempt to discuss the ultimate resolution or intrinsic resolution of a resist because the minimum printed feature of the resist will potentially vary from tool to tool.
Sensitivity or photospeed is the dose (amount of energy per unit area) required to produce the desired feature in the resist. The term sensitivity and dose also have potentially confusing descriptive nomenclature.
--[p32]-- Image contrast is the difference in the maximum and minimum intensity of an aerial image divided by their sum and is shown in Eq. (3). Image contrast is a useful general term, but does not provide information regarding the gradient or slope of the aerial image at the line edge, so other terms are more commonly used. The image log slope (ILS) is the slope of the logarithm of the aerial image, usually defined at the nominal edge of the designed pattern<sup>156</sup> and is shown in Eq.
--[p35]-- Dill and coworkers were the first to describe the basic lithographic exposure process with a mathematical model.<sup>160e162</sup> They used three parameters A, B, and C to describe the intensity of light in the resist and how it changes over exposure time due to photochemical reactions which occur during exposure. The parameters have become known since then as the Dill parameters; e.g., C is referred to as the Dill C parameter. These models can be used for UV, DUV, and even EUV patterning.
--[p30]-- CD is a term that is commonly used to describe the measurement of a feature printed in a resist, along with the terms linewidth or feature width.<sup>24</sup> CD is a more general term for the measurement of a feature and the terms are often used interchangeably, but resolution most precisely defines the smallest feature that can be printed or resolved.
Resolution and CD for resist features is most commonly measured by SEM and industrially this is done using a specialized version called a CD-SEM.

--[p430]-- Many alternatives such as 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidon, acetone, aqueous alkaline solutions such as 0.26 N tetramethylammonium hydroxide, or proprietary strippers such as AZ-100 (1-aminopropan-2-ol/dipropylene glycol methyl ether) or AZ-400T (1-methyl-2-pyrrolidone/1,2-propanediol/ tetramethylammonium hydroxide) are available, dependent on the properties of the resist and substrate.
Alternatively, a dry etching technique that incorporates oxygen plasma can strip the photoresist without damaging the device structure underneath.
--[p429]-- The acid-catalyzed deprotection of the base resin or dissolution inhibitors is triggered by the supply of thermal energy during a postexposure bake, which can be seen in Fig. 1C. It should be noted that in such a reaction the acid is not consumed. One acid molecule may contribute to the deprotection of several resin or inhibitor molecules. Fig. 1D shows the concluding step in the processing sequencedthe chemical development of the resist.
--[p430]-- The developing step of the lithographic process transforms the image that was irradiated with UV into a physical mask structure on the substrate. To remove the photoresist structures produced after use, or for rework, a photoresist stripper can be used.
--[p429]-- The base resins are generally extended chains of molecules, which are insoluble in a developer. When struck by a photon, the PAG produces a photoacid, catalytically removing acid-labile groups from the resin, or decomposing the dissolution inhibitor, leading to a solubility change. The process steps with a chemically amplified resist are illustrated by Fig. 1.
--[p428]-- 12.1 INTRODUCTION
The phenomenal surge in interest towards nanometer-sized electronic devices and circuit architectures has been propelled by expectations of further miniaturization and significantly lower costs of manufacture. This miniaturization has been possible due to microlithography and nanolithography, which have played a dominant role in decreasing the dimensions of electronic devices. This has been made possible by photolithography.
--[p429]-- Soluble areas of the resist are dissolved, whilst less soluble areas are retained.
A photoresist can be described as either positive tone or negative tone. The difference between these is that if the exposed areas are rinsed away when developed with a solvent it is said to be positive tone, while if the exposed areas remain postdevelopment, it is negative tone.
--[p429]-- To produce a uniform coating of the photoresist on to a semiconductor substrate, it is depositeddby spin coatingdfrom a solution of the polymer in a casting solvent.
The semiconductor substrate coated with a photoresist is baked on a hot plate to remove the majority of the residual casting solventdthis is known as a postapplication bake (PAB).
--[p428]-- For the production of semiconductor devices, patterning of the substrate is undertaken, to select areas where subsequent microelectronics processing steps can be employed, such as etching, deposition, diffusion, or ion implantation for doping. This technique of producing patterns is referred to as “lithography,” which is used to physically “mask off” certain areas of the substrate, whilst leaving other areas free for future processing.
--[p428]-- The aim of the lithographic process is therefore to protect selected areas of the device that are not to be modified during a particular processing stepdlike an etching processdwhich is achieved by coating that area with a protective layer.
--[p429]-- The first step in the lithography process is that the contaminants on the surface of silicon, which may result in poor adhesion and form defects in the photoresist film, must be removed by using cleaning chemicals. Often this is followed by the application of an adhesion promoter (such as hexamethyldisilazane) to improve the adhesion between the photoresist and the substrate that the device will be made from.
--[p429]-- In addition to evaporating the casting solvent from the photoresist film, this thermally anneals residual stress, in the photoresist film, that has occurred during spin coating. Fig. 1A illustrates that both the dissolution inhibitors and the PAG are distributed relatively homogenously within the photoresist, which is the ideal case.
In order to initiate the reaction in the appropriate areas of the photoresist a pattern is produced on the film by projecting light through a chrome photomask.
--[p429]-- The photoresist is irradiated with ultraviolet (UV) radiation. This causes the exposed areas of the photoresist to undergo a chemical transformation, for instance altering the solubility of these areas of the photoresist to the development solution. Fig. 1B depicts the interaction of incident light on the central part of the resist, which initializes the PAGs to produce a latent image of acid within the photoresist.
--[p429]-- The lithography mask to protect a selected area of a device is produced by creating a pattern of the desired feature size in a material referred to as a “photoresist.” The photoresist is “photo” sensitive, and it “resists” chemical and physical attack of the underlying substrate. The photoresist material is typically an organic polymer that consists of a resin, dissolution inhibitors, and/or photoacid generators (PAG), as described in previous chapters.

===== [p132-132] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 3.3 POTENTIAL ROLE IN LITHOGRAPHY (4块) =====
--[p132]-- The energy of the electron also determines its mean free path, i.e., the average length the electron travels the material. Fig. 3 shows experimental data for the inelastic mean free path as function electron energy.<sup>19</sup> It is relatively long at energies below 10 eV and can be on the order of nanometers. The mean free path has its minimum between 10 and 100 eV and increases again for higher energies.
--[p132]-- 3.3 POTENTIAL ROLE IN LITHOGRAPHY
Having given an overview of electron-induced processes that lead to the dissociation of molecules, the question is: what is the role of these interactions in the nextgeneration lithography? This issue is complex, as there are many parameters involved. We have seen that (among others) the energy of the electron determines the reaction rate and the outcome of the reaction.
--[p132]-- If sub-10-eV electrons dominate the reactions in the exposure of the resist or precursors, their relatively long mean free path can contribute to image blur and loss of resolution in the final pattern. Therefore, the electron energy potentially determines the spatial resolution in the next-generation lithography.
However, the most striking aspect regarding electron-induced chemistry is the limited amount of informationdthere is simply a lot that we do not know.
--[p132]-- Clearly, more work is necessary before that we can rationally design and optimize materials for the next-generation lithography. Yet, some general trends can be distinguished from what we know. To facilitate the discussion, three aspects of electron-induced chemistry are highlighted here: its effect on the cross section, its effect on the spatial resolution, and the rational design of novel materials.

===== [p44-49] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.5.4 PHOTOACID GENERATOR CHEMISTRY AND PHYSICS (39块) =====
--[p47]-- The higher energy can cause significant bond breaking, secondary electron generation, additional photon generation, and localized heating. These are all potentially important effects that should be considered for EUV and e-beam exposures, however, one of the most important effects is the change in acid generation mechanism.
--[p46]-- If the PAG has low absorbance at the exposure wavelength, then sensitization can be a more important reaction, especially if the resist is more strongly absorbing. The resist itself can sensitize the PAG in this case.
--[p46]-- It is also common for some specialized resists and coatings to add a small molecule sensitizer that absorbs strongly to enhance acid generation when both the resist and PAG have low absorbance at a particular wavelength such as CARs designed to operate at i-line and other UV wavelengths.
--[p45]-- While ionic onium salt PAGs are the most commonly used in lithographic applications, there are also a number of different types of nonionic PAGs which have received attention and use .<sup>79,278</sup> Some classes of nonionic PAGs include nitrobenzyl esters,<sup>279e288</sup> oximes,<sup>289</sup> dicarboximides,<sup>290</sup> sulfones,<sup>291</sup> a-sulfonyloxy ketones, and chloromethyl triazines. Examples of a compound from the oximes and dicarboximide family is seen in Fig. 15.
--[p48]-- Electron affinity is a measure of the energy change when an electron is added to a neutral atom to form a negative ion, and more negative electron affinity corresponds to a more favorable reaction.
--[p45]-- The onium salts have a cation that is a chromophore, which strongly affects absorption characteristics and quantum yield and an anion that determines the type of photogenerated acid. The iodonium and sulfonium salts are usually in the form of diaryl- or diphenyliodonium and triaryl- or triphenylsulfonium because the aromatic groups provide good absorbance at DUV and much better acid generation efficiency compared to cations such as trimethylsulfonium.
--[p45]-- The full mechanism of acid generation is generally known, but is complicated and can change depending on environment, whether the PAG directly absorbs the photon or if it undergoes excited state energy transfer from a sensitizer, and if it goes through in-cage or out-of-cage reactions.<sup>273e277</sup> Sulfonium salts are excited, a carbonesulfur bond is broken, the cation molecules usually reform as neutral molecules, and the anion abstracts a hydrogen atom (from the surrounding matrix or the cation products) to form the acid. The cation bond cleavage leads to rearrangement products that are either two molecules, (diphenylsulfide and benzene) or one molecule (phenylthiobiphenyl), which can have multiple isomers as shown in Fig. 16.
--[p47]-- Photons of this energy can primarily excite electrons into higher energy orbitals and minimal bond breaking occurs in the bulk resist matrix at low exposure doses. EUV with a wavelength of 13.5 nm has a photon energy of about 92 eV and e-beam tools typically have incident beams electrons ranging from 10 to 100 keV. At this higher energy, atoms determine absorbance rather than molecules or bonds, and thus all materials tend to strongly absorb.
--[p44]-- The most commonly used PAGs for lithography are ionic PAGs in the family of onium salts, usually sulfonium or iodonium salts, which were extensively studied and characterized by Crivello and coworkers.<sup>255e268</sup> Their popularity stems from the fact that they can be relativity easily synthesized by a variety of methods, they usually have good solubility in common casting solvents, and they are very efficient at generating acid under exposure due to their high quantum yield.
--[p48]-- (12) therefore likely plays a significant role in acid generation because increasing the probability that the reaction will occur (through increasing electron affinity) increases the acid generation yield in many studies.
--[p46]-- Both mechanisms can occur simultaneously, but the absorptivity of the resist matrix surrounding the PAG, the absorptivity of the PAG itself, and the exposure wavelength can make one mechanism more dominant than the other. If the resist is relatively transparent at the exposure wavelength and the PAG absorbs strongly, then direct excitation is the primary photolysis pathway. This is common for many DUV resists that use onium salt PAGs.
--[p48]-- For many organic materials common to resists, this energy level is around 10e20 eV, although inelastic collisions can continue in some materials at energies as low as 10 eV.
--[p48]-- (12) has an important contribution to overall acid generation. Studies have compared multiple different PAGs in a common resist and many found that the acid generation efficiency appeared to increase with increasing reduction potential or electron affinity of the PAG.<sup>78,314,315</sup> Reduction potential is a measure of the tendency of a species to acquire electrons and can be measured by techniques such as cyclic voltammetry.
--[p46]-- Direct excitation involves the direct absorption of a photon by the PAG molecule itself, which leads to an excited state, and ultimately the generation of the photoacid and other products. Electron transfer sensitization differs because the PAG molecule does not directly absorb the photon. Another molecule, called a sensitizer, absorbs the photon to enter an excited state where it can then transfer an electron to the PAG to lead to the bond cleavage and acid generation.
--[p44]-- 1.5.4 PHOTOACID GENERATOR CHEMISTRY AND PHYSICS
One of the most critical components to CARs is the PAG. A PAG is a compound that can generate an acid upon absorption of light. The photon absorption event promotes the PAG to an excited state and the return to the ground state can cause bond cleavage, which starts a series of reactions and rearrangements that ultimately results in the formation of an acid.
--[p49]-- E-beam typically starts with a much higher energy primary electron of around 50e200 keV and it can generate a much larger number of secondary electrons.
--[p45]-- Triphenylsulfonium salts usually have sufficiently good solubility in common casting solvents to be used directly, although further functionalization of the aromatic rings may be desirable. Diphenyliodonium salts have more limited solubility, so as a result, iodonium PAGs are frequently used in the form of bis(4-tert-butylphenyl)iodonium salts which have better solubility. The anion is chosen to produce a particular acid.
For example, tosylate anion is used to produce tosic acid, triflate anion for triflic acid, and so on.
--[p48]-- (11) where a recombination of a secondary electron with a radical cation can produce an excited state species that can undergo a sensitization-type reaction to produce a photoacid as described earlier for UV and DUV exposures. Another mechanism that appears to play a very significant role is the capture of an electron by the PAG to generate a photoacid as shown in Eq. (12). Electron capture leads to an excited state similar to photon absorption.
--[p45]-- The acid generation mechanism of nonionic PAGs varies from family to family. These PAGs are typically synthesized using a sulfonyl chloride and end up with an ${ \mathrm { R S O } } _ { 3 }$ group bonded to another atom such as carbon or nitrogen where the R group determines the type of sulfonic acid that will be generated. Photolysis often involves the breaking of NeO or CeO bond to generate the ${ \mathrm { R S O } } _ { 3 }$ group, which will form the sulfonic acid.
--[p47]-- The radicals generated during these processes could carry out their own reactions such as rearrangement, which removes atoms or breaks bonds, or reactions which form new bonds. The bond-forming reaction effectively cross-links the material and is the basis for the imaging of many negative-tone nonchemically-amplified resists for e-beam such as the calixarenes.<sup>310,311</sup>
--[p49]-- Likewise, the probability of interaction of each individual incident electron with a thin resist film is much lower than per incident EUV photon because the mean free path for a 100-keV primary electron is on the order of several hundred or a thousand angstroms in most organic materials.<sup>318</sup> The reduced number of incident e-beam electrons that interact with the film is somewhat offset by the higher per incident yield of secondary electrons.
--[p47]-- The PAG photolysis mechanism changes when exposed at EUV and e-beam because the energy of the incident beam is so much higher than at UV and DUV and materials interact with these higher energy sources differently. DUV wavelengths of 248 and 193 nm have photon energies of 5.0 and 6.4 eV, respectively. Absorptivity is determined by molecule and bond structure and the resist matrix typically has low absorbance.
--[p44]-- This means that at equivalent molar loading, these PAGs will generate more moles of acid at a particular dose compared to most other PAGs, which allows for better sensitivity in the resist. Use of ionic PAG-type molecules also allows for relatively easy change of the anion to generate different strengths of photoacid<sup>269</sup> and to create novel compounds such as photodecomposable bases (PDBs).<sup>270e272</sup>
--[p47]-- $$
