The radical cation can then participate in a number of reactions. It can react with another molecule to form a proton adduct and a radical. It can undergo an electronic relaxation in an Auger process to generate another secondary electron. Another secondary electron could recombine with it to form an excited state neutral species. It could also potentially directly fragment to form radical species.
--[p44]-- While the PAGs can be configured to generate a large number of different types of acids, they most commonly are used to generate either strong sulfonic acids such as p-toluenesulfonic acid or even stronger superacids such as trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (triflic acid) and other fluorinated acids such as nonaflic acid or fluoroantimonic acid $\mathrm { ( H S b F _ { 6 } ) }$ .
--[p47]-- While many more specific details can be found in Chapters 2 and 3, the mechanism for EUV and e-beam exposure will be briefly described later.
An EUV photon will behave similarly to a lower wavelength photon in terms of many of its physics such as diffraction, absorption statistics, etc. However, when it is absorbed by organic material, the higher energy 92-eV photon causes far more reactions than a lower energy DUV or UV photon.
--[p48]-- The secondary electrons carry out their own sets of reactions as they will move through the resist in a series of elastic and inelastic collisions. If the secondary electron has sufficient energy, it can carry out reactions similar to Eq. (10) to generate even more secondary electrons. Eventually, the electron will lose enough energy that it can no longer generate any more secondary electrons because the probability of inelastic collisions become very low.
--[p45]-- Photolysis of 2-nitrobenzyl esters is slightly different because a cyclic intermediate is formed, but the resulting photoacid is the same. This compound has also found use in many other applications including polymers and protecting group chemistry where it can be made into both nitrobenzyl esters and ethers to yield photolabile protecting groups.<sup>292e295</sup>
--[p48]-- The understanding of the physics in these systems is still incomplete, however, because some additional studies have found no direct correlation between photospeed and the reduction potential in EUV exposure of a methacrylate-based resist.<sup>317</sup> It is possible that the resist matrix has a strong role to play as well because some resists have more easily accessible hydrogens to contribute as the protons on the final acid.
--[p47]-- While direct excitation of the PAG to generate photoacid is possible, it is usually not the dominant mechanism<sup>309</sup> because of the higher energy of the photon and because both the polymer and PAG typically have very similar absorbance which leads to more polymerephoton events than PAGephoton events. The EUV photon will typically cause ionization of any material it hits which produces radical cations and ejects a high energy secondary electron. This reaction is illustrated in Eq. (10).

--[p49]-- EUV acid generation mechanisms can also be due to direct EUV photon excitation (although it currently appears to play a smaller role) and out-of-band radiation direct excitation. --[p44]-- There are large number of different structures and families of PAG molecules that have been studied, but some PAG families commonly used in lithography are shown in Fig. 15.
PAGs can be generally broken down into one of two types: ionic or nonionic, and a large number of different families or classes of materials fall under these two types. Ionic PAGs are typically salts and nonionic PAGs are neutral organic compounds.

--[p46]-- While ionic and nonionic PAGs have many differences, they are similar in the physics that govern the photolysis reactions, which appear to change when the exposure source changes from UVand DUV to e-beam and EUV. ===== [p372-373] Mainstreaming inorganic metal-oxide resists for high-resolution lithography > 10.3.1 HafSOx SOLUTION CHEMISTRY (12块) =====
--[p373]-- Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and electrospray ionization mass specwherein the planar $\mathrm { H f } _ { 4 }$ cluster (Fig. 9) is a major component. --[p373]-- The solution chemistry is dynamic, as clusters continuously oligomerize, eventually precipitating as the $\operatorname { H f } _ { 1 8 }$ sulfate cluster. Bound peroxide, excess hydrogen peroxide and sulfuric acid, and refrigeration suppress condensation and oligomerization to maintain high $\mathrm { H f } _ { 4 }$ solution concentrations. As such, peroxide and sulfate enhance cluster solubility.
Their roles in radiation exposure and the lithographic development process are examined in Sections 10.3.2 and 10.3.3.

--[p274]-- This has been validated in earlier studies using thin film buckling to measure modulus<sup>90</sup> as shown in Fig. 47.<sup>91</sup> Higher resist modulus allows for more resistance to capillary forces and therefore better pattern collapse performance.
Many of these types of materials show somewhat unique contrast behavior due to their imaging mechanism, based on cationic polymerization and cross-linking and development in organic solvent.
--[p274]-- Likewise, the significant volume change often observed with the loss of a protecting group could lead to other imaging problems. The small molecule starting materials appear to lead to less swelling during development than similar polymeric systems because the smaller unexposed materials dissolve faster and because the final network structure has higher cross-link density than similar polymer systems; this will be discussed further in Section 8.7.4.
--[p274]-- This reduction in mobility makes it hard for the network to grow larger and restricts the mobility of all molecules in the matrix as the polymerization proceeds. Since the surrounding molecules are restricted, increasing the amount of initiator (i.e., increasing the dose and producing more photoacid) does little to further increase cross-linking.
--[p276]-- $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ for these systems can start below room temperature for the uncross-linked resists and increase to $2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ or higher when fully cured.
--[p276]-- Organic solvent is used as developer because most of these materials lack appropriate functional groups to be soluble in standard aqueous base developer. Adding phenolic or carboxylic functionality to the molecule can allow for aqueous base development but that introduces additional complexity to the patterning process as discussed in Section 8.7.7. The resists often have a rapid response in increasing thickness at low dose because the cross-linking reaction is so efficient.
--[p276]-- If the $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ of the system is too high relative to the PEB temperature, very little cross-linking can occur.<sup>93</sup> The plateau occurs because the $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ of the material increases with extent of conversion until it is substantially higher than the PEB and mobility drops too far to allow further cross-linking. Increasing the PEB temperature increases the plateau value because the difference between PEB and $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ is decreased.
--[p276]-- These resists can have multiple plateaus with increasing PEB temperature because the $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ continues to increase with conversion until sufficiently higher conversion is obtained to maintain full NRT.<sup>93</sup> Some resists have sufficiently low $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ to reach an NRT of one with no PEB (i.e., full cure at ambient temperature),<sup>94</sup> while others must be heated to well above $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ depending on how high $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ is for the material.
Two other observations to note regarding these materials’ contrast curves is that they are often developed in organic solvent, and that they respond rapidly at low dose.
--[p276]-- The contrast curves show an E<sub>0</sub> of effectively $0 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ (zero dose). This means they have good sensitivity but can lead to further problems as discussed in Section 8.7.5.
--[p274]-- The reduction in diffusivity of the active species helps to provide good resolution, although this can be improved even further through reaction engineering as will be discussed in Section 8.7.5. Negative-tone imaging has also regained some attention recently due to the potential for improved imaging due to the better image contrast using a light field mask,<sup>3e5</sup> although it is as yet unclear how big of a benefit this is in these materials.

Commonly studied epoxide functionalized polyphenol type molecular resist.
causes of the good performance in these materials, there are several major potential benefits of this resist design. Since they operate by a no-mass loss reaction process (ring opening), there are reduced concerns regarding outgassing compared to resists based on acid-catalyzed deprotection where the smaller deprotection products are often volatile.
--[p274]-- One other potential benefit in this type of resist design is the improved mechanical properties in the final cross-linked structure compared to uncross-linked polymers and molecular resists which should improve pattern collapse performance.
--[p276]-- The second effect is to shift the value of the normalized remaining film thickness (NRT) at the plateau up with increasing temperature until complete film thickness is retained at sufficiently high temperature. As the epoxide groups are converted and the system cross-links, the glass transition temperature $\mathrm { ( T _ { g } ) }$ increases.
--[p274]-- This behavior has been observed in numerous other solid state cross-linking systems, and spectroscopic studies confirm that epoxide and oxetane conversion plateaus give rise to the plateau in film thickness.<sup>92</sup>
Changing the PEB temperature has two effects on contrast behavior. One is to change the slope in the kinetically controlled region at low dose because lower temperatures reduce the kinetic rates as described by the Arrhenius equation.
--[p274]-- The extent of polymerization increases linearly with initiator concentration for a fixed polymerization time since the total conversion of monomer into polymer is controlled solely by the number of active polymerization centers. The plateau region at higher doses occurs because the polymerization becomes diffusion controlled.<sup>92</sup> This happens because the crosslinked network has significantly less mobility than the initial small monomer molecules and photoacids.
--[p274]-- Epoxide and other cationic cross-linking resists will also have some level of intrinsic diffusion control because the active species is not the small molecule photoacid, but the cationic active centerdan oxoniumdthat is attached to an ever-growing chain and/or network. Likewise, the glass transition temperature of the resist increases with the cross-linking, which slows the reaction as it proceeds.
--[p274]-- One of the biggest challenges for sub-20-nm resist features is collapse that is caused by the potentially large capillary forces experienced by the resist lines during the development and rinse steps.<sup>87</sup> Such capillary forces will continue to increase as the features sizes shrink, and this is exacerbated in polymeric resists by the drop in mechanical modulus that most polymers experience as their critical dimensions shrink.<sup>88,89</sup> Cross-linked resists will inherently have higher moduli than conventional polymeric materials because the entire structure is held together by covalent bonds rather than the relatively weaker cohesive energy that keeps polymer chains together.
--[p274]-- Characteristics common in the contrast curves of these materials can be illustrated using the curve for 4-Ep as shown in Fig. 48. These materials often show a linear region at low dose followed by a curve into a relatively flat plateau region at higher dose. The linear region is generally due to a kinetically controlled polymerization reaction.

--[p210]-- Unfortunately, the olefin sulfone polymers are not only highly sensitive to high-energy photons but also break down readily under plasma or reactive ion etching. --[p154]-- The standard process for fabricating EUV-IL gratings based on the direct patterning of HSQ by e-beam lithography has therefore been carefully optimized to produce high-quality masks on fragile 100-nm thick $\mathrm { S i } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 }$ membranes in a straightforward manner.<sup>5,35</sup> Yet, the use of HSQ is limiting because of the low sensitivity of the material (i.e., the need for high e-beam doses) and the poor efficiency of the grating due to the low absorption of silicon oxide at EUV.<sup>7</sup> It is clear, that to be able to pattern with single-digit nm resolution with EUV-IL, it is of paramount importance to be able to create high-resolution gratings with high-diffraction efficiencies that are furthermore geometrically uniform and defect free by a simple fabri
--[p153]-- The use of highly efficient masks is also important to have as small exposure times as possible as any natural mechanical instability during the experiment will deteriorate the aerial image produced and will also limit the ultimate resolution that can be achieved by EUV-IL.
--[p153]-- The diffraction efficiency of the gratings at EUV wavelengths is inherently low (1e4%), and it depends not only on the geometry (pitch, material thickness, duty cycle: the ratio between linewidth and pitch) but also on the optical properties of the grating.<sup>24,33</sup> Sufficiently high flux $( { \mathrm { m J } } / { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 2 } )$ is therefore required for each exposure.
--[p155]-- Although Mo gratings are highly efficient at EUV wavelengths, this type of fabrication process is still very complex as it involves an RIE for pattern transfer into Mo, together with a final buffered hydrofluoric etch to remove the remaining $\mathrm { S i O _ { x } }$ atop the gratings.<sup>9</sup> This not only significantly reduces the final mask yield but also adversely affects its quality.

===== [p57-61] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.6.2 PHOTOACID DIFFUSION (27块) =====
--[p59]-- Reducing diffusion length can improve resolution and LER, but it can also have a negative effect on sensitivity because each acid can carry out fewer deprotection events. This can be offset by increasing the overall PAG loading in these systems.
--[p59]-- Later work showed they are an important tool for controlling acid diffusion as well. Base quenchers work by neutralizing the photoacid to eliminate its ability to carry out deprotection and other reactions.<sup>200</sup> They are now commonly loaded into the resist at 5e30% of the PAG loading; too high and the resist may fail to pattern.
--[p59]-- Reducing diffusion length improves resolution and LER, but the attachment of the PAG to the polymer also helps improve the uniformity of PAG distribution in the resist by limiting aggregation or segregation of the typically polar, ionic, small molecule PAGs which are usually physically blended into a less polar large molecule resist polymer.
--[p61]-- At constant dose, the reduction in space width with increased PDB loading is much lower than conventional base quencher as shown in Fig. 21B. The use of a PDB provides an additional advantage on top of the reduction in the sensitivity penalty in that it actually increases the acid and deprotection gradient at the line edge even further that can be achieved through the use of conventional base quencher as shown in Fig. 21C.
--[p60]-- $E _ { \mathrm { s i z e } }$ increases with base loading, but the acid gradient at the line edge also increases. As the base loading increases, the beneficial effects of base loading on the gradient tend to plateau, but the sensitivity penalty continues to increase as shown in Fig. 20D. There is thus a good benefit obtained by adding a small amount of base to the resist, but at much higher loadings the dose penalty tends to outweigh the benefit to resolution and LER.
--[p61]-- One type of material that satisfies this property is photosensitive cation such as triphenylsulfonium or diaryliodonium (commonly used as PAG cations) with an anion that is strongly basic until exposed when it is decomposed to a more neutral species. Some examples of these types of anions are hydroxides, alkof materials have been termed PDBs or photodecomposable quenchers.<sup>271,473e477</sup>
--[p61]-- While base quencher provides many advantages to patterning performance, it comes with a high cost to sensitivity because the base additives are uniformly distributed throughout the film. This means that many photogenerated acids are neutralized in the higher dose exposed regions, which is undesirable, to get the desirable neutralization in the low dose and unexposed regions. One solution to this is to use a base quencher that is decomposed in the high dose regions independently of photoacid.
--[p59]-- Base quencher can have a strong effect on resolution because its concentration is on the order or greater than the acid concentration at the edge of the exposed areas, so the small number of acid molecules, which might have diffused a long distance to affect resolution and LER, are neutralized before too significant damage is done.
--[p57]-- Very low acid diffusion can thus lead to poor sensitivity and potentially bad LER due to the statistically distributed photoacids. If the acid diffusion is too high, then the photoacids will diffuse outside of the nominally exposed area and the final developed pattern will be wider than desired. This is illustrated in Fig. 19. High acid diffusion can thus lead to poor resolution although the sensitivity may be good because each individual acid can cause a higher number of deprotection events.
--[p60]-- At constant dose, increasing the base loading causes a reduction in space width (for positive tone) because the acid concentration in the film uniformly drops as seen in Fig. 20A. Eventually the base loading gets so high that the resist will not pattern because the acid concentration is below the threshold for patterning. If the dose is changed for each base loading, then the space width can be held constant as shown in Fig. 20C and D because the threshold is at the same position in each case.
--[p59]-- In the middle of the exposed areas, the higher local dose causes a generally higher concentration of acid such that the base is effectively all neutralized and the remaining acid can react with the resist.
--[p60]-- Thus these figures would represent the space centered at $x = 0$ assuming a positive-tone resist. Fig. 20A and B shows change in base loading relative to PAG at constant dose $( E _ { \mathrm { s i z e } } )$ and changing CD or space width and Fig. 20C and D shows change in base loading at constant CD and changing $E _ { \mathrm { s i z e } } .$ .
--[p59]-- Many studies have shown that this approach can improve resolution and LER.<sup>220,222,467e469</sup> Attaching the cation of the PAG to the polymer has shown only limited improvements over blended PAGs,<sup>470</sup> while attaching the anion of the PAG to the polymer main chain has shown good improvements in both resolution and LER over blended PAGs.<sup>227,233</sup> Attaching the PAG anion directly to the polymer chain has a strong effect on reducing diffusion length because the acid size is now as big as the largest species in the system, the resist polymer; in the case of the cationically attached PAG, the acid is still a free, small molecule.
--[p61]-- These types of materials reduce the sensitivity penalty of using quencher because there is lower base concentrations at higher doses in the middle of the exposed regions compared to conventional base, as shown in Fig. 21A which is made using a similar simple exposure model as Fig. 20. As the dose increases, the difference in concentration actually increases as more base is photodecomposed in the high dose regions.
--[p61]-- Both simulation and experimental studies have shown improved LER through use of PDBs, but also improved exposure latitude and CD uniformity at lower dose.<sup>315,478,479</sup>
--[p58]-- Increasing the $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ of the resist tends to decrease the acid diffusion length. This is because the relative difference between the PEB temperature and the $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ of the resist has a strong effect on the overall mobility in the resist and therefore the acid diffusivity.<sup>459e463</sup> When the PEB temperature is well below the $\mathrm { T _ { g } , }$ the resist is a glassy solid and diffusion of small molecules in the resist is low.
Similarly, above the $\mathrm { T _ { g } , }$ the resist behaves more like a liquid and diffusivity is high.
--[p59]-- Some studies have also suggested that the overall acid generation efficiency in polymer-bound PAG systems is actually improved at EUV compared to conventional blended so the reduced effectiveness of each acid is offset by the fact that more acids are generated per photon.
Base quenchers were originally added to CARs intentionally to help with issues due to environmental base contamination as discussed in Section 1.5.2.
--[p57]-- Acid diffusion is an important parameter in CARs that can strongly affect resolution, sensitivity, LER, CD uniformity, and a host of other patterning metrics. It is therefore critical that acid diffusion is controlled. Three methods are commonly used to control acid diffusion: increasing the $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ of the resist, increasing the anion size of the photoacid, and addition of base quencher.
--[p57]-- 1.6.2 PHOTOACID DIFFUSION
Another important issue for high resolution CARs is photoacid diffusion because it has strong and opposite effects on resolution and sensitivity and also has an effect on LER. PAGs are distributed throughout the resist film and are converted to photoacids during exposure. At the end of the exposure, there is some spatial distribution of photoacids.
--[p59]-- One of the most important effects of base is that it can effectively increase the chemical gradient between high and low dose regions.<sup>201</sup> Increasing the chemical gradient at the line edge will generally improve LER but it can also lead to better overall patterning because the contrast between high and low dose regions is higher. The trade-off is that the dose required to pattern the resist tends increase with increased base loading.
--[p61]-- If the Dill C for base decomposition were lower, then the increase in $E _ { \mathrm { s i z e } }$ with increasing PDB would be higher and increase in gradient lower until the extreme case of conventional base quencher were reached as in Fig. 20D. The improvement in deprotection gradient at the line edge would lead to improved LER over the baseline resist while the sensitivity penalty is much less than conventional quencher.
--[p59]-- This is because more acids (i.e., more dose) are required to reach the same final feature size as base increases.
Some of the effects of base loading are demonstrated in Fig. 20, which shows some simplified model calculations of acid concentration for different base loadings. The space width or pattern size is taken based on specifying a threshold of acid; if acid concentration is above the threshold, then the resist is removed.
--[p58]-- The $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ of the resist can be increased by many methods such as changing the polymer backbone, increasing the molecular weight, or by putting on monomer units with bulky groups or that cause increased hydrogen bonding.<sup>464</sup> While this approach has been used successfully to improve resolution by reducing the diffusion length,<sup>465</sup> its utility can be limited because changing the resist polymer to increase $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ can potentially have strong negative effects on other lithographic properties such as solubility.
Increasing the anion size of the photoacid has been shown to decrease the acid diffusion length.
--[p57]-- A subsequent PEB step is done where the acids diffuse in a random walk process and deprotect the resist to induce a solubility switch that is converted to a relief pattern upon development. If the acid diffusion length is too low, then the original spatial distribution of photoacids is not effectively blurred out and the pattern may not correctly resolve until a sufficiently high dose is used to create an effective connected network of deprotected resist.
--[p61]-- This is because each unit increase in dose has a double effect on the resist to both increase acid concentration and decrease base concentration. At EUV, the situation is more complicated because every photon or secondary electron spent decomposing a base is not available to generate an acid and vice versa, but the general effect should be similar.
--[p61]-- The end result is that the improvement in gradient is now much more closely related to the increase in $E _ { \mathrm { s i z e } }$ as shown in Fig. 21D. In this case, the change in normalized properties with PDB is exactly the same because the Dill C for base decomposition in the model was set the same as the Dill C parameter for acid generation.
--[p59]-- This is because higher molecular weight and larger molecular volume species have a more difficult time moving through the resist and jumping between its free volume pockets. One method that has been used is to put bulky groups on the anion of a conventional blended PAG system, and this has shown improved resolution.<sup>464,466</sup> Another approach that has received much attention is the use of PBPs where the PAG is covalently attached directly to the resist’s main polymer chain.

===== [p125-127] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 3.1 INTRODUCTION (13块) =====
--[p126]-- First of all, electron scattering starts playing a role, leading to electrons having a spectrum of energies (rather than just one well-defined energy) and a having an average traveling length in the material. In addition, as we will see, electron-induced reactions are fundamentally different from the photochemistry
The role of electron-induced chemistry in lithography techniques. (A) A schematic drawing of EUV lithography.
--[p125]-- In FEBIP, the desired functionality (e.g., a conducting path) is added directly, without the need for a resist. Currently, the FEBIP is only technique
While in high-throughput lithography ultraviolet light is currently used to expose the resists, the next generation of integrated circuits will be produced using EUV light (13.5 nm). The change to EUV light means that the key processes in resists will be induced by electrons.
--[p125]-- Electron-induced chemistry plays a role in a variety of phenomena, for instance in the radiobiological damage to DNA due to high-energy radiation,<sup>1</sup> in the aging of high-voltage insulators,<sup>2</sup> in plasma processing,<sup>3</sup> and in polymer chemistry.<sup>4,5</sup> When high-energy radiation (e.g., X-rays, electron beam, and ion beams) interacts with molecules, it can directly excite and/or ionize the target molecules or release low-energy electrons that in turn induce the excitation or ionization. The excitation or ionization can lead to dissociation of the molecules, which may then react with neighboring molecules to form new reaction products.
Microlithography and nanolithography is one of the fields in which electroninduced chemistry plays a key role.
--[p126]-- The resist, a thin layer of photosensitive or electron-sensitive material is locally exposed to EUV light. After the exposure, the resist is developed for further processing. (B) A schematic drawing of EBL. The process is the same as in (A) but now using a focused electron beam instead of EUV irradiation. (C) A schematic drawing of FEBIP. Gaseous precursor molecules and a focused electron beam are codirected to the sample.
--[p126]-- The precursor temporarily adsorbs on the sample surface, where it is dissociated by (secondary) electrons.
used in, e.g., ultraviolet lithography. In photochemistry, radiationless transition from higher excited states to the lowest excited state is generally faster than chemical reactions. The outcome of photoinduced reactions therefore does not depend on the state to which the molecule is excited.
--[p127]-- In this chapter, the different mechanisms are explained by which electrons can induce reactions in matter. It is also briefly described how these mechanisms potentially contribute to the effects that are relevant for the next-generation lithography. Processes that do not lead to reactions, such as elastic scattering or vibrational excitation (heating of the target) are not discussed here.
--[p127]-- For more extensive overviews of all fundamental mechanisms involved in electron interactions and electron-induced chemistry, see the excellent overviews by, e.g., Moore et al.<sup>7</sup> and Ma¨rk.<sup>8</sup>
--[p125]-- Instead of using a resist film, volatile precursor gases are used in FEBIP. The precursor molecules are brought to the sample using a gas injection system, adsorb transiently on the sample, and dissociate when exposed to a focused electron beam. The fragmented precursor molecules either leave a solid residue [in the case of focused electron beam-induced deposition (FEBID)] or react with the underlying substrate to form gaseous products (in the case of etching).
--[p125]-- After a development step, the remaining patterned resist acts as a protective layer on the silicon wafer for further processing. In the final step, the desired functionality is added (e.g., conductive paths in an integrated circuit). Fig. 1A and B shows a schematic drawing for extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography and electron beam lithography (EBL), respectively. A very similar process is focused electron beam-induced processing (FEBIP), schematically shown in Fig. 1C.
--[p126]-- Instead of the photon-induced chemistry in ultraviolet lithography, EUV light is ionizing. The ionizing nature is what connects EUV lithography, EBL, and FEBIP: the changes in the radiation-sensitive material (the resist or the volatile precursor) are the result of reactions with electrons.
The shift from photon-induced to electron-induced brings about key changes to the lithography process.
--[p127]-- In this chapter, we will see that this is different for electron-induced reactions, where the energy of the incoming electron plays a role in determining the dissociation path. In EUV lithography, these new chemical pathways will affect the throughput and the pattern resolution.
To optimize these patterning techniques, it is a key to understand the role of electrons in the lithography processes and of low-energy electrons in particular.
--[p125]-- In standard lithography processes, (typically) silicon wafers are processed to add functionality such as, e.g., conducting paths in a circuit. To achieve this, the wafers are usually coated with photosensitive or electron-sensitive resists, traditionally thin polymer layers, which are then patterned. The patterning is achieved by exposing the resist for instance to light or to a focused electron beam, which changes the solubility of the resist locally.
--[p125]-- 3.1 INTRODUCTION

===== [p224-224] Chemically amplified resists and acid amplifiers > 7.2.2 RESOLUTION-LINE WIDTH ROUGHNESS SENSITIVITY TRADEOFF (4块) =====
--[p224]-- One concept explored was the use of acid amplifiers in EUV CARs.<sup>31</sup> Acid amplifiers are molecules that are triggered by photogenerated acids to yield a catalytic cascade of acid to effectively lower the dose necessary for acid production. The acid amplifier molecule should be thermally stable for adequate resist shelf life and should not diffuse too far during the post-exposure bake (PEB) step.
--[p224]-- Kruger et al.<sup>32</sup> reported on the first fluorinated sulfonate esters as acid amplifiers that can produce catalytic amounts of triflic acid (Fig. 5). They also designed a series of fluorosulfonic acids,
Reproduced from KrugerS, Hosoi K, Cardineau B, Miyauchi K, Brainard R. Stable, fluorinated acid amplifiers for use in EUV lithography. Proc SPIE 2012;8325:832514.
and they successfully patterned them with a champion result 2.1-nm line-edge roughness for a 50-nm dense pattern.
--[p224]-- 7.2.2 RESOLUTION-LINE WIDTH ROUGHNESS SENSITIVITY TRADEOFF
CAR resist performance has been driven by three main performance criteria: resolution, line-width roughness (LWR), and sensitivity. These criteria are actively being pursued for optimum performance simultaneously. It has been recently noted that there indeed may be a difficult tradeoff in optimizing all three criteria simultaneously.<sup>29</sup> Some researchers are even giving the so-called RLS tradeoff the term, “triangle of death”.
--[p224]-- Since resolution is primarily improved by acid diffusion control and quencher concentration (higher is better), the sensitivity of a CAR is thereby limited. A similar tradeoff exists for LWR versus sensitivity. This issue is especially relevant for EUV lithography where a lack of EUV photons is creating a need for very fast resists. Fig. 4 shows the effect of the RLS tradeoff on LWR versus dose.<sup>30</sup>
Many clever ideas have been attempted to improve the RLS tradeoff.

The modern world is thoroughly populated with integrated circuits (ICs) and other microelectronic devices. ===== [p23-24] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.3.3 EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET LITHOGRAPHY (13块) =====
--[p23]-- Part of this delay is due to concerns over the production readiness of various aspects of the tool and process which will be discussed later, but also due to continued advances in multiple patterning which have kept pace with the technology roadmaps until now, although at a very high, and increasing, cost.
EUV radiation covers the wavelength range from 10 nm up to about 120 nm and also can overlap with a region considered soft X-rays.
--[p24]-- Although EUV can be considered a form of optical lithography, the interactions of an EUV photon with a resist are significantly different than a DUV photon, due to the much higher energy at EUVand the typically higher absorbance at EUV. An incident 13.5-nm EUV photon has about 92 eVof energy compared to 5.0 and 6.4 eV for the DUV wavelengths of 248 and 193 nm, respectively. This energy difference means there is a significantly different photon flux onto the resist at equivalent doses.
--[p23]-- Fortunately, the use of multilayer film stacks of alternating materials can produce reflecting optics with reasonable efficiency.<sup>50</sup> The most commonly used EUV reflector stack consists of multiple alternating layers of molybdenum and silicon, which shows around 70% reflection efficiency with a peak wavelength of 13.5 nm.<sup>51</sup>
EUVexposure tools for manufacturing will require multiple mirrors (6 to 12 ) to project a sufficiently high fidelity image.
--[p23]-- The wavelengths that are the most lithographically interesting are in the range of 11e14 nm. Considering the Raleigh criterion shown in Eq. (1), this wavelength range would potentially represent a substantial improvement in resolution over 193-nm DUV; however, there are many important differences in the physics and tool design when the wavelength is dropped into the EUV.
--[p24]-- There are approximately 10 photons/nm<sup>2</sup> at EUV for a dose of 15 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>, while there are 146 photons/nm<sup>2</sup> at the equivalent dose at 193 nm. At DUV, the photon is absorbed by the resist and it temporarily excites an electron in a molecule to an excited state before returning to the ground state. When the 92-eV EUV photon is 59 absorbed by the resist, a photoelectron of about 80 eV (on average) is generated.
--[p23]-- This is important because it implies that any defects buried in the multilayer can have an effect on the projected pattern.<sup>54,55</sup> These defects will be difficult to find using conventional defect analysis because they will be very small scale and potentially invisible to many inspection methods as they are buried. As a result, a specialized technique had to be developed even to inspect EUV masks for defects based on actinic inspection. 56e58
--[p23]-- 1.3.3 EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET LITHOGRAPHY
EUV lithography has received substantial attention in the last 10 years as a “next wavelength” replacement for 193-nm DUV lithography.<sup>11</sup> Over this time, it has been predicted to be only a “few” years from commercial implementation multiple times, but has not yet been used in high volume manufacturing.
--[p23]-- The reflective mask requires off-axis illumination and this combines with the effect of the thickness of the mask absorber to create shadowing effects,<sup>53</sup> which degrade pattern quality and must be accounted for in mask and system design. The EUV light that is reflected from a multilayer is some cumulative distribution of the reflections at interfaces between all the layers.
--[p23]-- Since all materials absorb at these wavelengths, the system must be run in a vacuum rather than in air and transparent optics cannot be used in the way quartz can be used in the DUV.
--[p24]-- The chemistry and physics that occur in a resist during EUV exposure are therefore as much related to e-beam exposure as they are related to DUV exposure, although it is ultimately a combination of the two.
--[p23]-- As of spring 2016, a lab demonstrated power of 200 W had been reported, but sources in actual field demonstration units were around 80 W.<sup>52</sup> The low source power also means that EUV resists need very good sensitivity which will be discussed later.
EUV masks have also required significant work. In addition to reflective optics, EUV uses a mask composed of a reflective multilayer.
--[p24]-- The photoelectron will scatter through the resist and generate more secondary electrons (around two to five total secondary electrons for typical organic resists) in a manner similar to the cascade of secondary electrons generated by scanning electron microscope (SEM) or e-beam lithography interactions.
--[p23]-- Given the reflectivity of 70% for each mirror, only 1e5% of the generated photons will actually reach the wafer. This loss means that EUV light sources need sufficiently high power to provide the required wafer throughput to make EUV economically viable. Progress in EUV source power has been slow and has been among the top, if not the top concern/roadblock for implementation of EUV commercially. Current estimates suggest a source power of 250 W will be needed with long-term reliable operation.

===== [p167-169] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.3.6 ACID DIFFUSION (11块) =====
--[p167]-- 4.3.6 ACID DIFFUSION
In CARs, the ionization triggered by a single EUV photon is amplified so as to produce several acid units by a photoacid generator (PAG). The deprotection action of photoacids takes place in a volume defined as the deprotection sphere. Photoacid is then designed to spread through the photoresist to smooth out the nonuniformities at the edges and at the sidewalls between exposed and unexposed area.
--[p167]-- Acid diffusion was traditionally accomplished by a thermally activated process, which takes place mostly during a PEB of the resist. A typical PEB process is carried out for few tens of seconds at temperatures that are usually lower than that of the post application bake (PAB)dapplied after the initial spin coatingdto prevent any change in the material.
--[p169]-- 8 ~ \mathrm { n m } ^ { 8 \ddagger }$ and has the spatial profile shown in Fig. 18.
Resists with large acid diffusion length were intended for pre-EUV lithography, where sidewall roughness was a major issue (due to, among other things, standing optical waves in the resist).
--[p169]-- The minimization of the LER needs tuning of not only the diffusion length but also of the deblocking reaction capture range. The relationship<sup>84</sup> between these quantities is shown in Fig. 19.
--[p168]-- As the acid diffusion becomes more and more relevant to the total resist blur, it is technologically important to estimate its effect and seek ways to tune it. Several studies have investigated the effect of PEB and PAB temperature. Evidence that acid diffusion is a thermally activated process is provided by a study on the PEB temperature,<sup>80</sup> carried out at ranges $\mathrm { T } = 8 0 { - } 9 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ .
--[p167]-- During the PEB, acid diffuses statistically from the exposed areas of the photoresist (where the photoacid concentration is considerably higher) toward the unexposed areas. This diffusive process continues until their depletion or until their neutralization. The latter is accomplished by adding a quencher to the resist formulation, which has typically a concentration of about 1/10th that of the PAG.
--[p169]-- Roughness in EUV lithography has instead a different origin, mostly the stochasticity of photons and of distribution of chemically active PAGs, both of which have significantly smaller characteristic lengths than sidewall roughness. Moreover, for the goal of high resolution, EUV resists are being designed with two possible strategies: by reducing the acid diffusivity and by increasing the PAG concentration.
--[p169]-- The latter strategy cannot be implemented easily due to the changes in related chemical parameters of the resist.
Instead, low acid diffusivity is a viable route to reducing CD broadening, due to acid molecule movement, thus enabling high resolution. In addition, the acid diffusion length affects the LER of patterned structures, which is an important figure-ofmerit in EUV lithography quality.
--[p167]-- As such, acid diffusion is predominantly a stochastic process, which has been traditionally modeled as Fickian. It must be noted that acid diffusion effects act along with electron blur to smooth out the contour of the latent image: in a patterned resist, the two phenomena add in quadrature and are not easily discernable from each other.<sup>52,84</sup>
--[p168]-- The reaction rate plot versus reciprocal temperature shows a linear behavior, indicating a thermodynamic process, which obeys Arrhenius law behavior and a minimum blur of z4 nm. In another study, it was shown that the PAB has a modest effect on the acid diffusion, whereas even $+ 1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ variation of PEB temperature doubles the acid diffusion length<sup>85</sup> as shown in Fig. 17.
--[p169]-- Theoretical models, which combine quantum efficiency and total blur, also provide useful information to estimate of the blurring and spatial distribution of distance between photoabsorption and photoacid generation. Using an analytical model based on the extended NijboereZernike theory, the diffusion parameter was studied as a function of temperature and duration of the PEB.<sup>86</sup> Using a hybrid model, some researchers reported that the sensitization distance was $4 . 9 \pm 0 .

===== [p163-165] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.3.4 IMAGE BLUR (8块) =====
--[p163]-- 4.3.4 IMAGE BLUR
One of the most fundamental and elusive phenomena in EUV lithography that limits resolution is the electron blur. The generation of secondary photoelectrons in photoresists is accomplished by a photosensitive molecule in the formulation, which is ionized by absorption of an EUV photon. In the cascade process, additional SEs trons travel through the resist before interacting with the PAG molecule and triggering photoacid generation.
--[p164]-- Researchers from the State University of New York measured the amount of PAG-saturated outgassing to indirectly estimate the depth of penetration of an electron beam in photoresist in the 80e2000-eV range.<sup>77</sup> According to their model of low-energy electron scattering, the distribution of the depth of energy loss events for 80 eV electrons in photoresist peaks at w2-nm depth and drops to around zero beyond 5-nm depth.<sup>77</sup> Nevertheless, a few SEs can still travel as far as 30 nm through the material as indicated by their spatial distribution shown in Fig. 14.<sup>78,79</sup>
Another assessment of the electron blur was provided by a study of the temperature dependence of total resist blur for a CAR at varying post-exposure thermal treatments.
--[p164]-- A first understanding of the behavior of electron blur was provided by the analysis of the inelastic mean free path (IMFP) of electrons in matter. An empirical description of the IMFP was first provided by Seah and Dench<sup>74</sup> several decades ago. Since then, a number of equations have been developed to accurately describe the IMFP as function of electron energy.
--[p164]-- For example, the TPP-2M model developed by Tanuma et al.<sup>75</sup> provides the IMFP for a broad range of elements, all of which show the same trend (Fig. 12).
The energy of SEs resulting from direct photoionization processes when exposed to EUV was measured by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and was found to be around 80 eV (Fig. 13).<sup>76</sup> Using the theoretical values for IMFP,<sup>74</sup> it is expected that electron blur will be below 5 nm.
Experimental measurement of the electron blur in situ presents a considerable challenge.
--[p165]-- Indeed, the SE blur is basically invariant with temperature, whereas other sources of resist blur are thermally activated. The absolute acid diffusion lengths after exposure were calculated using a PROLITH model, and it was possible to estimate the statistics of distance between the location where photon is absorbed and where photoacid is generated. The resulting histogram, shown in Fig.
--[p164]-- In addition to electron blur, the latent image in the resist is formed as a combination of many other reactions, each of which has its own characteristic length: acid diffusion (in CARs), deprotection variability, flare, aberrations, out of band radiation, and mechanical vibrations. All these terms add to the total image blur, and thus make it challenging to evaluate the effect of electron blur on its own.
--[p165]-- 15, indicates that such distance peaks at w2.4 nm and is globally <10 nm.<sup>80</sup> Finally, an estimate of the electron blur, derived indirectly by the measurement of the exposure kinetic constant Dill parameter C, in a simulation study, found that this distance ranges from 2.1 to 3.3 nm.<sup>81</sup>
--[p163]-- Because the PAG reaction occurs in a slightly different spatial location to where the photon was initially absorbed, the latent image will not exactly match to the aerial image. This effect represents the most fundamental limitation to the achievement of high resolution in the patterned material and has great technological importance for lithography application. In the case of non-CARs, the same effect will be manifest, although through other reaction pathways.

===== [p172-173] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.3.7 PEB AND DEVELOPMENT (12块) =====
--[p172]-- Developing the photoresist is the lithography process step where the exposed (positive-tone resist) or unexposed (negative-tone resist) parts of the resist are selectively dissolved in the developer solution. For positive-tone resists, the developer is usually an alkaline, aqueous solution with some additional surfactant to improve the wetting of the wafer and thus the uniformity of the process. For negative-tone resists, the developers are typically solvents.
--[p172]-- The amount of acid generated is relatively small, and its diffusion length limited, and therefore, it is very important to ensure that it is not neutralized by environmental alkaline species.<sup>2</sup> This problem was already recognized in the early 1980s when T-shaped resist profiles were obtained as the waiting time in between exposure, PEB, and development increased.
--[p172]-- 4.3.7 PEB AND DEVELOPMENT
During the PEB deprotection reaction, acid-labile groups on the CAR polymer matrix that block its dissolution in an alkaline aqueous solution are attacked by the acid produced during exposure.
--[p172]-- In this chapter, development of positive-tone CARs is considered as an example system.
Aqueous base development of CARs is among the key processes in modern lithography. In it, the sinusoidal intensity modulation of the exposing light has to be converted into (ideally) step function like profiles in the resist. Therefore, in designing high-performance resists, good control over their dissolution in the aqueous developer is of utmost importance.
--[p173]-- The values of the constants $r _ { m a x } , r _ { m i n } , m _ { t h } .$ , and n can be derived experimentally. An example of a development curve based on Mack’s model is seen in Fig. 22. Two regions in the curve are of particular interest, firstly the inflexion point or $m _ { t h }$ where the second derivative of the development rate with respect to the inhibitor concentration is 0. This point marks the transition from low to high development rate in the exposed resist.
--[p172]-- Commercially available resists, however, do not behave ideally but can be modeled accurately using the so-called Mack development model.<sup>91,92</sup> In the CAR developing process, the deprotected resist monomers are soluble in the developer and the model assumes that the development rate of the resist depends on the amount of deprotected inhibitor groups in each resist monomer, n, called the dissolution selectivity. According to the model, the development rate of the resist r is given by:
--[p173]-- In the equation, $r _ { m a x }$ is the maximum development rate achievable for the given combination of developer and resist, m is the relative inhibitor concentration in the resist (for completely unexposed resist this is 0), $m _ { t h }$ is the threshold inhibitor concentration where developing starts, and $r _ { m i n }$ is the minimum development rate that is assumed to be unrelated to the inhibitor concentration in this model.
--[p173]-- Second, the knee of the curve (denoted by \* in Fig. 22) is of particular interest as this region defines the quality of the edges in the developed resist structures. The smaller the development rate is around the knee, the better defined the edges of the developed resist are.
--[p173]-- $$
r = \frac { r _ { m a x } ( ( a + 1 ) ( 1 - m ) ^ { n } ) } { a + \left( 1 - m \right) ^ { n } } + r _ { m i n }\tag{14}
$$
where:
$$
a = ( 1 - m _ { t h } ) ^ { n } \frac { ( n + 1 ) } { ( n - 1 ) }\tag{15}
$$
--[p173]-- Further important parameters in the development process are the mass transfer rates (via diffusion) of the developer to the surface of the resist and of the dissolved resist into the developer as well as the reaction rate at the resist surface, the latter being the rate-limiting factor in a typical development setup where the amount of developer is sufficient.
--[p172]-- This skin formation on top of the resist was due to basic substances in air (e.g., N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone) being absorbed on the top of the film, reacting and neutralizing the acid product after exposure.<sup>47</sup> For this reason, any delay in between the EUV exposure and PEB step might result in line width and sensitivity variation.<sup>2,90</sup> Amine filters or activated carbon air filters are now common in industry.
--[p172]-- For an optimal outcome of the lithography process, the transition between the developed and nondeveloped areas in the resist has to be as steep as possible. Therefore, a highly nonlinear dependence of the developing rate between the exposed and nonexposed areas is desired.

The ring parameter is defined as the mass of carbon atoms in the resist that are in a ring structure divided by the total mass of the resist.
--[p43]-- Etch resistance to plasma, especially oxygen plasma is an important property for resists.<sup>244,245</sup> The two most commonly used correlations for estimating etch resistance in resists are the Ohnishi parameter<sup>246</sup> and the ring parameter.<sup>247</sup> The Ohnishi parameter is defined as the total number of atoms per monomer divided by the number of carbon atoms minus the number of oxygen atoms.

--[p43]-- Partially protected polymers can also show improved adhesion to substrates, which often have polar groups. Likewise, dissolution performance may be better, with less swelling when using partially protected polymers. One of the advantages of polymeric resists is that their high number of functionality per molecule allows high levels of tuning and control over polarity and other properties that is often missing in small molecule resists, which tend to be more restricted in structure.
--[p43]-- Because a potentially huge list of polymers has been narrowed down to a few that satisfy most of these requirements, new polymeric resists can be made with a focus on lithographic properties and little worry about these. However, satisfactory performance regarding these properties are no longer a given with many new materials under investigation such as those based on smaller molecules or particles, so the learning curve must be undertaken with each new platform.<sup>236e243</sup>

The etch resistance of PHOST and other similar materials such as APEX or ESCAP types is sufficiently high for most patterning applications, but is slightly lower than novolac because of the additional nonring carbons in the polymer backbone.
--[p43]-- This was determined based on the observation that materials with higher numbers of ring structures had better etch resistance, so increasing the ring parameter leads to a decrease in the etch rate. At the limit of high etch resistance for organic materials would be things such as graphene and fullerenes, which are almost entirely composed of carbon atoms in ring 248 structures.
--[p43]-- The switch to 193-nm lithography once again required a switch in polymers because the absorbance of aromatic rings is too high at 193 nm to produce uniform exposure profiles through the depth of the film. Acrylates with no aromatic groups were found to have appropriately low absorbance, but suffered from poor etch resistance because of the lack of carbon in a ring structure and the higher relative number of oxygen atoms.
--[p43]-- There has been much work on incorporating fullerenes into resists or even directly functionalizing fullerenes for use as resists or hard mask materials.<sup>249e254</sup>
Novolac-based resists used in UV lithography have relatively high etch resistance because they are primarily aromatic rings with only a few additional atoms in the polymer structure.
--[p42]-- 1.5.3 RESIST PHYSICAL PROPERTIES AND ETCH RESISTANCE
The number of different types of polymers that have been evaluated for use as resists or could be considered for use is staggeringly large. Much work went into narrowing down the potential options to the handful of polymers that were ultimately chosen. An ideal resist material should fulfill long list of properties including solubility in “fab-friendly” organic solvents, and excellent film-forming characteristics.
--[p43]-- Early work on the polymeric CARs showed that partially protecting the polymer (i.e., blocking some of the polar functional groups and leaving others unprotected) led to better overall performance in a variety of areas; the APEX type shown in Fig. 13 demonstrates a partially protected PHOST. The better performance was due to several reasons.
--[p43]-- The solution to this issue that gained the most widespread application was the introduction of the adamantane group which can be seen on the left monomer for 193-nm resists in Fig. 13. Adamantane is a multicyclic group that consists of four cyclohexane rings connected together in a chair-type configuration.
--[p43]-- The sensitivity of a partially protected polymer is better than a fully protected polymer because the number deprotection reactions required to reach the solubility transition are less. As a result, the optimal number of protecting groups is often the minimal amount required to prevent dissolution in developer, so as to maximize sensitivity, although it is necessary to balance this with other properties such as LER or resolution, which may be optimized with higher protection levels.

===== [p19-22] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.3.2 DUV LITHOGRAPHYd248 nm AND 193 nm, IMMERSION, ANDMULTIPLE PATTERNING (21块) =====
--[p21]-- This process has an advantage in that it can, in theory, be applied to any general pattern, but it is highly sensitive to overlay error, which is the error between the alignment of each mask to the underlying pattern.
Another commonly used method of double patterning is called self-aligned double patterning. It involves the deposition of a conformal coating of a film onto a single resist pattern.
--[p21]-- BCPs are of interest because they can phase separate to length scales that are commensurate with desired lithographic patterns. DSA is the method whereby the self-assembly is spatially cued or controlled to produce lithographically useful phase-separated structures that are at a smaller pitch than is accessible from a single exposure step.
--[p20]-- One way to describe multiple patterning is that it provides a way to continue scaling through the use of added process complexity (by requiring multiple repeats of an existing process) rather than added tool or technology complexity (such as by modifying optics, changing wavelength, etc.). This description is obviously oversimplified because specially designed tools will improve the process, but it illustrates that the method could, in theory, be applied with existing equipment.
--[p19]-- The first major commercial production of wafers using DUV exposure tools was in 1990 to produce wafers with a critical dimension (CD) of $0 . 9 \mu \mathrm { m } .$ .<sup>28</sup> Mercury lamps have a weak peak around 254 nm (around 10% or less the intensity of the g-, h-, and i-line peaks), and the use of Hg-Xe lamps extends the usable range down to 220 nm with a stronger peak at around 248 nm.
--[p22]-- Several different ways to control DSA of BCPs have been investigated<sup>44</sup> such as graphoepitaxy,<sup>45</sup> chemoepitaxy,<sup>46,47</sup> or various combination methods. A chemoepitaxy process is illustrated in Fig. 5. Conventional lithography is used to pattern an UL to produce areas with different chemical affinity for each block of the BCP.
--[p21]-- This process is slightly simpler than LELE and has less stringent overlay error requirements, but is generally limited to a more restrictive set of patterns such as alternating lines. This process can also be repeated a second time on the first sidewall patterns to effectively quadruple the original resist pitch in a process known as self-aligned quadruple patterning.
--[p20]-- A similar approach was taken to implement so-called immersion lithography, and consists of introducing a fluid between the final lens and wafer.<sup>30</sup> This fluid, which has a higher refractive index than the air that is typically between the lens and wafer, changes the optical paths of exposure light and effectively results in a higher NA in Eq. (1).
--[p20]-- The strict definition of the resolution, defined by the Rayleigh criterion in Eq. (1), relates to the separation, rather than the feature size, of two objects and thus when the pitch between objects is relaxed the feature size can be reduced further, for instance by aggressive resist processing, exposure dose bias, etc. By patterning in multiple steps, closely spaced features can be separated into different patterning stepsdeffectively relaxing the pitch.
--[p20]-- The NA is higher because $N A = n _ { i }$ sin $\theta ,$ where $n _ { i }$ is refractive index and q is the propagation angle of light.<sup>31</sup> The NA of a “dry” exposure system does not go beyond 1.0; otherwise, the exposure light will be totally reflected back at the lens/air interface.<sup>32</sup> Use of ultrapure water as an immersion fluid (index 1.44 at 193 nm) has allowed production of tools with 1.35 NA capability and a resolution down to 45-nm halfpitch.<sup>33</sup> This 45-nm half-pitch is approximately the current resolution limit for single optical patterning in production today.
--[p20]-- Given the lack of an easily accessible lower wavelength exposure tool at the time, an alternative approach was developed to further improve the resolution of 193-nm lithography and continue feature shrink. It has long been known that the resolving power of an optical microscope can be improved if the air gap between the objective lens and the sample is filled with a high refractive index oil.
--[p19]-- 1.3.2 DUV LITHOGRAPHYd248 nm AND 193 nm, IMMERSION, ANDMULTIPLE PATTERNING
As feature sizes shrink, tool optimization generally reaches a limit meaning that $k _ { 1 }$ cannot shrink much more and NA cannot increase further. This means that resolution cannot be reduced unless the wavelength of light is reduced as shown in Eq. (1). This was a major driver for the investigation of DUV exposure tools in the 1980se1990s because the lower wavelengths allow for better resolution.
--[p21]-- The method involves first depositing a film stack consisting of one or more hard masks onto the wafer. One exposure is done near the resolution limit of the tool and this pattern is etched into the underlying film stack. A second exposure pattern that is offset from the first pattern is then carried out and transferred into the UL. The combined pattern from the two different exposures is at double the pitch of each individual pattern. The process is demonstrated in Fig. 3.
--[p19]-- These tools use a series of quartz lenses and a mask similar to UV lithography to generate the aerial image, which is translated by the photoresist into a relief image. Significant research and development went into an even lower wavelength of 157 nm which used $\mathrm { F } _ { 2 }$ excimer lasers, but it was ultimately abandoned due to difficulties finding a suitable replacement for quartz as a lens material.<sup>29</sup>
--[p22]-- Much progress has been made on evaluating DSA as a potential method for pitch multiplication<sup>48</sup> and improving defectivity,<sup>37,49</sup> however, it has not yet been implemented industrially for commercial semiconductor production.
--[p19]-- However, industrial application of DUV is almost entirely done using excimer lasers to produce the light used for exposures. The earliest DUVexposure tools used a wavelength of 248 nm, which is produced by a KrF excimer laser. As these tools were further optimized, there was a transition to a lower DUV wavelength of 193 nm produced by an $\mathrm { A r F }$ excimer laser to further improve the ultimate resolution of the printing system.
--[p20]-- Multiple patterning is a method that allows printing of patterns that are smaller than the single exposure lithographic resolution limit through the use of multiple process steps to print a single layer. Multiple patterning is the most general description of the process, but it was first used in the form of double patterning (equivalent to two single exposures) and then later quadruple patterning was developed and implemented (equivalent to four single exposures).
--[p21]-- The film can then be removed by a selective etch everywhere but on the sidewalls of the original resist. The resist is then removed and the remaining sidewall pattern will be at a smaller pitch and resolution than the original resist. Transfer of this remaining sidewall pattern into the substrate completes the process. This method is illustrated in Fig. 4.
--[p21]-- Multiple patterning techniques using directed self-assembly (DSA) of organic materials such as block copolymers (BCPs) have received much interest.<sup>35e43</sup> BCPs are polymers composed of two or more discrete blocks of homopolymers that are covalently joined together; some examples of BCPs include polystyrene-block-polymethylmethacrylate (PS-b-PMMA) or polystyrene-blockpolydimethylsiloxane (PS-b-PDMS).
--[p22]-- The different areas can be produced by chemical modification of the UL through plasma treatment or by selective removal of areas in the first UL and a deposition of another material such as a brush polymer. Finally, the BCP is coated onto the patterned UL and annealed. Because each block has different affinity for each area of the UL, specific blocks are aligned to create the directed self-assembled pattern.
--[p20]-- There was significant investigation into higher refractive index fluids than water, which would improve resolution even further, but these were never implemented because a technique called multiple patterning, which could provide superior resolution, was rapidly developed and employed first.<sup>33</sup>
--[p20]-- The application of multiple patterning as an industrial production process was in many ways a change in the paradigm of scaling that had driven the semiconductor industry for most of its lifetime.
Although there are many different potential ways to implement double and multiple patterning,<sup>34</sup> only a few will be briefly reviewed here. One method is known as Litho-Etch-Litho-Etch (LELE) and it involves two lithographic exposure and etch steps to create a single layer.

===== [p37-39] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.5.1 NONCHEMICALLY AMPLIFIED RESISTS (12块) =====
--[p38]-- The development rate in the novolac resin is strongly dependent on the loading and state of the DNQ. With no DNQ, the resin has a dissolution rate of around 10e100 nm/s. The logarithm of the development rate decreases linearly with added DNQ until it is on the order of 0.1e1 nm/s at 25-wt% loading. The exposed resist shows a similar increase in development rate with photoreacted DNQ content up to around 100e 1000 nm/s for a fully exposed resist with 25 wt% loading.
--[p39]-- The benefit of non-CA resists such as these is that they tend to have very high resolution because they do not tend to suffer from acid diffusion like many CARs (discussed later).
--[p39]-- They are unfavorable for production lithography that requires high throughput because they all generally have poor sensitivity; however, work has been carried out with the goal of creating nonamplified systems with greatly improved sensitivity.<sup>180e189</sup> While their poor sensitivity has limited non-CA resist application in industrial device production, their high resolution has made them highly used in research and development.
More information on nonchemically amplified resists can be found in Chapter 6.
--[p37]-- 1.5.1 NONCHEMICALLY AMPLIFIED RESISTS
Nonamplified resists encompass a large range of resists that are used for a number of applications. Since 1972,<sup>28</sup> the most widely used UV resist is a non-CA positivetone resist known as diazonaphthoquinoneenovolac, or DNQ/novolac.<sup>174</sup> Novolac is a polymer resin made by condensation of phenols and formaldehyde, often using methyl-substituted phenols.
--[p38]-- This rearrangement proceeds by loss of nitrogen followed by rearrangement to form a ketene and finally reaction with water (usually found in the environmental air and sorbed into the resist) forms an indene carboxylic acid; an overview of the process is seen in Fig. 11. The carboxylic acid is highly soluble in aqueous base solutions, and so the DNQ dissolution inhibitor becomes a dissolution promoter.
--[p38]-- The other reason is that the original DUV scanners had only about 10% as much power at DUVas the UV lamps, so very high sensitivity resists were required to maintain wafer throughput (a similar problem is currently being seen at EUV).<sup>28</sup> Since the quantum yield of DNQ conversion cannot be significantly improved, the sensitivity could not be increased enough. When used in higher energy systems such as e-beam and EUV, another issue is observed.
--[p37]-- The DNQ functionalized molecule that is commonly used in DNQ/novolac resists therefore usually contains several DNQ groups.<sup>174</sup>
When 15e30% by weight DNQ molecules are added to a novolac resin, the DNQ strongly inhibits the dissolution of the resin in aqueous base through strong hydrogen bonding interactions with the phenol groups. Upon exposure to UV light, DNQ undergoes a reaction known as the Wolff rearrangement.
--[p38]-- The absorbance of these resists is very high at 248-nm and below, so there is a significant gradient in light intensity through the thickness of the film which has a negative impact on patterning.
--[p39]-- The most common non-CA resists used in e-beam are polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA),<sup>177</sup> a methyl styrene-chloromethyl acrylate copolymer known as ZEP,<sup>178</sup> and HSQ.<sup>179</sup> The first two materials are positive-tone resists that undergo a solubility change that is driven by reduction in molecular weight of the polymer due to secondary electronecaused chain cleavage. HSQ is a negative-tone resist that undergoes cross-linking when reacted with electrons.
--[p38]-- The ketene intermediate requires water for conversion to the carboxylic acid, but e-beam and EUV are done in high vacuum systems, which remove most of the water in the film and in the environment. Lack of available water changes the mechanism and results in cross-linking of the DNQ intermediates to the resin rather than generation of the dissolution promoter.<sup>176</sup>
The other place that nonchemically amplified resists find major use is in e-beam lithography.
--[p37]-- The phenol groups on novolac are sufficiently acidic to react with base to form phenolate salts, which render the resin soluble in basic aqueous solutions. DNQ is a small molecule that is sensitive to UV light. It is often functionalized as a DNQ sulfonate (typically at the fourth or fifth position on the naphthoquinone ring) and several of these are reacted with a multifunctional phenol forming sulfonate esters.
--[p38]-- This behavior is illustrated in the so-called Meyerhofer plot.<sup>175</sup> DNQ/novolac works so well as a resist because the dissolution rate difference between exposed and unexposed regions can be 4e5 orders of magnitude.
DNQ/novolac was, and indeed still remains, an excellent resist system for i-line UV lithography, but it could not be used for 248-nm DUV lithography for two reasons.

===== [p301-307] Negative-tone organic molecular resists > 8.7.7 AQUEOUS BASE DEVELOPED EPOXIDE MOLECULAR RESISTS (27块) =====
--[p306]-- This likely is due to the additional cross-linking mechanism between epoxides and phenols and the higher $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ of TPOE-3Ep, which slows down the cross-linking kinetics and reduces the efficiency of cross-linking. It does show a desirable shift in $\mathrm { E } _ { 0 }$ away from zero dose.

--[p302]-- One approach that has been examined is the use of molecular resists that are intrinsically water soluble due to their specific structure.<sup>94</sup> Some of these structures are shown in Fig. 81. The materials are water soluble because of their small polar nature. Condensation and photolysis/radiolysis reactions converting a nanocluster to metal oxide.
--[p359]-- In condensation, represented by the top reaction, two nanoclusters react to form a larger cluster with water loss. As this process continues, larger clusters grow to oligomers and polymers, thereby decreasing solubility and dissolution rate. Hence, conditions driving dehydration such as spin coating, post-application bake, postexposure bake, and vacuum time will affect lithographic performance.
--[p359]-- M represents an oxo-hydroxo nanocluster containing three or more metal atoms, and L represents a radiation-sensitive ligand.
Photochemistry-by-design can be realized with a radiation-sensitive ligand (L) attached to the cluster. This ligand provides first-level condensation control. If ligand (L) substitutes for eOH or otherwise sterically hinders its reactivity, background condensation can be reduced. Radiation exposure breaks the MeL bond.

--[p432]-- PMMA was spun on the Au-coated substrate to an overall thickness of approximately 800 nm. Fig. 5 shows that the PMMA is unable to block the light. --[p432]-- The borosilicate glass was sputter coated with a thin Au film to provide an adhesion layer so that the PMMA could bond. --[p437]-- The effect is illustrated in Fig. 11AeD. The resultant dark area photoresist thickness, following exposure and development decreases (left to right, A to D), corresponding to a reduction in azo dye number density as the SML nanocomposite film thickness is reduced (left to right) due to increased transmission of light in the masked areas. --[p432]-- As the borosilicate glass provides a good optical substrate for the photomask, the PMMA must be put directly on the surface of the glass substrate. First, the Au thin film is a good conductor (2.2 mU/cm); this is necessary as the PMMA needs to be patterned using an e-beam direct writer.
--[p436]-- It is this optical contrast that is required at i-line wavelengths for transferring a microscale pattern from the nanocomposite resist to a photoresist. Fig. 10B shows that, as the number density of azo dyes (due to the increased film thickness) increases in the PMMA resist, it’s effectiveness as an i-line mask improves. --[p434]-- SML2000 resist is an organic nanocomposite material that is comprised of 9.5% of Sudan Orange, 2.5% of Sudan Black, 3% of trans-Stilbene, and 3% 4-phenylazophenol, supported by 82% PMMA. The chemical structures of the molecules are shown in Fig. 7. These azo dye materials were chosen specifically for their optical properties because the region of interest is between 320 and
450 nm. These azo dye materials will absorb i-line radiation (as illustrated in Fig.
--[p435]-- 8) at 365 nm, and it is this wavelength that is used to expose the well-known novolac resin photoresist S1813.
It was anticipated that the inclusion of the azo dyes should have minimal effect on the PMMA electron beam resist properties, as this resist operates primarily via chain scission process, rather than chemical amplification (which might be interrupted by extraneous additives).
--[p431]-- Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) is an organic electron beam (e-beam) resist well known to the scientific and industrial communities and generally considered to be the industry benchmark; it can produce features with a geometry of 10 nm.<sup>1,2</sup> However, to achieve such geometries, the resist film thickness must be around 40 nm, and hence, it has a limit of approximately 4:1 in pattern aspect ratio.<sup>3,4</sup> The main physical constraint to this is the generation of secondary electrons (SEs), which contribute to the proximity effect as they are scattered in arbitrary directions away from the desired exposure area. This cannot be avoided, so the maximum achievable aspect ratio of PMMA is approximately 4:1 when patterning with an acceleration voltage of 30 kV.
--[p437]-- To test the quality of the SML2000 resist as an optical mask, a pattern consisting of a grating with 30-mm wide lines was fabricated. This pattern was successfully transferred to the S1813 photoresist, which had a thickness of 1.3 mm. The S1813 photoresist was patterned using i-line wavelength and is shown in Fig. 12.
--[p436]-- Specifically, the “dark area” or opaque region defines the portion of the mask that is meant to block the exposing radiation. Conversely, the “light area” is the region where exposure of the resist is intended. ===== [p119-120] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.5.2 OUTLOOK AND RESEARCH NEEDS (7块) =====
--[p120]-- Synchrotron methods used in chemical dynamics may also be able to contribute to this goal. Experiments can be conducted on size-selected clusters,<sup>61</sup> 63 64 or core shell nanoparticles coated with variable-thickness resist films.
--[p119]-- 2.5.2 OUTLOOK AND RESEARCH NEEDS
EUV absorption in resist films can be significantly increased by incorporating high cross-section atoms. Furthermore high cross-section atoms will tend to localize subsequent reaction cascades, since excited molecules will emit two or three relatively slow SEs, instead of one relatively fast SE in the case of carbon excitation. Localized, simultaneous energy release has the potential to increase EUVL pattern resolution and reduce line-edge roughness.
--[p120]-- Modern computation methods can predict molecular excitation processes<sup>39,56,57</sup> and subsequent relaxation through Auger emission and fragmentation.<sup>58</sup> <sup>60</sup> Combined theoretical and experimental works on molecular systems can be of particular value, as these can help to refine theoretical approaches and validate methods that can later be applied to systems where direct experimental investigation is less practical.
--[p120]-- Particle-beam experiments have some important advantages relative to experiments on solid substrates spin coated with resist films, since radiation damage and electrostatic charging artifacts are eliminated, and wide ranges of parameter space can be efficiently explored by dynamically varying particle size, coating thickness or composition.
--[p119]-- Gas-phase electron scattering experiments on the same molecular components can elucidate the SE radiation chemistry. My colleagues and I at the Lawrence Berkeley National Lab are now working in this area.<sup>14</sup>
Theoretical work on the molecular components of EUVL resist systems also has a vital role.
--[p119]-- Gas-phase experiments on molecular components of EUVL resist systems can determine the absolute EUV X-ray absorption cross sections of molecules, the number and energy distribution of SEs, and the molecular fragmentation patterns. Synchrotron experiments using variable energy photon sources can unravel the contributions of different molecular orbitals, and quantify both primary electrons and photoelectrons.
--[p120]-- We are also working in this area at the Berkeley Lab.<sup>15</sup>
Full understanding of the initial steps of EUV molecular excitation and reaction can be a very important step in the development ofoptimized EUV molecular resist systems for high sensitivity and high-resolution pattern transfer. Even when the distribution of initial reaction products is known, understanding the reaction cascade in condensed systems will be challenging.
