===== [p130-131] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 3.2.2 ELECTRON IMPACT IONIZATION (5块) =====
--[p131]-- The total partial cross section refers to the probability of forming a particular ion. Two partial cross sections are indicated on the vertical diagram in Fig. 2B. Determining the absolute total and partial cross sections for DI (rather than relative cross sections) is important for many industrial applications (such as, e.g., for plasma processing and EUV lithography).
However, absolute cross sections are not straightforward to measure and have only been determined for a limited number of molecules.
--[p131]-- If these decay channels are dissociative, we speak of dissociative ionization (DI). For large polyatomic molecules, there can be a large number of decay channels. Reaction products are the primary ions and neutral (radical) fragments, where the primary ions can decay further into secondary ions. Predicting the reaction products and providing quantitative for the dissociation of molecules is difficult; ab initio calculations can only be done for relatively small systems.
--[p131]-- 2B shows two examples of such potential curves for $\mathrm { A B ^ { * } { } ^ { + } }$ (dark gray curve) and $\mathbf { A } \mathbf { B } ^ { \prime \ast ^ { + } }$ (light gray curve) above a ground state AB (black curve). Directly after the interaction event the reaction products are the excited cation ABþ\* and the free electrons, both the incident (now scattered) electron and the ejected electron. Different decay channels are open to the excited cation from its new potential curve.
--[p131]-- The threshold for electron impact ionization depends on the molecule but is usually at about 10 eV. Above this energy, the cross section increases strongly and smoothly with increasing electron energy. The total ionization cross section, i.e., the probability of forming an ion (integrated over all electron scattering angles, and without specifying which ion is formed) reaches a maximum for most molecules at about 70e100 eV and drops again for electron energies above that.
--[p130]-- 3.2.2 ELECTRON IMPACT IONIZATION
In electron impact ionization, a passing electron ionizes a molecule (or an atom) to leave an excited positively charged ion. Similarly to electron attachment, the
FrankeCondon principle applies to electron impact ionization. The ionization occurs on a time scale of about 100 as,<sup>7</sup> during which the molecular system goes from the initial potential curve to a given final interaction potential curve, all at the same nuclear separation. Fig.

===== [p175-178] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.3.10 PATTERN COLLAPSE MITIGATION STRATEGIES (21块) =====
--[p176]-- Apart from HMDS, a number of organic underlayers that promote the adhesion of the resists are commercially available.<sup>34</sup> These films are typically spin coated on the wafer (final thickness from a few to a few tens of nanometer) and baked at relatively high temperature (higher than for any of the bakes required by the resist itself) before resist application.
--[p176]-- The mechanical properties of the resist itself are naturally important as stiffer and more mechanically robust resists are less prone to deformation due to the capillary forces.<sup>98</sup> The mechanical properties of inorganic resists typically more resemble those of ceramics than those of polymers. Therefore, they are less prone to deformation (and collapse) in the presence of capillary forces.
--[p176]-- As capillary forces that occur when the wafers are dried are the root cause for pattern collapse, the most efficient way to mitigate pattern collapse is to eliminate any process steps where liquideair interface reaches the resist surface. The most effective technique is critical point (or supercritical) drying .<sup>102,103</sup> In this technique, the developed sample is brought, still immersed in rinse liquid, to a special chamber where liquid carbon dioxide (CO ) is then added.
--[p176]-- Therefore a common approach is to treat the wafers with hexamethyl disilazane (HMDS) beforehand.<sup>100</sup> The HMDS can be applied either by spin coating or by exposing the wafer to HMDS vapor, the latter being the preferred technique as this technique results in a monolayer coverage of the substrate.<sup>101</sup> The HMDS molecules have a hydrophilic end group that binds to the native oxide surface of the wafer and a hydrophobic group that provides an excellent adhesion for most organic resists.
--[p177]-- After spin coating, the wafer may be baked to remove the solvents. Finally, the encapsulating material is removed in a dry-etch step, leaving behind only the original inorganic resist structures (Fig. 25G).
DDRMs have to meet a specific set of requirements to work well. First of all, the material has to be well miscible with the rinse liquid used in the process. It also has to wet the resist well so that no air bubbles or unfilled areas are formed.
--[p178]-- More recently, dry developing CARs that undergo a selective silylation of the exposed areas upon contact to a gaseous silylating agent have been developed.<sup>110,111</sup> Here, the exposed (silylated) areas of the resist become more resistant toward ${ \bf O } _ { 2 }$ plasma etching by which the resist can now be developed as the unexposed areas are easily removed in the process.
--[p178]-- First, increasing the resist thickness has been found to decrease the LER,<sup>95</sup> and second, the etching resistance of the resist is improved, that is, deeper structures can be etched using the resist as an etching mask before it is fully removed by the etching process.
On a historical note, dry developing of resists was first investigated<sup>107,108</sup> in the early 1970s.
--[p175]-- Moreover, the resist should have a certain thickness for effective pattern transfer using etching. Another way to prevent pattern collapse is choosing a rinse liquid (or introducing an additional rinse step in another liquid) with smaller surface tension than that of deionized water that is the most common rinse material.
--[p175]-- 4.3.10 PATTERN COLLAPSE MITIGATION STRATEGIES
Several strategies for reducing pattern collapse during drying of the wafers can be inferred from Eq. (16). First, as the aspect ratio A is the dominant factor in the equation, reducing it by decreasing the film thickness is particularly appealing. This, however, has been found by many researchers<sup>34,95</sup> to result in increased LER in the resist structures.
--[p178]-- Naturally, neither the DDRM nor its solvent should damage the resist or other materials on the wafer in any way. Furthermore, the material should not shrink during the baking as this would lead to uneven surface and be detrimental to the uniformity of the etching processes. Last but not least, in the case of CARs, the etching selectivity between the DDRM and the resist should be good enough to allow for removal of the resist without significant damage to the DDRM itself.
--[p178]-- In the case of DDRP for inorganic resists, the requirements for the DDRM are similar to those in the case of CARs apart from the requirements that have to do with etching selectivity. For inorganic resists, the DDRM should be removed easily and completely by dry etching so that no damage to the resist occurs.
As DDRP mitigates pattern collapse in the patterned structures, it also allows for patterning the resist at increased aspect ratios. Along with this come several advantages.
--[p177]-- In DDRP, an encapsulating layer is spin coated on to the wafers while they are still wet after developing and rinsing processes, and this layer is subsequently removed via dry etching. Hence, as the wafer is not dried at any point of the process, no capillary forces act on the resist structures, and the root cause for pattern collapse is eliminated. The process was first suggested for CARs in 2013 by Sakamoto et al.<sup>105</sup> The process flow of DDRP for organic resists is shown in Fig.
--[p177]-- Due to higher etch resistivity of inorganic resists, the DDRP process for them is simpler than that for CARs,<sup>106</sup> as seen in Fig. 25EeG. The beginning of the process is identical to the case of CARs in that the resist is exposed, developed, and rinsed normally. Again, the wafer is not dried, but an encapsulating material is dispensed and spin coated on it while it is still wet (Fig. 25E), burying the resist structures (Fig. 25F).
--[p176]-- Then, the temperature and pressure inside the chamber are slowly increased above the so-called supercritical point of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } ,$ , where the densities of its gaseous and liquid state are equal. Above the critical point, the pressure (and the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } )$ from the chamber can be slowly released leaving behind the dry sample.
--[p177]-- In the next step, a dry-etching step (an etch back) is performed to expose the top of the buried photoresist (Fig. 25C). Finally, the photoresist is removed in another dry-etching step leaving only the DDRM pattern on the wafer (Fig. 25D) to be used in further processing steps. It is worth emphasizing that the process results in image reversal of the original resist pattern.
--[p176]-- The technique has been found to effectively mitigate pattern collapse in high aspect ratio resist structures.<sup>104</sup> As the process involves no liquidegas interfaces, no capillary forces are present. However, critical point drying is a very slow technique and limited to small samples, and thus not appropriate for HVM.
Dry develop rinse process (DDRP) has recently attracted attention as an HVM compatible pattern collapse mitigation strategy.
--[p178]-- At the time, mitigating pattern collapse was not the main motivation of the work, but rather to be able to carry out the exposure, development, and pattern transfer in a single high vacuum step, thus limiting the number of process steps and exposure of the wafer to the ambient environment in an effort to improve the yield and to reduce defects.<sup>49</sup> At first, polymers that evaporated almost fully upon expo-Subsequently, polymers that develop upon heating after electron beam exposure were developed.<sup>109</sup> However, in both cases, plasma etching was required to completely develop the images.
--[p177]-- For use with positive-tone resists, the DDRM was dissolved in an aqueous solvent and for negative-tone resists in an organic solvent to ensure a good mixing with the rinsing liquid (deionized water or organic solvent, respectively). After spin coating the DDRM, the wafer is baked to remove any solvent residue from the encapsulating film so that the resist structures are completely buried underneath (Fig. 25B).
--[p175]-- This approach has been studied in several reports.<sup>96,97</sup> Furthermore, designing the patterns so that the spacing between the resist structures (D) is maximized may be considered, where applicable.
--[p177]-- 25AeD. First, the wafer is exposed, developed, and rinsed as usual. After rinsing, the wafer is not dried (Fig. 25A) but an encapsulating material (dry develop rinse material, DDRM) is dispensed and spin coated on the still wet wafer. Sakamoto et al. used a silicon-based polymer for encapsulating the resist.
--[p176]-- The optimization of the adhesion between the resist and the surface of the wafer is very important as delamination of the resist is perhaps the most common reason for pattern collapse in resist structures with aspect ratios less than three.<sup>34,94</sup> The surface of the wafer where the resist is to be spin coated often does not provide sufficient adhesion to the resist as water or other impurities may be adsorbed on $\mathrm { i t } ^ { 9 9 }$ or the resist may simply not stick well to the material to be coated. Therefore, in most cases, the wafers are pretreated or primed before resist application. Organic resists typically stick best to hydrophobic surfaces while the surface of the wafers is intrinsically hydrophilic due to the native oxide layer.

===== [p438-445] SML electron beam resist: ultra-high aspect ratio nanolithography > 12.4 SML2000 ELECTRON BEAM PERFORMANCE (26块) =====
--[p443]-- It is evident that the inelastic scattering and BSE processes inside the SML2000 resist under 100-kV exposure differ from conventional PMMA. The generation of SE does not occur because the energy associated to the PE is large and not enough energy is lost as it travels through the polymeric material for inelastic scattering process to occur. Therefore, the proposed patterning mechanism is that the incident primary electrons travel through the
--[p441]-- When a PE crosses the material boundary from the resist to the silicon substrate, it loses its energy and the electron slows down and comes to rest. As it slows down, the number of collisions that the PE experiences increases and SE are generated. The distance that the PE travel is tens of microns into the silicon substrate before coming to rest, therefore, the distance that the SE are back scattered into the underside of the resist is far away from the write field.
--[p441]-- Hence, there is a higher level of BSE into the underside of the PMMA resist. This can be seen from Fig. 15.

===== [p490-490] Next generation lithographydthe rise of unconventional methods? > 14.2 BEYOND OPTICAL: STATE-OF-THE-ART IN NGL (4块) =====
--[p490]-- To date, a wide variety of tricks and unconventional patterning methods<sup>21,22</sup> to go beyond classic photolithographic limits. However, continued scaling is difficult, and major challenges occur for all NGL approaches, making significant further technological progress necessary. For the paradigm shift toward postoptical lithographic solutions the currently most promising top-down successors will be briefly introduced in the following section.
--[p490]-- • Furthermore, economic factors dictate a high effectiveness of the lithographic process throughput, costs, exposure dose, and extended process windows;
Finally, a reliable method to transfer a narrow feature from the resist layer into the underlying substrate must be existdpattern transfer capability, etch resistance/selectivity, and opportunity for direct patterning of functional materials.
--[p490]-- Thus, the accuracy and repeatability of the patterning process becomes ever more important: process latitude, CD control, linewidth control, reproducibility, line-edge roughness (LER);
• Any multilevel lithography process requires overlay registration and alignment capabilities, whereby the downscaling increases the requirements enormouslydoverlay registration/overlay alignment accuracy;
--[p490]-- 14.2 BEYOND OPTICAL: STATE-OF-THE-ART IN NGL
NGL tools and solutions are necessary to circumvent fundamental optical limitations. New lithographic approaches should meet several key requirements to successfully lead from micro toward nanofabrication<sup>4,19,20</sup>:
• Ability to reduce the MFSs: high lithographic resolution, contrast, and sensitivity;
• When the CDs shrink, the controllability of the process within strict tolerances will be more critical.

===== [p445-451] SML electron beam resist: ultra-high aspect ratio nanolithography > 12.5 PUSHING THE RESOLUTION LIMITS (28块) =====
--[p445]-- 12.5 PUSHING THE RESOLUTION LIMITS
It is evident that the SML resist exhibited nanostructures with a 10:1 aspect ratio using an acceleration voltage of 30 kV, as it was shown that it prevented the primary electrons from scattering laterally and reduced the number of SEs from being generated and exposing the resist laterally. Hence, a reduction to the contribution of the proximity effect was realized. Therefore, this suggests that the resolution limits of the resist have not been fully explored.
--[p450]-- Due to the decreased number of collisions with atoms in the SML300 resist, the electron mean free path of is larger when compared to PMMA, and the electrons travel further into the silicon substrate, and the PMMA resist has a greater risk of BSEs exposing its underside, which cases the tear drop shapes seen in Figs. 23A and 24A.
--[p445]-- This is significant, as it can be seen from Fig. 20 that SE are scattered at angles larger than 80 degrees in arbitrary trajectories away from the primary beam.<sup>3</sup> These electrons expose the PMMA resist laterally, contributing to the proximity effect.
--[p445]-- 21A and B, the number of SE generated is almost zero at 30 kV when compared to PMMA. Hence, their contribution to the proximity effect will be considerably less.

===== [p385-386] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.1 INTRODUCTION (11块) =====
--[p385]-- 11.1 INTRODUCTION
As the semiconductor industry continues to push the limits of 193-nm immersion lithography, many predict extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography will be necessary to print the features needed for future technologies. At these extremely small feature sizes, however, conventional polymeric EUV resists are encountering enormous hurdles which must be overcome.
1. Etch resistance. The ultimate purpose of a photoresist is to protect the underlying substrate from an etch process.
--[p385]-- If photoacid created in the exposed region diffuses into the unexposed region, image contrast is lost.<sup>7</sup> We predict that as resolutions continue to improve, the control of photoacid diffusion required to print the small features needed by the semiconductor industry will not be possible.
4. Optical density (OD).
--[p385]-- As resolutions improve, the sizes of patterned features in resist films are approaching the radius of gyration of the resist polymers (w1<sub>e</sub>5 nm).<sup>3</sup> At these resolutions, the patterned features appear to be composed of discrete components rather than a continuous film, limiting line-edge roughness (LER).
--[p386]-- Through the remainder of this chapter, the current status, synthesis, and lithographic evaluation of compounds made from Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Pd, Sn, Pt, and Bi will be discussed.
--[p386]-- Carbon and silicon tetrafluorides are volatile gasses, resulting in the low etch selectivity oforganic-resist films on silicon substrates. Most metal fluorides are solids at room temperature, and so we predict MORE resists to have significantly better etch selectivity than organic resists.
• No acid diffusion. Since these films are not chemically amplified, photoacid diffusion is not a concern.
High nonchemically amplified reactivity.
--[p385]-- As the microelectronics industry improves resolution, the resist film thickness must concomitantly decrease to prevent pattern collapse. Organic-resist film thicknesses are near the limits of being able to protect the substrate from the etch process.<sup>1,2</sup> We predict the etch processing of thin-organic films will not be capable of meeting the needs of future lithography nodes.
2. Resolution approaching the polymer radius of gyration.
--[p385]-- In future technology nodes, we predict LER improvements will be incapable of surpassing the size of individual polymer segments and thus will not meet future LER goals.<sup>4e6</sup>
3. Resolution approaching the acid diffusion length. One of the biggest challenges today with chemically amplified systems is the control of acid diffusion.
--[p386]-- We predict that by tuning the reduction and/or oxidation potential of the metals, highly sensitive nonchemically amplified systems are possible.
Selection of MORE materials. To identify high EUV OD elements, the OD for all elements on the periodic table was calculated at standard state density and compared to carbon (Fig. 1). Elements were then selected based on OD, cost, toxicity, and radioactivity.
--[p386]-- In order to overcome many of the problems discussed for organic polymer resists, we have developed a novel class of inorganic resists, which we have named molecular organometallic resists for EUV (MORE). MORE is a class of photoresist materials made from inorganic or organometallic compounds or clusters which are chosen from high OD metals throughout the periodic table. We predict that MORE materials will have significant benefits over organic polymer systems.
• High EUV OD.
--[p385]-- The OD of carbon is relatively low in EUV.<sup>8</sup> As film thickness decreases, the amount of absorbed dose will also decrease.<sup>9</sup> Even the darkest organic polymer films are incapable of absorbing more than w30% of the light at 20-nm film thicknesses. This low film OD ultimately results in a poor sensitivity due to the inefficient absorption of photons.
--[p386]-- Since some metals in the periodic table are more than 10 times darker than carbon, highly absorbing resist films can be made.
• High mass density. Inorganic films typically have a mass density 5e10 greater than polymer films. By increasing the mass density of the resist films, reduction of secondary electron blur is possible.
Excellent etch rates. The etch process typically involves the reaction of radical fluorine with both the resist and substrate.

--[p209]-- An early negative-tone acrylic resist, known as “COP” developed at Bell Laboratories, is a copolymer of glycidyl methacrylate and ethyl acrylate.<sup>58</sup> In the absence of added cationic initiator, cross-linking proceeds via cationic mechanisms, as described comprehensively by Al-Sheikhly and McLaughlin.<sup>59</sup> The radiation-produced cationic species open the oxirane ring producing an oligomeric cation, which undergoes further addition reactions with available oxirane groups.

--[p130]-- An example is the attachment of near-zero energy electrons to gaseous $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ to form stable $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { - }$ ions.<sup>17</sup> In radiative cooling, the transient ion emits a photon to form a stable negative ion.

--[p130]-- The second channel is DEA, which is favored when the resonance lifetime is relatively long (in the order of a vibrational period or longer).<sup>16</sup> It occurs when the interaction potential of the transient negative ion is dissociative and one of the fragments has a positive electron affinity. The transient ion $\mathrm { \bf A B } ^ { - }$ or $\mathbf { A } \mathbf { B } ^ { - * }$ dissociates into a neutral (usually) radical and an ion.

--[p129]-- This typically occurs at slightly higher energies (w5 to $\sim 1 5 \mathrm { e V } ) .$ 12 The second classification type depends on whether the new state is energetically above or below the ground state or the excited state of the initial molecule. --[p128]-- The cation can be in its ground state $( \mathsf { A B } ^ { + }$ , not shown), or can be exited $( \mathsf { A B } ^ { \star + }$ and $\mathsf { A } \mathsf { B } ^ { \prime \star + }$ , dark and light gray curves, respectively). The cation can decay, in this example into $\mathsf { A } ^ { + } + \mathsf { B }$ or $\mathsf { A } + \mathsf { B } ^ { + }$ , respectively.
--[p129]-- Rather it can contribute, e.g., to electron energy loss in the solid through elastic scattering (if the molecule falls back to its ground vibrational level) or by leaving the initial molecule vibrationally, rotationally, or electronically excited. For molecules that are adsorbed on a surface, this process may contribute to desorption of the entire molecule to the gas phase.
--[p129]-- Amongst others things, these aspects make electron attachment challenging to calculate and model. Full calculations are rare; acetylene is one example where ab initio and experimental results are available.<sup>10,11</sup>
Electron attachment is a resonant process, which can be classified in two ways.<sup>12</sup> The first classification depends on the number of electrons that are involved in the electron capture.
--[p130]-- The interaction potential of that transient negative ion determines which decay channel is open and therefore determines the outcome of the electronemolecule interaction. The relation between electron energy and dissociation yield is schematically shown in the vertical diagram in Fig. 2A, to the left of the potential axis. As mentioned, the influence of the electron energy makes DEA fundamentally different from the photochemistry used in, e.g., ultraviolet lithography.

--[p130]-- In DEA, this is different; the energy of the incoming electron plays a role in determining the interaction potential of the resonance, which in turn determines the dissociation path.
The last two decay channels are associative attachment and radiation cooling, both stabilization processes that can occur when the initial molecule has a positive electron affinity. In associative attachment, the resonance decays through energy transfer to neighboring molecules.
--[p129]-- In contrast to the short timescale of the electronic transition (during which the electron is captured), the lifetime of the resulting transient state can vary greatly. Lifetimes are mostly in the picosecond range but can also be as long as milliseconds, such as for $\mathrm { S F } _ { 6 } ^ { - }$ for example. 15
Once the system is in its transient state, there are four channels to relax: autodetachment, dissociative electron attachment (DEA), associative attachment, and radiative cooling.
--[p128]-- Schematic diagram of electron attachment interaction potentials for a molecule AB interacting with an electron. (A) In DEA, an electron is captured by a molecule that is in its neutral ground state (AB, black curve) to form a transient anion $( \mathsf { A B } ^ { - }$ , dark gray curve), or an excited transient anion $( \mathsf { A } \mathsf { B } ^ { \star - }$ , lightgraycurve). One of the decay paths for the transient ion is to dissociate.
--[p128]-- The threshold for DI is higher than for ${ \mathsf { D E A } } ,$ as it is determined by the ionization potential of the resulting cation $( \mathsf { A } ^ { + } \mathsf { o r } \mathsf { B } ^ { + } )$ and the bond dissociation energy of AB. (c) In ND, a neutral electronically excited state is formed, in this example $\mathsf { A B } ^ { \star }$ (dark graycurve) and $\mathsf { A B } ^ { \prime \star }$ (light graycurve).
--[p128]-- If the excited state is repulsive, the molecule dissociates into neutral reaction fragments $( \mathsf { A } + \mathsf { B } ^ { \star } )$ . Dissociation can also occur from an excited bound state if the molecule is sufficiently vibrationally excited (in this example $\mathsf { A } + \mathsf { B }$ , vibrational excitation not shown). The threshold energy at which ND occurs (indicated on the vertical scale) is lower than for DI, as the ionization energy does not need to be overcome.
--[p129]-- In this case, an electron is captured in an unoccupied orbital of which the interaction potential is “shaped” such that the electron needs to pass through a centrifugal barrier to enter or leave. The centrifugal barrier is a highly localized, induced potential barrier, associated with the high angular momentum of the electron.
--[p130]-- According to Kasha’s rule, in photochemistry the radiationless transition from higher excited states to the lowest excited state (through rapid vibrational relaxation) is generally faster than chemical reactions. The outcome of photoinduced reactions does therefore not depend on the state to which the molecule is initially excited.
--[p129]-- Single-particle shape resonances can decay relatively easily, as the energy of the transient ion is higher than the ground state of the parent molecule, and only a single electron is involved. Therefore, the lifetime of these resonances is relatively short<sup>12</sup> and generally favors the autodetachment decay channel, where the molecule returns to its neutral state. This type of electronemolecule interaction therefore is not likely to contribute directly to the resist chemistry.
--[p129]-- In a single-particle resonance, the electron is captured in to an empty molecular orbital, while the other electrons do not change configuration. This occurs typically at the lower range of energies, from 0 up to about 5 eV. Alternatively, the resonance can be core-excited. When forming the anion, the incoming electron excites one of the electrons of the molecule itself before being attached (two electron and one hole).
--[p129]-- The electron capture brings the system on the resonant interaction potential (dark and light gray curve in Fig. 2), a different interaction potential than before the event. It is important to note that the new ground state energy (of the transient negative ion) can be higher than the ground state energy of the initial molecule, which means that the new state can be thermodynamically unstable. In addition, the occupation of the orbital can be accompanied by an excitation of the molecule.
--[p129]-- This is apparent for instance from the angular distributions of electrons that scatter due to such resonance s.<sup>13,14</sup> Alternatively, the energy of the new state can be lower than the ground or excited state of the neutral. This is the case for electronically excited molecules that have a positive electron affinity. These core-excited resonances will have a lower energy than the neutral excited states; such resonances are called Feshbach resonances.

===== [p346-348] Positive molecular resists > 9.4 CURRENT STATUS, NEW CONCEPTS, AND CHALLENGES (11块) =====
--[p347]-- For the increase of absorption, popular choices are the incorporation of fluorine atoms and the use of inorganic or organometallic components. On the other hand, for the differentiation of the acid diffusion extent from the deprotection reactions kinetics, increase of $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ and the use of protecting groups with low energy of activation are most often tried.
--[p348]-- Under e-beam exposure, a 135-nm film of TAS-t-Boc<sup>67</sup> resolved lines down to 50 nm with an LER of 3.96 nm. Although this is an excellent performance regarding LER, changes in feature size induced by acid diffusion were significant in this resist system.
--[p346]-- Indeed, according to the information provided by Naulleau et al., as of 2013, progress in resist performance improvement appears to have been very slow in recent years.<sup>67</sup>
On the other hand, many efforts in the lithography field have, as their target, been overcoming the RLS problem. In a representative study with the participation of many players from different EUV processing sites,<sup>68</sup> some clues to beat the RLS problem have been proposed.
--[p348]-- The synthesized triarylsulfonium was found to be comparable in performance to commercial triphenylsulfonium when used as a PAG. The modification of the triphenylsulfonium ion by the addition of methyl groups and t-Boc protecting groups to the phenyl rings made the photoproducts of the PAG sufficiently bulky to prevent the relatively high outgassing levels that might be expected from such an onium salt PAG.
--[p347]-- Furthermore, novel ideas such as acid amplification (AA) and the use of photodestructive acid (PDA) units are constantly proposed [see for instance Ref. 62,76]. The relevant efforts affect all types of lithographic materials, but small organic molecules probably offer advantages for material differentiation in a reliable and reproducible manner. It is even possible to design well-characterized single component systems in the case of molecular resists.
--[p347]-- One such direction seems to be the increase of the film quantum efficiency. PAG content increase seems to help if material inhomogeneity problems can be successfully addressed.
During the last years, reviews of lithographic material experts,<sup>54,55,62,69e79</sup> mostly from industry but also from academia, have presented progress of work on molecular resists and, in particular, on positive molecular resists.
--[p347]-- Examples of attaching the PAG to the basic molecular structure and of addition of high-absorbing groups have been presented and will be briefly discussed here.<sup>80,81</sup>
A single molecule photoresist composed of tris(4-(tert-butoxycarbonyloxy)- 3,5-dimethylphenyl) sulfonium hexafluoroantimonate (TAS-t-Boc) (Fig. 18) was successfully synthesized, characterized, and imaged under DUV (248 nm) and e-beam exposures.
--[p346]-- 9.4 CURRENT STATUS, NEW CONCEPTS, AND CHALLENGES
The previous sections discussing the development of positive molecular resists by a good number of research groups clearly demonstrates that new classes of novel molecular materials have emerged as a result of this effort. Quite a few viable approaches for developing lithographic materials with sub-30-nm resolution capabilities under processing conditions similar to the ones used for positive-tone polymeric resists have been identified.
--[p346]-- Since the exposure mode envisioned as a successor to the current 193 immersion photolithography tools is EUV, these materials have to meet the strict requirements posed for EUV lithography to be widely accepted as resists in semiconductor manufacturing. Thus, in addition to resolution and LER requirements, sensitivity needs to be very high to compensate for the low output of EUV exposure systems.
--[p347]-- In these studies, it is clear that the effort continues involving all the types of materials discussed previously, but little information is provided regarding the specific structures under investigation. In addition, increase of EUV radiation absorption by using elements of high EUV absorbance in the resist formulation and differentiation of acid-diffusion processes from the extent of the deprotection reactions are routes that are also being investigated to beat the RLS problem.
--[p346]-- At this point, it is necessary to address the wellknown RLS (resolution, LER, sensitivity) problem, schematically represented with a triangle (Fig. 17) encountered in chemically amplified systems .<sup>65,66</sup> As has been discussed in these publications, the simultaneous optimization of all three requirements is a formidable task.

===== [p468-468] Alternative resist approaches > 13.2.3 HIGH-ABSORBANCE APPROACHES (4块) =====
--[p468]-- 13.2.3 HIGH-ABSORBANCE APPROACHES
EUV photons are said to be “expensive” which alludes to the great difficulty in producing a bright EUV source and the low reflectivity of the EUV optical system, particularly when all of the mirrors are considered, see Chapter 5.
--[p468]-- As discussed in Section 13.2.1, the continuing reduction in the maximum usable resist thickness, due to the worsening issue of aspect ratio-related pattern collapse during development, caused concerns that EUV-resist films were in fact too transparent, leading to the available EUV photons being inefficiently utilized. This led in turn to a significant amount of work to increase the absorbance of the resist materialda diametrically opposite approach to that seen in Section 13.2.2.
--[p468]-- Increasing absorption via metal oxide and organometallic resists has already been examined in Chapters 10 and 11, while metal-organic composite approaches will be described in Section 13.2.4 of this chapter.
This section will focus on modifications of more traditional organic-resist systems, via the halogenation of either the polymer or the PAG. The use of halogenated polymers to increase sensitivity in non-optical-resist materials has a long history. Taylor et al.
--[p468]-- demonstrated that the sensitivity of negative-tone X-ray resists could be increased by the incorporation of chlorine into the polymer.<sup>45</sup> The most effective class of material investigated was poly(chloroalkyl acrylates), which were examined at chlorine wt% between 26.6 and 52.3. Poly(2,3-dichloro-1-propyl acrylate) with a chlorine wt% of 38.7% demonstrated a sensitivity of 7 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> for 0.437-nm X-ray

===== [p417-417] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.6.1 LIGAND STRUCTURE (2块) =====
--[p417]-- 11.6.1 LIGAND STRUCTURE
In the literature, transition metal oxalates have been made with a variety of different ligands.<sup>84,86</sup> It is reasonable that the physical properties of the film may be related to the structure of the ligands bound to the metal. To investigate the effect of ligand structure, three amine and/or imine ligand-types (L) were selected: ethylenediamine (EN), 2,20-bipyridine (BPY), and phenanthroline (PHEN).
--[p417]-- For each ligand-type, compounds of the form $\mathrm { L } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C o } ( \mathrm { o x a l a t e } ) \cdot \mathrm { P F } _ { 6 }$ were made and evaluated. Compounds containing EN (60) and PHEN (62) ligands were found to be insoluble in common solvents (Fig. 39). Compound 61, containing the BPY ligand, has good solubility in polar solvents such as acetonitrile.

===== [p49-55] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.5.5 MOLECULAR RESISTS AND INORGANIC RESISTS (43块) =====
--[p55]-- Modifying the ligand appears to provide an opportunity to tune sensitivity up and down.<sup>440</sup> More information on these resists can be found in Chapter 13.
Another recently developed class of inorganic resists that have shown interesting results are the so-called molecular organometallic resists for EUV (MORE).
--[p50]-- Molecular resists have the additional advantage of being small molecules which means they can be synthesized to produce a very well-defined distribution of molecules or even be truly monodisperse. This can lead to very homogeneous films and minimal segregation of components, which can improve LER. Many different synthesis and separation techniques exist that can make these materials repeatedly with high levels of control at the molecular level.
--[p53]-- Despite all the potential advantages of molecular resists, they have not shown the compelling improvements in LER or resolution as hoped. While much work has been done on these materials, very few have reported LER values of below 4 nm, and most report values on the order of 4e8 nm. These LER values are commensurate with many polymeric resists and even higher than many state-of-the-art polymer EUV resists.
--[p50]-- In contrast, many polymeric resists contain three, four, or more different monomers which all have different reactivity ratios that ultimately can lead to polymers with both molecular weight polydispersity and also high levels of variation in the order and number of functionality along each chain length. A series of studies on one particular molecular resist core have
--[p52]-- One such model was developed that predicts the glass transition temperature in these types of materials using a bond contribution model based on a library of over 50 compounds.<sup>416</sup> It is also possible to leverage accurate models developed to predict nonlithographic or general material properties for small molecules and apply them to correlate or predict lithographic properties.
--[p50]-- The typical radius for a molecular resist might be on the order of 1e2 nm, while a polymer resist could have a radius of gyration of 5e10 nm. This is visually demonstrated in Fig. 18. Small molecule resists should not suffer from chain entanglement like polymers, which can potentially lead to internal stress or swelling and pattern distortion.
--[p53]-- For negative-tone patterning, the small molecule starting materials appear to lead to less swelling during development than in similar polymeric systems because the smaller unexposed materials dissolve faster, while the final cross-linked structure provides good mechanical support. These materials are covered more thoroughly in Chapter 8.
--[p53]-- The general size disparity between resist polymers and molecular resists is not so large as compared to many industrially used polymers, so the overall reduction in molecular size may not be so great as originally thought. Although the precise molecular weight of polymeric CARs varies, many are on the order of2000e20,000 g/mol, which is not too substantially bigger than molecular resists, which most often have ranged from 500 to 2000 g/mol.
--[p55]-- Tin-based compounds were also made and they showed a range of sensitivities from 5 to 190 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> depending on ligand and functionalization.<sup>443,444</sup> More information on MORE resists can be found in Chapter 11.
--[p49]-- However, there are a large number of different designs and approaches that have been investigated including positive-tone molecular resists using different protecting groups and negative-tone formulations that undergo solubility switching or cross-linking through a variety of means such as epoxide functionalization and cross-linking or additional small molecule cross-linkers.<sup>239,371</sup> There are even some nonchemically amplified molecular resists that operate by cross-linking or through the use of photosensitive protecting groups .<sup>181,236</sup> More thorough information can be found in Chapters 8 and 9.
Given the success of polymeric resists, it might not be immediately clear why small molecule resists could be desirable.
--[p55]-- In addition to these materials, there has been a lot of work done on high sensitivity nanoparticle resists based on $\mathrm { H f O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { Z r O } _ { 2 }$ by Ober and others.<sup>437</sup> Organic ligands such as methacrylic acid are used to functionalize the nanoparticles. These ligands provide solubility to the particles to allow film casting and they are combined with a PAG to form a resist.

--[p54]-- Since metals are more highly susceptible to oxidation and reduction, it is possible that high sensitivity nonchemically amplified resists could be made that would show good resolution. The high reactivity combined with high absorbance suggests promise for very sensitive EUV resists. There are still many concerns that must be addressed before inorganic or organometallic find use in high volume manufacturing.
--[p53]-- One example is resist contrast; molecular resists have generally shown lower contrast than polymeric resists. Since LER is inversely related to the deprotection gradient at the line edge,<sup>417</sup> it is likely that lower contrast resists could have worse LER.
--[p53]-- Ultimately, LER has not significantly dropped in molecular resists compared to polymer resists because the dominant factors controlling LER are not molecular size related but are other causes such as relative immaturity of the platform, shot noise, acid diffusion, pattern collapse, and other issues which are not necessarily improved (or may even by hurt) by small molecule resists.
--[p52]-- One study correlated the log D predicted for molecular resists to their solubility in aqueous base developer to calculate whether or not a particular molecular resist would dissolve in developer.<sup>5</sup> This model can be used to ensure a target molecule will be sufficiently soluble in developer but also can inform regarding the specific number of protecting groups that might be needed to make a molecule insoluble.
--[p54]-- The high mass density of inorganic resists compared to organic resists means that there is also a possibility of reducing the secondary electron blur at EUV (which can potentially limit ultimate resolution). Inorganic resists also show much higher plasma etch resistance than organic resists. This would allow much thinner resists which should help improve pattern collapse.
--[p49]-- 1.5.5 MOLECULAR RESISTS AND INORGANIC RESISTS
Historically, almost all resists were based on polymeric resins. As discussed earlier, polymers have many intrinsic properties that make them favorable for use as resists, particularly the fact that many easily form good quality amorphous films upon spin coating and have sufficiently high glass transition temperature for processing. In recent years, there has been an increasing interest in resists based on small molecules, both organic and inorganic.
The organic small molecule materials were the first most widely investigated and have been called molecular glass resists or molecular resists.
--[p53]-- Despite the fact that LER was not substantially improved by molecular resists, many of the other advantages, such as monodispersity, compositional control, and predictive structureeproperty relations still hold true.
--[p54]-- These elements can have up to 10 times higher EUV absorptivity than carbon.<sup>425</sup> This greatly increases the resist’s ability to capture EUV photons compared to current organic polymers, which might capture less than 30% of the incident photons at a 20-nm film thickness. The photons not captured by the resist are effectively wasted dose, and dose is at a premium in EUV.
--[p53]-- It is also possible that the generally lower $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ in molecular resists compared to polymeric resists contributes because it could make them mechanically less robust during processing and may have reflow or pattern collapse issues. A lower $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ could also lead to increased acid diffusion, which reduces resolution.
--[p49]-- Many of the investigated molecular resists contained phenolic OH groups, which imparted intrinsic base developer solubility and were then protected with acid-sensitive tert-butyloxycarbonyl (often shortened as tBoc or Boc) to function as a positive-tone resist.
--[p55]-- Another highly investigated inorganic resist family is based on high Z oxohydroxo clusters, exemplified by HafSOx and ZircSOx. These resists were originally developed at Oregon State<sup>432</sup> and are now being developed with the goal of commercialization by Inpria Corp. These materials have shown very high resolution and low LER with moderate to good sensitivity under EUV and e-beam.
--[p49]-- To avoid crystallization and ensure amorphous, disordered film formation they possess nonplanar, irregular shapes such as branched or ring structures.
--[p53]-- The lack of a substantial improvement in LER is likely because factors other than molecular size are the current dominant source of LER. This is due to a combination of many different factors.
Because molecular resists are a younger platform, they have not had the many additional years of development and improvement that polymeric resists already have received that gives them generally good performance.
--[p49]-- This nomenclature came about because molecular glasses are low molecular weight organic compounds that readily form stable amorphous glasses and show glass transitions usually associated with polymers.<sup>322</sup> Molecular glass materials have been investigated for use in a number of different fields<sup>323</sup> such as photo- and electroactive materials for electronic, optoelectronic, and photonic devices and photochromic amorphous molecular materials in addition to studies for use as a resist. Molecular glasses can be used in resists in place of polymers because they can generally be cast as amorphous films as opposed to many common small molecules, which tend to crystallize.
--[p52]-- Because their chemical structures can be very well controlled, it is possible to systematically change groups and properties on the resist molecules and evaluate the effects on lithographic performance .<sup>238,240,414,415</sup> The well-defined structure of the resists compared to polymers also opens the possibility of creating quantitatively predictive models that allow rational design of improved materials or prevent the synthesis of inferior materials by evaluating the resist properties in silico beforehand. Such models would also allow for rapid screening of candidate molecules.
--[p53]-- Optimization of resist design is potentially easier in polymer resists because monomer ratios can be carefully changed and new monomers added to fine-tune resist performance with minimal effect on other properties, while small changes in molecular resist structure can have large effects on other properties that lead to overall worse performance.
--[p53]-- In particular, negative-tone molecular resists that operate by crosslinking to form polymers and networks have shown good promise and performance on par or better than many polymeric resists.<sup>239,241,251,311,335e337,382,419e424</sup> There are many reports of resolutions below 20 nm, several below 15 nm, and a few materials operating in a nonchemically amplified mode have sub-10-nm resolution.
--[p55]-- MORE is a class of photoresist materials made from inorganic or organometallic compounds or clusters, which are chosen from high optical density metals throughout the periodic table. There have been many variations on MORE resists.
--[p54]-- 428e430 It has demonstrated sub-5-nm resolution under He ion beam and e-beam lithography .<sup>430,431</sup> It successfully patterns at EUV with very good resolution, but suffers from relatively poor sensitivity under any exposure source. This limits its use in production manufacturing, but it will likely remain a highly studied resist for research and development for many years. More information on HSQ can be found in Chapter 10.
--[p54]-- One of the biggest potentia advantages is that they can have significantly higher EUV absorbance than organic resists because they contain elements with very high EUV absorption such as tin, zinc, hafnium, nickel, and cobalt.
--[p55]-- Several platinum- and palladium-based MORE resists were developed and studied.<sup>442</sup> Many of the compounds showed poor performance and inability to pattern, but oxalate functional compounds showed patterning performance and sensitivity on the order of 50 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>.
--[p54]-- In addition to organic small molecule resists, there has been an enormous amount of recent work and interest on resists based on inorganic and organometallic small molecules and nanoparticles. These materials are more thoroughly discussed in Chapters 10, 11, and 13. The interest in these types of resists is based on the fact that they offer multiple potential advantages over organic materials.
--[p55]-- They have shown Initial EUV studies showed sub-16-nm resolution at a dose of 71 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>.<sup>434</sup> Resolution at 11 and 8 nm have been achieved using EUV interference lithography. More high sensitivity formulations have shown 13-nm half-pitch features at 35 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>.<sup>435</sup> Work has continued to improve sensitivity down to 20 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>, which is comparable to many CARs.<sup>436</sup> More information on these types of resists can be found in Chapter 10.
--[p55]-- One approach was to use organobismuth compounds, patterning could be done based on photoacid scission of phenylebismuth bonds or photolytic decarboxylation of bismuth carboxylates.<sup>441</sup> The phenylebismuth approach yielded low sensitivity of 60 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> at EUV. The bismuth carboxylates showed different sensitivities depending on ligand, ranging from 30 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> for 100-nm resolution up to 120 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> which produced 21-nm resolution.
--[p50]-- There are a number of potential advantages that molecular resists can be theorized to possess over polymeric resists. If the absolute spatial size of the molecule in a resist determines the smallest effective “pixel” in the resist image that is formed during patterning and development, then molecular resists could provide better resolution and LER because they have a smaller pixel size.
--[p52]-- For example, the partition coefficient (P, but most commonly used in the logarithmic form as log P) and distribution coefficient (similarly log D) describe the ratio of concentrations of a compound dissolved in an organic and water phase at equilibrium and are often used as a measure of hydrophobicity. Accurate models have been developed for prediction of these parameters purely from molecular structure because they are used in a variety of fields.
--[p53]-- For example, adding a single protecting group can change the $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ of a molecular resists by $1 0 { - } 3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , and some protecting groups can drive $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ below room temperature.<sup>240</sup> Because LER is proportionally related to the local variance in deprotection,<sup>418</sup> molecular resists might also have a disadvantage because they generally have only a few protecting groups, which means completely soluble and insoluble molecules could be locally mixed together that might lead to worse LER. Polymer resists generally require multiple deprotection events per molecule, so the local variation in molecule solubility is potentially less.
--[p52]-- shown that not only does decreasing the distribution of the number of protecting groups on a molecule improves LER, but also controlling the absolute position to create monodisperse resists can improve LER even further.<sup>411e413</sup>
Molecular resists also provide a potential way to increase the understanding of the structureeproperty relations in resists.
--[p49]-- There have been molecular resists made based on a large number of different types of core molecules such as polyphenols,<sup>324e334</sup> cyclic molecules such as calixarenes<sup>176,310,311,335e354</sup> and Noria-type molecules,<sup>355e361</sup> starshaped molecules, 322,362e371 fullerenes and other fused polyaromatic compounds,<sup>251,254,372e393</sup> dendrimers,<sup>394e398</sup> cycloaliphatic groups such as cholates or cyclodextrin,<sup>397,399</sup> and even PAG type cores .<sup>180,243,408e410</sup> Some examples of molecular resists with different cores are shown in Fig. 17.
--[p55]-- While there are still some questions regarding the imaging mechanism, it appears that the photoacid sulfonic acid can displace the methacrylic acid ligand which causes a solubility change in developer leading to a negative-tone pattern.<sup>438,439</sup> This type of resist has shown resolution of 26 nm with a very high sensitivity of 4.2 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>.
--[p54]-- One major concern is that metal contamination of the semiconductor device could be catastrophic.<sup>426</sup> Purification of other metals from the metal of interest is expected to be difficult as well.<sup>427</sup> There is also the concern that some metals cannot be easily etched or stripped back off of the wafer after patterning.
One of the most highly investigated inorganic resists is HSQ.

--[p367]-- Hence, in these environments, water or oxygen must be involved in film modification.
The role of water in the exposure mechanism is not the only thing unclear in the mechanism. Exposure dose has been found to depend both on area exposed (not related to backscattering effects) and the sequence of the pattern write.<sup>16,37,43</sup> That is, the exposure of one area can sensitize an adjacent area.
--[p367]-- In fact, the same group previously observed<sup>37</sup> that exposed areas of films will react and expand when sitting in air, suggesting absorption of ambient $_ { \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } }$ or ${ \bf O } _ { 2 }$ by the film with time.
Water definitely diffuses in HSQ as noted by Ryan et al.<sup>38</sup> and Zhao et al.<sup>39</sup> who studied water uptake in HSQ films for low-k applications.
--[p367]-- They baked HSQ films above $3 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and exposed them to 100% humidity. A quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) was used to measure water uptake. The studies show variable water uptake between 0.4 and 2.2 weight percent with a water diffusion constant of $3 . 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 0 }$ cm/s.
--[p367]-- The water content before moisture exposure is not known, but generally, water is not identified in FTIR measurement for films baked under similar conditions.<sup>40,41</sup> At the very least, these studies show that HSQ is permeable to water.
Furthermore, in exposure tools with a low or no vacuum environment, there are indications that water and hydroxyls play a role in the exposure mechanism.
--[p367]-- Caster et al.<sup>42</sup> studied HSQ using near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy before and after 580-eV X-ray exposure (2.14 nm). They saw an increase in the oxygen content of the film after exposure. Vacuum levels were 0.2 Torr, a level where considerable water will exist at the film surface. Furthermore, after 157-nm exposure in various ambient conditions, Bloomstein et al.<sup>8</sup> found an increase of the SieOH peaks via FTIR.

===== [p386-387] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.2 SURVEY OF SIMPLE METAL COMPLEXES (4块) =====
--[p386]-- 11.2 SURVEY OF SIMPLE METAL COMPLEXES
To better understand the challenges faced by MORE, a large survey of simple metal complexes was tested. There are very few literature examples of films made by spincoating inorganic or organometallic molecules and no examples of EUV sensitivity. The work on MORE was started by performing a survey of simple metal complexes with the goal of answering the following questions:
• Will inorganic and organometallic compounds form high-quality, amorphous films?
--[p387]-- It is likely the poor sensitivities observed can be attributed to good ligand stability. To improve the sensitivities of MORE compounds, not only do photons need to be absorbed, but the ligands must be designed to undergo photolytic decomposition.
--[p386]-- • Will thin metal-containing films of MORE compounds be air stable?
• Will ligand decomposition in MORE films cause significant outgassing?
A large series of simple inorganic complexes were purchased or synthesized (i.e., transition metal diketonates, zinc carboxylates, and metal halides) and tested as EUV resists.
--[p387]-- Although many of the tested materials formed poor-quality films due to crystallization, precipitation, and nonwetting of the wafer, some of the materials formed good-quality, air-stable, amorphous films. The materials that formed goodquality films were tested using the XIL-II EUV interference lithography tool at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland and were found to have little outgassing but also poor sensitivities.

--[p293]-- This type of additive could be considered a photodecomposable nucleophile (PDN) because it is a nucleophile in the unexposed state but is “decomposed” to form nonquenching species under irradiation.

--[p475]-- High-resolution patterning of inorganic metal compounds was first demonstrated nearly 40 years ago with the creation of 5-nm holes in a film of NaCl.<sup>62</sup> While the patterned structures were not sufficiently robust for pattern transfer, smaller and more robust structures were created using various metal-b-alumina crystals.<sup>63</sup> A series of metal based resists capable of very high electron beam resolutions soon followed, including metal halides and metal oxides as reviewed by Saifullah. 64 By varying the exposure and processing conditions both positive- and negative-tone resists were realized, including in some cases the ability to write a pattern containing pure metal after exposure.

===== [p454-455] Alternative resist approaches > 13.1 INTRODUCTION (9块) =====
--[p455]-- As integrated circuit feature sizes continued to shrink in line with Moore’s Law,<sup>2</sup> it was recognized that shorter wavelengths of light would be required to meet future resolution requirements, as discussed in Chapter 1, leading to the development of deep ultraviolet (DUV) illumination lithography, initially with the rather dim mercury discharge lamp (254 nm) and subsequently using KrF excimer laser (248 nm)ebased tools, first prototyped at IBM by Jain et al.<sup>3</sup> However, at DUV wavelengths, the DNQ/novolac system was found to be excessively absorbing, preventing even exposure through the full thickness of the resist film, and leading to imaging problems such as sloped sidewall profiles.<sup>3</sup>
--[p455]-- Earlier chapters in this book have dealt with “traditional” polymer approaches to extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, together with molecular glass alternatives, and work in inorganic resists and organometallic complexes. In this chapter we review a wide range of alternative approaches to EUV-resist design.
--[p455]-- This led to the development in 1982 of the chemical amplification concept by Ito et al.<sup>6,7</sup> Here a single photon causes a photochemical reaction that releases an active species. Commonly it is a photoacid generator (PAG), which absorbs a photon and then forms an acid as the active species. The acid can then catalytically induce multiple reactions within the resist film both during exposure and upon postexposure heating.
--[p454]-- Early resists, supporting g-line (436 nm) and i-line (365 nm) ultraviolet (UV) exposure sources, derived from systems developed primarily by the reprographics industry, as discussed in a detailed review by Willson et al.<sup>1</sup> One of the first successful materials, which supported the nascent semiconductor industry for 15 years from 1957, was the Kodak Thin Film Resist.
--[p454]-- In these early systems the quantum yield, or number of reactions per photon, was at most one and more commonly in the range of 0.2e0.3. This meant that in practice several photons were typically required for each reaction, and thus the dose required to pattern the resists was generally high.
--[p455]-- While more transparent polymers, such as poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA)dlong used as an electron beam resist<sup>4</sup>ddemonstrated good sidewall control in DUV,<sup>5</sup> the low power of available sources required a significant increase in the resist sensitivity to meet industrial throughput requirements. Even improving quantum yields to the theoretical maximum of 1 (i.e., one reaction per photon) for the existing systems was insufficient.
--[p455]-- Such materials achieve orders of magnitude increases in sensitivity and have dominated semiconductor photolithography to the current day, as extensively reviewed by Ito.<sup>8</sup>
To date most resists have been based on organic polymers. However, the challenge of meeting the semiconductor industry’s miniaturization roadmap, discussed in the next section, is leading to increasingly adventurous approaches to resist development.
--[p454]-- 13.1 INTRODUCTION
The development of new photoresist systems has historically been driven by the performance requirements of the semiconductor industry.
--[p454]-- This negative-tone formulation contained a cyclized poly(cis-isoprene) together with a bis-azide that undergoes photolysis on exposure to UV light, crosslinking the polymer and rendering exposed areas insoluble in organic solvents. As resolution requirements increased beyond the capabilities of KTFR (minimum feature size w2 mm) the industry moved to positive-tone systems utilizing a base soluble resin novolac, combined with the photodecomposable dissolution inhibitor diazonaphthoquinone (DNQ).

===== [p358-358] Mainstreaming inorganic metal-oxide resists for high-resolution lithography > 10.1 METAL-OXIDE RESISTS (7块) =====
--[p358]-- For instance, electron-beam (e-beam) patterning produced 7-nm lines at 17-nm pitch in aluminum fluoride,<sup>2</sup> but the required dose exceeded that for HSQ by 1000.<sup>3</sup> Such doses are impractical for most uses.
Since Namatsu’s work, there has been a growing interest in inorganic resists. Like any resist, performance is evaluated by resolution, sensitivity, line-edge roughness, and etch resistance. There are several specific areas where inorganics are beneficial:
1.
--[p358]-- This encompasses reactions during deposition, bake, exposure, and development. By organizing this information, we hope this snapshot enable researchers to realize the full patterning potential of metal-oxide photoresists.
--[p358]-- HSQ and HafSOx are oxo-hydroxo nanoclusters and members of the growing class of inorganic materials known as metal-oxide resists. In lithography, these radiation-sensitive materials produce substantially metal-oxide patterned structures. Oxo-hydroxo nanoclusters present opportunities to circumvent limitations of conventional polymer resists and enable enhanced high-resolution patterning.
--[p358]-- Highly absorbing materials are needed for extreme ultra-violet (EUV) lithography are beneficial inorganic elements have significantly higher photoelectron absorption cross-sections than organics.<sup>4</sup> This increases sensitivity,<sup>5</sup> enables the use of thin layers that are less susceptible to pattern collapse, and thereby allows higher resolution.
2. Better pattern transfer: under most conditions, inorganics have higher dryetching resistance than organics.
--[p358]-- 10.1 METAL-OXIDE RESISTS
In 1998, Namatsu et al.<sup>1</sup> reported a breakthrough for inorganic resist materials; he showed hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) could be patterned with both high resolution and sensitivity. Previously, high resolution patterning of inorganic resists always required high exposure doses.
--[p358]-- In addition, they have uniquely demonstrated the necessary combination of resolution, line-edge roughness, and sensitivity to broadly support nanoscale research and commercialization.
The following discussion provides a historical perspective of oxo-hydroxo nanocluster systems HSQ, HafSOx, and related materials. We focus the current state of understanding surrounding their chemical reactions during lithographic processing.
--[p358]-- Consequently, resist patterns are more effectively transferred to diverse underlying materials.
3. Higher resolution: in lithographies where secondary electrons are generated, for example, EUV, e-beam and helium-ion beam, lateral energy deposition from the secondary electrons increases exposure width and decreases resolution. High Z inorganics reduce lateral energy deposition and enhance resolution.<sup>6</sup>

--[p135]-- 3.3.2 SPATIAL RESOLUTION
What determines the spatial resolution in topedown lithography, and how do we obtain control over it? The spatial resolution of EUV lithography, EBL, and FEBIP has progressed to the sub-10-nm regime. The first parameter determining the spatial resolution is of course the area illuminated by the primary irradiation; a smaller illuminated area simply means a higher spatial resolution.

As we have seen, the dissociation of precursors such as $\mathbf { M e C p P t M e } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { P t } ( \mathrm { P F } _ { 3 } ) _ { 4 }$ is dominated by DEA occurring near $0 \mathrm { e V } .$ Similarly, Cl- abstraction from $\mathrm { C C l } _ { 4 }$ $1 0 ^ { - 1 4 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ , also near 0 eV.

===== [p376-378] Mainstreaming inorganic metal-oxide resists for high-resolution lithography > 10.3.5 ADVANCES OF LITHOGRAPHIC RESOLUTION IN HIGH-Z METAL-OXIDE RESISTS (16块) =====
--[p377]-- Soon after Ekinci et al.<sup>74</sup> reported 8-nm resolution results at the same synchrotron beamline, and Peeters et al.<sup>75</sup> demonstrated 13-nm half-pitch performance on the ASML NXE:3300B EUV exposure system.
Thrun et al.<sup>76</sup> reported 22-nm SRAM features imaged by a variable-shaped e-beam direct writer.
--[p376]-- In parallel, research continued on mechanistic understanding within the newly funded NSF Center for Sustainable Materials Chemistry. This mechanistic work is detailed in the previous sections.
Continuing HafSOx e-beam studies, Telecky et al.
--[p377]-- Pollentier et al.<sup>65</sup> quantified ${ \bf O } _ { 2 }$ and $_ { \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } }$ outgassing, demonstrating HafSOx gas evolution removed organic material from the witness plate.
In 2012, Ekinci et al.<sup>73</sup> reported 11-nm half-pitch line-space HafSOx patterns by using EUV interference lithography.
--[p377]-- In 2010, Stowers, Telecky, and Grenville described initial EUV HafSOx patterning results at the International Symposium on Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography.<sup>70</sup> Collaborating with Patrick Nalleau and Chris Anderson, <16-nm resolution at $7 1 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ was realized with the LBNL Microexposure Tool,<sup>71</sup> and Roel Gronheid patterned 32-nm half-pitch contact holes with the ASML-IMEC Alpha Demo Tool.<sup>70</sup> These results further supported that the high-Z oxocluster had the advantages of high EUV absorbance even in thin inorganic resists. Such high absorbance, mitigates EUV photon-noise effects.<sup>5</sup> In addition, these thin resists did not exhibit capillary force induced patterned resist collapse prevalent in organic systems.
--[p377]-- In 2011, Stowers et al.<sup>72</sup> reported HafSOx formulation and process improvements to lower EUV dose and to produce 12-nm half-pitch lines with e-beam exposure. Coating uniformity was demonstrated on 300-mm wafers, defectivity was shown to be equivalent to a water film, etch rate was measured to be $> 2 8 4$ higher than HSQ with an $\mathrm { S F } _ { 6 }$ plasma, and a resist-strip process was developed for rework.
--[p378]-- EUV absorption coefficients near 20 $\mu \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 }$ and 40:1 etch selectivity relative to a typical carbon underlayer enabled the use of ultra-thin resist layers.
In 2016, DeSimone et al.<sup>79</sup> described the first integrated patterning process incorporating a negative-tone metal-oxide EUV resist to fabricate next-generation high-resolution devices.
--[p376]-- reported 18-nm half-pitch features written at $2 4 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ (30 keV) with line-width roughness as small as 1.6 nm.<sup>69</sup> Also, 193-nm optical interference lithography with ZircSOx produced 60-nm half-pitch lines at $2 5 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ .
--[p377]-- They also quantified resist exposure dose in terms of solution shelf life and post-coat delays.<sup>77</sup> Results confirmed exposure dose varied with these items confirming Inpria reproducibility observations. This variability has been attributed to HafSOx’s hygroscopic nature and the effects of humidity on changing its water content.
--[p376]-- 10.3.5 ADVANCES OF LITHOGRAPHIC RESOLUTION IN HIGH-Z METAL-OXIDE RESISTS
As mentioned in Section 10.3, development of high-Z resists was a deliberate attempt to take advantage of the atomic smoothness of oxo-hydroxide films investigated for printed electronics.
--[p376]-- HafSOx and ZircSOx were also found to be $9 \times$ and $7 \times$ more resistant than $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ to $\mathrm { C H F } _ { 3 }$ plasma etching, respectively, demonstrating their potential as directly patterned hardmasks.
In 2009, recognizing the material’s significant potential, Keszler and Andrew Grenville, Inpria Corp., CEO, received funding via an NSF small business innovation grant to support commercialization.
--[p376]-- In addition, as already mentioned, the peroxide acts as a radiation-sensitive ligand.<sup>67</sup> Initial 30-keV e-beam exposures proved noteworthye exposure doses for dissolution rate contrast were orders of magnitude lower than HSQ and other inorganic resists and isolated 15-nm lines were readily printed.<sup>68</sup> Working with Jeff Byers at Sematech Austin, Stowers and Anderson also demonstrated deep UV HafSOx patterning by using a 193-nm interference Amphibian tool.
--[p376]-- Both these lithographic results were important because the sensitivity was in a range that meant the high resolution and sensitivity necessary for commercial applications should be accessible. Stowers, working with
Olynick and Scott Dhuey the Molecular Foundry, subsequently demonstrated the high-etch resistance of the thin-patterned oxide by deep-etching Si with a Boschtype $\mathrm { C H F _ { 3 } / C H _ { 4 } { - } S F _ { 6 } / A r }$ plasma (Fig. 11).
--[p378]-- In this work, Inpria tin-oxide materials were integrated into IMEC’s 7-nm back end of line process as a block mask layer to pattern metal pillars as small as 21 nm. Resist exposure sensitivity was also reduced below 20 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>.
--[p378]-- Because the Inpria team first recognized the HafSOx sensitivity plateau and instability issues, they redirected their efforts to develop an improved EUV resist platform under Stephen Meyer’s leadership. This platform was based on new tin oxo-hydroxides. In 2015, Grenville et al.<sup>78</sup> described new, directly patterned tinoxide materials for high-resolution EUV lithography. Formulations produced 13-nm half-pitch features at 35 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> on ASML’s NXE:3300B scanner.
--[p376]-- Resist work began when Jason Stowers, a Keszler graduate student (who had worked with Brian Rice, Jeanette Roberts, Eric Panning, and Robert Bristol in the Intel EUV lithography group before graduate work at Oregon State University) brought both EUVexperience and chemistry know-how to advance the work. Collaborating with Jeremy Anderson, Stowers identified peroxide as a ligand that would bind to the HafSOx and ZircSOx clusters (Fig.
9), thereby improving their dielectric film performance and stabilizing them to background condensation reactions.
--[p378]-- The tin-based resists have also played roles in SHARP to advance EUV mask technologies<sup>80</sup> and in EUV interference lithography mask development to advance resolution.<sup>81</sup> Current and improved performance of these tin-based materials, which originated from research in HafSOx and continues to be informed by HafSOx fundamental studies, is very promising for the future success of EUV lithography.
