===== [p387-388] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.3 BISMUTH COMPOUNDS (5块) =====
--[p387]-- These approaches leverage the free-radical stability and acid cleavability of bismuthphenyl bonds. The two approaches for designing bismuth compounds as candidates for MORE through the exploration and synthesis of organobismuth oligomers are presented here.<sup>10</sup>
Approach 1: Scission of phenyl-bismuth bonds with acid.
--[p387]-- 11.3 BISMUTH COMPOUNDS
Bismuth is the largest nonradioactive element and forms highly dense oxides. Along with a high EUV OD and low-cost, nontoxic starting materials, bismuth compounds are excellent candidates for MORE. Although the literature on bismuth chemistry is well populated, the photochemistry literature on bismuth is not, and so two approaches were developed to create photosensitive bismuth resists.
--[p388]-- When triphenyl bismuth is treated with three equivalents of triflic acid, bismuth triflate, and benzene are formed.<sup>11,12</sup> Triphenyl bismuth is organic soluble, and bismuth triflate is water soluble.<sup>12</sup> By generating photoacids in a film containing a triphenyl bismuth compound, it is conceivable that the reaction of the photogenerated acid would cleave the bismuth-phenyl bonds and result in a change in the exposed region solubility.
--[p388]-- Approach 1 utilizes these properties by blending bismuth-phenyl oligomers with a photoacid generator (PAG).
Approach 2: Photolytic decarboxylation of bismuth carboxylates. Metal carboxylates have established photochemistry and are known to undergo photolytic decarboxylation reactions. It is possible this decarboxylation could result in the shift in solubility needed to generate contrast.
--[p388]-- Compounds of the type $\mathrm { B i P h } _ { 3 } \mathrm { X } _ { 2 }$ where X Cl and OOCeR are known in the literature and give a pathway for integrating carboxylate functionality into bismuth systems. Preliminary testing with these monometallic compounds, however, resulted in poor dissolution contrast. This poor contrast is likely due to the extremely high solubility of these monometallic compounds in organic solvents.
Approach 2 utilizes these carboxylate functionalities in much less soluble oligomeric bismuth-phenyl systems.

===== [p198-199] EUV lithography patterning challenges > 5 3 3 RLS PROGRESS (5块) =====
--[p198]-- 5 3 3 RLS PROGRESS
Described in Chapter 4 is the concept of the RLS (resolution/LER/sensitivity) tradeoff, which states that, in general, improving one of these properties tends to negatively impact another property. Fig. 10 is an example of this for sensitivity and LER. Fig. 11, on the other hand, shows that we have had a steady improvement in resolution over time, so the natural question arises as to whether or not this has come with some tradeoff in another parameter.
--[p199]-- We note that the Z-factor is most conveniently used when normalized against the target performance. In this form, it is known as the nano-Z-factor,<sup>29</sup> which serves as a convenient metric for tracking progress in resist performance.
Fig. 12 shows a plot of the nano-Z-factor for CA EUV resists from 2010 through 2015.
--[p199]-- The nano-Z-factor is computed relative to the 2019 requirements for 17-nm half-pitch as published in the 2013 edition of the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS).<sup>30</sup> The ITRS calls for a resist sensitivity of 15 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> and a line-width roughness of 1.4 nm, yielding a reference Z-factor of 1.44  10<sup>9</sup> mJ nm<sup>3</sup>.
The data show that the best CA resist is approximately 5 away from the target in terms of the nano-Z-factor.
--[p198]-- Arguably, the best way to quantify the RLS tradeoff is through the concept of a single metric referred to as the Z-factor,<sup>27</sup> which is derived from the analytic description of the stochastic photon-limited performance of a resist in terms of resist diffusion and absorbed photon count.<sup>28</sup> The Z-factor is defined as
$$
Z \propto R ^ { 3 } L ^ { 2 } S\tag{3}
$$
where R represents the resolution, L the LWR, and S the sensitivity.
--[p199]-- The shortfall is due almost exclusive to the LWR performance. We note that, for NCA materials, the best nano-Z-factor achieved has been 4.2 (the 2011 material in Fig. 11), with the shortfall here being mostly due to the poor sensitivity.

===== [p207-209] The chemistry and application of nonchemically amplified (non-CA) chain-scission resists > SCHEME 1 (20块) =====
--[p209]-- The incorporation of the styrenic monomer imparts superior dry etch resistance compared with the acrylic homopolymer and increases the glass transition temperature.<sup>48</sup> In addition, it is known that polymers of a-methylstyrene undergo chain scission,<sup>50,51</sup> and this property was thought to enhance the scission yield of the copolymer.
--[p208]-- Indeed Lai and Shrawagi<sup>41</sup> state that during e-beam exposure above $6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ cross-linking becomes the dominant reaction.
These observations led Tada<sup>42,43</sup> to prepare acrylates halogenated at the alphacarbon and at the ester side chain.
--[p208]-- More recently, the group of Willson<sup>44</sup> prepared a series of polyacrylates functionalized with ${ \mathfrak { a } } { \mathrm { - C F } } _ { 3 }$ and/or 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl ester substituents and measured their response to highenergy <sup>60</sup>Co gamma photons. Increases in sensitivity were the modest, with
G-values for scission ranging from 1.3 to 3.2, compared with G(S) 1.4 for PMMA.
--[p207]-- SCHEME 1
The mechanism of degradation of poly(methyl methacrylate) by high-energy radiation. Interaction with high-energy photons leads to formation of excited cations and ejection of secondary electrons. The radical cations degrade primarily by cleavage of side chain bonds and subsequent formation of main chain radicals at the a-methyl group. These macroradicals readily undergo b-scission to form terminal vinyl groups and (de-)propagation radicals. Heating leads to extensive depolymerization.
--[p209]-- Reichmanis et al.<sup>34</sup> confirmed prior to this that incorporation of 14 mol% of MCN into copolymers of MMA and OM resulted in up to an order of magnitude increase in sensitivity. Pittman et al.<sup>47</sup> reported similar yields of chain scission in copolymers of MCN and a-trifluoromethylacrylate.
--[p208]-- studied the X-ray sensitivity of a range of analogs of FBM in which the methylene unit adjacent to the ester linkage was modified with substituents, and reported clearance doses from 46 to 80 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>, compared with 2400 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> for PMMA. The increased sensitivity compared with PMMA is a result of the electron withdrawing nature of the fluorinated side-chain and the subsequent activation of the ester CeO bond to degradation.
--[p208]-- In these studies and many others, researchers recognized that sensitivity of the resist to incident photons could be enhanced by incorporation of comonomers or by use of more radiation-sensitive monomeric units. For example, Reichmanis et al.<sup>34e36</sup> studied the incorporation of low molar percentages of the comonomer 3-oximino-2-butanone methacrylate (OM) into PMMA.
--[p208]-- The sensitivity to deep ultraviolet (UV) exposure increased by a factor of around five compared with PMMA on addition of the highly absorbing monomer at levels of 3e9 mol%. However, the cross section to X-rays of these copolymers was not significantly increased compared with PMMA.
--[p208]-- Unfortunately, these polymers have low glass temperatures.
Substitution at the alpha-position of polyacrylates is another route to enhanced sensitivity to absorbed photons.
--[p208]-- In a related study,<sup>36</sup> the authors examined the effect of added sensitizers including 4-t-butylbenzoic acid, which provided a further 2.5 times increase in sensitivity over the pure copolymer with 6 mol% of OM to broad-band illumination from a Hg lamp and around nine times improvement on irradiation with monochromatic 240-nm light.
--[p208]-- In a systematic study, Yoshiaki et al.<sup>37</sup> reported that for nonhalogenated methacrylates the sensitivity to monochromatic UV light mirrored as expected the absorption spectrum and those small differences in sensitivity arose from differences in extinction coefficients. However, they found that the sensitivity of poly(hexafluorobutyl methacrylate) (FBM) is around seven times higher than for PMMA (20 mJ/ cm<sup>2</sup> at 20 kV). At around this time, Kakuchi et al.
--[p208]-- For example, Helbert et al.<sup>38,39</sup> studied the effects of high-energy gamma photons on the structure of poly(methyl a-chloroacrylate) of copolymers of this monomer.<sup>40</sup> The presence of the chlorine leads to dissociative electron capture at the CeCl bond, and consequently, yields of chain scission are 4e5 times higher than for PMMA (G(S) w7).
--[p208]-- Homopolymers and copolymers of trifluoroethyl <sub>a</sub>-chloroacrylate had sensitivities under e-beam exposure 70e250 greater than $\mathrm { P M M A } ^ { 4 3 }$ and did not switch tone at higher doses. Copolymers with methyl and phenyl methacrylate and methacrylic acid had similar sensitivity to the homopolymer but displayed superior thermal and adhesive properties.
--[p209]-- A widely used positive-tone resist introduced in the early 1990s by Zeon are the so-called ZEP resists.<sup>48,49</sup> The commercially available ZEP520A is a 1:1 copolymer of methyl a-chloroacrylate and a-methylstyrene, although its structure has not been fully described in the open literature.
--[p209]-- of the 2-hydroxyethyl side chains. The hydrophilic nature of the polymer leads to considerable problems during development arising from swelling, especially for high-resolution patterning, and both teams of researchers propose the incorporation of hydrophobic comonomers.
--[p208]-- However, measurement of the evolution of molar mass on irradiation revealed that the polymer also undergoes cross-linking reactions, with a radiochemical yield G(X) of close to 0.7. At higher doses (>10 kGy), the yields of both scission and cross-linking both decrease but cross-linking becomes relatively more important.
--[p209]-- Finally, the lithographic performance of the well-known biomaterials, poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (PHEMA), has been reported by Aviram et al.<sup>52</sup> and later by Vasilopoulou et al.<sup>53</sup> Both sets of researchers agree that the sensitivity to UV and electrons of PHEMA is significantly higher than for PMMA; however, they offer different proposals for the mechanism of degradation $\mathrm { ( E _ { 0 } } \sim 7 5 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ at w190 nm and 1 $\mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ at 10 kV).<sup>52</sup> Vasilopoulou et al.<sup>53</sup> proffered a mechanism consistent with loss of the ester side chain and subsequent b-scission, while Aviram et al.<sup>52</sup> suggest formation of methacrylic acid monomeric units by selective scission

20 $\mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ at 25 kV.
--[p209]-- The nitrile group is involved in the primary events on radiolysis as confirmed by the careful experiments by Dong et al.,<sup>46</sup> who identified from low-temperature electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy measurements the imide-radical precursor to the degradation products. The overall G-values for radical formation were reported by these authors to be 2.2 and 2.8 at 77K and 298K, respectively.
--[p209]-- The replacement of the chlorine with trifluoromethyl in the alpha-position reduced the yield of cross-linking to negligible amounts.
It is well known that polymers of methacrylonitrile (MCN) undergo chain scission on irradiation. The stable free radicals at room temperature arise from chain scission,<sup>45,46</sup> consistent with this observation.

===== [p56-57] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.6.1 EXPOSURE STATISTICS AND SHOT NOISE (12块) =====
--[p56]-- The low dose requirement is further worsened because the high energy of the EUV photon means that incident photon count is low and approaching shot noise levels and limits. For example, there are approximately 10 photons/nm<sup>2</sup> at EUV for a dose of 15 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>, while there are 146 photons/nm<sup>2</sup> at the equivalent dose at 193 nm.
--[p56]-- Another way of thinking about this is that the discrete nature of the photon limits the amount of information that one can transmit to the resist to enact a pattern. As the dose decreases, there will eventually be insufficient information received by the resist or too large of a variation in the information locally to properly pattern. There are many other studies and reviews that discuss the issue of shot noise and photon statistics in further detail.<sup>445e454</sup>
--[p57]-- This variation in the local concentration can potentially contribute to LER or failed patterning. This issue is made worse by the fact that many PAGs have a tendency to segregate and aggregate within the film.<sup>455,456</sup> Even low levels of aggregation will greatly increase the local variation in PAG concentration which could lead to worse LER and will negatively affect ultimate resolution capability.<sup>157,457,458</sup>
--[p56]-- Given the relatively high source power for many 193-nm tools, sensitivity can be slightly sacrificed for the goal of improving LER with minimal penalty to throughput. Unfortunately, EUV exposure has different restrictions and physics.
Two issues associated with EUV patterning have synergistic negative effects.
--[p57]-- This effectively determines the volume that the acid must deprotect to create a connected network of deprotection for development. The desired feature size is rapidly approaching the distance between photoacids. Increasing the PAG loading to 30 wt% can improve the photoacid distance to around 2e3 nm. The relative sparseness of photoacids and PAGs exasperates the statistics issue because it leads to higher standard deviation in the local average.
--[p56]-- Even with an ideal resist with high absorbance, this low numbers of photons issue could potentially limit absolute resolution and LER in the resist for EUV exposures at low dose, regardless if the tool itself has higher resolution. The other concern is not just absolute resolution but CD uniformity from line to line, which could be significantly affected by the high local variability in photons.
--[p56]-- 1.6.1 EXPOSURE STATISTICS AND SHOT NOISE
Since the single exposure resolution limit for 193-nm lithography has been reached several generations ago, the continued development of resists has focused on further refinement and expanding the process window rather than a strong push to improve resist intrinsic resolution.
--[p56]-- This would occur simply because of the statistical variation in photons, and modifying the resist would have little effect unless its absorbance were greatly increased (which can only be done by changing the atoms in the resist) or the photoacid generation efficiency were greatly improved.
--[p56]-- Because source power is so low and overall reflectivity of the EUV optics relatively low, resist sensitivity needs to be on the order of 10e15 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> to even begin to approach the required wafer throughput that would make EUV economical (see Chapter 5 for more details). This upper limit on sensitivity can greatly restrict resist design.
--[p56]-- Work has been carried out on optimizing 193-nm deprotection-based resists for use in negative-tone imaging in solvent development due to the potential for improved imaging due to the better image contrast using a light field mask.<sup>196e19</sup> <sup>8</sup> Since resist resolution is already at the tool limit, direct resist formulation and modification has often been focused on improving LER and LWR for these resists.
--[p57]-- It is not just the inhomogeneity of the photons that is a concern for exposure statistics, but also the inhomogeneity of the resist components such as PAG and protecting groups. For example, at 10 wt% PAG loading, the average distance between PAGs would be around 2e3 nm. At 15 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> dose, average distance between photoacids could be 2.5e4 nm depending on Dill C for the PAG.
--[p56]-- If only 30e50% of the incident EUV photons are absorbed throughout the thickness of the resist (typically 20e40 nm at EUV), this could lead to very sparse spatial distribution of photoacid that could cause poor LER.

--[p3]-- Marcus Kaestner

===== [p285-288] Negative-tone organic molecular resists > 8.7.5 METHODS OF CONTROLLING CATIONIC POLYMERIZATION AND/OR CROSS-LINKING (18块) =====
--[p286]-- In conventional polymeric resists based on acid-catalyzed deprotection, addition of base quencher and changing the diffusion length of the photoacid have been successfully used to control limit the spatial propagation of deprotection and thereby improve the resolution of the resists. Extensions of this approach to new platforms are successful only when the active species is a photoacid, so changing the intrinsic chemistry of the resist means new control methods must be developed.
--[p286]-- Epoxide functionalized, and other cationic polymerization, resists typically operate by photoacid initiated cross-linking in a negative-tone mode. Generally, the most important reaction that occurs is epoxide homopolymerization, as shown in Fig. 60. The photoacid (HX) first protonates the epoxide.
--[p287]-- This occurs because the oxonium is covalently attached to the chains and networks that form, so its mobility significantly drops as these chains get very large. Despite this drop in mobility, resolution will ultimately be limited because the spatial extent of propagation before significant slowing in the rate of cross-linking may be large relative to many desired features.
--[p288]-- 60 suggests that base might be very weakly effective or even ineffective because the photoacid is only short lived until it forms an oxonium. To investigate the effect of base,<sup>104</sup> different amounts of the commonly used base trioctylamine (TOA) were added to 4-Ep and the contrast curves are shown in Fig. 63. Base had little effect on contrast behavior even up to high loadings of base (up to equimolar with PAG), especially at the most important low dose region.
--[p288]-- A similar result was seen for five base quenchers tested<sup>30</sup> in a fullerene-epoxy system as discussed in Section 8.2.

--[p288]-- Conventional resists would show significant change in sensitivity and many would not even pattern at base loadings this high. In these epoxide and other cationic systems, the molar ratio of reactive groups to base can be 10e100: 1 so it would be statistically difficult for the photoacid to encounter a base before it reacts with an epoxide or other group to form the oxonium which appears to have minimal sensitivity to base.
--[p287]-- Groups that can act in this way are acidic groups such as phenols, alcohols, and carboxylic acids. These groups often

increase the glass transition temperature of the resists, which helps reduce the mobility of the oxonium. Additionally they introduce a new reaction pathway, which modifies the overall kinetics of the cross-linking.
--[p287]-- In addition to a limit in ultimate resolution, many of these types of materials with no additional reactive groups will show nonideal contrast behavior because the cross-linking reaction is so efficient. An example of this type of contrast behavior is shown in Fig. 61 for the resist 4-Ep with 5 mol% triphenylsulfonium hexafluoroantimonate (TPS-SbF ) as PAG.
--[p287]-- Finally, the polymerization occurs by repeated reaction between epoxides and the oxonium, which moves as the polymer grows.
Many molecular resists containing only epoxide reactive groups will actually show good resolution with no additional control methods because the intrinsic slowing down of the polymerization rate as the network grows.
--[p286]-- This step is more formally an equilibrium, although it lies far to the right-hand side for epoxides (other cationically polymerizable groups, such as oxetanes discussed in Section 8.7.3, are more balanced in the forward and backward rates, which reduces the effective initiation rate). The second step in the process is the reaction between an epoxide and the protonated epoxide from the first step; this step can be treated as an initiation step.
--[p287]-- This might explain why LER is so much worse for 4-Ep in EUV exposure (8e 9 nm; see Fig. 61) compared to e-beam exposure (shown in Fig. 57 and discussed in Section 8.7.4) because e-beam exposure will likely have better aerial image contrast.
One method of controlling or slowing down the overall rate of cross-linking is through addition of functional groups that introduce a different cross-linking mechanism or modify the overall mobility of the film.
--[p288]-- An alternative approach is exemplified by the xMT resist, discussed in Section 8.8.
Use of acidic groups to control cross-linking is a viable strategy, but it is important to have a more generalized additive that can have a large effect when added in small amounts and doesn’t require any change in the chemical structure of the resist.
--[p286]-- The active species after this step is no longer the photoacid but instead a positively charged oxygen known as an oxonium, which serves as the cationic active center. This change in active group is crucially important because many control methods developed for photoacid diffusion control will not directly transfer to these
Reproduced from Lawson RA, Chun JS, Neisser M, Tolbert LM, Henderson CL. Methods of controlling crosslinking in negative-tone resists. Proc SPIE 2014;9051:90510Q.
materials.
--[p288]-- The reaction is exemplified in Fig. 62 using a phenol group. The oxonium active center can react with the acidic group to stop the growth of that particular chain but because of the available proton the photoacid is regenerated, which can start the growth of a new chain. This reaction can therefore be considered a chain transfer. The new mechanism slows the overall rate of chain growth and cross-linking because the catalytic cycle is not simply a single step but now a multi-step process.
--[p286]-- Although polymerization and cross-linking in negative-tone epoxide-based resists is initiated with a photoacid, the active species is not a photoacid, so new methods of controlling these systems must be developed. This section discusses the imaging mechanism of these types of resists and methods that have been investigated<sup>104</sup> to control the extent of solubility switching.

===== [p103-104] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.1 INTRODUCTION (10块) =====
--[p103]-- This oversimplified model misses important aspects of the photoemission process. The most strongly bound molecular or atomic orbitals that can be excited by EUV X-rays will have the highest relative photoionization probability. This means that the initial photoelectrons will have relatively low kinetic energies, and the molecular ion will be left with a significant amount of residual internal energy.
--[p103]-- Molecular relaxation may generate additional SEs, followed by molecular fragmentation into radicals and radical ions. Relaxation processes are especially important when resist sensitivity is increased by incorporating high EUV cross-section atoms, which typically form strongly bound orbitals.
--[p103]-- The challenge for resist designers will be to develop molecular systems that can harness this simultaneous localized explosion of chemical energy in the form of low energy electrons, radicals, and ions for pattern generation.
It is very difficult to directly investigate the reaction products of EUV radiation chemistry in condensed systems such as thin-film photoresists.
--[p103]-- In discussions of EUVL radiation chemistry, it is often assumed, explicitly or implicitly, that a 92-eV extreme ultraviolet (EUV) photon is absorbed by a resist molecule, ejecting an outer valance electron through photoemission, and leaving behind a stable parent ion with negligible residual internal energy. Since molecular ionization energies are on the order of 10 eV, the secondary electron (SE) will have a kinetic energy (KE) around 80 eV.
--[p103]-- In contrast, reaction products, both SEs and radicals, can be directly observed in gas-phase photoemission experiments on isolated molecules.<sup>4</sup> Modern synchrotron sources have sufficient photon flux at EUV energies to allow coincidence experiments, where simultaneous detection of electrons and ions allows the study of molecular excitation and relaxation with exquisite detail.<sup>5,6</sup>
--[p103]-- Time-resolved transient spectroscopy has not been done due to the lack of femtosecond (fs)-pulsed EUV sources, although efforts are underway in this area, although efforts are underway in this area. Only molecular fragmentation products generated near the surface of a resist film have a chance to escape into the gas phase where they can be detected, and there is no obvious way to distinguish primary and secondary reaction products.
--[p103]-- 2.1 INTRODUCTION
The interaction of ionizing X-ray radiation with molecular resist films in extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUVL)<sup>1</sup> is fundamentally different from the resonant photochemistry of deep ultraviolet lithography, and is different again from interaction of ionizing electron beams with resists in electron beam lithography (EBL).
--[p104]-- The goal of this chapter is to describe EUVexcitation and relaxation processes by drawing on fundamental, theoretical,<sup>7,8</sup> and experimental<sup>9,10</sup> studies of molecular photoemission, electron transport,<sup>3</sup> radiation effects in biological systems,<sup>11</sup> and practical applications of X-ray photoemission spectroscopy (XPS).<sup>12,13</sup> I will also describe experimental<sup>14</sup> and theoretical<sup>15</sup> approaches to understanding fundamental processes in EUVL.
--[p103]-- These fundamental interactions must be understood on the molecular scale to design resist materials that efficiently absorb X-ray energy, and then harness that energy to drive chemical transformations leading to solubility changes and ultimately to pattern transfer.
--[p103]-- In their review of photoresist radiation chemistry, Kozawa and Tagawa<sup>2</sup> stated that “.it is technically nearly impossible to directly observe the reactions induced in ultrathin resist films by 92.5-eV EUV radiation.” The yield and energy distribution of SEs cannot easily be determined, since they undergo a complex chain of multiple elastic and inelastic scattering events before they can be detected, and only SEs generated near the film surface have a reasonable probability of escape.<sup>3</sup> Likewise radicals and radical ions exist only as transient species before undergoing secondary reactions with other components of the resist system.

===== [p481-481] Alternative resist approaches > 13.3 CONCLUSIONS (4块) =====
--[p481]-- It is therefore clear that there remains much potential to be discovered in these new platforms, but also that significant work both on performance optimization and on understanding the interactions of these new resists with existing processes, tools, and materials will be required.
--[p481]-- 13.3 CONCLUSIONS
In order to meet the continued scaling requirements of the semiconductor industry, materials previously thought to be highly controversial, such as metal containing resists, inorganic polymers, and heavily halogenated compounds, are now receiving serious consideration.
--[p481]-- Excellent progress has been seen with many of these materials, but the move away from traditional photoresist materials reintroduces previously solved problems in areas as diverse as solvent compatibility to elucidating the resist mechanism, alongside many others not dealt with here, such as postpatterning rework, resist strip, substrate contamination, and so on. This chapter has introduced several of the more novel approaches to enabling a workable resist to support EUV lithography.
--[p481]-- For materials with relatively little pedigree as photoresists, operating in a radiochemistry regime still to be fully understood and with limited access to EUV photons for exposure, these new approaches have made remarkable progress in a short period, in many cases challenging the performance of highly optimized conventional materials.

ATL, or achromatic spatial frequency multiplication, is another simple yet powerful IL technique with which one can produce high-resolution periodic images.
--[p155]-- ATL benefits from high throughput and great power efficiency as the aerial image is generated using the interference from all transmitted diffraction orders by the use of a broadband EUV source.<sup>8,41</sup> The small spatial coherence illumination requirements needed with this technique allows for the use of sources other than synchrotrons (lasers, discharge-based sources) to produce high-resolution patterning for material characterization or model nanostructure generation.<sup>41</sup>
--[p157]-- l _ { c } \gg 4 p \frac { \lambda } { \Delta \lambda }\tag{7}
$$
where $l _ { c }$ is the transverse coherence length of the beam. If we consider a grating with a 20-nm period and a beam with 4% spectral width, for example, $l _ { c }$ would have to be just over 2 mm. This would typically not be difficult to achieve even with nonsynchrotron EUV sources.<sup>41</sup>
The maximum distance $z _ { m a x }$ (Eq.
--[p158]-- (8)) at which interference is possible depends on the grating field size, period $p ,$ and the illumination wavelength l, where G is the side length of the grating:
$$
\quad z _ { m a x } = G \times { \frac { p } { 2 \lambda } }\tag{8}
$$
For ATL, the distance between the mask and the sample plane should therefore be larger than the achromatic Talbot distance but smaller than the maximum distance.
--[p158]-- Highresolution dot arrays with diameters as small as 15 nm at 100-nm pitch using HSQ have been produced at the XIL-II beamline of the SLS located at the Paul Scherrer Institute with ATL.<sup>8</sup> The XIL-II beamline has an undulator synchrotron source filtered by a pinhole to produce spatially coherent light of tunable wavelength/energy (70e500 eV) and a 4% bandwidth (Dl/l).
--[p158]-- This distance should also not be too large to minimize the side noninterfering fields due to the first-order diffraction. The first-order diffraction has the largest effect over the sample field size. The diffraction angle is calculated by the Bragg equation:
$$
{ \frac { \lambda } { p } } = \sin \theta\tag{9}
$$
Given the diffraction angle, the field size can be calculated from the gap between mask and sample plane, or vice versa:
$$
\tan \theta = { \frac { G - x } { 2 z } }\tag{10}
$$
--[p155]-- With Talbot lithography using a monochromatic light source, Talbot images are produced at exact periodic distances nz<sub>T</sub> (n-integer) from the grating and, therefore, the sample has to be positioned with high accuracy from the mask, limiting the depth of field of the technique. At integer multiples of the Talbot distance, the intensity distribution resembles that of the grating.<sup>41</sup> As can be seen in Fig.

===== [p327-328] Positive molecular resists > 9.1 INTRODUCTION (11块) =====
--[p328]-- In particular, the main motivation for considering small molecules instead of polymers has been the expectation that the line edges of the lithographic structures would have been potentially smoother when smaller size components were used in the lithographic materials (Fig. 1).
--[p327]-- The science underpinning lithographic material evolution has been covered by a number of excellent reviews and introductory presentations ,<sup>1e4</sup> where the different properties that have to be simultaneously met for a mature lithographic material, most commonly known as photoresist or simply resist due to its function in pattern transfer, are presented.
--[p328]-- In addition, proposals for using dendrimers instead of linear polymers as lithographic resist components can be considered as targeting the same direction. 13
Following these proposals, a new direction on lithographic materials development was launched. These new materials, which are based primarily on small organic molecules, are better known as molecular resists to be distinguished from the polymeric resists.
--[p327]-- The basic components of the lithographic materials used in production are even today almost exclusively organic polymers due mainly to their capability of forming uniform amorphous films from solution and the many ways they provide for the change of their solubility following limited chemical changes in the material induced by exposure to irradiation.
--[p327]-- The evolution of the lithographic materials used in semiconductor device manufacturing has been evolved in parallel with the introduction of new exposure equipment and technologies accompanying this new equipment, while further material properties had to be considered to meet the increased performance demands as the dimensions were shrinking.
--[p328]-- In technical terms, the line-edge roughness (LER) or line-width roughness (LWR) reduction has been envisioned as the parameter expected to be an inherent problem when using polymers that would be substantially improved with the use of small organic molecules. The relevant proposition<sup>12</sup> was made by the Shirota group in 2001, a group with long experience in working with amorphous films of small organic molecules known as molecular glasses.
--[p328]-- The proposition of using small organic molecules as possible successors of the polymers as main components of the lithographic materials started to gain attention only when the dimensions of the device features entered the sub-50-nm domain, and concerns that the polymer size could be a limiting factor for creating structures of adequate quality have risen.
--[p328]-- Since the best performing resists in production environment had been traditionallydafter the introduction of novolac-based resistsdthe ones of positive tone, a strong effort was directed to the development of positive molecular resists that could be processed, if possible, in a manner analogous to that of the common positive polymeric resists.
--[p328]-- Nevertheless, a significant effort was also directed toward the development of negative molecular resists, as shown in a number of early report s,<sup>14e16</sup> since it was reasonably expected that typical problems of polymeric resists such as swelling would not be encountered in negative molecular resists. In the present chapter, we will concentrate on the development of positive molecular resists, whereas Chapter 8 is devoted in this volume to the negativetone molecular resists.
--[p327]-- In addition, the rich chemistry that followed the introduction of the chemical amplification approach in the resist film has been presented in a number of reviews usually written by researchers with eminent contribution to the field.<sup>5e8</sup> Finally, more recent reviews covering the whole evolution of the resist materials have been also published in different sources.<sup>9e11</sup>
--[p327]-- 9.1 INTRODUCTION
The evolution of microelectronic technology during the last decades according to the famous Moore’s law has been enabled by the constant improvement of critical technologies including lithographic patterning equipment, processes, and materials capable for the formation of diminishing structures according to strictly defined requirements.

===== [p26-29] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.3.5 OTHER LITHOGRAPHY PROCESSESdION BEAM, SCANNING PROBE, AND NANOIMPRINT (25块) =====
--[p28]-- Even state-of-the-art production tools are expected to cost around one-tenth to one-fifth that of a top 193-nm stepper and provide even bigger savings over the potential costs of EUV tools.<sup>128</sup> It is the highest resolution technique that seems well suited to roll-to-roll printing or printing on curved surfaces.
Step-and-flash tools can have wafer throughput that approaches optical and EUV exposure tools, and it is truly the fastest of the alternative lithography techniques.
--[p28]-- There are also alternatives that combine the two techniques .<sup>120,121</sup> There is a variant of nanoimprint called soft lithography that uses an elastomeric mold to deposit monolayers or “ink” selectively on a surface.<sup>122e124</sup> This soft mold has the advantage of being able to print on uneven, patterned, or nonplanar surface. There have been some studies that have examined electrically or electrochemically transferring the pattern from the mold to substrate.<sup>125,126</sup>
--[p29]-- The mold master templates for nanoimprint are on the other hand exactly the size of the embossed pattern, so it is a much more significant challenge to write the mold master using e-beam lithography because the pattern sizes are much closer to the resolution limit of the e-beam tool. There are currently serious concerns over how many defects might be generated in the master mold due to mold patterning.
--[p29]-- Likewise, if the mold does not cleanly detach from the patterned resist, a defect can be generated. It is also possible to actually delaminate the top layers in a film stack on a wafer if the separation forces for the mold are too high or damage the top layers in the stack if the imprint pressure is too high. Studies have shown that defectivity is lower than expected when using an optimized step-and-flash process,<sup>129</sup> but the defectivity is still nonzero.
--[p27]-- The scanning probes were originally developed to observe physical, chemical, or biological interactions at the nanoscale and some of the more well-known are the scanning tunneling microscope and AFM.<sup>83,84</sup> While there is much variation in tools and methods in other lithographic techniques, scanning probe lithography uses a truly diverse set of methods whereby to modify and pattern the resist and surface.
--[p27]-- Ion beam lithography is a technique that uses focused ion beams to pattern a resist.<sup>12,13</sup> The technique has many similarities to e-beam lithography, but the ions are significantly higher mass than the electrons. As a result, there are many more secondary electrons generated per incident ion than the equivalent incident primary electron in e-beam, which improves throughput.
--[p29]-- Despite the considerable advantages, nanoimprint still has some disadvantages, the biggest of which is defectivity or at least the potential for defectivity. Because the mold directly comes in contact with the resist and substrate, there is a much higher probability of defect generation on both the mold (which will then propagate to further printings) and on the resist. For instance, if the resist does not correctly fill the mold feature, a defect can be generated.
--[p26]-- 1.3.5 OTHER LITHOGRAPHY PROCESSESdION BEAM, SCANNING PROBE, AND NANOIMPRINT
Beyond the most commonly used lithographic techniques discussed earlier, there are many other methods that have been investigated as well such as ion beam lithography, nanoimprint lithography, and scanning probe lithography. These techniques offer certain advantages and disadvantages compared to more conventional lithography.
--[p29]-- Defectivity can be improved by cleaning or replacing the molds after a certain number of patterns. One approach is to create a single master mold, which is then used to create multiple replicates. These replicates can be used to generate the molds actually used in the process and also create the replacement molds. While this improves defectivity, it also greatly increases the cost-of-ownership and the complexity of maintaining the tool.
--[p29]-- In optical lithography and e-beam lithography, absolute resolution is determined by combination of tool exposure conditions, wavelength of exposure, and resist chemistry and response. Nanoimprint is much less sensitive to resist chemistry and its resolution is almost entirely determined by the mold. As a result of these advantages, there are several commercial suppliers for nanoimprint.
--[p28]-- One commonly used method is to heat the resist film above its glass transition temperature and mechanically deform the polymer by the mold followed by cooling below $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ to lock the pattern into the polymer after the mold is removed.<sup>14e16</sup> The other commonly practiced approach is to start with a liquid monomer or polymer that fills the mold upon imprint and then UV-curing the liquid while in contact with the mold to create a solid polymer that remains after the mold is removed.<sup>18</sup> This technique has been named step-and-flash or jet-and-flash nanoimprint.
--[p28]-- In general, it has similar resolution to e-beam, but it is possible to use scanning probe to produce the highest resolution patterning that has yet been obtained by any method, the movement and specific placement of individual atoms .<sup>105,106</sup> (Although atomic resolution is possible, the extremely slow manipulation rates, the narrow process window, and the transformation of such fine manipulations into a usable, stable, and operational device thus far prohibits the breakthrough of atomic manipulation as an industrially applicable lithographic method.<sup>107,108</sup>) Most scanning probe techniques do not suffer from long-range proximity effects as in e-beam because the size scale of the probe limits the proximity size.
--[p29]-- Another challenge is overlay of the mold pattern to the underlying wafer structures, which is more challenging with nanoimprint than for optical as the underlying structures must be identified and the mold aligned and then physically moved to the wafer. Generation of the mold master template is also a nontrivial challenge.
--[p28]-- Nanoimprint has several advantages that make it very promising. It is capable of sub-10-nm resolution,<sup>127</sup> which actually makes it superior to current optical lithography. It is generally of low cost from a tool perspective, especially given its high resolution.
--[p28]-- One alternative lithographic technique that has shown promise for sufficiently high throughput is nanoimprint lithography.<sup>117e119</sup> Nanoimprint creates a pattern by pressing a mold into the resist to replicate the mold pattern. There are many various methods used to transfer the pattern from the mold into the resist or substrate.
--[p27]-- Recent improvements in ion sources and columns have greatly reduced the spot sizes possible, which have allowed for resolutions in helium ion beam lithography comparable to the best demonstrated by e-beam.<sup>79</sup> The advantages and disadvantages of ion beam over conventional optical lithography are similar to e-beam.
--[p27]-- Methods exist to carry out photon-induced changes<sup>95,96</sup> or even selective deposition of ink in dip pen lithography.<sup>97e101</sup> There is similarly a large number of electric fieldebased interactions with the surface, which can be used to pattern a surface.<sup>102e104</sup> These are discussed in Chapter 15.
Scanning probe lithography has its own set of advantages and disadvantages compared to other lithographic techniques.
--[p27]-- In addition to this, ion beam also has the advantage in that is does not suffer from long-range backscattering, so proximity effects are negligible. Heavy ions have a relatively large spot size that prevents comparable resolution to e-beam, but use of light ions such as helium allow much higher resolution.
--[p29]-- Since projection lithography prints a 4 reduction in the mask pattern size onto the wafer, patterning of the mask is generally done at a feature size 4 larger than will be printed. This is usually well away from the resolution limits of the e-beam tool usually used as a mask writer. The larger patterns on the mask also allow for higher sensitivity resists which increase mask throughput.
--[p28]-- The major disadvantage of scanning probe is its very low throughput compared to optical lithography and the difficulty in going up and down in length scales that can be more easily accomplished in e-beam. Much work has been done by attempting to improve throughput with a mix-and-match process<sup>110e112</sup> and multiple tip write arrays.<sup>113e116</sup> More thorough information regarding scanning probe lithography can be found in Chapters 15 and 16.
--[p27]-- It is generally one of the simplest lithography techniques in that it requires no complex optics, exposure sources, or vacuum conditions and the tools can often fit on a table top rather than requiring a dedicated bay or room. It is maskless, so arbitrary patterns can be rapidly created and written.
--[p28]-- It also is generally less damaging to sensitive materials than high energy electron beams.<sup>109</sup> Some scanning probe methods also allow for three-dimensional patterning by controlling the penetration depth of the probe. There is also an alignment and inspection advantage because the scanning probe can often be used to pattern a resist and then immediately image the patterned surface by changing the force, or turning off an applied heater or electric field on the probe.
--[p27]-- Its main disadvantage is low throughput due to the serial nature of patterning, but it can possess a one-to-two orders of magnitude higher sensitivity than e-beam.<sup>80</sup> Rapid progress in helium ion beam has encouraged extensions to other ion beams such as neon ion beam.<sup>81,82</sup> More thorough information regarding ion beam lithography can be found in Chapter 17.
Scanning probe lithography is based on the concept of using a nanoscale probe to modify a resist or surface.
The pattern is created by selectively positioning the tip of the probe, and this is therefore another maskless form of lithography.
--[p27]-- Some methods use force-induced interactions to indent<sup>85,86</sup> or nanoscratch<sup>87</sup> the surface or even to move individual atoms and molecules.<sup>88,89</sup> There are a whole series of thermally induced changes including thermomechanical changes,<sup>90,91</sup> direct evaporation,<sup>20,92,93</sup> and thermochemical changes.<sup>19,94</sup> Many of these are specifically reviewed in Chapter 16, which covers thermal scanning probe lithography.
--[p27]-- It is a maskless form of lithography, which allows high flexibility for arbitrary patterns (compared to optical lithography techniques, which require a mask) and its resolution is determined by the diameter of the ion beam and not the wavelength of light.

===== [p391-391] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.3.2 APPROACH 1: NONCATALYTIC ACID CLEAVAGE OF BISMUTH-PHENYL OLIGOMERS (4块) =====
--[p391]-- 11.3.2 APPROACH 1: NONCATALYTIC ACID CLEAVAGE OF BISMUTH-PHENYL OLIGOMERS
This approach is based upon the known acidolysis reactions of triphenyl bismuth. Upon exposure to excess triflic acid, the phenyl-bismuth bond is cleaved and replaced by triflate. Approach 1 utilizes this chemistry by combining the phenylbismuth oligomers with a PAG.
--[p391]-- Phenyl-bismuth oligomers blended with 25 wt% PAG were found to have sensitivities of $6 0 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } .$ . The poor photospeeds of this system may be due to its noncatalytic nature. Higher PAG formulations were not tested due to issues with PAG phase segregation.
--[p391]-- Curve (a) represents the GPC spectrum before treatment with acid and curve (b) shows after treatment. The elution times post-treatment are longer, and the resulting peaks are sharper, indicating a decrease in molecular weight.
Phenyl-bismuth oligomers were formulated with PAG and tested for EUV contrast. Contrast curve measurements were taken at the Berkeley Micro Exposure Tool but demonstrated poor photospeeds.
--[p391]-- Upon exposure, the photogenerated acid should cleave the phenyl-bismuth bonds, eliciting a change in solubility due to both a decrease in oligomer molecular weight and a change in polarity.
As a cursory test of this approach, oligomers were treated with acid and molecular weights were measured. Oligomers were treated with an excess of triflic acid and a GPC spectrum collected before and after treatment. The results of this experiment are shown in Fig. 6.

===== [p13-15] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.1 INTRODUCTION (22块) =====
--[p14]-- In Chapter 2, new insights into the mechanisms of EUV resist radiation chemistry are presented from the perspective of an examination of the fundamental interactions of soft X-rays with matter, photoionization, and molecular relaxation processes. These processes can lead directly to chemistry not present at longer wavelengths, but also to the production of low energy electrons which are important for EUV resists.
--[p13]-- 1, which shows the transistor dimension required to maintain Moore’s law along with a cross section of the photoresist pattern required to produce these dimensions.<sup>5</sup> Photoresists are the radiation-sensitive materials used for forming the relief patterns required to build up IC devices. As shown in Fig. 1, transistors have continued to shrink to where current feature sizes are sub-20-nm, and sub-10-nm features are only a few years away.
--[p15]-- Chapter 16 deals with thermal scanning probe lithography and introduces the new commercial thermal probe tool the Nano-Frazor from Swisslitho. Finally in Chapter 17, the recent development of the scanning helium ion beam lithography tool and its application to nanolithography is discussed.
--[p13]-- As features rapidly approach molecular and even atomic length scales, a number of technological challenges have arisen that threaten to halt this steady progress, and thus the entire IC industry.
The critical pieces required for scaling are both the materials and the processes used for lithography.
--[p15]-- The exposure mechanism is radically different to that of organic systems and is explained in depth, together with a review of processing. Chapter 10 also addresses an exciting new material class: high-Z nanocluster resists, examined via the prototypical hafnium peroxide sulfate (HafSOx). These depart in almost every way from the traditional paradigm of a photoresist, but nonetheless have demonstrated outstanding performance.
--[p15]-- From Chapter 6 onward, the book addresses resist chemistry. The first of these chapters presents progress in resists that operate via a mechanism of chain scission. These are typically known as nonchemically amplified resists, as one exposure event leads to a single chemical event in the resist. While such systems are typically considered to be quite insensitive, new work on high-speed variants is presented. Chemically amplified systems for EUV lithography are reviewed in Chapter 7.
--[p15]-- While EUV is covered extensively across the first 13 chapters, various other approaches are also under development. Chapter 14 presents a short review of the challenges and potential solutions of next-generation lithography. In Chapter 15, the topic of scanning probe lithography is examined in great depth, before focusing on electrical field interactions of a nanoprobe with resist, and approaches to scanning probe lithography throughput enhancement.
--[p14]-- Chapter 4 introduces the technique of EUV interferometric lithography, which has been used to generate many of the experimental results seen in later chapters. General resist material challenges are then examined and potential strategies are discussed. Chapter 5 introduces EUV lithography which uses more conventional optics, i.e., using a mask and projection optics rather than a grating for pattern generation, and a detailed analysis of the tool challenges faced by industry.
--[p14]-- For noncontact methods, the actinic radiation under consideration is typically far more energetic. This will be discussed in Section 1.3 of this chapter, together with a brief introduction to resist chemistry in EUVand electron beam lithography, alongside a review of current resist processes.
--[p14]-- Currently there is significant worldwide research effort both industrially and in academia into next-generation lithography processes such as extreme ultraviolet (EUV), advanced e-beam, nanoimprint, scanning probe, and ion beam lithography. There is likewise similar effort in both the industrial and the academic lithography arenas into next generation materials for lithography including numerous novel approaches to resist chemistry and ingenious extensions of traditional photopolymers.
--[p13]-- 1.1 INTRODUCTION
The modern world is thoroughly populated with integrated circuits (ICs) and other microelectronic devices. These devices are present in all aspects of society and are integral to the running of government, business, health care, transportation, security, and even domestic tasks.
--[p13]-- The doubling of the number of transistors per chip has been done by shrinking the sizes of the transistors. The shrink in feature sizes has been enabled in a large measure by advancements in lithography, which is the technique used to print the circuit features on silicon wafers during IC fabrication.<sup>4</sup> A visual example of the scale of shrink is shown in Fig.
--[p15]-- While many chemically amplified systems are proprietary, and results in the literature often presented without significant chemical detail, this chapter seeks to identify the major recent trends in chemically amplified systems.
To date the majority of resist systems have been based on polymeric materials. However, in the last two decades a significant amount of research into molecular resist systems has been undertaken.
--[p14]-- This book therefore aims to bring together some of the world’s foremost lithographic development scientists from the various communities to produce in one place a complete description of the many approaches to lithographic materials and process design, development, and characterization. Resist chemistry for next-generation lithography is likely to be quite distinct from the well-known process of photochemistry in current use.
--[p15]-- Good results as a photomask are indeed demonstrated, but serendipitously the resist has also been found to enable astonishingly high aspect ratio electron beam patterning, primarily due to the very low-density nature of the film. Electron beam patterning resist features with aspect ratios far beyond anything that could be achieved in other resists are shown.
--[p15]-- Film density is something that will be revisited in Chapter 13, as part of an examination of a selection of the other novel approaches that have been undertaken recently. The chapter addresses novel approaches to EUV lithography, including low and high absorbancy films and novel nanoparticle-based resists.
The last section of the book addresses several new approaches to next-generation lithography.
--[p13]-- Once found primarily in computers, ICs are now pervasive in almost everything one interacts with, including cell phones, automobiles, televisions, toys, even appliances such as refrigerators and coffee makers. They have changed the way people work, play, and communicate. The ubiquity of these devices has come about because their computing power has increased exponentially over time, while at the same time the cost per computing power has dropped.
--[p14]-- One of the most significant problems in EUV lithography relates to stochastic variations, both due to the high energy per photon, and thus low photon number per dose, but also the variability of multicomponent resist materials pushed to the limits of their performance. Chapter 5 introduces a new model to simulate these effects and identify areas of most concern. Finally the progress in commercial and research resists exposed on a mask-based EUV tool is reviewed.
--[p15]-- Chapter 8 examines a wide variety of negativetone molecular resist systems, primarily but not exclusively operating via crosslinking mechanisms, while Chapter 9 looks at positive-tone molecular resist systems, via, for instance, solubility switch mechanism (see Section 1.2 of this chapter for a discussion of resist tone). Another recent alternative to polymeric resists are inorganic resists. Chapter 10 introduces the most widely used of the inorganic systems, hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ).
--[p15]-- Another novel approach utilizing organometallic complexes is presented in Chapter 11. By selecting metal atoms of high EUV absorbance together with appropriate ligands to enable spin coating and development, a number of high-speed EUV resists have been demonstrated.
Chapter 12 takes a fundamentally different approach to resist development. A material initially developed to demonstrate high opacity in the UV, so as to allow its use as an electron beam writable photomask is presented.
--[p14]-- In Chapter 3 the examination of the EUV resist mechanism is extended further via a detailed analysis of the interactions of low energy electrons in the resist film, identifying the many productive (and nonproductive) reaction pathways available.
Chapters 4 and 5 investigate the process and patterning challenges facing EUV lithographydthe most likely next generation contender.
--[p13]-- This performance and cost has been enabled by the ability of the IC manufacturers to double the number of transistors per chip roughly every two years.<sup>1</sup> This trend is commonly referred to as Moore’s Law.<sup>2,3</sup> Gordon Moore observed this trend in 1965, and he predicted this scaling would continue for another decade. It continued not only for another decade, but it has continued for over 50 years. It started as an observation on scaling, but then became an industry mandate.

===== [p223-223] Chemically amplified resists and acid amplifiers > 7.2.1 EUV CAR RESIST REACTION MECHANISM (3块) =====
--[p223]-- Some workers have reported crosslinking reactions at higher dose leading to negative-tone behavior.<sup>24</sup>
Work to take advantage of this alternate mechanism has been reported. Incorporation of halides to increase absorption cross section has been reported.<sup>25e27</sup> Use of more easily reduced acid generators has led to sensitivity enhancement as well.<sup>28</sup>
--[p223]-- 3 depicts, ionizing radiation such as EUV is absorbed by the polymer matrix, allowing a cascade of secondary electrons of varying energies (5e80 eV), which can reduce the acid generator to produce acid.<sup>16</sup> This step is very different than optical lithography whereby the photoacid generator is directly photolyzed by the incoming exposure wavelength. Once the acid is produced, the normal steps of acid-catalyzed deprotection and acid diffusion are carried out.
--[p223]-- 7.2.1 EUV CAR RESIST REACTION MECHANISM
It is important to distinguish between the CAR-positive resist reaction mechanism for optical lithography versus EUV lithography. ===== [p488-489] Next generation lithographydthe rise of unconventional methods? > 14.1.2 THE WORKHORSE OF THE SEMICONDUCTOR INDUSTRY AND ITS PHYSICAL LIMITATIONS (8块) =====
--[p488]-- Thus, the exposure wavelengths were reduced during past decades from 435 nm (g-line), to 365 nm (i-line), and to 248 nm (DUV, KrF laser source, since 1998). However, as can be seen from Eq. (2), this scaling trend also leads to a decrease of the DoF. This has triggered the development of thinner resists and chemical-mechanical planarization based planarization methods. Current state-of-the-art DUV photolithography (ArF laser source) uses a shorter exposure wavelength still (l  193 nm).
--[p488]-- The inherent limitations of photolithography (currently most used: projection lithography technology<sup>7</sup>), respectively the resolution (minimum feature size [MFS]) and depth of focus (DoF), are specified by two scaling laws<sup>8</sup> given by Eqs. (1) and (2):
$$
\mathbf { M F S } = k _ { 1 } \cdot { \frac { \lambda } { \mathbf { N A } } }\tag{1}
$$
$$
\mathrm { D o F } = k _ { 2 } \cdot { \frac { \lambda } { \left( \mathrm { N A } \right) ^ { 2 } } }\tag{2}
$$
--[p488]-- In photolithography, photons transfer geometric patterns from a photomask to a photosensitive thin film, called a photoresist, which changes its solubility in a developer as a result of a photon-triggered chemical reaction. Due to the physical wave nature of light and optical diffraction and interference effects, fundamental limitations of the photolithographic process exist.
--[p488]-- To continue the downscaling trend, a variety of resolution-enhanced techniques (RETs) have been developed to push the resolution of photolithography far beyond the boundary described by the diffraction limit, described by Eq. (1).
--[p489]-- Today, the 22-nm and 14-nm nodes are manufactured with multipatterning immersion ArF lithography.<sup>15</sup> Intel claims that, 10-nm and 7-nm node patterning are achievable with conventional methods.<sup>16</sup> Estimated insertion of NGL methods (i.e., EUV, block-copolymer patterning, etc.) is at 7 nm and below.<sup>17</sup> The same trend is reflected on ITRS 2.0 technology roadmap (Fig. 2).
--[p488]-- To fulfill key industrial requirements for the 45-nm node target, and potentially on to the 10-nm node, optical lithography systems operating at 193 nm exposure wavelengths have been enhanced by RETs such as off-axis illumination,<sup>9</sup> immersion lithography,<sup>10</sup> multiple patterning, phase-shift mask lithography,<sup>11</sup> optical proximity correction,<sup>12</sup> source mask optimization,<sup>13</sup> and inverse lithography.<sup>14</sup>
--[p488]-- 14.1.2 THE WORKHORSE OF THE SEMICONDUCTOR INDUSTRY AND ITS PHYSICAL LIMITATIONS
Due to its simplicity and high throughput, the parallel photolithographic technique has dominated the route for semiconductor device fabrication for the past several decades and led to the current status of the integrated circuit.
--[p488]-- where l is the exposure wavelength, NA the numerical aperture of the lens system, and $k _ { 1 }$ (typically 0.5e0.8) and $k _ { 2 }$ (typically 0.1e0.5) are process-related constants. 4 In a lithography process, one seeks to minimize the MFS and maximize the DoF. To improve the resolution, with acceptable levels of DoF, the general trend has been toward illumination sources with shorter wavelengths and to increase of the numerical aperture of the projection lithography system.

===== [p451-452] SML electron beam resist: ultra-high aspect ratio nanolithography > 12.6 SUMMARY (5块) =====
--[p452]-- Therefore, it can be concluded that the SML2000 resist can be used to fabricate an optical photomask for the i-line wavelength. It was observed that the resolution of SML2000 achieved an aspect ratio of 10:1 at 30 kV. This was not expected as typically an aspect ratio of 4:1 is normal. Therefore, the resolution limits were explored.
To push the lithographic resolution limits of the resist, the resist thickness was decreased to 600, 300, and 50 nm.
--[p452]-- This led to the composite resist film exhibiting a large electron mean free path allowing the primary electrons to experience a reduced number of inelastic scattering events and achieve a greater control of the lateral scattering of the primary electrons.
--[p451]-- It was found that when the SML2000 resist film thickness was 2 mm the total transmission of the UV radiation was attenuated to zero. This provided a good optical contrast between dark and light areas of the mask as required for optical lithography.

It was found that the PMMA had high optical transmission at i-line wavelengths and as a result would have poor optical contrast for an optical photomask. For PMMA to perform as a photomask, modification of its transmission would be required. Azo dyes were introduced into the polymeric matrix to improve this optical contrast at the i-line wavelength. By the addition of multiple azo dyes into the e-beam resist, the i-line radiation was attenuated.

===== [p282-282] Negative-tone organic molecular resists > 8.7.4 EFFECT OF NUMBER OF FUNCTIONAL GROUPS AND COMPARISON TO POLYMERIC RESISTS (4块) =====
--[p282]-- Although there are many potential reasons for this result, one major factor could be the lower degree of functionality per molecule in cross-linking molecular resists compared to polymers. A study<sup>101</sup> was carried out that attempted to further understand this effect by comparing a series of small molecules and oligomers that had relatively similar sizes and varying the number of functional groups per molecule as shown in Fig. 56.
--[p282]-- 8.7.4 EFFECT OF NUMBER OF FUNCTIONAL GROUPS AND COMPARISON TO POLYMERIC RESISTS
Molecular resists were originally investigated based on the thought that using small molecules instead of polymers (i.e., macromolecules) would improve LER and potentially resolution through the effective reduction in the resist “pixel” size.
--[p282]-- While this may or may not actually be the case, many molecular resists actually tended to perform worse than the equivalent polymer for conventional positive-tone deprotection-based chemistry. Any potential pixel size advantages were lost or obscured because LER and resolution was limited by a lower overall resist performance.
--[p282]-- The origin of reduced performance was never fully elucidated, although the generally lower glass transition temperature of the molecular resist<sup>100</sup> and the reduced mechanical properties were likely major sources of the issue. However, one class of molecular resists that tended to outperform the polymeric equivalent was negative-tone crosslinking systems based on epoxide or cationic cross-linking.

===== [p131-132] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 3.2.3 ELECTRON IMPACT EXCITATION (5块) =====
--[p131]-- The threshold for ND is at about 4e6 eV, lower than the threshold for DI, because the fragments do not need to be ionized.<sup>7,12</sup> However, as ions are formed during DD, the threshold for that process is higher, about 10e15 eV, above which the cross section increases continuously. 12
Electron impact excitation has been studied extensively for atoms, as it is important, for e.g., plasmas and lighting.
--[p131]-- Second, the excited molecule can dissociate into two neutral radicals [neutral dissociation (ND)]. Two examples of ND are shown schematically in the diagram in Fig. 2C. The third possibility is dipolar dissociation (DD), where the neutral molecule dissociates into a cation and an anion.
--[p131]-- However, much less information is known for polyatomic molecules, which makes ND an unknown quantity among electron-induced reactions.
While charged particles (such as the ions released in DEA, DI, and DD) are relatively easy to detect, neutral reaction products are more difficult to qualify and certainly more difficult to quantify. As a result, little is known about the role of ND in electron-induced chemistry.
--[p132]-- As Moore et al.<sup>7</sup> summarize, total ND cross sections have only been determined for relatively small molecules, such as methane and fluorinated methanes. The cross section depends on the electron energy in much the same way as for electron impact ionization, although the cross sections tend to peak at a lower energy (around 70 eV, rather than around 100e120 eV).
--[p131]-- 3.2.3 ELECTRON IMPACT EXCITATION
In electron impact excitation, a passing electron excites a molecule (or an atom), to leave an excited neutral. It is similar to electron impact ionization and also has a short interaction time. In the case of a molecule, there are three decay channels for the excited neutral. First, the molecule can relax to the ground state by emitting a photon or by transferring energy to other particles if these are in the direct vicinity.
