===== [p18-19] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.3.1 ULTRAVIOLET LITHOGRAPHY (9块) =====
--[p19]-- Finally, projection printing has the big advantage of higher intrinsic resolution. The optical resolution limit for far field (Fraunhoffer) diffraction limited projection lithography is given by the Raleigh criterion shown in Eq. (1) where l is wavelength of radiation used, NA is the numerical aperture of the lens in the exposure system, and $k _ { 1 }$ is a process dependent factor that depends on a variety of factors and tool issues.
--[p19]-- Contact printing improves resolution to about the order of the wavelength of the light (and potentially, if not practically, higher), but puts the mask and resist at high risk of damage and defectivity due to the direct contact. Contact and proximity printing both require masks that are the same size as the wafers, and mask features the same size as the features to be printed in the resist.
--[p18]-- Although it has been replaced by other techniques and exposure sources for the highest resolution features, it is still commonly used for multiple levels of patterning at feature sizes of 0.3 mm and larger.<sup>23</sup> The origin of the UV light is commonly a mercury arc lamp, which has its own unique spectral emission characteristics. Three of the strongest emission wavelengths in the UV are at 436, 405, and 365 nm, which are commonly referred to as g-line, h-line, and i-line respectively.
--[p18]-- There are three different setups that are commonly used to pattern with UV lithography: contact printing, proximity printing, and projection printing. In contact printing, the mask is placed in direct contact with the wafer and photoresist. Proximity printing is similar except that a small gap is left between the wafer and mask. Projection printing collects light from the lamp using a series of lenses and focuses it onto the mask.
--[p19]-- Resolution for a lithographic process is the smallest feature that can be successfully printed with acceptable quality and control.<sup>24</sup> Proximity printing works in the near-field (Fresnel) diffraction regime and is resolution limited by the wavelength of light (l) and the gap between the resist and the mask (L) $_ { \mathrm { t o } } \approx \sqrt { \lambda L }$ , about 2e4 mm in practice.
--[p18]-- 1.3.1 ULTRAVIOLET LITHOGRAPHY
UV lithography has been the most used exposure source in the semiconductor industry for decades and is commonly used in many other industries that require patterning such as flat screen televisions.
--[p19]-- For many projection tools, $k _ { 1 }$ is below 0.5 and NA is near 1 (or even greater for immersion lithography), so resolution is actually smaller than the wavelength of light (compared to several times greater than the wavelength for proximity printing).
$$
R = k _ { 1 } \frac { \lambda } { N A }\tag{1.1}
$$
--[p19]-- Projection printing overcomes the defectivity issues because the mask is further away from the wafer and is protected by a pellicle,<sup>25e27</sup> which prevents particles from landing on the mask. Projection printing can also use masks with features larger than the optical patterns at the wafer level because the process allows for the reduction of the mask image, typically a 4 reduction in the mask features; this allows for easier mask production.
--[p18]-- The light from the open areas of the mask are then collected by another lens, which projects the pattern onto the wafer. Contact and proximity printing tools are less expensive than projection tools because of the simpler setup that requires much less sophisticated optics and so are commonly used in research and development labs; however, projection lithography is by far the dominant method in high volume manufacturing because it has several advantages over the other two techniques.

===== [p113-115] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.3.3 ATOMIC RELAXATION AND FRAGMENTATION IN MOLECULES (9块) =====
--[p115]-- Usually Auger relaxation is the dominant channel when it is energetically possible due to the speed of nonradiative electronic processes. This illustrates another complexity of molecular relaxation. The rate of an Auger process is strongly dependent on the overlap of the wave functions of the participating electrons.
--[p115]-- Molecules are not static, however, and as the atoms vibrate around their equilibrium positions, the overlap between the semicore $2 a _ { I }$ orbital localized around the oxygen atom and the more extended valence orbitals changes. The ultrafast Auger relaxation probability after the photoionization event depends on the instantaneous geometry of the molecule.
--[p113]-- 2.3.3 ATOMIC RELAXATION AND FRAGMENTATION IN MOLECULES
Following atomic ionization, the remaining electrons relax. Following molecular ionization, both electrons and atoms relax. The Born Oppenheimer approximation separates the electronic and atomic degrees of freedom. The molecular electrons relax on a few femtoseconds timescale, before the atoms have time to respond. Then the atoms adjust on a 50 fs ps timescale.
--[p114]-- Montenegro et al.<sup>43</sup> classified molecular relaxation processes in terms of increasing energy release: first “evaporation” of an H<sup></sup> radical, then “fission” where an $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ ion is ejected, and finally fragmentation into multiple radicals and ions.
Water provides a good example of molecular relaxation, as it is one of the few cases where the detailed experimental branching ratios are known as a function of the original ionization event.
--[p115]-- Table 2 summarizes the results of coincidence experiments, where both ions and electrons are detected.
When the HOMO or HOMO-1 molecular orbitals are ionized, the result is the stable parent ion $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ^ { + }$ . If HOMO-2 is ionized, the molecule is left with ${ \sim } 6$ eV of internal energy, and water is very likely to split into ions and radicals.
--[p115]-- When an $\mathrm { O H ^ { + } }$ ion is detected (70% probability) an H<sup></sup> radical must also be produced, even though it is not detected directly. When a $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ ion is detected (22% probability), the neutral fragment(s) could be either OH<sup></sup> or $\mathrm { O } ^ { \bullet } + \mathrm { H } ^ { \bullet }$
--[p115]-- The HOMO-3 or $2 a _ { I }$ orbital (BE 32.6 eV) will have the largest $\sigma _ { E U V }$ When this orbital is ionized, the excited molecular ion is left with w20 eV of residual internal energy, enough for Auger relaxation. Surprisingly, there is a 2:1 branching ratio between Auger relaxation, resulting in doubly ionized water which immediately fragments<sup>6</sup>; and fragmentation of singly ionized water without an Auger process.
--[p113]-- As the atoms move, the electron density remains in near equilibrium with the instantaneous molecular geometry. In general, bond lengths and angles are different for neutral and ionized molecules, and vibrational excitation may result from photoionization.
When an electron is removed from molecular orbitals below the HOMO, the molecule is left in an excited state with residual internal energy. The initial steps of molecular relaxation are similar to the atomic processes shown in Fig. 5A and B.
--[p114]-- If there is sufficient internal energy, the molecule will relax by a fast Auger process, resulting in a doubly ionized molecule and an additional SE. Multiply ionized molecules usually break into singly charged fragments to minimize Coulomb 43 energy.
Singly ionized molecules may also fragment when the residual internal energy exceeds the few electronvolt energy of chemical bonds. Molecular dissociation is usually faster than fluorescence processes (Fig. 5C).

===== [p71-72] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.7 CONCLUSIONS (9块) =====
--[p71]-- Modifying a resist to optimize or improve one or two parameters such as resolution and LER appears to always come at the cost of another parameter such as sensitivity. High sensitivity, low resolution resists such as CARs become much less sensitive as their resolution is improved to sub-20 nm. Low sensitivity, high resolution resists such as nonamplified resists begin to lose resolution capability as their sensitivity is improved.
--[p71]-- EUV seems a likely contender, but its introduction into manufacturing seems to always be 2 years away, so it is unclear when or if it will be used. E-beam, ion beam, and scanning probe all appear capable of the desired resolution, but throughput will always be a concern. Nanoimprint seems capable of the desired resolution, cost, and throughput, but fears regarding defectivity may prevent adoption for IC manufacturing. Or will optical lithography continue until the end of scaling?
--[p71]-- Options once thought almost impossible for use in manufacturing like inorganic and metal-containing small molecule resists have begun to receive serious consideration as conventional organic polymer resists may not be capable of meeting the combination of RLS required for EUV resists.
The challenges to resist design now appear to grow larger with every nanometer reduction in resolution below 25 nm.
--[p71]-- The features are so small that the stochastic nature of matter and light are beginning to play a significant role in the patterning results, and the current sensitivity requirements for EUV may not provide good enough statistics. The challenge of controlling photoacid diffusion in CARs has resulted in the development of several new materials, but control may still not be sufficient for the resolutions required in future generations.
--[p71]-- 1.7 CONCLUSIONS
There are a wide variety of materials and processes that have been used for lithography. Lithographic exposure tools have progressed to ever shorter wavelengths starting in the UV and moved down to the DUV at 193 nm. Advanced process techniques such as immersion lithography and multiple patterning have pushed optical lithography well beyond its intrinsic resolution limit. The tools and techniques that will be used in future generations of devices are uncertain.
--[p71]-- Ultimately it will be a balance of cost, benefits, and risk that determines which technique will be used in future devices or if scaling will continue as it has the last 50 years at all.
There have been an enormous variety of different types and families of resists investigated since the beginning of modern photolithography, but ultimately only a few have shown the correct combination of properties to find their way into high volume manufacturing.
--[p71]-- CARs and non-CARs are rapidly converging in performance as the resolution and sensitivity requirements continue to shrink. Pattern collapse may ultimately be the limiting factor for resolution as the capillary forces experienced in drying rapidly increase with decreasing spacing. This is made even worse by the rapid drop in material strength and modulus as the feature sizes decrease below 30e 40 nm due to the higher mobility chains at the surface and the increasing surface-to-volume ratios.
--[p72]-- Shrinking the feature size has been the drumbeat of the semiconductor industry for the last 50 years. This drumbeat appears to be slowing as the challenges grow larger with every new generation of device. Scaling will eventually stop, either due to the physical limits imposed by the finite size of atoms, or due to the economic cost required to continue scaling. As the challenges increase, so does the opportunity for innovation in the materials and processes for next-generation lithography.
This volume presents the most novel materials and processes currently under investigation for the next generation of lithography.
--[p71]-- These few were chosen at one time to operate at the cutting edge of resolution, and continue to find use for larger scale back end of the line processes while their descendants continue to push the limits of resolution. As the challenge of continued scaling has increased, so have the variety and types of resists.

Even at 65-nm patterns, there was noticeable bridging or swelling and the 35-nm patterns showed significant swelling induced failure of the patterns.
The data appeared to confirm the hypothesis that lower functionality materials have better resolution.
--[p284]-- Because fewer cross-links (lower conversion) are required to form the gelled network in higher functionality materials such as polymers and oligomers like SU-8, the network structure likely has a lower cross-link density than in the lower functionality molecular resists. Since the polymers and oligomers have a less dense network, they can imbibe more solvent during the development, which then leads to the swelling that causes bridging defects and pattern failure in dense features.
--[p284]-- Interestingly, dose-to-size increased as the degree of functionality decreased from $4 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ for 4-Ep, $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ for 3-Ep, and up to $7 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ for 2-Ep. This increase in dose is because more catalyst (i.e., photoacid) is required at a fixed PEB condition in order to achieve the higher extent of conversion that is required to gel, as functionality decreases.

--[p284]-- One major effect of the degree of functionality per molecule (f) is a change in the extent of conversion and cross-linking density in the final network. Flory-Stockmeyer theory suggests that functional group conversion at the gel point is proportional to 1/(f  1), so as the degree of functionality decreases, higher conversion is required to reach the gel point. The higher conversion should lead to higher crosslink density, which could have better mechanical properties and less swelling.

===== [p280-282] Negative-tone organic molecular resists > FIGURE 53 (6块) =====
--[p282]-- Although these results suggested that use of epoxide groups will lead to superior resist performance compared to using oxetanes, modifications of the resist to slow down the propagation rate of an oxetane system could lead to improved performance.
--[p282]-- Likewise, the initial slope of the contrast curve in 2-Ep at $9 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ is lower than 2-Ox because the propagation rate is slower for the epoxide, and the thickness plateau is higher in 2-Ep because the cross-link density is higher so less material dissolves out of the network.
--[p282]-- Previous studies of polymerization<sup>98,99</sup> of epoxides and oxetanes showed that the epoxides usually have higher initiation rates than oxetanes, while oxetanes tended to have faster propagation rates than epoxides. These studies also suggested that propagation rates of oxetanes are much higher than their initiation rates. The various rates of the two functional groups suggested that final network structure is different in epoxide systems compared to oxetane systems.
--[p282]-- can be seen in the 45-nm patterns; there are multiple points where the lines appear to be stuck together and other places where the line does not hold its shape (e.g., along the left edge).
The differences in 2-Ep and 2-Ox contrast curves and patterning performance can be potentially explained due to differing polymerization kinetics.
--[p282]-- One can think of epoxide cross-linking as a large number of slowly growing chains that suddenly form a high cross-link density network at relatively high monomer conversion. In the oxetanes, a smaller number of initiated chains rapidly polymerize to form linear units, which ultimately form a low cross-link density network. Thus, resolution is limited in 2-Ox because the lower cross-link density network is more likely to swell than the higher density 2-Ep.

===== [p39-42] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.5.2 CHEMICALLY AMPLIFIED RESISTS (17块) =====
--[p41]-- Significant work was also done on alternate 193-nm lithography resists based on cycloolefin-maleic anhydride alternating copolymers<sup>208e211</sup> and resists for 157-nm lithography.<sup>212e217</sup> While these materials and others did not directly find widespread use, many important things were learned from the studies that were applied to later resists.
--[p39]-- Newer CARs for EUV can have much higher PAG loading and may have the PAG covalently attached to the polymer as discussed later. The polymer contains acidic groups such as phenols (e.g., hydroxystyrene) or carboxylic acids (e.g., methacrylic acid) that can give the polymer aqueous base solubility, but have been blocked by protecting groups to make it initially insoluble in base.
--[p42]-- While this type of resist has not been universally adopted for use in the highest resolution industrial patterning (according to company reports), there appear to be many resist manufacturers that have begun investigating and using this 219,235   
technology.
--[p39]-- Irradiation of the resist film causes conversion of the PAGs into photoacids, which catalyze the deblocking of the protecting groups, often done at elevated temperatures $( 8 0 - 1 3 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ in a PEB step. Deprotection of the polymer’s acidic groups changes the polymer’s polarity and provides a high dissolution contrast between exposed and unexposed regions.
--[p41]-- The number and types of different polymers that have been evaluated for use as CARs is enormous.<sup>168e170</sup> This is compounded even more by the fact that many resists are copolymers composed of three or more monomers. Despite the large number of different materials that have been investigated, only a handful of polymers and monomers have been ultimately used in commercial CARs (at least only a handful have been disclosed by the resist manufacturers).
--[p42]-- These resists also show a reduced propensity for the PAG to segregate within the polymer compared to blended $\mathrm { P A G S } ^ { 2 3 4 }$ and this can allow for higher PAG loadings as well which will improve sensitivity and may improve other properties such as LER. Attaching the PAG anion to the polymer chain also reduces its diffusion length, which appears to lead to improved resolution and LER.
--[p39]-- Development done in aqueous base developer produces positive-tone images because the deprotected groups can react with base, while development done in certain organic solvents produces negative-tone images<sup>193e198</sup> because the exposed regions have more polar groups that have less affinity for organic solvent than the less polar unexposed protected regions. Fig. 12 shows an illustration of this patterning process.
In addition to PAGs, base is often added to resists, usually at a small percentage relative to the PAG.
--[p42]-- An example of an anion-bound PBP resist is shown in Fig. 14. This approach provides multiple advantages. One is that it can show improvements in outgassing because many of the small molecule fragments from the PAG photolysis are attached to the larger molecule chain.
--[p41]-- Chemical structures of some commonly used families of chemically amplified resists.
inhomogeneous distribution of environmental base in the film can cause T-topping in the resist where the top of the patterned feature is wider than the middle and bottom.
--[p41]-- Adding base quencher directly to the resist in the first place can improve these problems because there is such a large background level of base in the resist that the small amount of environmental base only very slightly changes the base concentration in the resist and thus only slightly changes the sensitivity.
--[p39]-- Sensitivity is better in CARs because a single photon absorption can generate a catalyst which carries out multiple reactions that affect the solubility of the resist resin.<sup>190e192</sup> This catalyst is almost always a strong acid that is generated by a compound known as a photoacid generator (PAG). The PAG is typically blended at 2e10 wt% with a majority resist polymer.
--[p41]-- Base quencher also helps because it tends to suppress acid deprotection in the low dose regions, but have minimal effect in the higher dose regions where it all has been reacted with photoacid. This tends to improve contrast because there is a sharper chemical gradient between high and low dose regions. It also can improve resolution by preventing diffusion of acid into low dose and unexposed regions and improves LER by a similar manner.<sup>204</sup>

--[p41]-- Most CAR formulations consist of a multifunctional copolymer resin with small molecule PAGs and base quenchers added to obtain the desired final resist
properties. A class of CARs has been developed where the PAG is not simply blended into the matrix, but instead is covalently attached to the polymer backbone. These materials are commonly called polymer-bound PAG (PBP) resists .<sup>218e233</sup> The PAG is usually an ionic onium salt that can be attached through the cation or through the anion.
--[p39]-- 1.5.2 CHEMICALLY AMPLIFIED RESISTS
CARs are the family of resists that are used today in the highest resolution patterning in semiconductor production. CARs overcame the two problems inherent with DNQ-novolac at DUV. They have much better sensitivity, up to two orders of magnitude better, and they have lower absorbance because the base polymer is changed from novolac to more transparent materials such as polystyrene copolymers at 248 nm and acrylates at 193 nm as will be discussed later.
--[p40]-- Base quenchers provide multiple benefits.<sup>199e201</sup> In a CAR with no added base, any small amount of environmental base that is absorbed into the resist can significantly change the sensitivity because base will very rapidly react with any photoacid to effectively reduce the acid concentration.<sup>202,203</sup> This problem caused significant issues when CARs were first used commercially because sensitivity would vary by two or three times the baseline condition.<sup>28</sup> Likewise,
--[p41]-- Some representative resists include poly(4-hydroxystyrene) (PHOST) with different degrees of protection (called APEX type),<sup>205</sup> styreneehydroxystyreneemethacrylate copolymers referred to as ESCAP type,<sup>206</sup> and purely acrylateemethacrylate-type polymers for 193-nm lithography<sup>207</sup> as shown in Fig. 13.

===== [p37-37] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.5 RESIST MATERIALS AND CHEMISTRY (5块) =====
--[p37]-- This generally works because the radiochemical event produces a catalyst, most often an acid, which can react with the surrounding resist matrix to mediate a cascade of reactions or initiate a chain reaction that modifies the properties of the resist in a way that can be exploited in relief image generation. 28 Thus, the required number of photons, or dose (to effect an equivalent solubility change) is greatly reduced in CARs.
--[p37]-- While the distinction between non-CA and CA resists has been clear in UV and DUV exposure, the differences are slightly less clear in EUV and e-beam because a single incident photon or electron can ultimately produce multiple reactive low energy electrons, which leads to quantum yield values of greater than one .<sup>60,171e173</sup> The more general rule followed now is that a system is a CAR if the electron or photon reaction leads to the production of a catalyst which could carry out multiple reactions and non-CA if the number of reactions is ultimately limited by the final number of electrons or photons.
--[p37]-- Many of the oldest families of resists such as bis-azide/rubber and DNQ/novolac were nonamplified resists, but were not so specifically named until later, after the development of CARs. CARs were so named because single photon absorption can cause multiple reactions, i.e., its impact is amplified.
--[p37]-- 1.5 RESIST MATERIALS AND CHEMISTRY
The rest of this book covers many of the most recent developments in resist materials in depth. This section provides an overview of many different types of resists and covers some of the most historically important resist families. More in-depth information reviewing a large number of different resists and their historical development can be found in the excellent reviews by H. Ito. 168e170
--[p37]-- Resists have generally been divided into classifications based on development tone (positive or negative) but have also been divided into two groups known as CARs and nonchemically amplified (non-CA) resists, or more simply nonamplified resists. Nonamplified resists generally can carry out at most one reaction per photon, i.e., their quantum yield is less than or equal to one.

===== [p213-214] The chemistry and application of nonchemically amplified (non-CA) chain-scission resists > 6.4 SUMMARY (7块) =====
--[p213]-- Contrast in these resists thus depends on factors such as (1) absorbance of photons and/or photon cross section and/or yield of secondary electrons, (2) extent of chain scission reactions, and (3) the extent of depolymerization reactions.
The design of non-CA resists was initially inspired by several decades of examination of the effect of high-energy radiation on polymeric materials.
--[p214]-- It remains to be seen, however, whether the generally lower sensitivity of the non-CA materials can be tolerated in a commercial setting, especially considering the continued concern with wafer throughput in current EUV lithographic tools.
--[p214]-- There are, however, other potential chemistries to be exploited, such as those of the poly(benzyl carbamate)s and poly(benzyl ether)s being developed as so-called self-immolative polymers primarily in the field of biomedical polymers.<sup>16,18,19</sup> Also not fully explored are what we might term “hybrid” systems, which undergo simultaneous chain scission and polarity switches.<sup>79,100</sup> It is clear that the potential for development improved approaches to non-CA materials does exist, and it is hoped that investment is made to explore these possibilities.
--[p213]-- If the polymer is thermodynamically unstable at the irradiation or postexposure annealing temperatures, extensive depolymerization reactions may occur. The decrease in molecular weight through chain scission and if relevant chain depropagation is the source of the contrast necessary for selective removal of exposed regions of the resist film.
--[p214]-- Those studies provided a detailed understanding of the structural factors contributing to high sensitivity to incident radiation. For example, detailed studies of the radiation degradation of poly(olefin sulfone)s identified this class of material as of interest for lithographic patterning. Likewise, the radiation sensitivity of the polymethacrylates was well established by the early 1960s.
--[p213]-- 6.4 SUMMARY
The chemistry of non-CA resists involves the interaction of the polymer with an incident photon or in the case of higher energy lithography (EUV and e-beam) with secondary electrons. For the materials considered in this review, namely positive-tone chain-scission non-CA resists, this interaction leads ultimately to cleavage of the polymeric main chain, either directly or through secondary processes such as beta scission (e.g., the methacrylate resists).
--[p214]-- The following two decades of research saw extension of this work and commercial exploitation of the technology; however, the invention of chemical amplification led to a dramatic decrease in interest in non-CA materials.
As discussed in this chapter, there is renewed interest in non-CA resists due to their demonstrated reduced LER compared with CA resists.

===== [p139-140] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 3.4 CONCLUSIONS (9块) =====
--[p140]-- It is clear that an extensive research effort is necessary to reveal how the fundamental mechanisms affect the throughput and the ultimate spatial resolution for lithography-related compounds.
--[p139]-- However, the cross section for a particular reaction channel by itself does not necessarily determine the sensitivity of a resist or precursor. Which channels are active is also determined by the electron spectrum at the surface or in the material, i.e., the electron energies that are available. In other words, the cross section for dissociation needs to be convoluted with the electron spectrum to obtain the final product yield.
--[p139]-- 3.4 CONCLUSIONS
As commercial, high-throughput lithography moves from ultraviolet light to EUV light, and with the continuing development of other lithography techniques, such as EBL and FEBIP, it becomes increasingly important to understand electroninduced chemistry. Theoretically, the fundamental mechanisms by which electrons can induce chemistry are well described. These processes are electron attachment, electron impact ionization, and electron impact excitation.
--[p139]-- Similar research efforts are necessary to develop improved compounds for EUV lithography and EBL.
Regarding spatial resolution, there is little direct evidence on the role of the electron energy. Sub-10-eV electrons can have a relatively long mean free path in a solid and can therefore contribute to image blur and a loss of resolution. FEBIP experiments on ultrathin membranes suggest that secondary electrons contribute to the dissociation of $\mathrm { W } ( \mathrm { C O } ) _ { 6 }$ .
--[p140]-- Tuning the resist or precursor to specifically select a reaction channel, such as with silacyclohexane shows the potential of this approach. Preliminary lithography studies show that the selectivity to DI does indeed lead to higher spatial resolution.
In conclusion, although an appreciable body of experimental data and theoretical calculations on electron-induced chemistry exists, much more is needed to fully model and optimize the key aspects.
--[p139]-- This is also expected for precursors, such as $\mathbf { M e C p P t M e } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { P t } ( \mathrm { P F } _ { 3 } ) _ { 4 }$ , which have dominant cross section at 0 eV, at which electrons have a long mean free paths. However, secondary electrons do not appear to play a main role in EBL using HSQ, where rather DI appears to dominate.
The rational design of resists or precursors to optimize reaction product quality for lithography is in its infancy.
--[p140]-- There are opportunities for highly selective and localized pathways, as electron-induced chemistry can be very robust. The stateof-the-art on rational compound design for electron-induced chemistry is currently in the FEBIP field. The dominant mechanisms are identified by systematically varying ligand types and molecule architectures in various reaction conditions (gas phase, condensed phase, and deposition experiments).
--[p139]-- FEBIP is the first lithography process for which a detailed understanding on the reaction channels has begun to appear. For example, for $\mathbf { M e C p P t M e } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { P t } ( \mathrm { P F } _ { 3 } ) _ { 4 }$ a significant amount of data has been produced over recent years. The dominant reaction is the loss of a single ligand, most likely due to DEA. At a resonance at about $0 \mathrm { e V , }$ this reaction will be predominantly induced by the secondary electrons.
--[p139]-- However, there are relatively little experimental data on the electron-induced dissociation of molecules and certainly on compounds for lithography.
There is only limited number of compounds for which the absolute total cross section has been determined. Typical cross sections are in the order of $1 0 ^ { - 1 6 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ but can also be as high as $1 0 ^ { - 1 4 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ at $0 \mathrm { e V , }$ as in the case of Cl- abstraction from CCl , through DEA.

===== [p137-139] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 3.3.3 RATIONAL DESIGN OF NOVEL MATERIALS (11块) =====
--[p138]-- Popular ligand types and molecule architectures are characterized extensively<sup>54</sup> and the effect of adding reducing groups (e.g., NH<sub>3</sub>) in the molecule is studied.<sup>55</sup> Results from gas phase, condensed phase, and deposition experiments are combined to identify the dominant mechanisms.<sup>41</sup> Systematically mapping a set of ligands for Au(I) and Au(III) compounds has lead to the first rational design of a novel FEBIP precursor, although the synthesis of the compound is yet to be demonstrated.<sup>56</sup>
A high-potential development for the next-generation lithography is tuning the resist or precursor to specifically select a reaction channel.
--[p137]-- 3.3.3 RATIONAL DESIGN OF NOVEL MATERIALS
The route to new and improved materials for lithography is through rationally tuning the starting material (i.e., resist or precursor) to electron-induced chemistry. The key issue is whether a molecule AB will dissociate upon capturing an electron and (if it dissociates) which reaction products are formed.
--[p139]-- As mentioned in the previous paragraph, low-energy electrons potentially limit the ultimate spatial resolution due to their relatively long mean free path. Possibly, the best spatial resolutions are obtained using a compound that is only sensitive to the primary particle, and insensitive to secondary, low-energy electrons. Recently, and for the first time, such a path-selective compound was reported.
--[p138]-- Regardless of whether the target molecule is, e.g., methanol, ethanol, or acetic acid, OeH bonds are broken at about 6.5 and 7.7 eV, while 9 or 10 eVare required to break CeH bonds.<sup>51</sup> The authors conclude that in the case of such core-excited resonances “the fragmentation occurs at the site of core excitation and the excess charge is carried away by one of the fragments.”<sup>51</sup> Another example of selectivity was found by Ibanescu et al.,<sup>52</sup> who studied DEA for a large number of asymmetrical ethers, $\mathsf { R } _ { 1 } { - } \mathsf { O } { - } \mathsf { R } _ { 2 }$ . They varied $\mathrm { R } _ { 1 } ,$ , studying for instance ethyl-methyl-ether, propyl-methyl-ether, and butyl-methyl-ether.
--[p138]-- Although minor cross sections were observed below 5 eV, the reactions occurred mainly at approximately the same energy (9.1, 8.5, and 8.0 eV for $\mathrm { R } _ { 1 } = \mathrm { e t h y l }$ , propyl, and butyl, respectively). These observations suggest the excitations (Feshbach, in these cases) are localized on a part of the molecule, rather than delocalized across the entire molecule.<sup>52</sup> Similar localization may occur in polymeric resists.
--[p138]-- There are opportunities, as electron-induced chemistry can be very robust, highly selective, and localized. For example, Prabhudesai et al. used the electron energy to select the site for H- desorption from organic molecules.
--[p139]-- Bjarnason et al.<sup>57</sup> demonstrated that 1,1-dichloro-1-silacyclohexane can be dissociated by DI and DEA, while silacyclohexane only fragments as a results of DI. The first FEBIP studies using the two precursors show that indeed there is an effect on the resolution, smaller features being written using the precursor that is only sensitive to DI.<sup>58</sup>
--[p138]-- The results show that the outcome of an electron-induced reaction can therefore be tuned using the molecular design.
One may argue that reaction conditions during lithography are much more complex than ideal lab conditions. For example, Ibanescu et al. only used electron energies 16 eV, while higher-energy electrons are also available in the resist in lithography conditions.
--[p138]-- They were surprised to find that, regardless of $\mathrm { R } _ { 2 } , \mathrm { R } _ { 1 }$ was released as a radical:
$$
\mathrm { R } _ { 1 } { - } \mathrm { O } { - } \mathrm { R } _ { 2 } + \mathrm { e } ^ { - }  \mathrm { R } _ { 1 } ^ { * } + \mathrm { R } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ^ { - }\tag{9}
$$
In addition, DEA predominantly occurred at approximately the same electron energy.
--[p137]-- Which reaction products are formed, depends on which bond are broken; this in turn depends on the molecular orbital in which the electron was absorbed and the affinity of the ligands. However, while radiation synthesis is a known method to develop new materials,<sup>4,49,50</sup> to my knowledge, there have been very few efforts to rationally design the precursors in order to obtain a specific reaction product.
--[p138]-- But selectivity can remain prominent under reaction conditions, as demonstrated for example by $\mathbf { M e C p P t M e } _ { 3 }$ , a popular FEBIP precursor. MeCpPtMe<sub>3</sub> yields basically the same reaction product quality under significantly 53 varying reaction conditions and incident beam energies.
Still, applying our knowledge of electron-induced chemistry to optimize the reaction product quality is in its infancy.
The state-of-the-art on compound design for electron-induced chemistry is currently in the FEBIP field.

--[p374]-- 10.3.3 HafSOx DEVELOPMENT
Conventional HafSOx develops in 25% aqueous TMAH with contrast near $1 0 . ^ { 6 2 }$ It is a negative-tone resist, hence unexposed regions dissolve during development. Aqueous hafnium speciation under such basic conditions has rarely been studied, as Pourbaix diagrams indicate that only solid $\mathrm { H f O } _ { 2 }$ exists at high pH.
--[p374]-- Consequently, the HafSOx system appears to enable a new type of chemical amplification, unlike the expose and bake processes of conventional chemically amplified polymer resists. Sulfate exchange and film neutralization drive formation of a highly insoluble product to create a high differential dissolution rate between unexposed and exposed regions. These processes likely account for the high sensitivity of HafSOx relative to most other inorganic resists.

===== [p186-188] EUV lithography patterning challenges > 5 1 1 INTRODUCTION (9块) =====
--[p187]-- This process is known as immersion lithography.<sup>4,5</sup> Progressing below 193-nm wavelength required a transition to reflective optics despite an attempt of transmission lithography at 157 nm. Reflection optics, however, are not new to lithography, and in fact, they were quite common in the early days of lithography<sup>6e10</sup> before the advent of line narrowed laser sources.<sup>11e13</sup>
--[p187]-- In addition to resolution, another key optical patterning metric is depth of focus (DOF), which can be written as
$$
D O F = { \frac { k _ { 2 } \lambda } { N A ^ { 2 } } }\tag{2}
$$
and describes the longitudinal distance over which the image contrast can be assumed to be constant. Similar to $k _ { 1 }$ in the resolution equation, $k _ { 2 }$ is another process dependent variable, but in general, it can be assumed to be on the order of 0.5.
--[p186]-- 5 1 1 INTRODUCTION
As described in Chapter 4, the unyielding push to patterning smaller semiconductor device features and maintaining Moore’s law have led to a continuous shrink in lithographic patterning wavelength with a transition to 13.5 nm now underway.<sup>1e3</sup> Fundamental optics theory teaches us that the half-pitch patterning resolution limit of an optical system can be expressed as
$$
R = \frac { k _ { 1 } \lambda } { N A }\tag{1}
$$
--[p187]-- Being inversely proportional to ${ \bar { N A } } ^ { 2 }$ , DOF decreases rapidly as a function of increasing NA. This parameter is important because it determines how one expects the quality of the image to evolve through the finite thickness of the resist and also determines how quickly the contrast degrades as the wafer is defocused. Fig. 2 shows the plot of image contrast as a function of defocus for an ideal 0.33-NA EUV system patterning
--[p188]-- 20-nm lines and spaces under the thin mask approximation and a partial coherence of 0.5. We see that with only 60 nm of defocus, the image contrast drops to 50%, which is often assumed to be the limit of what a resist process can handle. Ultimately, a resist process is evaluated based both on the resolution it can achieve at best focus as well as on the defocus range it can tolerate (tolerance to image contrast loss). Evaluating a resist under realistic DOF conditions is thus important.
--[p188]-- One of the benefits of EUV is that it relies much more strongly on the shrink in wavelength than NA to achieve the resolution compared to 193-nm lithography, thus it benefits from relaxed DOF. The first EUV production tools will have a NA of only 0.33.
--[p186]-- where l is the patterning wavelength, NA is the numerical aperture which represents the sin of the half angle of the optic exit pupil as observed from the wafer plane, and $k _ { 1 }$ is the so-called process parameter accounting for the somewhat subjective nature of the definition of resolution. For example, in the Rayleigh definition of resolution, $k _ { 1 }$ is 0.61.
--[p186]-- The absolute limit for $k _ { 1 }$ is 0.25 and the limit for NA in vacuum is 1, making one quarter the wavelength the smallest possible half-pitch one can pattern using conventional imaging methods. This represents the half period of the interference pattern created by two counter-propagating beams.
--[p187]-- Assuming fixed NA, the resolution equation shows us that wavelength shrinks lead directly to pattern shrink (increased pattern density), and the semiconductor industry has continuously made use of this fact as shown in the plot of Moore’s law in Fig. 1. 193i represents using 193-nm wavelength in combination with an immersion fluid, which leads to an effective wavelength given by l/n where n is the index of refraction of the fluid.

--[p360]-- The highest resolutions have been achieved using a high-contrast development process first discovered by Yang et al.<sup>15</sup> Overall, HSQ’s high-resolution capabilities at moderate sensitivities have made it a critical material for R&D prototyping in areas such as nanoelectronics, energy, plasmonics, and data storage.
While HSQ has been very useful as a resist in R&D settings, its wider use is limited.

4. The mechanism by which the radiation-exposed material develops to form a relief pattern.
--[p360]-- 10.2 HYDROGEN SILSESQUIOXANE
HSQ was first developed as a low-k dielectric. Subsequently, in 1998, Namatsu et al.<sup>1</sup> demonstrated the HSQ’s use as a high-resolution e-beam resist. Since then, it has also been shown to act as a resist under other radiation sources such as proton beam,<sup>7</sup> UV light<sup>8</sup> at 157 nm, $\mathbf { E U V } ^ { 9 , 1 0 }$ at 13.5 nm, and $\mathrm { E U V } ^ { 1 1 }$ at 46.7 nm.
--[p360]-- Soon after the initial resist demonstrations, instabilities in the material were observed.<sup>16e18</sup> Van Delft et al.<sup>17</sup> reported changes in contrast and sensitivity as a function of time between deposition and exposure. Clark et al.<sup>19</sup> discovered feature broadening in e-beam-exposed samples as a function of preexposure storage conditions; samples left in dry $\mathrm { N } _ { 2 } ,$ , air, or vacuum experienced broadening.
--[p360]-- The behavior of HSQ when processed as a dielectric: HSQ was initially used as a low-k dielectric, which was cured by heating to temperatures above $2 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ where reaction changes are more prevalent. Hence, there is a large body of literature on spinning and baking HSQ to optimize low-k conditions.
(The relationship between e-beam and thermal crosslinking reactions will be covered in Section 10.3.)
2.
--[p361]-- Spin and bake issues related to HSQ as a resist: In this case, we consider changes in HSQ when baked below $2 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , as higher temperatures cause significant preexposure crosslinking, preventing its use as a resist. Even at these low temperatures, the bake temperature, delay between exposure and development, and ambient conditions all play a part in resist performance.
3.
--[p360]-- The capability for very high resolution (sub-5-nm half-pitch) has been demonstrated with He ion-beam lithography<sup>12</sup> and e-beam lithography,<sup>13,14</sup> as exemplified in Fig. 3.
--[p360]-- These instabilities are mitigated with higher doses and stronger developers but at the expense of sensitivity.<sup>18</sup> Here, we will discuss the mechanism of HSQ exposure and development, with consideration given to instability. The HSQ discussion is broken into four sections:

===== [p105-106] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.2.1 ATOMIC PHOTOEMISSION (12块) =====
--[p105]-- For solids the BE is referred to the Fermi level, while for atomic and molecular systems<sup>17</sup> it is more useful to refer to the vacuum level, $B E _ { \nu a c u u m } = h \nu - K E _ { p h o t o e l e c t r o n } .$
The “cross section” s, with units of area, is way of describing the probability of molecular, atomic, and nuclear interactions with radiation.
--[p105]-- In addition to the X-ray absorption cross section, the inelastic and elastic electron-molecule scattering cross sections are important for EUV radiation chemistry, as are the molecular ionization and fragmentation cross sections for both X-rays and electrons. If the cross section is small compared to the physical area of the target, the interaction probability is small.
--[p106]-- Subshell cross sections decrease rapidly with increasing photoelectron KE, although the energy dependence can be more complex close to threshold.<sup>18</sup> The cross section also depends on the occupation of the orbital, so a filled d-level with 10 electrons will usually have a higher cross section than a filled s-level with only two electrons for similar BE. Calculated subshell cross sections for all the elements are tabulated by Yeh and Lindau.<sup>19</sup>
--[p106]-- The photoemission cross section is proportional to a dipole matrix element between the wave functions of the initial bound electron orbital and the final outgoing free electron wave. This matrix element involves an integral over the overlap of the two wave functions.<sup>18</sup> The phase of the outgoing wave oscillates with a wavelength proportional to $\mathrm { K E } ^ { 1 / 2 }$ .
--[p106]-- Cross sections for high angular momentum d and f orbitals can show a “delayed maxima.”<sup>20</sup> Unlike s and p levels, where the maximum cross section is very close to the threshold photon energy, the maximum for higher angular momentum states can occur 30 or 40 eVabove threshold. This is due to the so-called “centrifugal repulsion term” in the effective radial potential for a high angular momentum electron wave.<sup>20</sup> This effect can be important at EUVenergies, as seen in Fig.
2, where many of the 4d elements have large cross sections.
--[p105]-- 2.2.1 ATOMIC PHOTOEMISSION
The electronic structure of an isolated atom can be described as a series of 1-electron orbitals or energy levels, defined by the principal quantum number $n ( = I , 2 , 3 . . . )$ and the orbital angular momentum $l \left( s = 0 , p = I , d = 2 , f = 3 \right)$ , each with its own binding energy (BE).
--[p106]-- As the wavelength becomes smaller than the radial size of the bound electron orbital, the positive and negative phase contributions to the overlap integral tend to cancel out, resulting in a rapid decrease of the orbital cross section with energy. The decrease in cross section is faster for weakly bound valence orbitals than for core orbitals since their radial wave functions are more extended. For large KE, the cross section will drop $\mathrm { o f f } ^ { 1 8 }$ as KE <sup>3</sup>.
--[p105]-- In the nuclear and atomic physics literature, cross sections are sometimes expressed in units of “barns” or $1 0 \ ^ { \ 2 8 } \mathrm { ~ m } ^ { 2 }$ , the typical scattering cross section of an atomic nucleus, so 100 Mb, or megabarn, corresponds to an area of 1 $\mathring { \mathbf { A } } ^ { 2 } ( 1 0 \ ^ { 2 0 } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } )$
--[p105]-- If the number-density of targets is given by n, then the interaction mean free path $\lambda = 1 / n \sigma$ and the probability of photon absorption in a film of thickness t is $1 - e ^ { \ n \sigma t }$ .
--[p106]-- Each orbital has its own energy-dependent X-ray absorption cross section $\sigma _ { n , l } ( h \nu , Z )$ , sometimes called a “subshell cross section,” where Z is the atomic number.
--[p106]-- The radial wavefuction of a bound orbital has a radial node, where the phase of the orbital changes sign, when the orbital angular momentum l is greater that the principal quantum number n. This phase change also affects the matrix element overlap integral, and causes a so-called Cooper minimum in the subshell cross section around 10 20 eV above threshold.<sup>20</sup> Cooper minima occur for 3p, 4d, and 5f orbitals, as shown by Yeh and Lindau.<sup>19</sup>
--[p105]-- The binding energies of the occupied states are directly measured through photoemission experiment s on solid materials<sup>12</sup> where $B E _ { F e r m i } + \phi = h \nu - K E _ { p h o t o e l e c t r o n }$ represents energy conservation the BE plus the sample work function (f) is the difference between the incoming photon energy (hn) and the outgoing electron KE.

===== [p373-374] Mainstreaming inorganic metal-oxide resists for high-resolution lithography > 10.3.2 HafSOx THIN-FILM DEPOSITION, BAKE, AND EXPOSE (8块) =====
--[p373]-- Peroxide-free materials lose approximately 20% of their mass as water on heating to $2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ Sulfate decomposes and evolves as $\mathrm { S O } _ { 2 }$ near $8 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , so films retain sulfate through lithographically relevant baking and exposure steps.
--[p373]-- From O1s XPS spectra, baking increases the oxide peak corresponding to HFeOeHF and decreases the peak corresponding to HFeOH, indicating that a soft bake drives water loss and condensation (Fig. 2).<sup>61</sup> Stowers, working with Olynick at the Molecular
Foundry, first observed the $8 3 5 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ Raman peak corresponding to HF-bound ${ { \mathrm O } _ { 2 } } ^ { 2 - }$ in films containing peroxide.
--[p374]-- For patterning, the post-application bake temperature is typically $8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . At this temperature, compositions are substantially uniform through the film volume,<sup>62</sup> but a thin 1-nm crust rich in HF and deficient in sulfate forms at the surface.<sup>63</sup> As determined by QCM analysis, these films gain mass as ambient relative humidity rises and lose mass as humidity falls. The films effectively breathe $_ { \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O } }$ .
--[p373]-- 10.3.2 HafSOx THIN-FILM DEPOSITION, BAKE, AND EXPOSE
HafSOx solutions uniformly coat hydrophilic 300-mm wafers by spin coating. Compared with conventional polymer resists, films are quite thin, typically 15e 20 nm.
--[p374]-- Even in films baked at high temperatures, water resorption occurs via dissociative and molecular mechanisms.<sup>61</sup> Capping layers and other techniques have failed to yield means to control and stabilize film water content.
HafSOx films have been lithographically patterned by e-beam, 193-nm laser, and EUV exposures. Peroxide-free HafSOx does not pattern, so peroxide regulates relevant radiation-induced reactions.
--[p374]-- Stowers, working with Olynick and Ogletree at the Molecular Foundry, observed $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ( \mathrm { g } )$ evolution using mass spectrometry during ebeam exposure of HafSox. Similar results have been observed in electronstimulated desorption<sup>64</sup> and EUV outgassing studies.<sup>65</sup> $_ { \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } }$ has also been observed in EUVoutgassing work. By correlating the peroxide Raman signal to exposure dose and contrast, Amador et al.

--[p364]-- 10.2.2 HSQ EXPOSURE MECHANISM
The exposure mechanism in HSQ has most frequently been investigated with vibrational spectroscopies such as Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR)<sup>1,18,30e36</sup> a nd Raman spectroscopy.<sup>36</sup> Generally, the vibrational spectroscopy changes seen with e-beam-induced chemistry are similar to those observed upon heating of HSQ. --[p364]-- Similar radiation-induced changes were observed by other author s.<sup>18,30e35</sup> After development in aqueous tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH) and potassium hydroxide (KOH), Namatsu et al. found rapid dissolution of the unexposed material relative to the e-beam-exposed material. From FTIR studies, the following reaction for e-beam exposure was surmised (to date, this mechanism has not been fully substantiated, and some evidence against it is discussed in the following section):
$$

$$
$$
2 \mathrm { O } _ { 3 / 2 } \mathrm { S i } ^ { \cdot } + 2 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }  2 \mathrm { O } _ { 3 / 2 } \mathrm { S i O H } + \mathrm { H } _ { 2 }\tag{10}
$$
$$
2 \mathrm { O } _ { 3 / 2 } \mathrm { S i O H }  2 \mathrm { S i O } _ { 4 / 2 } + \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }\tag{11}
$$
--[p364]-- Namatsu et al.<sup>1</sup> were the first to study the HSQ e-beam-exposure mechanism using FTIR. They reported changes indicative of a shift from the cage to the networked structure. Decreases in the SieH peak (Table 1, peak 1) indicate the loss of SieH bonds, which is expected upon the formation of the network structure.
--[p365]-- Beyond the $\mathrm { S i H } _ { 4 }$ reaction,<sup>36</sup> there are surely other processes at play. For instance, besides $\mathrm { S i H _ { 4 } }$ desorption, Olynick et al. also observed the generation of significant amounts of hydrogen. However, the role of water in the reaction mechanism is unknown. During e-beam exposure, water was not detected in the gas phase above the background pressure,<sup>36</sup> putting the reaction in Eq. (11) into
--[p364]-- Olynick et al. combined Raman and FTIR to further study the e-beam-exposure mechanism. The observed both a decrease in the SieH peaks and the formation of $\mathrm { S i \mathrm { - } H } _ { 2 }$ peaks (Table 1, peak 2). This indicates that the redistribution reaction, identified thermally [Eq. (1)], also occurs with e-beam.<sup>36</sup> The reaction in Eq. (1) is illustrated in Fig. 5.

===== [p234-235] Negative-tone organic molecular resists > FIGURE 1 (8块) =====
--[p235]-- In contrast Section 8.7 focuses primarily on functional group rather than core structure and covers cationic polymerization and cross-linking of functional groups such as epoxides. Because this functional group has been used in resist designs for almost all core structures, a section is dedicated to better understanding the chemistry and physics of this group along with reviews of several polyphenol-based resists that use this chemistry.
--[p234]-- As the linewidth required continues to decrease and approaches the size of the polymers used in traditional resists, molecular resists offer a potential route to higher resolution with their smaller molecule size. They feature smaller, lower molecular weight components, which are produced with monodispersity (or much less polydispersity) and excellent compositional control. As the units are identical, a much more homogenous distribution in the film with a smaller free volume should be achieved.
This combination was expected to have a significant impact on line-edge roughness (LER), as illustrated in Fig.
--[p234]-- Despite the lack of substantial improvement in LER, negative-tone molecular resists have shown significant promise as higher resolution materials. As will be reviewed in this chapter, there are many reports of resolutions below 20 nm, several below 15 nm, and a few materials operating in a nonchemically amplified mode have sub-10-nm resolution.
--[p234]-- For negative-tone patterning, the small molecule starting materials appear to lead to less swelling during development than in similar polymeric systems because the smaller unexposed materials dissolve faster; this will be discussed further in Section 8.7.4.
This chapter is broken down into several sections, each usually based on the core molecular structure of the resist.
--[p235]-- As the pattern tone of a molecule is often determined by its functional groups, there will certainly be an overlap with positive-tone materials with the same molecular cores, but different functionalization (see Chapter 9). Sections 8.2e8.6 introduce fullerene, triphenylene, calixarene, noria, and polyphenol resists, respectively.
--[p235]-- Finally, Section 8.8 contains a wide variety of different core structures that are no less important or impactful but have been reported less frequently, such as dendrimers and cyclodextrins. While no review can be absolutely complete, the chapter endeavors to cover most of the common and widely reported molecular structures.

===== [p119-119] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.5.1 DIFFERENCES IN EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET LITHOGRAPHY AND ELECTRON BEAM LITHOGRAPHY (6块) =====
--[p119]-- Unlike EUVL, the HOMO is the most likely orbital to be ionized, and ionization cross sections<sup>54</sup> for deeper levels drop off as at least $1 / \mathrm { B E } . ^ { 2 }$ In most cases there will be little residual internal energy in the ionized molecule, and relaxation processes will be relatively unimportant. The molecular ionization cross section will have a relatively weak material dependence, unlike $\sigma _ { E U V }$ The average SE KE is w10 20 eV.
--[p119]-- 2.5.1 DIFFERENCES IN EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET LITHOGRAPHY AND ELECTRON BEAM LITHOGRAPHY
The fundamental relaxation processes for excited molecules are identical for EUVL and EBL. The differences arise from the distribution of excitations. Molecular relaxation is critically important in EUVL, especially if high s<sub>EUV</sub> atoms are involved.
--[p119]-- Quadrupole mass spectrometers or residual gas analyzers typically use 70-eV electrons for ionization, and fragmentation effects (cracking patterns) must be considered in spectral interpretation.<sup>55</sup>
--[p119]-- The challenge for resist designers will be to develop molecular systems that can harness this simultaneous localized explosion of chemical energy in the form of low energy electrons, radicals, and ions for pattern generation.
The EBL excitation process is fundamentally different. Fast w50-keV primary electrons excite molecules by inelastic electron scattering.
--[p119]-- Since the deepest levels have the highest photoionization probability, the photoelectrons will have relatively low energy, and molecules will be left with a significant amount of residual internal energy. Relaxation will generate additional SEs, followed by molecular fragmentation into radicals and radical ions.
--[p119]-- Radiation chemistry is driven by the generation of SEs isolated in space and time, rather than the localized explosion of EUVL.
HOMO ionization is the dominant EBL process, but fast primary electrons can also ionize deep core levels, although the relative cross section is much reduced. This is the basis of electron-excited Auger spectroscopy and microscopy.<sup>12</sup> Electron impact ionization can also fragment molecules.

--[p145]-- As mentioned, the jump from DUV to EUV involves many technological challenges. While those challenges are being resolved from the tool performance point of view, materials also need to be developed in parallel. --[p146]-- With EUV-IL, it is also possible to pattern several square mm in a step and repeat manner, making this technique considerably faster than e-beam lithography for the production of high-resolution nanostructures for academic research.<sup>8</sup> Aside from proving to be an enabling technique for patterning dense periodic and quasi periodic<sup>9</sup> structures with sub-10-nm resolution, such an achievement shows the great potential of using EUV-IL for the evaluation of the performance and ultimate resolution limits of different photoresists for future technology nodes and will be treated in this chapter.
--[p144]-- Yet, such predictions have been proven untrue time and time again due to constant developments in optical (stepper, repeater, and scanner) and exposure systems (contact, proximity, projection, and immersion), wavelength reduction (g-line: l 436 nm, i-line: $\lambda = 3 5 6$ nm, deep ultraviolet (DUV): KrF, $\lambda = 2 4 8$ nm; and ArF, l  193 nm), resist materials, topography reduction methods (chemical mechanical planarization), and other resolution enhancement methodologies over the years.<sup>2</sup>

In the simplest of terms, optical resolution (R) is proportional to the exposure wavelength l and inversely proportional to the numerical aperture (NA) of the exposure system, 3
$$
R = \frac { k \lambda } { N A }\tag{1}
$$
--[p145]-- Therefore, it is theoretically feasible to resolve features down below 4 nm with EUV lithography at 13.5 nm. Nonetheless, light sources with high efficiency or highly sensitive photoresist materials that can make this possible in HVM are still under development. In fact, the introduction of EUV radiation into photolithography systems has brought significant challenges. As all matter absorbs EUV, exposure within vacuum systems and reflective optics with multilayer coatings have to be developed.

--[p144]-- 4.1 INTRODUCTION
There is no doubt that lithographic performance in the semiconductor industry has been driven by the constant need of device (logic and memory) size miniaturization and productivity as dictated by Moore’s Law.<sup>1</sup> Nonetheless, resolution-related limitations have constantly threatened to end the semiconductor technology roadmap since photolithography was introduced as the workhorse of the fab four decades ago in the early 1970s.
--[p145]-- EUV light generation with high power and efficiency is still a formidable challenge. Other viable alternatives to optical lithography such as electron beam lithography (e-beam) that can meet the resolution requirements (but not the high throughput requirements of the semiconductor industry) have also been considered and were discussed briefly in Chapter 1. E-beam has been widely used for research applications or photomask fabrication.<sup>2</sup>
--[p146]-- Single-digit-resolution nanopatterning with extreme ultraviolet light for the 2.5 nm technology node and beyond. Nanoscale 2015;7:4031e7 and reproduced by permission of The Royal Society of Chemistry.
of EUV resists. These tools provide high-resolution aerial images, mimicking the aerial image of a scanner to a certain extent. Nevertheless, the tool costs are relatively high, in particular due to high-resolution optics.
--[p145]-- Current high-volume manufacturing (HVM) of semiconductor devices with sub-100-nm resolution is only possible with DUV-immersion lithography by multiple patterning which is rapidly becoming costly and complex. For this reason, extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography at $\lambda = 1 3 . 5$ nm (a photon energy of 92 eV) represents the future of photolithography. The maximum resolution that can be achieved by optical lithography methods is limited by light diffraction to l/4.
--[p146]-- 1) and 8-nm resolution dense patterning by the use of a Si-based and hafnium-based photoresist, respectively, has been demonstrated by using EUV-IL, which up to now is still the world record resolution for photon-based lithography.<sup>7</sup> The simple, well-defined, and high-resolution aerial image of EUV-IL makes it a powerful tool for photoresist development.

===== [p486-486] Next generation lithographydthe rise of unconventional methods? > 14.1 THE ULTIMATE DRIVING FORCE: MOORE’S LAW (3块) =====
--[p486]-- However, only by the development of new lithographic concepts, composed of both top-down and bottom-up approaches, might the trend of downscaling be continued in the future.
--[p486]-- The main aim of nanolithography is the creation of nanoelectronic devices and nanoelectromechanical systems, which possess innovative properties and functions due to their small size range of 1e10 nm. Thus, nanotechnology is becoming a widespread field of research and enables a wealth of new applications and visions. As transistor number per chip increases, each transistor becomes much tinier, quicker, and less expensive, providing an unprecedented increase in processor performance.
--[p486]-- 14.1 THE ULTIMATE DRIVING FORCE: MOORE’S LAW
Nowadays, rapid development of electronic devices is observed. The trend to miniaturization of integrated circuits is becoming more intense. To meet the growing demand for miniaturization, new and sophisticated nanolithography methods and associated technologies such as resist technology are being developed.

===== [p16-17] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.2 OVERVIEW OF LITHOGRAPHY PROCESS (11块) =====
--[p16]-- UV light is then shone through a mask, which selectively allows light through certain regions to generate a pattern on the resist. The mask has historically been made of quartz with chrome patterns on top that control where the light shines through the mask. The radiation pattern from the UV light induces chemical changes in the resist, which selectively modifies the solubility of the exposed regions in a liquid called developer.
--[p17]-- This etch process could be a wet or chemical etch where liquid chemicals selectively remove the underlayer (UL) while having a minimal effect on the remaining photoresist. However, it is more common that the etching is done using plasma etching where high energy particles selectively etch the UL compared to the remaining resist.
--[p16]-- Positive-tone resists are those where the exposed areas are dissolved during development; the solubility change is often due to chemistry that occurs during exposure or in the PEB which changes the polarity or functional groups of the resist. Negative-tone resists are those where the exposed regions are not dissolved during development and the exposed areas are dissolved instead.
--[p16]-- 1.2 OVERVIEW OF LITHOGRAPHY PROCESS
Lithography is the art and science of producing a pattern on a substrate. The term is used most often today in connection with semiconductor processing.
--[p16]-- Solubility change in these materials can likewise occur by many different methods, although two of the most common are cross-linking to form high molecular weight network structures and changes in functional groups of the resist which affect polarity.
Finally, the remaining pattern in the developed resist is transferred into the underlying film stack using an etch process.
--[p16]-- The most commonly used form of lithography in high volume manufacturing is optical lithography and a generalized overview of the process is shown in Fig. 2.
A highly simplified description of the process is as follows. The substrate (usually a silicon wafer) is usually coated with a thin film of a functional material or a multilayer stack of materials that could serve any number of roles such as low-k or high-k dielectric, etch-resistant hard mask, or conducting layer.
--[p17]-- Recent advances have even shown the possibility of atomic level control with the introduction of atomic layer etching.<sup>6e8</sup>
After all the desired modifications are completed in the underlying film stack, any remaining photoresist is removed through a plasma or chemical stripping process. This lithographic process is then repeated (sometimes multiple times) for each layer of the device to allow for fabrication of complete ICs.
--[p16]-- Photoresist, which is a photosensitive material that is typically composed mostly of an organic polymer, is then spin coated onto the film stack. The term photoresist is often shortened simply to resist which is also a more general term for these types of materials; especially since resists for many alternative and future exposure sources would not be exposed to photons but rather electrons, ions, or other physical sources of a pattern.
--[p16]-- The wafer is commonly baked after this exposure step [called a postexposure bake (PEB)] to further induce chemical change in the exposed regions.
The development step is next, and is where developer is poured or sprayed onto the resist and certain regions of the resist are dissolved, while other regions remain on the wafer. The exposed regions will either be dissolved or remain depending on the tone of the resist.
--[p17]-- Plasma etching allows a high level of control and selectivity at both the nanoscale and wafer size scale by changing the various parameters in the etch chamber such as etch gases and species, voltage, bias on the wafer, pressure, and local wafer temperature, among many others. By controlling the time and type of gases used, plasma etching can go from isotropic to highly anisotropic etching profiles.
--[p16]-- Additional adjectives are often used to more specifically define the technique such as optical lithography or photolithography (using UV light to generate the patterns), imprint lithography (a mold is pressed or imprinted into a material to generate the patterns), e-beam lithography (electron beams are used to generate the pattern), or EUV lithography.

===== [p222-222] Chemically amplified resists and acid amplifiers > 7.2 EUV CAR RESISTS (7块) =====
--[p222]-- Some of the reported ways to lower acid diffusion included high $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ polymer matrix,<sup>11</sup> hydrophilic polymer matrix,<sup>12</sup> large polar acid anion design,<sup>13</sup> Photoacid generator (PAG) anion incorporation in the polymer,<sup>14,15</sup> and the photodestroyable quencher<sup>16,17</sup> concept. With these methods of diffusion control, it has been shown that 13-nm hp is possible using CAR resists, see Fig. 2.
--[p222]-- It has been estimated that 4% of the radiation from the EUV exposure tool is unwanted OOB.<sup>18</sup> Roberts et al.<sup>19</sup> found the OOB sensitivity of the resists they examined can be estimated to within an order of magnitude using the resist absorbance value.
--[p222]-- 7.2 EUV CAR RESISTS
EUV CAR resists developed following the extensive learning curve already developed over the longer wavelengths. The first widely available EUV resists were simply extensions of the previously developed Environmentally Stable Chemical Amplification Photoresist (ESCAP) resists based on Poly(p-hydroxy)Styrene (PHS)/styrene/t-butyl acrylate polymers,<sup>7</sup> as shown in Fig. 1.
--[p222]-- These resists are robust with the necessary fast sensitivity required and reasonable resolution of 30-nm half-pitch (hp).<sup>8</sup> These resists were used extensively in the early tool development stage. As more was learned during the early resist development stage, it became clear that specific resist materials optimized for the 13.5-nm wavelength were needed.
--[p222]-- Other issues particular to EUV lithography have led to novel resist concepts. One particular issue is the effect of out-of-band (OOB) radiation on resist performance. OOB is unwanted wavelengths exposing the EUV resist. OOB wavelengths of greater concern are 248 and 193 nm.
--[p222]-- Resist designers use PAGs such as triphenyl sulfonium (TPS) extensively, but it has been shown that TPS has high sensitivity to OOB radiation.<sup>6</sup> What is really necessary for EUV is to design PAGs that have high sensitivity to EUV but little to no sensitivity to the longer wavelengths. Indeed, some novel PAGs with low sensitivity to OOB have been designed.<sup>20e22</sup>
--[p222]-- Some of the best early work focused on cycloaliphatic polymers as used in 193-nm resists versus phenol-containing resists as developed for 248 nm. Fedynyshyn et al.<sup>9</sup> found extensive matrix effects affecting overall resist sensitivity. Yamamoto et al.<sup>10</sup> found that proton donor source such as vinyl phenol can enhance acid generation in EUV exposure. One key insight was the necessity to control acid diffusion to enhance CAR resolution.

===== [p430-431] SML electron beam resist: ultra-high aspect ratio nanolithography > 12.2 PHOTOMASK PRODUCTION (10块) =====
--[p431]-- A pattern can be directly written into the resist, and this can then be used directly as the photomask. Once the mask had been created in this way, it could be used in production or replicated in to chrome masks via contact photolithography, which is significantly faster than EBL. This approach would significantly lower production costs, allowing rapid prototyping and significant reduction in the production cost of a chrome photomask.
--[p430]-- 12.2 PHOTOMASK PRODUCTION
Clearly, the photolithography process requires a photomask. The photomask is fabricated by depositing a chrome layer with a thickness of typically 100e200 nm on to a transparent substrate such as quartz or borosilicate glass. The chrome material and a transparent substrate offer a 100% contrast (i.e., incident light is completely blocked in the chromed areas), which provides the high-quality pattern definition into the resist.
--[p430]-- In this approach, a substrate is coated with a polymer thin film called an electron beam resist material, which is analogous to the photoresist used in photolithography. Features are patterned into the resist material using a beam of electrons. In a positive-tone electron beam resist, the mechanism of solubility change is typically via a reduction in the molecular weight of the polymer chains by electron-induced chain scission. This increases the solubility of the polymer in organic solvents.
--[p431]-- However, to produce a photomask from a single processing step, the optical properties of the resist film would be required to block g, h, and i-line UV sources (436, 405, and 365 nm) as well as KrF and ArF excimer deep UV (DUV) sources (248 and 193 nm).
--[p431]-- Once the pattern has been achieved in the electron beam resist, it must be transferred into the underlying chrome thin film. This can be achieved by a dry etching technique that requires an oxygen and/or chlorine plasma. The oxygen and/or chlorine ions in the plasma are accelerated towards the target chrome film. Whilst some physical sputtering occurs, the reaction is primarily chemical.
--[p430]-- Photomask sets represent a major portion of the cost-of-ownership in semiconductor fabrication, with up to 100 individual masks required for a chip fabricated with the current lithographic process of 193-nm double patterning immersion lithography.
Photomasks are produced using a technique called electron beam lithography (EBL). This is a standard technique used widely by the photomask industry to create a photomask with high-resolution features.
--[p431]-- The chrome that is directly underneath the electron beam resist will be protected from the oxygen and chlorine ions; after etching the electron beam resist is removed using an organic solvent, producing a fully fabricated photomask.
Clearly, there are a number of consecutive processing steps, each of which must be perfectly realized in order to produce a photomask.
--[p431]-- This, together with the low-throughput serial nature of EBL, makes it very difficult, and very expensive to produce a photomask. Therefore, there is a motivation to fabricate a photomask with one processing step, eliminating the need for an etch.
This can be achieved by replacing the absorbing material (usually a metal, e.g., chrome) with the electron beam resist, by spinning it on either borosilicate glass or quartz.
--[p431]-- In particular, due to the chemical (rather than physical) nature of the chrome plasma etch, it is difficult to achieve good pattern transfer. Lateral etch rates are typically high due to diffusion of etch species, and the process also suffers from significant loading and microloading effects (where the overall level of unmasked chrome, and the density of highresolution feature can both lead to variable etching rates).
--[p431]-- The chlorine and oxygen ions chemically attack the surface of the chrome, producing predominantly CrClO and $\mathrm { C r C l } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } .$ , which are volatile at room temperature. These volatile products are transported away by the use of a vacuum.

===== [p233-233] Negative-tone organic molecular resists > 8.1 INTRODUCTION (8块) =====
--[p233]-- Positive-tone systems developed in the aqueous base tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH) have tended to dominate industrial applications to the present day.
--[p233]-- Although research on novel and improved negativetone resists has steadily continued since the early ages of commercial photolithography, the semiconductor industry has gone through cycles of increasing and decreasing interest in negative-tone resists. One of the earliest workhorse materials for the semiconductor industry was the Kodak Thin Film Resistda negative-tone cyclized rubber and/or bisazide cross-linking system.
--[p233]-- The term molecular resist and molecular glass (MG) resist can effectively be used interchangeably, but the term molecular resist is less precise. Glasses are amorphous solids that have a glass transition from a hard brittle state to a soft “rubbery” texture below the melting point of the material. The glass transition temperature $\mathrm { ( T _ { g } ) }$ of the material needs to be sufficiently high to form stable thin films and allow thermal processing without impacting the patterned image.
--[p233]-- In order to achieve this, molecules with rigid cyclic cores such as polyphenols are used. To avoid crystallization and ensure amorphous, disordered film formation they possess nonplanar, irregular shapes such as branched or ring structures. Likewise, it is important to emphasize that this review will be focused on organic small molecules in comparison to other
--[p233]-- This was supplanted after about 15 years by a positive-tone diazonaphthoquinone/novolac (DNQ/novolac) resist due to swelling failures in the former as feature sizes reduced.<sup>1</sup> With the move from ultraviolet (UV) to deep UV (DUV) exposure wavelengths the sensitivity of DNQ/novolac proved to be insufficient, leading to the development of the chemical amplification (CA) concept.<sup>2</sup> The earliest commercial application of DUV lithography used a chemically amplified resist (CAR) with negative-tone imaging of tertbutoxycarbonyl (tBOC) protected polyhydroxystyrene (PHOST) using a solvent developer (anisole). This negative-tone development process was quickly supplanted by an aqueous base developed positive-tone CAR operating via a similar mechanism.
--[p233]-- These new materials became available through research efforts in developing new, better resists, and understanding their properties with the goal of improving performance. Similar to previous resist platforms, small molecule resists have seen a wide array of different approaches and design schemes with the same goals.
This chapter reviews work in the area of negative-tone molecular resists. These can be defined as resists based on small organic molecules that can form amorphous films.
--[p233]-- 8.1 INTRODUCTION
Negative-tone resists are materials whose solubility decreases upon exposure to radiation. This solubility change can occur in any number of different ways, but the two most common are a change in polarity or a substantial increase in molecular weight through cross-linking.
--[p233]-- However, negative-tone imaging has once again gained attention recently due to the potential for improved imaging due to the better image contrast using a light field mask.<sup>3e5</sup> In many of these instances, the shift in interest was driven by the technological superiority of the negative-tone resist or by the ability to access improved imaging capability with a different resist.
