Power requirements at the mask can then be determined by factoring in the losses in the imaging optics. For first generation commercial tools, we expect a total of six imaging mirrors, and if we assume an average reflectivity of 66% per mirror, we get a total efficiency of 8.27%.
--[p191]-- Given the significant challenge of achieving even this level of power with high availability, there are very significant constraints on further relaxing the sensitivity requirements from 15 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>. --[p191]-- Note that, as the technology pushes to higher NA in the future, the number of mirrors’ requirement would be expected to increase. --[p190]-- The driving requirement is wafer throughput, which must be set to be high enough for EUV to be more economically viable than the current approach of multiple patterning with 193i. In this example, we set the requirement to be 145 wafers per hour, which is considerably slower than 193i tools.

===== [p158-159] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.3.1 INTRODUCTION TO CHEMICALLY AMPLIFIED RESISTS (7块) =====
--[p158]-- The chemical amplification or sensitivity improvement results from the fact that the acid generated upon exposure (by photolysis of the PAG, also known as a sensitizer), catalyzes the deprotection reaction (cleavage of pendant groups on polymer side chains, i.e., the capped polyaldehyde molecules).<sup>49</sup> Photolysis of the PAG salt produces a local concentration of strong Brønsted acids.
--[p158]-- The main motivation for developing such an idea originated from the fact that the quantum yield (measure of the efficiency of the photochemical transformation, molecules transformed per photons absorbed, or the number of molecules transformed/sensitized per photons absorbed during exposure) for traditional Novolac resin photoresist with diazonaphthoquinone (DNQ) sensitizers, as typically used in the early 1980s, was quite low.<sup>49</sup>
--[p158]-- In the original chemically amplified system from Ito et al.,<sup>47e49</sup> a capped or protected poly(phthalaldehyde) and a photo acid generator (PAG)dcationic photo initiators, such as triarylsulfonium salts, that produce strong acids upon exposuredwere used.
--[p158]-- This allows dual tone imaging by just changing the developer/solvent solution.<sup>47</sup> The deprotection reaction in the early days of chemical amplification was originally designed for self-development but was later modified to for thermal development (thermally activated during a post-exposure bake, PEB) to prevent tool contamination.<sup>50,51</sup>
--[p158]-- During a subsequent postexposure bake, the acid product catalyzes the cleavage of pendant groups on the side chains of the polymer matrix. In this way, the polymer undergoes acidolysis that results in a polarity and solubility change. Exposed areas can then be selectively removed in a polar solvent such as an aqueous base or alcohol resulting in positivetone resist image.
Alternatively, unexposed areas can be selectively removed when a nonpolar solvent (anisole) is used resulting in a negative-tone resist image.
--[p158]-- 4.3.1 INTRODUCTION TO CHEMICALLY AMPLIFIED RESISTS
Ito et al.<sup>47e49</sup> from IBM introduced the chemical amplification concept (by means of an acid catalyst) in the early 1980s.
--[p159]-- The chemical amplification concept has become the foundation upon which state-of-the-art photoresist technology has been continuously designed and developed from the early 1990s with the introduction of the excimer DUV laser (KrF, $\lambda = 2 4 8$ nm, ArF, $\lambda = 1 9 3 ~ \mathrm { { n m } ) }$ 2

===== [p165-167] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.3.5 QUANTUM EFFICIENCY (5块) =====
--[p167]-- However, as mentioned previously, the QE needs to be higher in EUV than in the DUV photoresists because there are 14 fewer photons per unit volume at equal dose.<sup>60</sup> It has been shown for one CAR resist, that for a given level of photoacid produced in the latent image, the DUV QE was 0.33, while in EUV QE it was up to 2.08.<sup>52</sup> In other words, the QE at EUV increases in comparison to DUV, which acts to (at least partially) offset the lower number of photons for a given energy dose. In this regard, chemical amplification seems indispensable for EUV resist, owing to the lack of intense EUV sources.
A straightforward way of improving the QE is by increasing the concentration of PAGs in the resist (when feasible).
--[p165]-- The efficiency of forming the latent image from the aerial image is defined by the quantum efficiency, QE:
$$
\mathrm { Q E } = \frac { \# \mathrm { a c t i v a t e d ~ p h o t o a c i d s } } { \# \mathrm { a b s o r b e d ~ p h o t o n s } }\tag{13}
$$

The definition of QE requires knowledge of the number of activated photoacids and their initial concentration. This value can be derived with different techniques, for example, from the Dill parameter C (i.e., exposure kinetics) and the initial PAG concentration. The number of absorbed photons can be estimated from the exposure dose, provided that the absorption coefficient is known.
In chemically amplified photoresists, formation of the latent image is mediated by photoacid generators both at DUV and EUV.
--[p167]-- By doing so, values up to 3.5 were obtained in a poly(4-hydroxystyrene) polymer which is commonly used for EUV resists (Fig. 16). 83
However, increasing the concentration of PAGs is effective only up to a given amount; beyond that, no significant improvement is achieved, possibly due to a single SE ionized at EUV having insufficient energy to activate more than 4w5 PAGs. For CARs, it is therefore important to maximize the PAG chemistry to maximally exploit the energy from SEs.
--[p165]-- 4.3.5 QUANTUM EFFICIENCY
PAGs are not excited directly by the EUV light but via the secondary thermal electrons at energies <15 eV. In comparison, in ArF lithography, the DUV light directly triggers the photolysis of the PAG.<sup>82</sup> Acid generated from a PAG deprotects the polymer matrix, making it soluble to the alkali for the development. This chemical reaction takes place in a spatial region of the photoresist defined as the deprotection sphere.

===== [p161-163] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.3.3 RESIST ABSORPTION (14块) =====
--[p161]-- 4.3.3 RESIST ABSORPTION
The linear absorption coefficient defines the proportion of photons that interact while passing through a material. In the case of spin-coated photoresists, the optimum absorption is a tradeoff between efficiently harvesting the incoming light and the need to maintain a constant intensity throughout the film thickness. DUV and pre-DUV photoresists were designed to pattern critical dimensions (CDs) >100 nm and to coat at 200e800-nm thickness.
--[p161]-- • EUV photons are very expensive due to the complexity, cost, and limited power of EUV sources.
• Photoresists for sub-20-nm resolutions are designed to coat at w45-nm thickness and below (due to pattern collapse at high aspect ratios), which decreases their absorbance.
The photon density is about 14 times higher for 193-nm ArF excimer laser lithography in comparison to EUV at the same dose. Fig.
--[p163]-- Measurement of the photoabsorption coefficient contributes to a more complete understanding of the mechanisms that govern the generation of secondary photoelectrons. It is also worth mentioning additional studies that are shedding light on this phenomenon. An EUV photon has an energy of $\sim 9 2 \mathrm { e V } ,$ and upon absorption, it can excite high-energy core electrons (deep below the valence band).
--[p161]-- It has been reported that fluorine-based resists can improve the absorption from 5.2 to $7 . 0 \mu \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 }$ , but more development is required because the change in backbone polymers significantly affects acid generation, acid diffusion, catalytic chain reactions, and dissolution. Other studies have reported fluorinated versions of PMMA which could in principle provide up to $1 8 ~  { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ absorbance (up from $3 .
--[p161]-- 10 illustrates the significant difference between deep ultraviolet lithography and extreme ultraviolet lithography for relevant dose levels.<sup>60,61</sup> As fewer photons are absorbed per energy, photon shot noise becomes a major concern in EUV lithography.
--[p163]-- A completely novel approach for the incorporation of metal in EUV resists is the so-called metal-oxide resists, which are novel photoresists that can be patterned into pseudooxide. These materials are for the most part, nonchemically amplified.
--[p161]-- Conventional photoresists synthesized from organic polymers (which contain mostly oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen) have a linear absorption coefficient, a, ranging between 2 and 5 <sub>m</sub>m-<sup>1</sup> at EUV wavelengths.<sup>62</sup> For these <sub>a</sub> values, the EUV attenuation length in the photoresist is approximately 200e500 nm, and this results in little of the light being absorbed in the film.
--[p161]-- The incorporation of elements with larger photoabsorption cross-section $\sigma _ { a }$ (other than C, O, H) is one way of improving the resist absorbance. The absorption cross-section of elements is roughly proportional to the atomic number, and it is significantly higher in those elements where interaction between d-orbitals and photons is stronger. The atomic absorption cross-section,<sup>63</sup> at EUV, of elements from Z  1 to 86, is shown in Fig. 11.
--[p161]-- 8 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 }$ of a conventional FUJIFILM FEVS-P1101 series resist).<sup>66</sup> This is discussed in more depth in Chapter 13. The incorporation of metals is a viable way to synthesize negative-tone photoresists<sup>67</sup> based on organometallic carboxylate compounds of the type $[ \mathrm { R n M } ( \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C R } ^ { \prime } ) _ { 2 } ]$ with $\mathbf { M } = \mathbf { S } \mathbf { n }$ , Te, Bi, Sb, and is covered in Chapter 11.
--[p163]-- A different approach that has recently been undertaken involves the synthesis of photoresists based on nanoparticle/molecular metals. Incorporation of $\mathrm { Z r O _ { x } }$ and $\mathrm { T e O _ { x } }$ nanoparticles in a CAR has been demonstrated to reduce its transmittance by up to ${ \sim } 8 \%$ depending on the relative amount of oxide, compared to the original formulation,<sup>68</sup> as described in Chapter 13.
--[p161]-- Significant research effort is being devoted to the incorporation of highly absorbing elements into EUV photoresists while still retaining the functionality of the material. As Fig. 11 suggests, feasible materials that are being researched specifically for this purpose are: F, Hf, Te, Sb, Sn, Zr, and Bi. Fluorinated polymers have been investigated as the backbone polymers of EUV resists<sup>64,65</sup> owing to the large photoabsorption cross-section of fluorine atoms.
--[p161]-- These resists were mostly based on DNQ  novolac resins, compounds which yielded an absorption coefficient of about $0 . 5 \mu \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 }$ . At such values of absorption coefficient, about 80% of the incoming light is transmitted to the bottom of the resist, which guarantees both an adequate depth clearance and a limited sidewall slope. In EUV lithography, absorption becomes more relevant than in previous platforms for three reasons:
--[p163]-- A negative-tone resist based on a $\mathrm { H f O } _ { \mathrm { x } }$ core, covered in Chapter 10, achieved an estimated $1 6 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 }$ absorbance.<sup>69</sup> Experimental studies on these materials have reported a remarkably higher absorption (3e4 times higher, up to $1 9 . 2 \mu \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 } )$ than in conventional organic polymers.<sup>70</sup>
--[p163]-- The measurement of the energy of generated secondary electrons (SEs) was performed in a complex experimental setup and showed than these SEs have energy ranging between 12 and 50 eV and yield of up to four SEs per absorbed photon.<sup>71</sup>

===== [p329-330] Positive molecular resists > 9.2 GENERAL CHARACTERISTICS (9块) =====
--[p329]-- All these molecular materials have main component molecules bearing structural units composed of etch-resistant rings, mostly aromatic but in a few cases also cycloaliphatic, and they are functionalized with specific groups to provide substrate adhesion, enhancement of intermolecular forces for achieving acceptable film-forming properties, and solubility change upon exposure.
--[p329]-- 9.2 GENERAL CHARACTERISTICS
--[p329]-- Furthermore, thermal stability is usually an important issue since evaporation of molecular components from the resist material can occur at relatively low temperatures. In addition, sensitivity is usually a further issue since the mechanisms of chain scission and chain crosslinking either are not encountered or are not as effective a means for solubility change as in the case of polymers.
--[p330]-- On the basis of the previously mentioned characteristics, better control of materials properties is expected and, in addition, a deeper understanding of the chemical-structure lithographic performance relationships. Furthermore, as already presented in Section 9.1, the ultimate resolution and the quality of the structures obtained from the small molecule-based lithographic materials are expected to be superior compared to polymeric materials.
--[p330]-- The previously mentioned issues will be reviewed in more detail for the different families of the so far proposed molecular resists according to the information available in the relevant literature. Finally, the current status and the challenges, that the development of molecular resists has to overcome, will be discussed.
--[p329]-- The basic chemical families of molecules investigated so far as main components of positive molecular resists are star-shaped molecules, polyphenols, cyclic molecules such as calixarenes and pilararenes, ladder-type molecules, the most studied family of which is noria, fused aromatic derivatives including fullerene derivatives, derivatives of polycarbocyclic aliphatic compounds, and finally, materials that are based on crosslinked molecules which can exhibit positive resist behavior.
--[p329]-- In the case of molecular resists, film formation is usually a key issue since, in these materials, intermolecular forces from chain entanglements are not present to help, as is the case for polymers. Adhesion to the substrate is also not as effective as in the case of polymers since each molecule has limited number of contacts with the substrate.
--[p329]-- More complex architectures, such as cyclic molecules containing many aromatic rings were proposed later in an effort to meet the strict performance requirements of the lithographic materials and successfully compete with polymeric resists as will be described in the next section.
In all cases, the components of molecular resists are well-characterized compounds and it is reasonably expected that they have advantages over polymeric materials in terms of purity and reproducibility.
--[p329]-- Thus, molecular resist materials are usually based on the chemical amplification approach and, in particular, on the presence of a number of protecting groups that in acidic environment are removed exposing hydrophilic groups to allow development in aqueous base developers. A generic structure showing the basic design scheme for the first positive molecular resists is presented in Fig. 2.

--[p410]-- 11.5.2.1 Anionic ligand decomposition
As stated previously, each cluster is composed of a 2 cationic core bound by two charge-balancing anionic ligands. One possible mechanism for the observed photosensitivity of these clusters is a photolytic decomposition of the anionic ligands. Homolysis of the carbonyl could result in the generation of a radical carboxylate, followed by the loss of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and reduction of the tin-oxide core (Fig. 31).
--[p412]-- Comparison of bond dissociation energy and $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { S I Z E } }$ led to a change in the originally predicted mechanism. When bond dissociation energy was compared with $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { S I Z E } } ,$ no correlation was observed (Fig. 33A). There was, however, an observed correlation between ligand molecular weight and $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { S I Z E } } ,$ which increased proportionally with the molecular weight of the anion (Fig. 33B).
--[p410]-- Since this mechanism involves the breaking of a bond, the relative sensitivity of these clusters should correlate directly with bond energy.
In order to test the effect of the ligand structure, a series of clusters with different anionic ligands were made. In 1998, Eychenne-Baron et al.<sup>57</sup> reported on the synthesis of compound 51.

===== [p378-378] Mainstreaming inorganic metal-oxide resists for high-resolution lithography > 10.4 METAL-OXIDE NANOCLUSTER PATTERNING MATERIALSdPRESENT AND FUTURE (4块) =====
--[p378]-- 10.4 METAL-OXIDE NANOCLUSTER PATTERNING MATERIALSdPRESENT AND FUTURE
While HSQ and HafSOx patterning represent breakthrough inorganic resist performance, drawbacks persist. Solution stability and variable film water content compromise reproducibility and performance. Concentrated TMAH development is unacceptable in the commercial fab environment, and sensitivity plateaus are too low for commercial applications.
--[p378]-- Hence, continued HSQ, HafSOx, and similar material studies should greatly advance understanding of deposition, radiation, and dissolution mechanisms affecting lithographic performance. While broad impacts are likely to be associated initially with photoresist applications, such directly patterned materials could one day be directly integrated as functional materials to enhance device performance.
--[p378]-- To address these issues, the Inpria resist team applied the HSQ and HafSOx learnings described in Sections 10.2.1, 10.2.2, 10.3.2, and 10.3.3 to create new tin-oxide nanoclusters that fill all HSQ and HafSOx performance gaps, while providing higher EUV absorption. As noted in Section 10.3.5, these materials have already been integrated into semiconductor manufacturing processes, moving from lab to fab and supporting EUV introduction for high-volume manufacturing.
--[p378]-- HSQ and HafSOx will continue to serve as model systems supporting research, both as resists to fabricate devices and to explore the limits of nanoscale lithography. As inorganic materials, their chemistries make possible application of unique in situ analytical techniques to examine patterning mechanismsdtechniques that are, for example, not readily applied to organic-material studies.

--[p263]-- 8.5 NORIA RESISTS
The name Noria stems from the Latin, meaning waterwheel. Noria can be thought of as an extension of calixarenes and is synthesized using a similar approach. It is produced by a condensation reaction of resorcinol with 1,5-pentanediol in a one-pot procedure with high yield w83%.
--[p264]-- As Noria-Ox does not dissolve in 0.26 N TMAH and the industry prefers alkaline development, the original oxetane group was replaced with another one that carries secondary hydroxyl groups as welldNoria-GOx. ===== [p402-403] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.5.1.1 Development of Sn-1 solubility hypothesis (6块) =====
--[p402]-- We hypothesize the latter tin compound (31) forms 6-coordinate complexes, which can dramatically increase solubility. The dibutyltin oxalate is constrained to a 4-coordinate complex, allowing intermolecular coordination, ultimately resulting in the formation of an insoluble network structure. The dibutyltin diformate, however, can be oriented such that the carbonyl oxygens are coordinating with the tin, preventing cross-linking and resulting in a significantly more soluble product (Fig. 20C).

(C) The lone-pair carbonyl electrons can rearrange, forming a soluble monomeric structure for the dibutyltin diformate. The lone-pair electrons on the oxalate, however, are constrained from intramolecular rearrangement to fill the empty tin-binding sites. This forces intermolecular coordination to occur, resulting in an insoluble, network structure.
--[p402]-- 11.5.1.1 Development of Sn-1 solubility hypothesis
Through experimentation with alternate Sn-1 compounds, a solubility hypothesis was developed. Three other Sn-1 compounds were synthesized using formic acid, catechol, and tert-butyl catechol. The catechol complex (29), like the oxalate complex (28), is insoluble. The tert-butyl catechol complex (30) is a semisoluble solid, and the formic acid complex (31) is a semicrystalline solid with excellent solubility in organic solvents (Fig. 20B).

===== [p104-105] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.2 EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET MOLECULAR EXCITATION (7块) =====
--[p105]-- The details of the X-ray molecule interaction process must be considered to understand the origin of these differences in absorption, and their implications for resist chemistry.
--[p104]-- Finally, there is a structural reorganization in the excited molecule, with changes in atom positions, often causing the molecule to fragment into radicals and radical ions. These steps are described in detail in the following paragraphs.
In chemically amplified DUV resists, UV photons are selectively absorbed by photoacid generators, causing molecular dissociation into anions and cations. The
Three-step process of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) molecular photoionization.
--[p104]-- (A) A 92-eV EUV photon is absorbed. The most strongly bound molecular orbital that can be excited by EUV has the highest excitation cross section. A relatively slow secondary electron is emitted. (B) The molecule is left with significant residual internal energy. The electrons will rapidly reorganize (few femtoseconds) to reduce internal energy by emitting an Auger electron if this is energetically possible. (C) Now the atoms will reorganize (100e1000 fs).
--[p104 [表]]-- If the molecule is doubly ionized, or if it has residual energy greater than a few electronvolts, it will fragment into radicals and radical ions.

--[p104]-- 2.2 EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET MOLECULAR EXCITATION
The three-step EUV excitation process<sup>1</sup> is shown schematically in Fig. 1. First, an EUV photon is absorbed, and an SE is emitted. The most strongly bound molecular orbital that can be excited by EUV usually has the highest excitation cross section. Second, the molecular electrons reorganize to reduce the residual internal energy in the molecule, often emitting a second SE in an Auger process.

other molecular components in the resist system are tailored to be relatively weak UV absorbers. During the postexposure bake, the ionic components chemically amplify the impact of the UV absorption event, increasing resist sensitivity.
--[p105]-- The chemical amplification strategy is less appropriate for EUVL, as it reduces pattern resolution, increases noise and line-edge roughness.<sup>16</sup>
In EUV lithography, all components of the resist system can absorb EUV X-rays, but the X-ray absorption depends strongly on atomic composition. ===== [p188-189] EUV lithography patterning challenges > 5 1 2 EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET OPTICS AND MASK (8块) =====
--[p189]-- Also, because the system is reflective, the mask illumination is required to be off axis as shown in Fig. 5A. This combined with the fact that the mask absorber pattern has finite thickness (on the order of 70 nm) causes a shadowing effect in the plane of reflection as shown in Fig. 5B. The shadowing impacts the light going down to the multilayer surface as well as the light reflected back up from the multilayer.
--[p189]-- Moreover, in reality, the EUV light is not just reflected from the top surface of the multilayer, but rather the reflection is distributed from within the bulk of the multilayer, which further exacerbates the shadowing of the reflected light.
--[p188]-- 5 1 2 EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET OPTICS AND MASK
Although basically an extension of optical lithography, EUV lithography cannot rely on conventional transmission lenses and masks as used in the past. The strong absorption of all materials in the EUV regime requires a switch to reflective optics. Obtaining high reflectivity at EUV, however, is not trivial and depends on the use of near-normal incidence Bragg (multilayer) coatings<sup>14</sup> allowing optics with reasonable throughputs to be fabricated.
--[p189]-- In the EUV regime, such exposure systems typically rely on a two-bounce Schwarzschild system as the imaging optic providing a field of view on the order of 0.2 mm. An example of such a tool is the Berkeley MET tool<sup>16</sup> schematically depicted in Fig. 4 along with a photograph of the projection optic.
Just as with the optics, the mask in EUV lithography must also be reflective multilayer.
--[p188]-- Current manufacturing class EUV tools<sup>1</sup> operating at 0.33 NA utilize six mirrors in the imaging system and approximately four in the illuminator. Further adding the source collector optic and
FIGURE 3
the mask, a typical tool<sup>15</sup> (Fig. 3) might have 12 multilayer surfaces, which will yield a total reflectivity of around 1%.
--[p189]-- Because this shadowing effect only occurs in the plane of reflection, horizontal and vertical features on the mask will print differently; however, much of the effect can be compensated for by properly biasing the features on the mask or through optimization of the mask architecture and materials.<sup>17</sup>
--[p188]-- The multilayer of choice for EUV lithography is molybdenumesilicon enabling reflectivity near 70% at 13.5 nm. A typical multilayer is comprised of 40 bilayers with a bilayer thickness of approximately 7 nm. The relatively low reflectivity places significant constraints on the number of mirrors that can be used in both the illuminator which transports and shapes the light from the source to the mask as well as in the imaging optic itself.
--[p189]-- The complexity of the manufacturing tool in terms of the number of optics is driven by the large field size required in full chip production (on the order 26-mm wide); however, such a large field is not needed for resist testing alone. To support such testing, a class of smaller field tools referred to as microfield exposure tools is typically used.

===== [p109-111] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.2.5 PHOTOEMISSION AND SHAKE-UP (8块) =====
--[p109]-- The most well-known core-level shake-up process occurs in double-bonded hydrocarbon molecules (alkenes) when a C 1s electron is excited in XPS. There is a $\pi \to \pi ^ { * }$ shake-up satellite line with a relative intensity of w10% shifted to 6.7 eV higher BE due to the simultaneous shake-up excitation of a second electron from the p bonding orbital to the $\pi ^ { * }$ antibonding orbital. 12
--[p111]-- These orbitals are the most likely to be excited at 92 eV, and this means more residual energy is left in the excited molecule after photoemission, which can drive relaxation processes and molecular fragmentation.
--[p110]-- The same group has developed powerful theoretical methods to study shake-up effects in larger molecules.<sup>39</sup> In the case of benzene, they found that the probability of direct photoemission from the seven outer valence orbitals, with binding energies of 9 17 eV, was between 80% and 90%. On the other hand, photoemission from the three inner valence orbitals, with binding energies of 19, 23, and 27 eV, was associated with very strong shake-up effects.
--[p110]-- Direct emission probabilities were no more than 10%, and the remaining intensity was split among at least six to eight shake-up lines, each with 2 40% of the total intensity.<sup>8</sup> These shake-up lines are quite difficult to resolve or assign in experimental spectra, especially when shake-up lines from multiple molecular orbitals overlap. Shake-up effects are expected to become more important with increasing molecular size, particularly for molecules with aro-8 matic character.
--[p109]-- 2.2.5 PHOTOEMISSION AND SHAKE-UP
More recent work by Cederbaum and collaborators<sup>37</sup> has shown that molecular orbital theory breaks down due to correlations, or interactions, among valence electrons during ionization. In a “shake-up” process, as shown in Fig. 4, absorption of one X-ray photon can change the energy levels of two electrons. One electron is ejected, and a second is excited to an unoccupied level in the molecule.
--[p109]-- In a “shakeoff” process, both electrons can be ejected.<sup>38</sup> Usually shake-up and shake-off processes are much less likely than direct single-electron photoemission from core levels. Each shake-up process will reduce the intensity of the direct photoemission line, and create a satellite line with reduced KE, while increasing the residual internal energy in the molecular ion.
--[p110]-- Shake-up reduces the photoelectron KE, while increasing the residual internal energy of the molecular ion. “Shake-off,” where both electrons are ejected from the molecule, is also possible, but less likely.
Strong molecular shake-up processes from inner valence (semicore) orbitals have important implications for EUVL.
--[p110]-- Shake-up in molecular photoemission. When an incoming photon [double-line magenta arrow (gray in print versions)] ejects an electron from a molecular level (open circle), a second electron can be excited or “shaken $\mathsf { U p } ^ { \prime \prime }$ to an unoccupied state [curved magenta arrows (gray in print versions)]. Multiple electron excitation effects are strongest when inner valence levels are photoexcited.

===== [p24-26] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.3.4 E-BEAM LITHOGRAPHY (15块) =====
--[p25]-- Backward scattering tends to cause dense features to receive a higher effective dose than sparse features because the backward scattered electrons from neighboring features contribute to the total dose while the sparse features have few neighbors.
--[p25]-- 70 Multiple-beam e-beam lithography is potentially the most advanced option at this time, and improves throughput by massively parallelizing the beams that pattern the wafer.<sup>71</sup>
The most important radiationematerial interaction in optical lithography at UV and DUV wavelengths is direct photon absorption to temporarily excite a molecule to an excited state as discussed earlier.
--[p25]-- The electrons which scatter through the resist as described earlier and shown in Fig. 6 can be considered forward scattering of the electrons because most of the electrons are scattered at small angles forward into the resist. There is another scattering phenomenon that is important in e-beam lithography called backward scattering. This occurs when electrons are scattered at much higher angles from the substrate backward into the resist.
--[p26]-- When the electrons get much lower in energy (<10e20 eV), they can undergo additional types of reactions and can be scavenged by some compounds in the resist. This can lead to excited state compounds that can carry out further reactions that are potentially similar to DUV excited state reactions.<sup>78</sup> This change in imaging mechanism will be discussed further in later sections.
--[p24]-- Compared to UV, DUV, and EUV lithography, e-beam lithography is a maskless form of lithography in that it requires no mask because the deflectors and coils allow arbitrary deflection of the finely focused beam. Indeed, e-beam lithography is the technique that is most commonly used to pattern the masks used in other forms of lithography.
--[p25]-- A standard single beam e-beam tool can take several hours to expose a single wafer and up to several days for some complex masks or templates. This time will be longer as the desired spot size is decreased to improve resolution. Patterning in e-beam can also take more time because the highest resolution resists are often nonchemically amplified resists which require much higher doses than the chemically amplified resists (CARs) commonly used in optical lithography.
--[p24]-- The flexibility of e-beam allows almost any arbitrary geometry to be programmed and patterned, although certain applications that require high fidelity and alignment in circular patterns such as bit-patterned media will use more specialized tools that allow for a circular rotating stage.<sup>60,61</sup>
Among the many different types of commonly used lithography, e-beam is widely considered to have the highest resolution, especially when using 50 to
100 keV primary electrons.
--[p25]-- In e-beam lithography, the radiationematerial interaction is very different and is in many ways significantly more complex.<sup>72</sup> High energy primary electrons (typically 50e100 keV) enter the top surface and scatter through the resist by a series of elastic and inelastic collisions. The inelastic collisions cause a loss of energy and generate multiple secondary electrons.
--[p26]-- Electrons are of a sufficient energy that they can cause direct bond cleavage of some groups. This type of reaction drives the solubility transition in some resists where insoluble higher molecular weight polymers are reduced to soluble lower molecular weight molecules by bond cleavage. Electrons may also cause crosslinking in other groups, which gives a negative-tone-type behavior as less soluble larger molecular weight species are formed.
--[p25]-- The low throughput has historically limited e-beam lithography to mask making and research and development purposes; however, work has been carried out and continues on methods and tool designs which could improve throughput such as projection e-beam,<sup>63e66</sup> multiple-beam,<sup>67,68</sup> shape-variable beam, 69 and reflective beam.
--[p25]-- Features as small as 5 nm and below have been fabricated using e-beam lithography.<sup>62</sup> Although e-beam lithography has resolution capability that far exceeds current production DUV tools, it has significantly slower throughput, which limits its use in high volume commercial manufacturing. Throughput for a modern optical lithography scanner exceeds well over a hundred wafers per hour.
--[p25]-- This is known as the proximity effect<sup>75</sup> and proximity effect correction<sup>76,77</sup> is a method that attempts to correct this effect by using models that estimate the effective dose as a function of geometry, and then change the programmed dose at each location to obtain the desired final deposited dose.
The scattered electrons can have many different chemical and physical effects on the resist.
--[p25]-- Backward scattering is more likely when electrons encounter higher Z elements as are commonly found in the inorganic substrates. It is a concern because its effects are felt over a much larger dimensional range, up to microns away from the incident beam rather than the nanometer length scale for forward scattering.
--[p25]-- The secondary electrons can likewise scatter through the resist with similar physics and generate even more additional free electrons. In this manner, a single incident electron can generate a large cloud of electrons. This cloud of electrons often has a teardrop-shaped interaction volume with the resist as shown in Fig. 6. The electron trajectories and secondary electron generation can be simulated using Monte Carlo techniques.<sup>73,74</sup>
--[p24]-- 1.3.4 E-BEAM LITHOGRAPHY
E-beam lithography uses a focused beam of electrons to directly expose a resist. The electron gun is often a tungsten thermionic emission cathode.<sup>23</sup> The beam is focused onto a very small spot size that can be less than 10 nm using a series of condenser lenses and beam deflection coils.

===== [p341-343] Positive molecular resists > 9.3.5 CYCLIC MOLECULESdCALIXARENES AND RELATED STRUCTURES (10块) =====
--[p341]-- 9.3.5 CYCLIC MOLECULESdCALIXARENES AND RELATED STRUCTURES
Cyclic molecules have usually a number of repeated units and, in this respect, resemble polymers but they are well-defined structures. The most popular class of such compounds are calixarenes. In Fig. 14, a specific example from the calixarene family is shown. The calixarenes appear in diverse cyclic structures with a varying number of aromatic units per cycle.
--[p341]-- In addition, calixarenes with more than one cycle have been also investigated and molecules of related structure, the pilararenes, have been also recently introduced and will be discussed.
The calixarenes have dimensions of w1 nm. It has been demonstrated that several calixarene derivatives form molecular glasses with a number of desirable characteristics including high $\mathrm { T _ { g } } .$ .
--[p341]-- These materials were first proposed for lithographic applications as negative resists by Fujita et al. in 1996 and 1997.<sup>14,47</sup> Despite their low sensitivity, they attracted attention in different nanolithography applications since they can provide sub-10-nm resolution.
--[p342]-- The best lithogaphic performance was reported for a formulation based on calix[4]resorcinarene (5 wt% solution in propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate [PGMEA]) with the PAG triphenylsulfonium 2-(phenoxy)tetrafluoiroethane-1-sulfonate (5% with respect to the resist) and trioctylamine (0.12 wt%, with respect to the resist) as base quencher for a film approximately 100-nm thick using 0.026 N TMAH for development.
Later,<sup>50,51</sup> the Ober group reported on nonchemically amplified materials with DNQ. The structures investigated are shown in Fig. 14.
--[p341]-- The dissolution inhibition of DNQ was studied, and formulations of positive molecular resists allowing development in 1.5 wt% TMAH were obtained demonstrating a sensitivity of $3 0 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ and a contrast of 2.8.
Calixarene compounds have subsequently been investigated as components of molecular resists by other groups. Ober et al. have worked mostly with calixarenes of a single cycle containing either four or six phenolic units.
In 2006, Chang and Ober reported<sup>49</sup> sub-50-nm lithography in EUV using calixarene derivatives.
--[p341]-- Later, in 1999, positive-tone variants were introduced when a molecular resist based on calixarenes and diazonaphthoqinones (DNQ) was proposed by Nakayama and Ueda.<sup>48</sup> The synthetic procedure for the calixarene component was based on cyclization of p-benzyloxyphenol and paraformaldehyde in the presence of a base. Highly transparent films were obtained from solutions in ethyl lactate.
--[p343]-- The pilararenes have been introduced recently by Ogoshi et al.<sup>52</sup> A synthetic route is presented in Scheme 3.<sup>53</sup> Resists based on these molecules were reviewed recently, along with calixarenes having more than one cycle, as components of high-performing positive molecular resists.<sup>54</sup> Details on resist formulations are not given in this review, which covers recent developments on molecular resists based on cyclic molecules.
--[p341]-- The $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ of different materials was found to be in the $1 7 0 { - } 2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ range depending on the substitution. The films were transparent at 300 nm, allowing the use of this material in i-line (365 nm) lithography. On the other hand, the optical density at 248 nm was $0 . 3 \ \mu \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 }$ so that it can be used in KrF eximer laser lithography as well.
--[p343]-- In addition to the mentioned calixarene-related compounds, noria-based formulations, which will be discussed next, are covered in the same review. High-quality lithographic features in the sub-30-nm domain were presented.
In a recent article published by the Dow team in 2013, positive-tone molecular resist materials were discussed.<sup>55</sup> Although structural details are not given, the materials are reported as having calixarene cores.
--[p343]-- In this publication, it is stated that the molecular glass materials if properly designed could have physical properties very similar to polymeric materials while offering superior performance in LER/LWR improvement. Promising lithographic performance of such materials was reported in this publication raising hopes that molecular glasses can be a viable alternative choice to polymeric materials as lithographic materials for next-generation lithography.

===== [p178-178] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.4 CONCLUSIONS (4块) =====
--[p178]-- All these aspects need to be considered when developing the next generation EUV materials for photolithography. Furthermore, IL has been shown to be a simple yet powerful technique that does not require the use of expensive high NA optics, imaging systems, or masks. In particular, IL with the use of transmission diffraction gratings offers many advantages such as achromaticity, insensitivity to misalignment, infinite depth-offocus, and the possibility to pattern large areas.
--[p178]-- For this reason, several approaches have been proposed to improve the performance of EUV materials such as the incorporation of elements with large photoabsorption cross-sections to improve resist absorbance, the synthesis of photoresists based on nanoparticle metals, or the creation of novel non-CAR resists that exhibit higher absorption in comparison to conventional organic polymers and can be patterned into pseudooxides.
--[p178]-- It has been widely used not only for the characterization and development of novel EUV materials but also for the fabrication of high-resolution periodic structures. In fact, structures down to 8- and 7-nm HP in resolution, the smallest feature sizes that have been patterned by photon-based lithography, have been accomplished by EUV-IL.
--[p178]-- 4.4 CONCLUSIONS
In this chapter, lithography process inhibitors and challenges such as electron and acid blur, pattern collapse at high aspect ratios, and photon shot noise, to name a few, have been explored as we seek to meet the resolution, LER, and sensitivity performance requirements set for future semiconductor device technology nodes. The simultaneous improvement of these parameters in CARs at EUV is difficult due to inherent tradeoff relationships between each one.

===== [p117-117] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.4.2 MOLECULAR RELAXATION IN CONDENSED FILMS (7块) =====
--[p117]-- Inter-atomic electronic processes such as ICD and ETMD, while slower than direct Auger processes, are still fast compared to the atomic relaxation and fragmentation discussed in Section 2.2.3.
--[p117]-- 5C, where further standard, or “intraatomic” Auger relaxation is not possible. One such process, Intercoulombic decay (ICD),<sup>44,45</sup> is similar to Penning ionization.<sup>46</sup> In Penning ionization spectroscopy, metastable excited He atoms are produced by inelastic electron scattering, where one He electron is excited from the 1s to the 2s energy level.
--[p117]-- ICD is a similar process, in that internally excited atoms, molecules, or molecular ions can transfer energy to near-neighbors through nonradiative Coulomb interactions when fast intra-atomic Auger processes are energetically forbidden.
An atomic ICD process is shown schematically in Fig. 8. An excited 2 ion “A” does not have sufficient residual internal energy for Auger decay into a 3 ion, but it does have enough energy to ionize a neighboring atom “B” through ICD energy transfer.
--[p117]-- Here both charge and energy are transferred in an atomic relaxation process. This process was first identified in the relaxation of a $\mathrm { N e } ^ { + + } \mathrm { K r } _ { 2 }$ cluster after Ne photoemission followed by Auger relaxation to $\mathrm { N e ^ { + + } }$ . Similar processes seem likely in condensed molecular system as well.
--[p117]-- The metastable $\mathrm { H e } ^ { * }$ atom has around 20 eV of internal energy, but it cannot decay by an Auger process since He has only two electrons, and radiative decay from 2s to 1s is dipoleforbidden and hence very slow. When $\mathrm { H e } ^ { * }$ collides with a neutral molecule, He relaxes to its ground state, transferring its internal energy to the target molecule through the Coulomb interaction and ionizing it.
--[p117]-- 2.4.2 MOLECULAR RELAXATION IN CONDENSED FILMS
The fast electronic relaxation and Auger electron emission processes discussed in Section 2.3.1 will also be very similar in gas and condensed phase, except for small energy shifts due to the dielectric environment. However, some new intramolecular relaxation processes become possible in condensed systems when molecules or ions are left in metastable excited states, as in Fig.
--[p117]-- ICD processes are also possible between molecules<sup>47</sup> and have been observed in aqueous systems.<sup>48</sup> ICD rates depend strongly on the separation between the participating atoms, and may be modulated by vibrational motion.
Stumpf et al.<sup>49</sup> described another relaxation process for excited- or ground-state dications. This electron transfer mediated decay (ETMD) process is shown schematically in Fig. 9.

===== [p226-227] Chemically amplified resists and acid amplifiers > 7.2.3 POSITIVE-TONE EUV CAR RESISTS (8块) =====
--[p227]-- The question became whether or not one wanted to attach the PAG through the cation and allow the acid anion to diffuse or rather attach through the PAG anion to reduce acid diffusion. Thackeray<sup>6</sup> reported on the improved resolution achieved when copolymerizing the acid anion of the PAG with methyl adamantyl methacrylate, hydroxyvinyl naphthalene, and a hexafluoroalcohol unit, as shown in Fig. 7.
--[p227]-- Another interesting class of EUV CAR resist, the so-called polymer-bound PAG (PBP) systems, has been developed. Initial work was done by Gonsalves, where he reported copolymerization of (phenyl methacrylate)dimethyl sulfonium triflate with ethyl adamantyl methacrylate and vinyl phenol to make PAG cation-bound resist polymers.<sup>40,41</sup> These polymers exhibited fast sensitivity and reasonable resolution down to 50 nm.
--[p227]-- Many workers have tried to design MGs, most notably Nishikubo who developed the NORIA system.<sup>36</sup> One of the challenges of replacing polymer with MGs is that it is difficult to build thermal and mechanical properties into the MG. If the glass transition temperature is too low, for instance, the photoacid diffusion becomes too large to control image blur. Also, it is difficult to build dissolution contrast in an MG resist, which limits the overall lithographic performance.
--[p227]-- NORIA-based positivetone resists have been developed by Yamamoto et al. with adamantyl ester protecting groups.<sup>37</sup> This type of resist resolved 22-nm hp as reported by Maruyama.<sup>38</sup> Frommhold et al. have recently reported on a fullerene-based resist whereby protecting groups were selectively grafted on the fullerene structure to yield high-resolution resists.<sup>39</sup> Chapters 8 and 9 describe, in more depth, negative- and positive-tone MG resists, respectively.
--[p226]-- Ultimately, ESCAP-type resists were capable of 30-nm hp patterning with exposure doses in the $1 5 { - } 2 0 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ range. Meanwhile, EUVL Infrastructure Development Center (EIDEC) in Japan was doing early screening on novel resist concepts with their own EUV exposure unit.<sup>33</sup> They were an early proponent for molecular glass (MG)-based resist.
--[p226]-- The MG concept was built upon the thesis that polymers were too large for ultrafine patterning in the sub-30-nm regime. PHS polymer, for instance, at 10-kDa molecular weight is estimated to have a radius-of-gyration of 3 nmdabout 10% of the critical dimension target.<sup>34</sup> By making discrete MGs, such as calixarenes, one can reduce the average molecule size to less than 1 nm. The formulations were modified by Brainard et al. to thinner thicknesses and higher PAG loadings.<sup>7</sup> These resists served as early-learning vehicles for patterning and measuring acid yields.

===== [p421-421] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.7.2 PALLADIUM AND PLATINUM (2块) =====
--[p421]-- 11.7.2 PALLADIUM AND PLATINUM
Four series of palladium and platinum resists were made and tested, each exploring a different functional group. Azide groups did not result in imaging. Carbonate groups resulted in negative-tone patterns but suffered from solubility and sensitivity issues. Oxalate groups resulted in reasonably good positive-tone imaging, capable of patterning 30-nm hp lines at $5 0 \mathrm { m J } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ .
--[p421]-- The photoproducts were also analyzed by NMR, and the reaction appears to proceed through a decomposition of the oxalate group, liberating $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ gas.

===== [p205-206] The chemistry and application of nonchemically amplified (non-CA) chain-scission resists > 6.2 THE CEILING TEMPERATURE (8块) =====
--[p206]-- The ceiling temperature phenomenon has been reviewed by a number of distinguished authors<sup>13e15</sup> and remains important not only in the field of lithographic materials but increasingly in the chemistry of switchable and responsive biomaterials.
--[p205]-- 6.2 THE CEILING TEMPERATURE
The usual experience of polymer chemists is that polymerization reactions proceed via the consumption of monomeric species to the formation of a high polymer. This reaction proceeds with the upper rate constant $k _ { p }$ in Eq. (1). However, if the reaction is conducted at a sufficiently high temperature, reverse reactions, with rate constant $k _ { d } ,$ can become appreciable.
--[p206]-- We define the temperature at which this occurs as the ceiling temperature, $T _ { c } ,$ and can write:
$$
T _ { c } = \frac { \Delta H _ { p } } { \Delta S _ { p } }\tag{2}
$$
The net forward reaction does not proceed at temperatures above the ceiling temperature, where $\Delta G _ { p }$ becomes positive. However, it should be noted that the polymeric species $( P _ { n }$ and $P _ { n + 1 } )$ referred to in Eq. (1) are polymeric radicals, not the dead polymer chains.
--[p205]-- Such phenomena have been discussed for over six decades; for example, in a remarkable 1953 issue of the Discussions of the Faraday Society on the chemistry of free-radical reactions, Dainton and Ivin<sup>13</sup> had already described the key elements on these reactions.
$$
P _ { n } + M \mathop {  } _ { k _ { d } } ^ { k _ { p } }\tag{1}
$$
--[p206]-- Under normal circumstances, isolated and purified polymer chains have undergone termination reactions, and the end groups are capped or nonradical in nature.
--[p206]-- We know that the activation energy of the depolymerization reaction is greater than that of the propagation step by the difference in enthalpy of the two states, and therefore, as temperature is increased the rate constant of depropagation increases faster than that for propagation. Consequently, a temperature may be reached in which the reverse reaction is favored. At this point, the change in the Gibbs free energy of the forward and reverse reactions becomes zero.
--[p206]-- Polymers that undergo spontaneous depolymerization on removal of a capping agent have been “rebranded” as self-immolative polymers and suggested to have broad application in drug delivery and other aspects of biomedical sciences.<sup>16e21</sup> Much learning of relevance to the design of lithographic materials can be found in these articles from an apparently unrelated discipline.
--[p206]-- This means that polymers with accessible ceiling temperatures may in fact be highly stable above $T _ { c } .$ An excellent example of this is polyformaldehyde, an early commercial polymer from the DuPont company, which requires capping with acetate groups to render it thermally stable.<sup>14</sup> These polymers are more correctly termed “metastable,” as they will undergo depolymerization on generation of the macromolecular radical species, by, for example, cleavage of the terminal unit.

===== [p111-112] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.3 EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET MOLECULAR RELAXATION 2.3.1 ELECTRONIC RELAXATION IN ATOMS (8块) =====
--[p111]-- $\mathrm { I } ^ { 1 2 5 }$ decays to $\mathrm { T e } ^ { 1 2 5 }$ by capturing a 1s electron, leaving an excited state atom with 35.4 keV of residual internal energy.
--[p111]-- The excited atom either decays by fluorescence, with a 7% probability, or by an Auger cascade, with a 93% probability.<sup>41</sup> Monte-Carlo calculations of possible decay paths predicted the emission of between 5 and 44 Auger electrons, with an average of 22, and many of these electrons had kinetic energies<sup>41</sup> between 15 and 50 eV.
Relaxation can have a big impact on the radiation chemistry of resist materials incorporating high $\sigma _ { E U V }$ atoms.
--[p111]-- 2.3 EXTREME ULTRAVIOLET MOLECULAR RELAXATION 2.3.1 ELECTRONIC RELAXATION IN ATOMS
When the most weakly bound electron is removed from an atom by photoemission, the result is a stable ground-state ion, and the photoemission BE is very close to the equilibrium ionization energy.
--[p111]-- 5B schematically illustrates one possible Auger process.
Depending the number of occupied orbitals above the core hole, there may be a large number of possible Auger processes, each resulting in different final states and different kinetic energies for the ejected Auger electron.<sup>12</sup> If the residual internal energy exceeds the third ionization energy, a second Auger process will result in a triply ionized atom.
--[p112]-- These atoms have high cross sections because they have deeper levels, and these deep levels are the most likely to be photoionized, leaving behind a highly excited ion with much of the original X-ray energy. Consider iodine. The 4 $d$ orbital, with a 60-eV $\mathrm { B E _ { v a c } } .$ , is far more likely to be ionized at EUV energy than the 5s level at 19 eV or the 5p at 10 eV. After emitting a 32-eV photoelectron, the excited ion will be left with 60 eV of residual internal energy.
--[p111]-- The BE measured by photoemission for more strongly bound orbitals is actually the energy difference between the initial state, a neutral atom, and the final state, an excited ion with a core hole (missing electron) as shown in Fig. 5A. Excited ions quickly relax to their ground state. If the residual internal energy in the excited ion exceeds the second ionization energy, then the ion will decay by a fast, nonradiative Auger process within a few femtoseconds, ejecting a second electron. Fig.
--[p112]-- Auger electrons up to w41 eV could be emitted, since the iodine second ionization energy is 19 eV. Fig. 6 shows an experimental gas-phase Auger electron spectrum after Xe 4d photoemission.<sup>42</sup> The Xe spectrum should be rather similar to iodine as the main difference in electronic structure is one additional 5p electron. At least two dozen possible Auger transitions are observed, producing electrons with kinetic energies between 8 and 36 eV.
--[p111]-- If there are no energetically allowed Auger processes, the isolated excited ion will undergo a much slower radiative decay process and emit a photon (Fig. 5C). Fluorescent decay times range from nanoseconds for dipoleallowed transitions to microseconds and longer for triplet-singlet or dipoleforbidden transitions.
Highly excited atoms can release large numbers of Auger electrons in an Auger cascade. Radioactive iodine isotopes such as $\mathrm { I } ^ { 1 2 5 }$ are used in cancer therapy.

===== [p147-148] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.2.2 ACHROMATIC DIFFRACTION GRATINGeBASED EUV-IL (6块) =====
--[p147]-- 4.2.2 ACHROMATIC DIFFRACTION GRATINGeBASED EUV-IL
--[p147]-- To overcome the need for temporal and spatial coherence, the use of achromatic interference lithography (AIL) using transmission-diffraction gratings (wavefront division scheme) has been widely used.<sup>11,12</sup> With AIL, the resulting interference pattern is independent of the wavelength used and can therefore be used using a wide spectral width beam and spatial coherence is not required.<sup>4,11</sup> The use of IL schemes, that make use of transmission-diffraction gratings, allow for achromaticity, and thus, a monochromator is not necessary.
--[p148]-- The resulting mutually coherent beams interfere at a certain distance along the beam direction. The aerial image produced by two-beam IL has a period P that is half of the original mask grating period $P _ { g }$ when first order (m 1) diffracted beams are used (Eq. (3)):
$$
P = \frac { \lambda } { 2 \sin \theta _ { m } } = \frac { P _ { g } } { 2 m }\tag{3}
$$
--[p148]-- High-resolution patterning can be easily accomplished by the interference (forming a standing wave, intensity peaks, and nodes) of two or more spatially coherent beams through a transmission diffraction grating as shown schematically in Fig. 3. With EUV-IL, a spatially coherent incident beam of EUV light l is diffracted by linear gratings patterned on a partially transparent membrane at diffraction angles $\theta _ { m }$ (m denotes the diffraction order).
--[p147]-- There have been several other EUV-IL schemes that have also been studied such as amplitude division interferometers using gratings as beam splitters.<sup>4</sup> In this chapter, only achromatic Talbot lithography (ATL) and a diffraction gratingebased division method will be described.
--[p147]-- IL with the use of transmissiondiffraction gratings, therefore, offers many advantages such as achromaticity, insensitivity to misalignment, infinite depth-of-focus, and the possibility to pattern large areas in one shot.<sup>4,12,14</sup> Needless to say, multiple grating fields with different periodicities and even multiple configurations can be patterned on a single mask.

===== [p109-109] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.2.4 MOLECULAR PHOTOEMISSION (5块) =====
--[p109]-- Binding energies are reduced by a few electronvolts due to polarization of the dielectric environment, which screens the core hole,<sup>13</sup> and there are additional small “chemical shifts” in BE caused by electron density changes around the atom due to bond formation.<sup>12</sup>
Valence-level photoemission changes in important ways.
--[p109]-- 2.2.4 MOLECULAR PHOTOEMISSION
When atoms come together to form molecules, their electronic structure can be described in terms of bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals formed from interactions between the outer valence electrons of the constituent atoms.
--[p109]-- A ground-state molecular ion Mþ is formed when one electron is removed from the HOMO. Isolated organic molecules typically have ionization energies between 9 and 14 eV.
Core-level photoemission is almost unchanged when atoms are combined into molecules and solids.
--[p109]-- Each orbital has its own BE, and the orbitals are populated by valence electrons starting from the most strongly bound orbitals.<sup>36</sup> Orbitals can hold at most two electrons of opposite spin, by the Pauli exclusion principle, but high-symmetry molecules may have several “degenerate” orbitals of the same energy.
The “highest occupied molecular orbital” (HOMO) contains the most weakly bound electrons, and the empty “lowest unoccupied molecular orbital” (LUMO) comes next in energy.
--[p109]-- Molecular orbitals are shifted in energy relative to atomic levels as chemical bonds are formed, and the number and energies of these orbitals are seen directly in photoemission spectra of simple molecules.<sup>9</sup> In fact gas-phase photoemission was considered to be the first direct experimental proof of the physical relevance of molecular orbital theory.<sup>17</sup> When electrons are removed from bonding orbitals, molecular vibrations are excited, in exact analogy to the Franck Condon effect in optical spectroscopy. High resolution spectra for small molecules often show clearly resolved vibrational series.<sup>9</sup>

===== [p421-421] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.7.3 TIN (Sn-1) (3块) =====
--[p421]-- The ligand (L) was compared within a set of five carboxylate ligands. For most, the sensitivity correlates with ligand molecular mass, suggesting the ligand does not play a role in the photoreaction but rather acts as an unreactive spacer, preventing the reaction from occurring. Interestingly, the sensitivity of the acrylate and methacrylate ligands does not follow this trend. Both ligands, well known to undergo free-radical polymerization, are more sensitive than would be expected.
--[p421]-- 11.7.3 TIN (Sn-1)
A large number of organotin compounds of the formula $\mathbf { R } _ { 2 } \mathbf { S n L } _ { 2 } \left( \mathbf { S n - } 1 \right)$ were made, tested, and compared. The organic group (R) was compared within a set for butyl, phenyl, and benzyl. The sensitivity for these systems correlates with the CeH bond dissociation energy of the organic group, suggesting homolytic cleavage of the $\mathrm { S n - C }$ bond.
--[p421]-- It is conceivable that the organic group (R) cleaves photolytically, generating a radical which then acts as an initiator causing cross-linking in the film.

===== [p118-118] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.4.3 REACTION CASCADES IN CONDENSED FILMS (3块) =====
--[p118]-- The excited molecular ion will relax on a fs ps timescale through a combination of Auger electron emission, energy transfer or electron capture from neighboring molecules, and fragmentation into radicals and radical ions. These secondary particles will induce a cascade of secondary reactions among neighboring molecules on a ps ms timescale.
Secondary reactions induced by ionizing radiation can be quite complex, and are outside the scope of this chapter.
--[p118]-- 2.4.3 REACTION CASCADES IN CONDENSED FILMS
When a molecule absorbs an EUV photon, more than 90 eVof energy is deposited in a single event. Some of this energy is carried away by the primary photoelectron, but a substantial amount of residual internal energy is left behind, especially when a strongly bound orbital of a high cross section atom is photoionized.
--[p118]-- The radiation chemistry of liquid water has received the most concentrated attention,<sup>50</sup> but this is an area of current research. Table 2 summarizes gas-phase $_ { \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } }$ relaxation. In condensed water, $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ^ { + }$ will typically react with another water molecule to produce a $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } ^ { + }$ ion and an OH radical.<sup>50</sup>

===== [p108-109] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.2.3 GAS-PHASE MOLECULAR SPECTROSCOPY (6块) =====
--[p109]-- Brion and collaborators used inelastic electron scattering to determine absolute oscillator strengths for electron scattering from atoms<sup>31</sup> and small molecules,<sup>27,32</sup> which in the limit of small momentum transfer are closely related to the absolute photoabsorption cross sections, as shown in Fig. 3.
--[p108]-- Variable energy photoemission experiments give detailed insight into molecular structure.<sup>20</sup> Sweeping the X-ray energy through an excitation edge, as in the near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure experiment, allows resonant processes to be investigated.<sup>29</sup> Near-ambient pressure photoemission methods allow high-quality molecular photoemission data to be collected.<sup>30</sup>
--[p108]-- 2.2.3 GAS-PHASE MOLECULAR SPECTROSCOPY
Gas-phase photoemission spectroscopy is a powerful tool to investigate molecular electronic structure, chemical dynamics, and radiation chemistry. Early work used laboratory photon sources, either Al or Mg $k _ { \alpha }$ XPS sources<sup>17</sup> at 1254 or 1487 eV, or He 1a or 2a UPS sources<sup>9</sup> at 21.2 or 40.8 eV.
--[p109]-- High-intensity synchrotron X-ray sources make coincidence experiments possible, where electrons and ions from single molecular events are detected simultaneously allowing molecular relaxation to be studied in detail.<sup>5</sup>
Gas-phase electron scattering experiments can also provide important information for EUV radiation chemistry.
--[p108]-- Synchrotron light sources are ideal for molecular studies.<sup>4</sup> Variable photon energy allows photoemission and relaxation processes to be separated, since photoelectron energies depend on X-ray energy while Auger electron energies do not.
--[p109]-- Garcia and collaborators have investigated inelastic electron scattering from small molecules, including water,<sup>33</sup> toluene,<sup>34</sup> and phenol,<sup>35</sup> measuring integrated and differential cross sections for internal excitations and ionization.

===== [p111-111] Molecular excitation and relaxation of extreme ultraviolet lithography photoresists > 2.2.6 MOLECULAR SHAPE RESONANCES (2块) =====
--[p111]-- This leads to molecular “shape resonances” that can modulate the photoemission cross section.<sup>20</sup> Shape resonances are also important in dissociative electron attachment, where capture of slow electrons by stable molecules can cause molecular fragmentation.<sup>40</sup>
--[p111]-- 2.2.6 MOLECULAR SHAPE RESONANCES
There is another unique feature of molecular photoemission that is important near threshold. When the out-going photoelectron has low KE, it “feels” the electrostatic potential of the molecule. --[p363]-- Generally, resolution, sensitivity, and contrast decrease with increasing bake temperature because there is less differential networking between the radiation exposed regions and the areas only exposed to the bake. ===== [p206-207] The chemistry and application of nonchemically amplified (non-CA) chain-scission resists > 6.3.1 POLYMETHACRYLATES (5块) =====
--[p206]-- The chain scission mechanism of the degradation of PMMA had been established some 60 years ago<sup>22</sup>; however, the definitive studies of the mechanisms of degradation did not appear until the advent of high-resolution spectrometers several decades later .<sup>11,23e30</sup> The initial reactions of PMMA on interaction with high-energy photons are cleavage of the ester side chains, forming gaseous products and main-chain radicals (Scheme 1).
--[p206]-- 6.3.1 POLYMETHACRYLATES
As introduced mentioned previously, the earliest materials examined as resists for DUV lithography were based on PMMA.<sup>1</sup> Indeed PMMA remains a benchmark material for non-CA resists and for the manufacture of masks for photolithography.
--[p207]-- Bowden<sup>32</sup> found that the sensitivity of a resist depends not only on the nature of the polymer but also on its molecular weight and molecular weight distribution and increased with deceasing molar mass dispersity. The development dose was found to decrease with increasing G(S) for the polymethacrylates examined. Similar observations on the effect of molecular weight were reported by Lai and Shepherd.<sup>33</sup>
--[p207]-- In early studies, Thompson et al.<sup>31</sup> and Bowden<sup>32</sup> reported the properties of PMMA as potential X-ray and electron beam (e-beam) resists and in the former work examined the effect of incorporation of heavy atoms to enhance the sensitivity of PMMA to X-rays.
--[p206]-- The main-chain radicals can further undergo b-scission to form the propagating radical and a chain-end double bond. Direct main chain scission at the a-carbon is believed to be playing a minor role in the degradation pathways.

===== [p297-299] Negative-tone organic molecular resists > 8.7.6 UNDERLAYERS FOR EPOXIDE FUNCTIONALIZED MOLECULAR RESISTS (11块) =====
--[p299]-- Cross-linking between the resist and UL can occur during the PEB through either residual epoxide groups or phenolic hydroxyl groups at the surface of the UL.
--[p297]-- 8.7.6 UNDERLAYERS FOR EPOXIDE FUNCTIONALIZED MOLECULAR RESISTS
Most positive-tone materials use an added organic monolayer such as hexamethyldisilazane (HMDS) or precoated organic UL to improve adhesion to the typically inorganic substrates encountered in semiconductor manufacturing. Conventionally used epoxy adhesives typically bond quite well to inorganic and metal substrates.
--[p297]-- Some studies have indeed reported issues with negative-tone epoxide resists dewetting during coating and during the postapply bake before patterning but no apparent dewetting during the postexposure bake.<sup>93</sup> Likewise, development in aqueous base instead of organic solvent can lead to additional adhesion loss because the base developer tends to highly wet the native oxide surface.
--[p297]-- One reason is that the epoxides could potentially directly react with hydroxyl groups found in oxides that form on many inorganic surfaces, such as silanols found on the surface of wafers with a native oxide. This reaction would proceed similarly to that shown in Fig. 62. Thus, it is possible that these materials might have better adhesion on native oxide silicon wafers rather than those on HMDS primed or UL-coated wafers.
--[p299]-- Reproduced from Lawson RA, Narcross H, Sharp B, Chun JS, Neisser M, Tolbert LM, et al. Optimizing performance in cross-linking negative-tone molecular resists. Proc SPIE 2015;9425:94250A.
The UL was created to leverage the reactivity of epoxides to allow covalent bonding of the resist directly to the UL. This was accomplished by putting functional groups into the UL molecules that can react with the epoxides in the molecular resists during the PEB step. Lawson et al.
--[p299]-- The UL GT1 showed improvements in adhesion of a base developed epoxide molecular resist (called TPOE-3Ep, and discussed further in Section 8.7.7). A dot and/or column pattern on native oxide silicon had clear delamination issues when developed in aqueous base TMAH, but the delamination was eliminated by the use of the UL as shown in Fig. 77.
--[p297]-- Indeed, HMDS priming was not typically used for most patterning of these materials for this reason. However, an added monolayer or UL improves adhesion during the both development step and also improves the surface energy match between resist solution and substrate during wafer spin-coating. Since the epoxide reaction with substrate will only occur during the PEB step, an UL might be needed in order to get good quality coating of the small molecule resists.
--[p297]-- This could lead to delamination during development, which is not encountered during solvent development.<sup>110</sup> Thus, there is still a need for UL materials for these types of resists, but they must not lose the capability to directly bond to the resist that is possible with a native oxide. One such UL has been developed that has these properties and also appears to provide sensitivity improvements.<sup>111</sup>
--[p299]-- The UL also showed improvements for a very low $\mathrm { T _ { g } }$ difunctional molecular resist,<sup>93</sup> which showed wetting and adhesion issues during spin-coating and in organic solvent MIBK development. The UL significantly improved its performance as shown in Fig. 78, suggesting the UL has fixed the problem through better adhesion and reduced wetting of the resistesubstrate interface.
--[p299]-- TBAB is an optimal catalyst for the reaction because it does not inhibit cationic polymerization unlike many other phenol-epoxy cross-linking catalysts.<sup>112</sup> Because the thermal crosslinking of the UL required higher temperatures (150e200 C) than the typical PAB step (90e120 C) for these resists, minimal thermal cross-linking between resist and UL will occur except in presence of acid in exposed regions during PEB. An illustration of this process flow is shown in Fig. 76.
--[p299]-- created the UL called GT1 by combining PHOST with the 4-Ep molecule at an equimolar ratio of epoxide (Ep) to phenolic hydroxyl (OH) groups and thermally cross-linking the UL, using a catalyst of tetra-butylammonium bromide (TBAB) loaded at 5 wt%, in a bake step before coating the resist. By putting the identical resist molecule directly into the UL, there should be an optimal surface energy match between the two materials.

Throughout the scope of this work, MORE resists were successfully made from Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Pd, Sn, Pt, and Bi. ===== [p363-364] Mainstreaming inorganic metal-oxide resists for high-resolution lithography > 10.2.1.3 Improvingreproducibility: issues due to delaybetween spin/bake and exposure (4块) =====
--[p364]-- It has also been suggested that a vacuum-dry is a better alternative to a $9 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ bake.<sup>29</sup> Both approaches have subsequently been adopted in the literature without it being clear if one is better than the other.
--[p364]-- Even if the delay causes a higher effective exposure dose (features can be broadened with delay), the stronger developer dissolves this material. Post-application bakes as low as $9 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ are recommended to reduce delay affects.
--[p363]-- For instance, Clark et al.<sup>19</sup> showed that w25-nm features broadened tens of nanometers over the course of a 1 hour exposure in an e-beam.
Henschel et al.<sup>18</sup> found that stronger developers and lower post-application bake temperatures reduced delay affects, as detected by sensitivity and contrast measurements. Presumably, this is because the dissolution contrast in the film increases with the strong developer.
--[p363]-- 10.2.1.3 Improvingreproducibility: issues due to delaybetween spin/bake and exposure
Delays between the spin, bake, and exposure, and the storage conditions during delay, can affect contrast, resolution, and sensitivity.<sup>17,19</sup> Post-bake and postexposure delay is unavoidable in serial exposure processes such as direct-write e-beam. Unfortunately, it has been found that feature size is a function of the time in the tool before the feature is exposed.

===== [p174-174] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.3.8 CONTRAST CURVE (4块) =====
--[p174]-- The slope of the contrast curve near the x-axis intercept is called the contrast of the photoresist or $\gamma$ (dashed line in
Fig. 23). The higher the value of $\gamma ,$ the stronger is the distinction between the development rates on the exposed and unexposed parts of the resist. Therefore, $\gamma$ is a useful figure-of-merit of a photoresist.
--[p174]-- From the intercept of the x-axis, one can extract the dose-to-clear (or the clearing dose) of the photoresist, that is, the minimum amount of energy required to fully remove the exposed resist in a given development process, an important indicator of the sensitivity of the photoresist. It is important to notice that this value is different (always smaller in the case of positive photoresists) from dose-to-sizedthe amount of energy required for the desired feature size.
--[p174]-- To plot such a curve, the resist is exposed using various doses through a small opening in a mask and all the doses are developed using the same development process. Then the thickness of the resist in the exposed areas is measured (typically using either ellipsometry, profilometry, or an atomic force microscope), normalized, and plotted against the logarithmic values of the exposure dose (see the example in Fig. 23).
--[p174]-- 4.3.8 CONTRAST CURVE
A contrast curve (also Hurter-Driffield/H-D or characteristic curve) is a commonly used tool in characterization or development of photoresists. It was first introduced by Hurter and Driffield<sup>93</sup> in 1890 for the characterization of photographic plates. In a contrast curve, the normalized thickness of the photoresist that has undergone the development process is plotted against its exposure dose.

===== [p375-375] Mainstreaming inorganic metal-oxide resists for high-resolution lithography > 10.3.4 HafSOx SUMMARY (3块) =====
--[p375]-- The net result is a sensitive inorganic resist. High resolution derives from small nanoclusters with radii $4 \times$ smaller than the average radii of gyration of polymers comprising conventional chemically amplified resists. In the HafSOx system, planar clusters allow both deposition and dissolution approximating single-molecule precision.
--[p375]-- This cluster growth produces a differential dissolution rate between exposed and unexposed film regions. During concentrated TMAH development, peroxo hydroxo hafnium clusters likely dissolve from unexposed regions; this high-pH hafnium chemistry requires additional research. TMAH neutralizes unexposed film regions and extracts sulfate to produce an insoluble hafnium-oxide hydroxide. These processes amplify the differential dissolution rate between unexposed and exposed portions of the film.
--[p375]-- 10.3.4 HafSOx SUMMARY
From a solution mixture of $\mathrm { H f O C l } _ { 2 } \cdot \mathrm { x H _ { 2 } O } , \mathrm { H _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } ( a q ) }$ , and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ( \mathrm { a q } )$ in water, spincoated and baked films produce a crosslinked hydrous gel prepared for exposure. E-beam, EUV, and deep UV exposures cleave the peroxide bond to produce new intercluster HFeOeHF linkages and cluster growth.

===== [p55-55] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.6 CHALLENGES IN MODERN RESIST DESIGN (3块) =====
--[p55]-- Feature shrink has progressed to the point where even measuring these quantities is complicated by potential bias introduced by the measurement techniques themselves. This section briefly reviews many of these challenges.
--[p55]-- 1.6 CHALLENGES IN MODERN RESIST DESIGN
There are a number of challenges faced by resists as feature sizes continue to shrink. One of the major challenges for current and future resists is meeting the process requirements for resolution, LER, and sensitivity. It is difficult to simultaneously optimize these properties because a number of different chemistry and physics effects affect each property in different ways. Some of these include shot noise and photon statistics, and acid diffusion.
--[p55]-- On top of the three directly measured resist parameters are issues such as pattern collapse and resist adhesion, which can severely limit resolution, but are difficult to directly quantify. All of these measurable properties are also potentially affected by changes in the basic physics of polymers as they are confined to dimensions below 100 nm, which can have effects such as significant drops in elastic modulus, glass transition temperature, development behavior, and diffusivity.

How will these processes change in condensed molecular films?

--[p112]-- 2.3.2 RESONANT PHOTOABSORPTION

===== [p146-147] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.2 EUV-IL AS A CHARACTERIZATION ANDNANOPATTERNING TOOL (2块) =====
--[p146]-- 4.2 EUV-IL AS A CHARACTERIZATION ANDNANOPATTERNING TOOL
Interference lithography (IL) is a simple technique that does not require the use of high NA optics, imaging systems, and masks, which are expensive for EUV. In IL, resist-coated substrates are exposed to a periodic aerial image produced by interference of multiple coherent beams. This interference pattern exists within the volume of space defined by the overlapping beams and is invariant normal to the substrate.
--[p147]-- For this reason, the depth-of-focus is for all purposes infinite, and thereby, the aerial image created by interference is insensitive to variations between the mask and the substrate. Ultraviolet (UV) IL has been used in production since the 1990s to create large-scale gratings.<sup>10</sup> In the UV and visible regions, lasers are typically used due to their high coherence properties.<sup>11,12</sup>
