===== [p417-417] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.6 METAL OXALATE COMPLEXES (3块) =====
--[p417]-- To better understand the lithographic properties of this series of MORE compounds, three properties of these materials were studied through structural variation: ligand structure, central metal, and oxalate loading.
--[p417]-- Over the course of the last 100 years, the synthesis of different transition metal oxalate complexes has been thoroughly investigated.<sup>80,82e87</sup> In this section, we will investigate the lithographic properties of a series of different transition metal oxalates of the structure $[ \mathrm { M L } _ { 3 } ] \mathrm { X } _ { \mathrm { n } } ,$ where M is a transition metal, L is a bidentate ligand, and X is a charge-balancing counter ion.
--[p417]-- 11.6 METAL OXALATE COMPLEXES
Transition metal oxalates are a class of compounds with known photochemical reactivity at wavelengths longer than EUV (UV/visible) and so were investigated as MORE materials. The thermal and photochemical reaction of transition metal oxalates has been thoroughly studied in the literature.<sup>76,80,81</sup> The oxalate decomposes, generating 2 M equivalents of carbon dioxide and reduces the metal by two electrons (Fig. 38).

===== [p401-401] Molecular organometallic 11 resists for EUV (MORE) > 11.5 TIN COMPOUNDS (2块) =====
--[p401]-- 11.5 TIN COMPOUNDS
Tin compounds have myriad literature examples, high EUVoptical densities and low oxidation potentials, making them ideal candidates for MORE. However, although the tin literature is vast, there exist few examples involving photochemistry and none involving exposure to EUV radiation. Here, is presented the investigation of tin compounds as candidates for MORE through the exploration and modification of known tin complexes.<sup>25,26</sup>
--[p401]-- Two classes of tin compounds have been investigated for EUV sensitivity: Sn-1 compounds and Sn-12 clusters. The Sn-1 compounds contain a single tin atom, with four, potentially photoactive, ligands. The Sn-12 clusters are oxoclusters containing 12 tin atoms found to undergo EUV photochemistry during preliminary trials and for which possible exposure reactions have been investigated. The following section will describe the syntheses and exposure results for both material types.

===== [p18-18] Overview of materials and processes for lithography > 1.3 LITHOGRAPHIC EXPOSURE SOURCES AND PROCESSES (6块) =====
--[p18]-- The most commonly used exposure sources are UVand deep UV (DUV) light generated by a mercury lamp or laser. Modifications in DUV lithography at 193-nm wavelength have led to a technique that is called immersion lithography. This exposure wavelength has been extended even further to smaller feature sizes through the use of double and multiple patterning as will be discussed later.
--[p18]-- Each of these exposure sources and processes typically has its own specific type of resists with unique properties that allow them to work well for that source, although some resists can be used across multiple platforms. This section will focus on the sources and techniques and a more thorough discussion of resists will be given in Section 1.5.
--[p18]-- Some examples of this include nanoimprint lithography<sup>14e18</sup> where the resist pattern is made by pressing a mold into the resist to replicate the mold pattern or scanning probe lithography 19e22 where the pattern is made by selectively scanning a nanoscale probe such as an atomic force microscope (AFM) tip over the surface of the resist and modifying the resist through thermal, chemical, or electrical changes.
--[p18]-- Work has also been carried out on use of ion beam lithography which uses focused beams of ions to pattern the resist.<sup>12,13</sup> There have also been extensive developments in lithographic processes where the resist is not exposed to a radiation source, but instead is physically modified in some other way.
--[p18]-- Intense research and development has been carried out on the application of EUV lithography for future generations of IC manufacturing.<sup>9e11</sup> Electron beam (e-beam) as a source of exposing radiation has been used industrially for mask production for many years and is used commonly in research and development applications due to its very high resolution and ability to rapidly produce a wide variety of patterns.
--[p18]-- 1.3 LITHOGRAPHIC EXPOSURE SOURCES AND PROCESSES
When discussing lithographic imaging, it is important to specify the radiation source used to expose the resist and transfer the pattern. Although much of the lithography process is similar or the same with differing sources, it is important to understand the differences between each type of commonly used exposure source and how the choice of exposure source affects the choice and optimization of resist material.

===== [p175-175] Theory: electron-induced chemistry > 4.3.9 PATTERN COLLAPSE (3块) =====
--[p175]-- 4.3.9 PATTERN COLLAPSE
One of the major problems faced by photoresists patterned to the highest resolutions is the permanent adherence of two or more neighboring structures to each other $( \mathrm { i . e . } ,$ stiction) due to electrostatic or van der Waals forces (Fig. 24A). This phenomenon is called pattern collapse.
--[p175]-- In order for pattern collapse to occur, the structures first have to be brought into contact with each other at some point of the process, most often due to capillary forces present when the wafer is dried after the resist developing and rinsing processes (Fig. 24B). This may occur either due to bending or breaking of the resist or its delamination from the substrate. 94
--[p175]-- The maximum stress experienced by the resist due to the capillary forces during the drying process $\sigma _ { m a x }$ <sub>x</sub> is given as<sup>94</sup>:
$$
\sigma _ { m a x } = { \frac { 6 \gamma A ^ { 2 } } { D \cos \theta } }\tag{16}
$$
where $\Upsilon$ is the surface tension of the rinse liquid, A the aspect ratio (or height-towidth ratio H/W) of the resist structures, D the spacing between them, and q the contact angle between the resist and the rinsing liquid (Fig. 24B).
As can be inferred from this equation, pattern collapse becomes a severe problem with decreasing HPs and increasing aspect ratios.

===== [p351-351] Positive molecular resists > 9.5 CONCLUSIONS (3块) =====
--[p351]-- In addition, certain materials can find application outside the traditional semiconductor manufacturing, for instance, in the area of organic electronics (star-shaped, fullerene, fused ring derivatives) and in microsystems.
--[p351]-- 9.5 CONCLUSIONS
The current status of molecular resists performance indicates potential for the development of mature lithographic materials based on small organic molecules in the near future. Nevertheless, their expected advantages over the polymeric lithographic materials have not been demonstrated yet. Much effort has been devoted to processing and stability issues that proved difficult to address successfully.
--[p351]-- Thus, the expected improvement over polymeric resists in LER issues has not yet been convincingly demonstrated. On the other hand, the research effort in this area has provided novel materials and a plethora of new chemical routes that can be further exploited if this effort is further supported and particularly if more academic groups enter the field.

===== [p491-491] Next generation lithographydthe rise of unconventional methods? > 14.2.2 NANOIMPRINT LITHOGRAPHY (3块) =====
--[p491]-- 14.2.2 NANOIMPRINT LITHOGRAPHY
Instead of the exposure of resist materials by energetic beams, nanoimprint lithography (NIL) replicates nanostructures by embossing a resist-coated substrate with a 3D master mold to circumvent the limitations of diffraction or scattering .<sup>49e51</sup> The basic principle of NIL is to use a mold to emboss a polymer film (Fig. 3), either by softening the polymer thermally during imprint or by starting with a liquid polymer that is UV-cured during imprint.
--[p491]-- NIL methods with corresponding materials used are summarized in Table 1. Presently, NIL is a commercial technology and finds a use in photonic, microelectronic, and bioapplications.<sup>51,62e65</sup>
--[p491]-- The patterned polymer can be directly used as a functional layer (e.g., lenses, microfluidic channels) or as a mask for subsequent processing.<sup>52</sup> Even in the earliest publications from Chou et al.,<sup>53e55</sup> this simple concept showed high-resolution capabilities down to the 10-nm regime. Various NIL methods are differentiated depending on the curing process applied, which will also set the required specifications for mold and resist materials.

--[p83]-- PMMA behaves as a positive tone resist for low dose ranges and exhibits negative tone behavior when it is exposed to high doses for both beams (Fig. 10A).<sup>43,44</sup> A reduced layer thickness is observed in the negative tone region and the trend of decreasing thickness continues with increasing dose. This may be caused by shrinkage of the resist under heavy bombardment by energetic particles.
--[p83]-- The sensitivity enhancement of HIBL compared to EBL is therefore confirmed, with a gain of 60 in the positive tone region and a gain of 42 in the negative tone region, while having similar contrast values of w1. The HSQ sensitivity values (extracted from Fig.
--[p83]-- The PMMA sensitivity values are 2 and $1 2 0 \mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ , in HIBL and EBL respectively, after identical resist preparation and development processes, and negative tone resist behavior begins at 60 and $2 5 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } ,$ respectively.
--[p83]-- 17.3.2.1 Sensitivity
Sensitivity indicates the amount of incident energy required to produce the chemical reactions in the resist for pattern definition. For positive tone resists, such as PMMA, it is usually defined as the dose that leads to a full clearance of resist; for negative tone resist, such as HSQ, it is often defined as the dose necessary to achieve 50% of the film’s original thickness after development. The sensitivity can be determined from plots of normalized resist thickness vs.
--[p83]-- 10B) are 31 and $1 3 7 \mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ in HIBL and EBL respectively, whilst the contrast values, obtained from the tangent at half-height on the dose response curve, are approximately equal for the two different beams at around 2.1. The results show that Heþ ion exposure is w4.4 times more effective than electron beam, in exposing HSQ at the same beam energy.
--[p84]-- For both resists, HIBL exposure is substantially more efficient than EBL without compromising the resolution, which means that much lower doses are required in HIBL, while a good contrast is obtainable in the formed patterns. This effect is due to a significantly larger low-energy SE yield from the energetic helium ions compared to an electron beam of the same energy, which is in agreement with the modeling results from the previous section.

Likewise, the contrast can also be calculated from the slope of the falling (positive tone) or rising (negative tone) part of the response curve. ===== [p17-18] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.4.3 Electrochemical material deposition (15块) =====
--[p17]-- 15.2.4.3 Electrochemical material deposition
As well as field-induced material modification reactions, an electric field and/or a tunneling/field-emission current can also trigger localized material deposition reactions. This has been used to create in situ solid-state nanostructures underneath the nanoprobe.
--[p17]-- The implementation of traditional electron-beam-induced deposition concepts into STM-based lithography, firstly demonstrated by Ehrichs et al.<sup>153</sup> to write 20-nm cadmium structures, has led to the direct patterning of a multitude of materials, for example iron,<sup>154,155</sup> aluminum,<sup>156</sup> gold,<sup>157</sup> titanium,<sup>158</sup> and also silicon.
--[p18]-- However, based on the hydrophilic nature of polar molecules (1-octene, alcohols), the presence of water should be avoided to prevent water contamination within the formed liquid menisci.<sup>162,165</sup> Based on this lithographic method, Rolandi et al.<sup>166</sup> demonstrated high-speed patterning of sub-50-nm fluorinated amorphous carbon film features at velocities up to cm/s.
--[p17]-- Reduction | Tip (+) | $2 { \mathsf { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathsf { O } } \to { \mathsf { O } } _ { 2 } \uparrow + 4 { \mathsf { H } } ^ { + } + 2 { \mathsf { O } } { \mathsf { H } } ^ { - }$
Reduction | Surface (-) | $4 \times ( 0 + \ e ^ { - } \to \mathsf { R } )$
To improve the LAO process, Tello and Garcia<sup>161</sup> tried to replace the water by other organic liquids, such as ethyl alcohol. Instead of the growth of the respective compounds on the silicon surface.
--[p17]-- The deposition process can be initiated either starting from gaseous precursor molecules, called STM-chemical vapor deposition (CVD), or from a liquid phase, which operates via a field-induced organic liquid meniscus (see LAO-processes, Section 15.2.4.1) within the tipesample junction.
--[p18]-- They proposed a multistep process involving the capture of CO inside the nanogap due to a field-induced diffusion process (application of extreme high electric fields up to 30 V/nm), followed by the activation of the molecules, and subsequently the formation of the carbonaceous deposit with presence of some oxygen onto the positively biased sample surface.
--[p18]-- Garcia et al.<sup>160</sup> demonstrated the creation of carbonaceous depositions (sub-25-nm dots) directly from stable precursor gases, such as carbon dioxide, in ambient conditions.
--[p17 [表]]-- In a typical setup, the STM-CVD process is carried out at UHV conditions while the STM operates in field emission mode. Commonly bias threshold values<sup>160</sup> are above 4 V, although the exact value is dependent mainly on the precursor gas. However, the purity of the deposit material can be diminished by carbon contamination, and thus generally inorganic precursor molecules are preferred over organic ones.
--[p18]-- The deposition of carbon-rich material, usable as an etch mask for subsequent process steps, is caused by a field-induced decomposition of the solvents, 162e165 such as ethanol, 2-propanol, octane, 1-octene, perfluorooctane, and hexadecane. The field-induced formation and manipulation of nanometer-sized liquid menisci plays a crucial role with respect to the spatial confinement of the electrochemical reaction.
--[p18]-- Moreover, Spinney et al.<sup>168</sup> collected carbon-based material from a glassy carbon substrate and redeposited it onto a gold thin film by simple voltage/bias polarity control. In addition to carbon nanostructures, Torrey et al.<sup>169</sup> was able to write sub-30-nm germanium nanostructures at velocities up to 100 mm/s, utilizing the precursor diphenylgermane, present as a liquid thin film.
--[p17]-- 159 The fieldemitted, low-energy electrons (3e30 eV) interact with the gaseous precursor molecules, which are located within the electron beam of the biased probeesample junction. The respective electronemolecule interaction, commonly an excitation of organometallic precursor molecules, causes a decomposition process with subsequent material deposition underneath the nanoprobe.
--[p18]-- Electrons are injected from the tip into unoccupied molecular orbitals of a precursor (electric-field direction plays important role), which leads in turn to fragmentation of the molecule, resulting in pure germanium deposition onto the surface.
--[p18]-- In general, nanostructures were formed at both sample bias polarities (tip grounded), although the structures are significantly smaller at negative polarities. The material growth rate can be significantly modified by modulation of the organic solvent composition.

--[p4]-- 15.1.1 SCANNING PROBE MICROSCOPY AND SCANNING PROBELITHOGRAPHY SETUP
The simplest path to scanning probe lithography (SPL) is to use conventional scanning probe microscopy (SPM), and by applying excessive force on the tip, to modify the surface of the sample. In SPM, a sharp probe is raster scanned across the sample (in the X and Y directions), and the surface geometry (Z direction) is detected via changes in the forces appearing between the probe and the sample.

===== [p92-93] Scanning helium ion beam lithography > 17.3.3 HIBL WITH FULLERENE DERIVATIVE MOLECULAR RESIST (9块) =====
--[p92]-- However, the resists have relatively low sensitivity in EBL (from 200 to $2 0 { , } 0 0 0 { \mu } \mathrm { C / c m } ^ { 2 }$ ; one to three orders of magnitude less than required for commercial resists), which limits their application.<sup>56,57</sup>
--[p92]-- In our group, we have investigated using HIBL to expose thin films prepared by spin coating silicon with a methanofullerene derivative of $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ dissolved in anisole (HM-01, Irresistible Materials Ltd.).<sup>58</sup> The doseeresponse curves for HM-01 in EBL and HIBL are shown in Fig. 17C, where the normalized resist thickness was plotted against the logarithm of dose.
--[p92]-- However, such thin layers of resist can cause significant issues due to insufficient protection of the substrate underneath during subsequent pattern transfer processes. Hence, resists that exhibit high etch resistance, as well as high resolution, are needed in nanolithographic applications.
--[p93]-- This is comparable to the best achievable with state-of-the-art EBL, despite being carried out using a tool not optimized for lithography, and with standard processing conditions.
--[p92]-- Due to their carbon-rich nature, fullerene derivative resists exhibit high etch durability; $\mathrm { e . g . }$ , double that of SAL601 (a high durability commercial resist) and almost eight times than that of silicon in plasma etching.<sup>55</sup> This increased material selectivity along with their high-resolution potential make fullerene derivative resists attractive for nextgeneration-lithography.
--[p93]-- The best results to date are continuous and well-defined lines with a pitch of 17 nm and a 0.5 line-space ratio (line width of w8.5 nm) and resolvable but broken densely packed lines with a pitch of 12 nm and a 0.5 line-space ratio (line width of w6 nm).<sup>58</sup> These patterns, produced with line doses of 0.09 and 0.04 nC/cm, respectively, are shown in the HIM images and corresponding contrast line profiles in Fig. 18.
--[p92]-- 17.3.3 HIBL WITH FULLERENE DERIVATIVE MOLECULAR RESIST
From the previous section, it is clear that patterns of the highest resolution have been formed in resist layers with thicknesses less than 10 nm. This is because the beam broadening through scattering increases with depth from the surface and so smaller feature sizes can be defined as the thickness of the resist is decreased.
--[p92]-- Recently, a new class of negative tone fullerene-based molecular resists was developed in an effort to provide a good balance of these desirable properties.<sup>10</sup> Having a small molecular size, down to w0.7 nm (Fig. 17A), and a molecular weight of w1000 Mw $( \mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ plus the side chains), fullerene resists offer great potential to improve lithographic resolution and reduce line edge roughness compared to conventional polymeric resists (Fig. 17B).
--[p92]-- HM-01 exhibits negative tone behavior with a sensitivity of 40 and $2 0 { , } 0 0 0 { \mu } \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ in HIBL and EBL, respectively. There is a 500 times improvement in sensitivity in HIBL compared to EBL for this resist, which results in a significantly reduced required current and exposure time and an improved efficiency.
High-resolution sparse and dense line arrays with various pitches were patterned using HIBL in w10-nm-thick HM-01.

===== [p50-53] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.2 ADVANTAGES OF THERMAL SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY (17块) =====
--[p51]-- The patterning throughput of TSPL and electron-beam lithography at highest resolutions is similar. Nonchemically amplified electron-beam lithography resists such as hydrogen silsesquioxane require a higher exposure dose than lowerresolution chemically amplified resists, hence slowing down electron-beam patterning. However, as TSPL evaporates the resist directly and instantly, no development is required after patterning.
--[p52]-- Pixels in the immediate vicinity of each other may geometrically merge, but there are no long-range effects such as in electron-beam lithography.
High-energy electron radiation may also cause damage to electronic devices.
--[p51]-- One order in magnitude improvement in resolution results in a five orders of magnitude decrease in areal throughput. Different resists and beam currents may be used with electron-beam lithography, with varying resolution and throughput. Nevertheless, exposing entire wafers with electron-beam lithography is time intensive and usually not feasible for lower end electron-beam writers that are typically used in the research domain.
--[p53]-- As the patterning space is much more accessible, it is also much easier to make modifications and tailor the machine to individual applications. In addition, work pieces do not need to be vacuum compatible.
--[p51]-- The pattern is defined in software and written directly into the resist without prior fabrication of a mask template. Mask-less patterning is well suited for research applications and prototyping, where typically many different variants of a design are tested. While mask-less methods allow the flexibility of modifying patterns without additional cost, they are sequential in nature.
--[p52]-- In an overlay application, topographical features from lower layers are used as the alignment template. After spin coating the resist, some residual topography remains at the surface of the resist. The topography is imaged before patterning, and a cross correlation between the underlying and the surface topographies can be used to compute and correct for alignment errors. It is not necessary to complicate layout designs by placing area-consuming alignment marks around devices. 33
--[p50]-- 16.2 ADVANTAGES OF THERMAL SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY
As evident from the name, thermal scanning probe lithography uses a heated probe for structuring of the resist material. The hot probe is brought into contact with the surface, to locally decompose and evaporate the resist. As illustrated in Fig. 1, a voltage is applied between the probe and the work piece substrate (or, alternatively, to an electrode above the cantilever) to generate an electrostatic pull-in force.
--[p51]-- Without the need to first develop the resist, the inbuilt AFM topography imaging can be used for quality inspection. The user is given immediate feedback about the patterning success without reloading the work piece into a separate metrology instrument and the need to locate the patterned area. 21
The charged particles used in electron-beam lithography have drawbacks. Charge is deposited in the resist and work piece substrate during patterning.
--[p52]-- Arbitrary-depth 3D patterns can be created with this method in a single patterning step. Methods for 3D electron-beam lithography have also been developed, but these usually require additional steps such as thermal reflow and accuracy and choice of geometry are limited.<sup>30</sup>
The volume of the tip and its heater are minimized to maximize the achievable heating rates. The thermal time constant of the heaters used by SwissLitho are calculated<sup>31</sup> to be around 6 ms.
--[p52]-- If charges are trapped in the device layer or substrate material of a device, its characteristics and voltages may change or degrade due to extra gating .<sup>25,26</sup> Sensitive materials such as graphene are also known to be damaged directly by the electron beam.<sup>27,28</sup> As the principle of thermal scanning probe lithography does not rely on charge, such damage mechanisms have not been observed.<sup>29</sup> Typical operating conditions and resist thicknesses of thermal scanning probe lithography also show good thermal insulation between the hot tip and device layers, so thermal damage is unlikely.
A unique capability of thermal scanning probe lithography is the ability to control the penetration depth of the probe pixel by pixel.
--[p53]-- The second alignment type is stitching individual patterning fields together. In this case, the inherent surface roughness of the resist may be used as position reference. The statistical nature of the surface roughness of the resist is unique in each location. During writing, a field is imaged with an extra margin around the written pattern. The topography in this margin is used as an alignment reference after a coarse positioning step.
--[p50]-- The deflection of the probe and the penetration depth can thus be controlled by modulating the force voltage. This simple actuation mechanism minimizes the accelerated mass to only the probe, thus maximizing the actuation speed.<sup>21</sup> TSPL can pattern complex surface topographies in one step.<sup>20</sup>
Thermal scanning probe lithography is a mask-less lithography method.
--[p52]-- This allows the patterning interaction to be turned off practically instantaneously. Thus, writing and imaging with the same probe can be interleaved without causing spurious “exposure” of the resist. Moreover, interleaved patterning and imaging allows the implementation of a closed-loop depth feedback 32 loop to make the overall patterning process robust and accurate.
Topographical features on the substrate may be used for pattern alignment. This may be done in two ways.
--[p52]-- The deposited charge influences the exposure of nearby areas. This is known as the proximity effect. Complex dose-adjustment simulations are typically carried out to achieve pattern fidelity at the highest resolutions.<sup>24</sup> In thermal scanning probe lithography, there is a depth-dependent lateral broadening of a written pixel, as the tip is cone shaped.
--[p53]-- Mathematically, the information content in a 1-mm square field is sufficient for nanometer accuracy position offset calculations. The final position accuracy is limited by the mechanical positioning of the system.<sup>34</sup>
TSPL is carried out in ambient environment. Therefore, the mechanical setup is much simpler compared to electron-beam writers. This reduces maintenance complexity and effort.
--[p51]-- However, its resolution is still limited by the wavelength of the laser used,<sup>23</sup> resulting in resolutions around or just under 1 mm.
Electron-beam lithography is a long-established and de facto standard method for research prototyping and mask writing at length scales below 1 mm. An interesting observation made by Marrian et al.<sup>22</sup> is the scaling of area throughput with resolution, which seems to hold true for all mask-less lithography methods.
--[p51]-- Writing a pattern pixel by pixel reduces the area throughput compared to mask lithography methods, where an entire field can be exposed at once.<sup>22</sup> Other mask-less lithography methods include laser writing lithography and ion and electron-beam lithography.
Laser writing lithography has the advantage of comparatively high-area throughput. Today, it is capable of patterning full wafers in less than an hour, reaching similar throughput to UV mask lithography.

===== [p76-77] Scanning helium ion beam lithography > 17.2.2.2 Secondary electrons characteristics (10块) =====
--[p77]-- ^ { 2 3 , 2 4 }$ In contrast, for electron beam irradiation, there are a large number of SEs at energies ranging from a few eVs to the full primary beam energy and the energy distribution of SEs peaks in the range of 5 to 15 eV as shown in Fig. 7B.
--[p77]-- This suggests that with further helium ion source developments, a higher operating voltage will further enhance the SE yield.
Knowing that more SEs are generated by the helium ion beam than the electron beam, an understanding of the energy profiles of the SEs becomes important. Petrov et al. studied the energy distribution of SEs obtained from a gold sample exposed to 35-keV helium ions.
--[p77]-- SEs with higher energies travel further than those that have a lower energy, and SEs of more than 100-eV energy are known to have a very long range in resists and cause modifications in a relatively large region around the impact site.<sup>31</sup> This effect contributes greatly towards the proximity effect in EBL and limits pattern fidelity and resolution.
--[p77]-- On average 2 to 8 SEs are generated by each $\mathrm { H e ^ { + } }$ , substantially higher than the 0.5 to 1.25 per incident electron in EBL.<sup>17,27</sup> The large number of SEs makes reactions such as bond-breaking or cross-linking more efficient, resulting in higher resist 28   
sensitivities.
Ramachandra et al. described a Monte Carlo simulation techniqueeIon Induced SE or “IONiSE”- for the modeling of SE production by ions. Fig.
6 shows the normalized SE yield as a function of the normalized beam energy for electrons, $\mathrm { H e } ^ { + }$ ions, and protons.
--[p76]-- A $\mathrm { H e ^ { + } }$ beam generates a much higher SE yield compared to an electron beam. Due to its larger mass, the helium ion can transfer only a small fraction of its energy to an electron on collision.
This allows the helium ion to excite more electrons before its energy dissipates.
--[p77]-- The low-energy SEs excited by the helium ion beam makes HIBL favorable for creating ultra-dense patterns due to the consequently reduced proximity effect.
--[p77]-- This gives the helium ion beam an $\mathrm { E / E _ { \mathrm { m a x } } }$ value of 0.03e0.06 which is an equivalent 30% to 40% of the maximum SE yield $( \delta / \delta _ { \mathrm { m a x } } = 0 . 3 - 0 . 4 )$ , indicated by the gray box on Fig. 6. In contrast, the $\mathrm { E / E _ { m a x } }$ value for electrons at 30 keV is at 100 to 300dfar off the right hand side of the chartdwhich results in a much smaller percentage of the maximum SE yield.
--[p77]-- The SE yield from the incident helium ions reaches a maximum when the beam energy is between 500 keV and 1 MeV $\mathrm { ( E _ { m a x } }$ for helium ions), whereas the SE yield from energetic electrons reaches a maximum at a very low beam energy between 100 and 300 eV $\mathrm { ( E _ { m a x } }$ for electrons).<sup>23</sup> A beam energy of 30 keV is widely used in both electron and HIBL.
--[p76]-- 17.2.2.2 Secondary electrons characteristics
Low-energy SEs are often considered as the most important drivers of the local chemical conversion of resist molecules in lithographic applications. In principle, ion beam lithography follows the same mechanism as EBL, since they both generate low-energy SEs. All SEs along the $\mathrm { H e ^ { + } }$ trajectory are relevant if they have sufficient energy for bond-breaking or cross-linking reactions.
--[p77]-- The majority of SEs excited by $\mathrm { H e ^ { + } }$ ions have an energy of $2 \mathrm { e V }$ or less, and over half of the generated SEs have energies less than 3 eV. Furthermore, the energy distribution peaks at w1 eV and there are almost no SEs with energies above 20 eV as shown in Fig. $7 \mathrm { A } .

===== [p68-70] Scanning helium ion beam lithography > 17.1 INTRODUCTION (16块) =====
--[p69]-- The finite penetration depth of low-energy electrons limits the thickness of the resist; forward scattering also reduces resolution as the resist thickness increases.
--[p69]-- In EBL, electron beams generate low-energy secondary electrons (SEs) to activate the physical/chemical reactions in the resist materials. FIB lithography adopts the same principle but more SEs are generated, hence, the process is more efficient and therefore potentially faster.. In FIB lithography, proximity effects are negligible due to the very low number of ions that are backscattered.
In theory, densely packed patterns with a resolution comparable to the FIB probe size are achievable.
--[p68]-- 17.1 INTRODUCTION
Lithography is a process where an arbitrary pattern can be accurately and repeatedly produced in a specialized layer of material on a substrate by inducing a chemical modification. Typically, that pattern is then transferred to another functional layer through a traditional etching or lift-off process.<sup>1</sup> Lithography facilitates the drive for ever-decreasing dimensions of semiconductor devices and is therefore a keystone of the nanotechnology revolution.
--[p69]-- field ion source (GFIS) over 20 years ago<sup>9</sup>; however, deficiencies in column technol  
ogy halted its progress. Recently, developments in light ion sources and columns 10   
have made subnanometer spot sizes possible, whilst limiting sample damage.   
With the shorter ion range, weaker forward scattering and smaller lateral diffusion
of yielded SEs, FIB lithography can now reach resolutions comparable to the best demonstrated by well-established EBL.
--[p70]-- For example, sub-20-nm pitched features have been demonstrated with neon ion beam lithography.<sup>13,14</sup>
In the following sections, the working principles of the helium ion beam system as well as the unique properties of the ionesolid interactions in HIBL will be described. Analysis of the key features that enable high-resolution nanofabrication will also be presented.
--[p69]-- It is used daily for mass production of integrated circuits, which, at the time of writing, are being shipped with feature sizes corresponding to the 14 nm technology node.<sup>2</sup> However, alternative lithography methods can be more favorable for low-volume fabrication where the requirement for a photomask is a disadvantage. For example, electron beam lithography (EBL) is a common direct-write method that uses a focused electron beam to expose resist.
--[p68]-- Resist-based lithography is the most prevalent approach where resist materials that are sensitive to energetic photons or particles are exposed.
There are many lithographic approaches currently implemented in industry as well as in research. Optical lithography is the most common topedown patterning method that allows for cost-efficient, high-volume fabrication of microelectronic and nanoelectronic devices.
--[p69]-- For heavy ions such as gallium, the large beam spot size makes it difficult to reach comparable lithographic resolution to EBL. Other constraints are substrate damage and contamination produced by the ion impact.<sup>8</sup> Both factors have inhibited large-scale applications of heavy ion beam lithography in resist patterning.
For light ions such as helium, w200-nm resolution was demonstrated using a gas
--[p70]-- However, this has minimal effects on applications such as rapid prototyping for nanoscale devices where wafer-scale mass production is not required. The area on a sample surface that can be exposed without stage movements tends to be smaller for FIB lithography than EBL; however, this can be conquered by good alignment techniques that enable the stitching of write fields to produce the complete pattern.
The helium ion microscope (HIM), introduced by Carl Zeiss SMT, Inc.
--[p70]-- in 2006, based on GFIS technology, is a new entry into the field of FIB lithography.<sup>10,11</sup> It produces a subnanometer ion beam probe, which can be used for high-resolution, high pattern-density nanolithography, as well as for imaging. Reported state-ofthe-art helium ion beam lithography (HIBL) performance is comparable to the best EBL achievements<sup>12</sup> but with a one to two orders of magnitude higher sensitivity.
--[p69]-- However, EBL suffers from long-range proximity effects at high energies due to backscattered electrons (BEs), as discussed in Chapter 12, and this effect significantly limits its performance. Although the proximity effect has been demonstrated to be minimal when adopting low beam energies (15-nm half-pitch structures were obtained<sup>5</sup> at 2 keV), patterning thick resists proves to be difficult at this energy level.
--[p70]-- Second, the ultimate resolution in ion beam lithography is defined and limited by the diameter of the FIB rather than the wavelength of the exposing irradiation.
Nonetheless, there are also disadvantages that limit ion beam lithographic applications. Due to the nature of serial write, the throughput is lower than that for a parallel technique, hence, it is not as economically favorable for large area, or high-volume, fabrication.
--[p69]-- Proximity effect correction (PEC) in EBL was developed to enhance lithographic accuracy and resolution; however, these commercial software packages are optimized for high throughput of highly hierarchical design topologies consisting mainly of a relatively low-density arrangement of rectangular-shaped features and can be costly.<sup>7</sup>
Another method is the lesser known, but highly versatile focused ion beam (FIB) lithography.
--[p69]-- EBL at energies of 30 keV and above is well established for sub-20-nm nanofabrication and a minimum feature size of below 10 nm has been demonstrated.<sup>3,4</sup>
The high-resolution masks and templates fabricated by EBL have enabled highvolume nanoscale patterning technologies including optical and nanoimprint lithography. Furthermore, EBL is used for rapid prototyping of new device designs.
--[p70]-- Being the workhorse of nanoscale lithography, EBL has benefited from not only the high brightness of the Schottky source of electrons, but also decades of incremental innovation and engineering of apparatus around the source. HIBL techniques are, on the other hand, in their infancy but showing great potential. The success of the HIM in lithography encourages extensions of this technology to produce beams of other ion species.
--[p70]-- Compared to parallel lithography approaches including conventional optical lithography, FIB lithography has two main advantages. First, its mask-less approach offers good flexibility in writing arbitrary patterns, similar to EBL. For single-item or low-volume runs, it is a relatively low cost and high efficiency option. In parallel techniques, the masks have to be fabricated first to transmit radiation accurately, which can be time-consuming and expensive.

===== [p94-95] Scanning helium ion beam lithography > 17.3.4 EVALUATION OF EUV RESISTS USING HIBL (5块) =====
--[p95]-- Arrays of 40-nm pitched circular holes and lines patterned in HIBL and EUVL were shown to be comparable in resolution, indicating that HIBL could find use as a rapid characterization and prescreening tool for EUV resists.
--[p94]-- For the introduction of EUVL, development of high-performance EUV resists is of key importance and involves characterizing resist, for instance their sensitivity, resolution, and pattern uniformity. Currently, EBL is often used to prescreen EUV resists<sup>59</sup> partly due to its flexible direct-write approach, which means that no mask is required for complex arbitrary patterns. However, due to its pronounced proximity effect, PEC is often required for high-density pattern definition.
--[p95]-- The full clearance of the positive tone resist was reached at a dose of 0.085 ions/nm<sup>2</sup> in HIBL and 12.8 photons/nm<sup>2</sup> in EUV, suggesting that a single 30-keV helium ion is as effective as 150 EUV photons. This is mainly due to the fact that energetic helium ions excite more SEs during inelastic collisions along the trajectory before all energy is dissipated, whilst each EUV photon excites far fewer SE along its path.
--[p94]-- 17.3.4 EVALUATION OF EUV RESISTS USING HIBL
Another promising application of HIBL is in the evaluation of resists for extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUVL). In EUVL, a pattern is projected onto the resist using extreme ultraviolet light via a patterned mask. Due to its parallel nature, the high throughput technique is being developed as a promising next-generation lithography candidate.
--[p94]-- As an alternative to EBL, HIBL has a clear advantage of having a greatly reduced proximity effect.
Maas et al. used 30-keV HIBL to expose chemically amplified EUV resist for sensitivity and resolution characterization for the application of EUV resist prescreening. Doseeresponse curves of chemically amplified EUV resist using 30-keV HIBL and 92-eV EUVL showed highly similar shapes and close contrast values, but with a large difference in the sensitivities.

===== [p49-50] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.1 HISTORY (10块) =====
--[p50]-- The main difference between the lithography, and the data storage, application is the removal of the resist for lithography rather than its reversible indentation in data storage.<sup>20</sup>
--[p50]-- Successful trials were carried out with crosslinking chemistries for binding species to a surface,<sup>13</sup> as well as thermal conversion of precursors to organic electronics<sup>14,15</sup> or the reduction of graphene oxide to graphene.<sup>16</sup>
--[p50]-- The probes were optimized for small tip radius (down to 5 nm), to maximize data density.<sup>18</sup> The actuation of the probes was also designed for the modulation of indentation depth to store multiple bits per indentation. Furthermore, a topography sensor with electrical readout was integrated on the cantilever. This allowed the use of parallel cantilever arrays with low technical overhead.<sup>19</sup> These optimizations are also ideal for high-resolution, 3D lithography.
--[p50]-- Diamond indenters were used for lithography even before the invention of the AFM.<sup>3</sup> A more refined approach is to use diamond tip AFM probes for scribing arbitrary-depth patterns.<sup>4</sup> Other patterning approaches involve the various nonmechanical interactions between the tip and the substrate material.
--[p49]-- The high resolution and comparative simplicity of the instrument are also attractive properties to explore probe-based lithography approaches.
The simplest method is to use a probe for scribing directly into a work piece.
--[p49]-- 16.1 HISTORY
Probe-based microscopes such as the scanning tunneling microscope (STM) and atomic force microscope (AFM) revolutionized the ability to image materials and topography down to the nanometer, and even subatomic, length scales.<sup>1,2</sup> Compared to electron-beam imaging and patterning instruments, which require complex electron optics and operate in vacuum conditions, scanning probe instruments generally have a much simpler design.
--[p50]-- The topic of this chapter is thermal scanning probe lithography (TSPL). TSPL uses heat transfer as mechanism for defining the pattern. A dedicated TSPL instrument is available from SwissLitho, called the NanoFrazor.<sup>12</sup> The primary application of SwissLitho’s TSPL machine is thermal decomposition and evaporation of a resist material.
--[p50]-- For example, the tunneling currents of an STM may also be used for local anodic oxidation.<sup>5</sup> The high electrical field (gradient) between tip and substrate may result in electron emission and can be used for the desorption of resist molecules<sup>6</sup> or the deposition of a resist from precursor material.<sup>7</sup> A commercial control system for STM lithography using field interactions to move hydrogen atoms<sup>8</sup> is made by Zyvex Labs.<sup>9</sup> With a focus on biological applications, probe-based instruments have been developed for the deposition of material, either in a dip pen fashion<sup>10</sup> or using hollow probes.<sup>11</sup>
These and other scanning probe lithography techniques are described in Chapter 15.
--[p50]-- More generally, thermal scanning probe lithography may also be applied to any heat-activated chemical or physical process, so long as its activation temperature can be reached. Various chemical reactions have successfully been triggered with heated silicon AFM probes.
--[p50]-- The heated probe technology used by SwissLitho was originally developed at the IBM Research Laboratories.<sup>17</sup> The probe-based data storage project “Millipede” at the IBM Labs in Zurich was a significant contributor to the evolution of thermal AFM probes. In this project, heated probes were used to soften and reversibly indent a polymer layer to store data.

--[p24]-- promising tool for nanoscale prototyping and high-resolution mask and NIL mold fabrication, given its high potential, including
• the possibility of closed-loop lithography<sup>1</sup> including preimaging, overlay alignment, and postimaging for feature inspection;

To overcome the hurdle of low throughput, different strategies and/or their combinations can be applied. These include increase of the patterning speed by the introduction of high-speed scanners<sup>207e209</sup> in combination with reduction of the required “interaction time”<sup>166,210</sup> for patterning, for example, lowering the needed electron dose in FE-SPL, which requires high-sensitivity resist.
--[p24]-- Alternatively, a combination of different lithographic methods in a so-called mix-and-match/hybrid lithographic strategy<sup>211e213</sup> can be employed. In addition, it is possible to scale up the physical processes by either the utilization of cantilever/tip arrays,<sup>214e217</sup> or the introduction of conductive stamps mimicking parallel tips.<sup>214,218</sup>

===== [p56-56] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.4 PATTERN TRANSFER PROCESSES FROM PPA (3块) =====
--[p56]-- 16.4 PATTERN TRANSFER PROCESSES FROM PPA
Like most lithography methods, the pattern template is created in a resist layer and needs to be transferred into the final working material. Depending on the intended application, different approaches may be used to transfer patterns from PPA into the substrate material.
A selection of the main approaches to transferring written patterns are set out in the following sections.
--[p56]-- These will need to be adapted to the user’s specific application, materials, available equipment, and available etching chemistries. Therefore, the focus here will be on the steps that are required to develop the final recipe for the transfer process. As a starting point, typical etch rates and etch rate contrasts can be taken from literature.<sup>44,45</sup>
In the following sections, pattern transfer methods for different applications are outlined.
--[p56]-- Two-dimensional lithography at high resolution similar to electron-beam lithography is usually transferred using multiple stacked resist layers. The multilayer stack can be used for etching into the substrate as well as liftoff processes. Threedimensional patterns are transferred using a different approach to layering or simply in one go. A less common approach to replicating the written patterns would be the formation of mass replication stamps.
PPA is also uniquely suitable to the directed assembly and subsequent fixation of nano particles on a work piece.

===== [p62-63] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.4.4 MASS REPLICATION TECHNIQUES (5块) =====
--[p63]-- The galvanization process requires careful control of conditions, so the resulting Nickel master has an appropriately high quality and is free from internal stresses. This process was carried out by a specialist companydApplied Micro Swiss. Subsequent injection molding with the template gave a faithful replication down to the nanometer scale.<sup>51</sup>
Galvanic plating is possible as PPA does not dissolve in water.
--[p62]-- 16.4.4 MASS REPLICATION TECHNIQUES
Like any mask-less lithography technique, the flexibility of TSPL is ideal for prototyping application. However, due to the sequential nature of patterning, its throughput is not suited for mass production. Similar to mask lithography, parallelization can be achieved with a master stamp that is then imprinted.
The general recipe follows the steps illustrated in Fig. 7. A pattern is written into a sufficiently thick PPA layer (Fig. 7, Panel 1).
--[p63]-- However, water may penetrate the interface between the PPA and the substrate, for example, a silicon wafer. This is prevented if the surface of the substrate is hydrophobic, eg after silanization using hexamethyldisilazane (HMDS) or similar. Silanziation did not adversely affect the ability to spin coat PPA.
--[p63]-- Two master stamp materials and techniques have successfully been tested with TSPL-written structures. A simple and quick trial with a soft UV nanoimprint (NIL) method called “SmartNIL” was successful. Further evaluations are ongoing, but no special precautions were necessary for creating the NIL stamp. 50
The second master template was made for a true mass fabrication technology, injection molding. In this application, a hard Nickel master stamp was created with galvanic plating.
--[p62]-- An appropriate material for the master stamp is applied to the layer (Fig. 7, Panel 2). Once the layer is finalized, the PPA can be removed, either thermally or with solvent (Fig. 7, Panel 3). Finally, the imprinting is carried out (Fig. 7, Panel 4). The master is formed with the same depth and shape as the template. If the required depth exceeds the capability of the TSPL, additional hard-mask layers may be added for depth enhancement, following the 3D transfer recipes described earlier.

===== [p12-12] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.1.4 Motion and manipulation (Atoms, Molecules, Nanoparticles) (6块) =====
--[p12]-- After careful cleaning of the sample surfaces, interference effects of electron waves could be made visible by the STM-based construction of quantum structures, called quantum corrals.<sup>69,70</sup> In general, atomic and molecular designs involve the complex positioning of adsorbents, which require sufficient drift stability and the suppression of thermally activated diffusion processes. Thus, most experiments were carried out at cryogenic temperatures.
--[p12]-- res,<sup>34,75</sup> nanoparticles, and other nanoobjects,<sup>74</sup> for example, nanocrystals, nanotubes, DNA, and even proteins.
--[p12]-- However, in some circumstances, for example, the manipulation of atoms embedded in surfaces instead of weakly bonded adatoms, the working temperature can be increased.<sup>71e73</sup> Recently, it has been demonstrated that AFM is also capable of manipulating and rearranging at the single atomic level, even at room temperature.<sup>72</sup> Despite the ultimate resolution capabilities, remaining challenges concerning the extreme slow manipulation rates, the narrow process window, and the transformation of such fine manipulations into an usable, stable, and operational device prohibit the breakthrough of atomic manipulation as an applicable lithographic method.<sup>53,74</sup> In general, the same strategies and techniques can be utilized to move, position, and manipulate molecular structu
--[p12]-- Typically, atom-by-atom relocation is performed by approaching the STM tip toward the atom and subsequently moving the probe in constant current mode over the surface.
--[p12]-- Due to the close proximity, the tip is almost in mechanical contact with the atom, and the chemical nature of the tipeatom interaction is the main driving force behind the adsorbent translation.<sup>53</sup> Besides force-based interactions,<sup>65</sup> further effects like excitations by tunneling electrons<sup>67</sup> or tip-induced electric fields<sup>68</sup> allow the repositioning of adsorbents in a controlled manner.
--[p12]-- 15.2.1.4 Motion and manipulation (Atoms, Molecules, Nanoparticles)
The ultimate lithographic resolution, uniquely defined by single atomic manipulation, was demonstrated in 1990 by the pioneering work of Eigler and Schweizer,<sup>65</sup> and Weiss and Eigler.<sup>66</sup> By applying a low-temperature, UHV STM, they demonstrated the rearrangement of adsorbed Xe atoms on single-crystal metal surfaces.

===== [p17-17] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.4.2 Electrochemical modifications: oxidation and reduction of selfassembled monolayers (2块) =====
--[p17]-- 15.2.4.2 Electrochemical modifications: oxidation and reduction of selfassembled monolayers
Beside the direct surface modification described in LAO, the same process of electrochemical nanolithography can be applied to LangmuireBlodgett films and SAMs. Thus, additional chemical functionality can be introduced on the surface of highly ordered monolayers by oxidation or reduction reactions (Table 1).
--[p17]-- Further information is provided elsewhere.<sup>60,79,148e152</sup> In contrast to modification reactions, scanning probe-induced cathodic electrografting can directly pattern alkynes on hydrogen-terminated silicon surfaces by the creation of covalent bonds via an oxidation reaction.<sup>149</sup>

===== [p53-54] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.3.1 TEMPERATURES (7块) =====
--[p54]-- As the overall cantilever geometry has a longer thermal time constant than the tip heater, a short-heating pulse $( 1 0 - 3 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { s } )$ limits the thermal spread into the surrounding cantilever structure and, with it, the probability of damage due to overheating. If such high temperatures are required for custom applications, for example, local triggering of chemical reactions, the activation times should be appropriate.
--[p54]-- The conical tip shape has a thermal resistance associated with it, as does the interface between the tip apex and the surface of the work piece. The heat flow into the contact point between tip and surface thus depends on the exact tip geometry. Topographical patterning requires sharp tips with a small opening angle to maximize patterning resolution and minimize depth-dependent pixel broadening. However, higher temperatures will actually be reached with blunter tips with a larger opening angle.
--[p53]-- The temperature of the heater is calculated from the I-V characteristics of the resistive heating element. The electrical resistance of doped silicon increases with temperature, as the number of charge carriers is dominated by the doping level and thus stays broadly constant. The mobility decreases due to the increased scattering.
--[p54]-- As a general rule, the achievable temperatures with the silicon tip are sufficient to trigger processes that are activated below $2 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in static conditions on a hot plate. 35
The highest temperatures, above circa $8 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ , are typically applied in a pulsed mode for increased robustness.
--[p53]-- At a characteristic temperature, the resistance decreases again, as the number of thermally activated charge carriers is larger than the number of dopantinduced charge carriers. The resistance is then dominated by the increasing number of carriers rather than the decreasing mobility.<sup>31,36</sup>
The main energy transport process to the substrate is conduction through the tip. Convection and radiation seem only to play a minor role.
--[p54]-- The heat flow out of the contact point depends on the thermal conductivity of the substrate material. On a silicon substrate, a buffer layer of around 30e50 nm of polymer provides sufficient insulation to allow patterning of polyphthalaldehyde (PPA). Standard chemical activation energy calculations show that shortinteraction times require higher temperatures to trigger chemical processes.
--[p53]-- 16.3.1 TEMPERATURES
SwissLitho thermal scanning probes use resistive (Joule) and thermoelectric (Thomson) heating of the tips. The cantilever is formed as a loop, and a voltage is applied across the legs of the cantilever. A region of lower doping below the tip forms a resistor to localize the heated area. In practice, temperatures of up to 1000 C can be reached by the resistive heating element at the base of the tip.<sup>31,35</sup>

===== [p82-83] Scanning helium ion beam lithography > 17.3.1 GENERAL PROCEDURE AND CONSIDERATIONS FOR HIBL (13块) =====
--[p83]-- More recently, sub-10-nm HIBL patterning on fullerene-derivative resists has been demonstrated. Another study used HIBL as an alternative approach to EBL for prescreening EUV resists, resulting in sub-20-nm patterns. The next section will describe the work carried out in this nascent field to date, before evaluating the potential of HIBL as a nanopatterning technique.
--[p82]-- This has been made possible by the extremely bright source and the unique ionesolid interactions as described in the previous section. HIBL is a promising alternative to well-established EBL, with sensitivity enhancement, higher resolution and reduced proximity effect. However, it follows similar process steps to those in conventional EBL.
First, a radiation sensitive material (the “resist”) is applied as a thin film to a substrate before exposure to the energetic helium ions.
--[p82]-- Throughput is a measure of the number of features patterned per second and indicates the speed of the lithographic technique. A high resist sensitivity means less exposure time is required, which allows faster beam writing, hence leading to a higher throughput and higher writing efficiency.
During the exposure, apart from the native raster-scan generator in the HIM, a compatible external pattern generator is often employed to steer and blank the beam in order to form complex patterns.
--[p82]-- Resists are categorized into two types: Positive tone resists go through scission of polymeric chains on exposure and become more soluble in the developer.
--[p83]-- A pattern file can be imported and the beam will trace along the pattern in a serial writing style. Dose variation can be achieved by means of changing beam current, the dwell time, and the pixel spacing of the beam.
After the exposure, a developer is used to remove either the (exposed) fragments from the positive tone resist or the (unexposed) noncrosslinked molecules from the negative tone resist. This is done by immersing the sample in the developer solution.
--[p82]-- Resists with higher contrast are generally capable of being patterned with smaller features than those with lower contrast. Other important factors in lithography are sensitivity and throughput. Sensitivity indicates the quantity of incident energy required to produce the desired chemical reactions in the resist for pattern definition. Beam species, landing energy, resist thickness, and development processes are known to have a substantial impact on the sensitivity of a resist.
--[p82]-- A number of chemical and mechanical properties make resist materials appropriate for a given lithographic processes. Resolution is used to specify the reproducibility of the printing of minimum sized features under conditions of reasonable variation. The contrast of a resist is the rate of polymer chain scission/cross-linking upon exposure and is determined by the rate of change in solubility with increasing dose.
--[p82]-- 17.3.1 GENERAL PROCEDURE AND CONSIDERATIONS FOR HIBL
The field of HIBL was kick started with the development and commercial release of the HIM (Orion Plus, Carl Zeiss) based on GFIS technology. In addition to its application in the field of high-resolution imaging, HIM is also an emerging nanofabrication technique that has found many applications in the sub-10-nm regime for ultra-high-resolution and high-density patterning.
--[p83]-- Due to the inseparable relationship between exposure and development, when a pattern shows underdevelopment, it could be due to underexposure; likewise, if a pattern appears to be overdeveloped, it could be overexposed. From resist spinning to the development process, HIBL consists of various steps and involves complex chemical and physical reactions.
--[p83]-- Several groups have made breakthroughs into the sub-10-nm patterning regime, using HIBL on the high-resolution HSQ and PMMA resists.<sup>12,40,41</sup> The best results achieved in terms of feature size are comparable to the best results in EBL but with a sensitivity improvement of one to two orders of magnitude at the same beam energy. These studies also reveal that HIBL exhibits a very low proximity effect and makes pattern density irrelevant to pattern definition.
--[p83]-- Longer polymers are less mobile and more resistant to the developer, and hence, they take longer to dissolve.<sup>38,39</sup> The process can be accelerated by using a higher concentration of developer but this can degrade the resolution. In addition to the strength of the developer, the temperature and the duration of the development are also contributing factors that could affect the development results.
--[p82]-- An example of a high-resolution positive tone resist is poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), which is composed of long chain polymers that will break into smaller fragments upon exposure and become more soluble.<sup>35,36</sup> Negative tone resists become less soluble due to cross-linking reactions, where smaller molecules combine into larger ones, leading to a decrease in solubility.<sup>37</sup> Hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) is a good example of a high-resolution negative tone resist.
--[p83]-- Hence, there are a large number of parameters that can affect the final result and understanding impacts of these parameters is very important when carrying out lithography experiments.

===== [p56-56] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.3.5 CROSSLINKING REACTIONS (2块) =====
--[p56]-- 16.3.5 CROSSLINKING REACTIONS
Crosslinking negative lithography on the other hand has been found to be more challenging to achieve. It is important that the crosslinked material is anchored all the way to the substrate to avoid washing off during development. An interaction between resist and substrate material (or underlayer) may help to achieve this, though a concrete example of such a material combination is lacking.
--[p56]-- As the heat is applied to the surface, and the substrate is at ambient temperature, there will be a thermal gradient across the material to be crosslinked. This generally limits the depth of material that can be crosslinked. Worse, materials that soften or melt before crosslinking may flow onto the tip and, crosslink there, rather than on the substrate.

===== [p64-64] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.5 CONCLUSIONS (2块) =====
--[p64]-- 16.5 CONCLUSIONS
Scanning probe lithography is a versatile mask-less lithography method ideally suited for proptotyping applications. It is capable of patterning at highest resolutions below 20 nm, as well as shaping in 3D in a single step. The integrated imaging gives immediate feedback to the operator about the patterning success without the need for laborious development and separate metrology steps. In comparison to electronbeam patterning, charge-related issues and damage are avoided.
--[p64]-- After lithography, the written structures can be transferred into the substrate using standard cleanroom machines and techniques. Despite its thermal decomposition, the PPA resist has similar etching behavior to other resists such as PMMA. Recipes and guidelines for selecting parameters are described for 2D dry etching transfer, 3D transfer, as well as liftoff, imprint master fabrication, and capillary assembly of nanoparticles.

===== [p73-73] Scanning helium ion beam lithography > 17.2.2 IONeSOLID INTERACTIONS (1块) =====
--[p73]-- 17.2.2 IONeSOLID INTERACTIONS

===== [p63-63] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.4.5 GUIDED PARTICLE ASSEMBLY (5块) =====
--[p63]-- Finally, the substrate is placed on a hot plate at circa 200 C to evaporate the remaining PPA and deposit the particles on the substrate. 38
As PPA decomposes and evaporates at the glass-transition temperature, there is no appreciable flow and correspondingly no further lateral movement of the particles.
--[p63]-- It was also found that the evaporation is very clean, so that the particles are deposited directly on the surface of the work piece also have good electrical contact after fixation.<sup>38</sup>
--[p63]-- 16.4.5 GUIDED PARTICLE ASSEMBLY
Many novel devices are based on nano-sized objects, usually particles or tubes. These are often fabricated separately and need to be placed in an appropriate spot where they can interact with other circuitry (optical or electronic). A technique for guided assembly of particles from solution is capillary-assisted particle assembly (CAPA).
--[p63]-- Most CAPA is carried out from aqueous solution, which does not affect the PPA. Prior silanization (HMDS) of the substrate surface prevents water penetration and liftoff of PPA. Other solvents need to be tested for compatibility.
Fig. 8 shows a sketch of the guided particle assembly technique with TSPL. The PPA layer on a silanised substrate is patterned with suitable trap structures (Fig. 8, Panel 1). The CAPA can be carried out directly on the patterned PPA (Fig. 8, Panels 2 and 3).
--[p63]-- Capillary forces drive nano-objects into prepatterned traps or holes from where they can be transferred to the work piece surface.<sup>52</sup>
Several features of TSPL make it suitable for creating traps for CAPA. The topography-based overlay alignment technique allows precise alignment with prepatterned device features. Moreover, the unique thermal evaporation property of PPA makes the transfer of particles to the surface very simple.

===== [p20-20] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.4.7 Current/charge resist exposure (7块) =====
--[p20]-- In the context of electron-based patterning, PMMA-based resists and SAL601 were used as positive and negative tone resists for electron field emission SPL (FE-SPL), respectively.<sup>10,53,199,200</sup> Lines with width of 20 nm in negative tone and 80 nm in positive tone were demonstrated.<sup>10</sup> Negative tone FE-SPL was performed on calixarene (Fig. 8). Recently, negative tone FE-SPL applied to fully aromatic low-weight molecular glasses was demonstrated.<sup>201,202</sup>
--[p20]-- Thus, they undergo a number of scattering effects before reaching the resist/substrate interface under the influence of the electric field.<sup>4,196</sup> In contrast to EBL,<sup>4,196</sup> no UHV conditions are required. The low energy of the incident electrons eliminates proximity effects resulting in an enhanced resolution and pattern fidelity. In addition, the bias polarity and relative humidity play role in patterning.<sup>197,198</sup>
--[p20]-- As in EBL, resist tone switching is observed in SPL. Depending on the dose applied, either negative tone or direct ablation (self-development: Fig. 9A) of resist can be triggered. By applying relatively high doses ( 400 nC/cm), M-profile negative tone lines can be achieved after wet development (Fig. 9B). The mechanism of self-development is connected with initial cross-linking of resist and is speculated to be oxidative degradation of material.
--[p20]-- The positive tone (self-development) on calixarene resist was discovered by Rangelow et al.<sup>203,204</sup> Subsequently, writing with closed-loop FE-SPL of negative tone and self-developed patterns on calixarene resist was demonstrated (Fig. 10).<sup>205</sup> Tone switching was observed in polymers (PMMA, PS and PHS) as well.
--[p20]-- 15.2.4.7 Current/charge resist exposure
In the same manner as electron-beam lithography (EBL), tip-based, field-emitted low-energy electrons (<100 eV) can be directly used to induce cross-linking or chain scission. Chemical processes involved in resist exposure all require an energetic threshold; operation below this threshold allows imaging without writing. 4,5,10,11 Only electrons with sufficient energy can cause the required chemical changes in resist.
--[p20]-- However, even at higher doses (>1000 nC/cm), no switch to self-development mode was observed for the fluorinated molecular glass resist UBT7.<sup>202</sup> The ultimate resolution of both positive and negative tone resist patterning with SPL, with the resist selfdevelopment method, was dense lines with 12.5-nm half pitch (Fig. 11) and sub-5-nm single lines (Fig. 12) written on calixarene resist.<sup>1,2,18</sup>
--[p20]-- Typically, voltages in the range of 10e100 V are applied in order to operate in FowlereNordheim electron field emission regime. The behavior of the emitted electrons is quite different in comparison to EBL. The low-energy electrons in SPL have a mean free path below 2 nm within the resist.

===== [p89-92] Scanning helium ion beam lithography > 17.3.2.3 High-resolution patterning (10块) =====
--[p91]-- This study also included fabrication of 5 nm clearly resolved half-pitch lines with no resist residuals between features and resolvable 4-nm half-pitch lines with clear contrast but resist residues (Fig. 16). The optimal line doses were 110 and 90 pC/cm, respectively.
--[p92]-- Li et al. went on to demonstrate successful transfer of the nested L structures produced by HIBL in HSQ to a UV resist layer a via a nanoimprint process. This approach is particularly attractive because it takes advantage of the highresolution capabilities of HIBL to produce sub-10-nm features in resist whilst avoiding the potential issue of subsurface damage and defects induced by the energetic helium ion beam.
--[p90]-- The thicker the resist, the more scattering the beam will undergo and therefore the broader the exposed feature will be. This result shows that the resist layer thickness is an important parameter in high-resolution lithography and suggests that a thin resist with thickness equal or less to the escape depth of the SEs may enhance the lithographic results in the subnanometer regime.
Results from a different study on HIBL with HSQ by Li et al. are presented in Fig.
--[p89]-- Experimental HIBL investigations using PMMA have resulted in line widths of around 15e20 nm being achieved.<sup>41,42</sup> For example, we have demonstrated clearly resolved 20-nm-wide lines in 20-nm-thick PMMA layers on silicon, with an optimum line dose of w3 pC/cm (Fig. 14).
--[p91]-- 15C and D and demonstrate the wide dose window for HIBL high-resolution patterning: 12-nm half-pitch nested L shapes were patterned in 12-nm-thick HSQ on silicon using line doses of 120 and 320 pC/cm.<sup>53</sup> It can be seen that both doses resulted in well-defined line features with similar qualities. This relatively large process window increases the reproducibility of the high-resolution patterns.
--[p89]-- The demonstrated line widths in PMMA are well in excess of the resolution limits of the helium ion probe, indicating that resolution is being limited by properties of the PMMA resist such as molecular size rather than by the HIBL technique itself.
Higher resolution feature definition with HIBL, at sub-10-nm scales, has been demonstrated by several groups, using HSQ resist. One study looked at the effect
of HSQ resist thickness on ultimate feature size limits.
--[p91]-- This line dose is an order of magnitude lower than the dose required for HSQ in EBL for the fabrication of similar features.<sup>54</sup> These findings on sensitivity and resolution are consistent with the results obtained from the high-resolution investigations by Winston et al. and Sidorkin et al.<sup>12,41</sup> Moreover, the 4-nm half-pitch lines provided, for the first time, experimental evidence of HIBL exceeding the highest reported EBL resolution to date, which is a 4.5-nm half-pitch.
--[p92]-- Furthermore, it may be possible to reuse the HIBL-formed nanoimprint master stamps to reproduce patterns many times over at low cost, paving the 53 way toward higher throughput and mass production.
--[p90]-- Sparsely placed dot arrays were patterned in HSQ resists with identical helium ion beam exposures and subsequent development processes, the only variance being the resist thickness (Fig. 15A and B).<sup>40</sup> The results reveal that the average dot size for the 55-nm-thick HSQ (Fig. 15A) is 14 nm, which is more than twice the average size of 6 nm achieved on the 5-nm-thick HSQ (Fig. 15B).
--[p89]-- 17.3.2.3 High-resolution patterning
As explained in Section 17.2, the HIM is capable of generating a subnanometer probe size owing to the extremely high brightness GFIS and the use of helium gas. Furthermore, the highly localized ionesolid interactions make it theoretically possible to fabricate features of comparable size to the beam spot. Modeling work described in the previous section suggests that HIBL is expected to achieve higher resolution patterning than EBL.

===== [p14-14] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.3.2 Dip-pen nanolithography (5块) =====
--[p14]-- 15.2.3.2 Dip-pen nanolithography
Dip-pen nanolithography (DPN), firstly developed by Piner et al.<sup>99</sup> represents a very popular direct-write, constructive nanolithographic method. In general, molecular ink transport from the nanoprobe toward the surface represents the key process in this technique.
--[p14]-- This technique is called electrostatic DPN.<sup>107</sup> Additional DPN capabilities can be achieved by the implementation of reactive inks for etching,<sup>108</sup> molecular biology applications,<sup>74</sup> or inorganic inks.<sup>109</sup> Furthermore, DPN can be combined with electrochemical processes. For example, this has been shown by Li et al.<sup>110</sup> whereby metal salts coating a cantilever are dissolved, electrochemically reduced into metals, and deposited on the surface.
--[p14]-- Its high flexibility and simple control capabilities make it to an attractive tool to deposit multiple compounds precisely and selectively in a sequential or parallel manner.<sup>100,105</sup> Beside the standard molecular transport mechanism, which is facilitated under ambient conditions by a water meniscus between the tip and the sample, Nelson et al.<sup>106</sup> developed a thermally based DPN method.
--[p14]-- It allows patterning on various surfaces with lateral resolutions down to 15 nm.<sup>100e104</sup> In this manner, DPN is similar to nanoimprint lithography (NIL) microcontact printing, but a nanoprobe is used instead of a stamp.
--[p14]-- Here, a probe heats metallic ink, which is solid at room temperature, but begins to flow at relatively low melting temperatures. Alternatively, metallic nanoparticles can be deposited from the tip by the electrostatic interaction generated by charge separated caused by friction between the tip and the surface.

--[p84]-- 17.3.2.2 Proximity effect
The proximity effect is defined as the unintentional exposure of resist surrounding the impact site of the primary incident beam. It is caused by backscattered primary particles and is a common issue in EBL.<sup>45</sup> Simulation results presented in the previous section suggest that the low yield of backscattered helium ions and the subsequent limited generation of SEs by backscattered ions leads to a smaller proximity effect in HIBL compared to EBL.
--[p85]-- Beam broadening is also minimized by using a resist layer with a thickness of only 5 nm, however, this ultrathin resist may be impractical when the patterns need to be transferred into a subsequent layer by etching or lift-off.
Another way of analyzing the proximity effect in HIBL is a quantitative approach where experimental results are fitted to the proximity function for determination of the proximity parameters.
--[p86]-- The proximity parameters a and $\beta$ represent the range of forward scattered electrons and BEs, respectively, and h is the ratio of energy deposited by the backscattering to the forward scattering component. This formula describes the absorbed dose at a distance r from the primary incident beam due to effects of both forward scattering of the incident focused electron beam in resist and the backscattering of electrons from the substrate.
--[p87]-- Care must be taken when comparing PSF results as they are affected by many parameters including the resist, the exposure tool/process, the pattern development process and metrology. However, the HIBL PSF results indicate a slightly reduced forward scattering range and a much reduced backscattering range compared to EBL.
--[p84]-- To verify this experimentally, three approaches have been adopted.
The first method is a qualitative approach, which compares individual patterns at different densities. If dimensions and shapes of a specific pattern remain identical regardless of the density, the conclusion is that proximity effect is negligible. Fig.

--[p88]-- In summary, all three approaches to analyzing proximity effect suggest that it is significantly smaller in HIBL compared to EBL. This advantage enables HIBL to achieve high-resolution and high-density patterning without applying complex and costly PEC.
