===== [p73-76] Scanning helium ion beam lithography > 17.2.2.1 Interaction volume (12块) =====
--[p76]-- This suggests that a smaller interaction radius at the sample surface can be achieved at high beam energies. Currently, the typical operating voltage for a helium ion source is around 30 keV, but advances in source technology may further improve the resolution by increasing the operating energy.
--[p73]-- 17.2.2.1 Interaction volume
Having a small beam spot size is the first step in achieving subnanometer resolution imaging and patterning. Another key element is the unique interaction of the primary energetic helium ion beam with the target at and just below the surface. When a particle beam dwells on a sample surface, a chain of reactions happens, not only at the initial point of impact from the incident beam, but also quite widely and deeply into the material (see Fig. 3).
--[p74]-- ions mainly lose their energy through inelastic collisions where electronic stopping dominates. Compared to electrons at the same energy, 30-keV helium ions lose about 50 to 100 times more energy during this process.<sup>22</sup> Abundant low-energy SEsdwith energies typically below 20 eVdare created, which have short mean free paths of the order of a few nanometer s.<sup>23,24</sup> These are localized close to the beam path and cause insignificant lateral straggle at the surface.
--[p73]-- The incident particles lose energy in two ways as they travel through the sample: (1), nuclear stopping via momentum transfer to the target atom nuclei and (2), electronic stopping via interaction with the target electrons.<sup>20</sup> Nuclear stopping depends on the ion velocity as well as the charges of two colliding atoms, whereas electronic stopping is determined mainly by the charge state of the ion and its velocity.
--[p76]-- The beam broadening at a depth of 20 nm is only 1 nm for the helium beam compared to 5 nm for the electron beam.
A Monte Carlo simulation of helium ion trajectories in bulk silicon reveals differences in the resulting interaction volumes under different beam energies (Fig 5). As beam energy increases, the beam becomes more directional and collimated along the path in the sample and the ion range increases.
--[p73]-- For high-energy ions, electronic excitation and ionization occur during electronic and this dominates at the start of the ion track. Energy loss through nu  
clear interactions dominates near the end of the ion track, creating recoil atoms.   
These recoil atoms also lose energy in the same ways as the primary ions, forming   
a collision cascade. In the first 10 to 100 nanometers from the surface, energetic Heþ
--[p74]-- As $\mathrm { H e ^ { + } }$ ions penetrate through the target, nuclear stopping becomes dominant, creating recoils and causing greater lateral straggle far below the target surface.
The finite volume excited and affected within the sample by the primary beam is called the interaction volume. Its shape and size are usually determined by factors such as charged particle species, the angle and landing energy of the incident beam, and the sample material composition (mass and density).
--[p74]-- The interaction volume provides strong indications of the subsequent generation of SEs and hence ultimately determines the performance of a lithographic technique. A smaller interaction volume results in SEs generated from a small area localized around the incident beam and allows for higher resolution.
A good way of visualizing the interaction volume is by modeling the trajectories of charged particles in the sample. Fig.
--[p74]-- 4 illustrates a comparison of modeled trajectories of incident and BEs and ions using Monte Carlo simulations (CASINO for EBL and SRIM for HIBL). The $\mathrm { S E _ { 1 } }$ SEs are excited directly by the primary beam, and $\mathrm { S E } _ { 2 }$ by scattered ions/electrons exiting the surface. For both simulations, the particle beams have an energy of 30 keV and expose an infinitely thick silicon sample at an incident angle normal to the surface.
--[p74]-- The low ion backscattering fraction from the substrate back into resist layer is especially favorable in lithography, leading to a reduced proximity effect compared to EBL,<sup>25</sup> and facilitating high-density patterning.
Although the estimated smallest spot size can be controlled down to 1 nm in EBL systems, the lateral straggle of the electrons near the surface is significantly wider, due to a large yield of high energy BEs just below the sample surface.
--[p76]-- They excite further $\mathrm { S E } _ { 2 }$ and this cascade of electron production over a fairly large volume limits the resolution of EBL. In the lithographic context, additional resist material will be exposed which degrades the pattern fidelity. This relatively large interaction volume limits the resolution in EBL regardless of the probe size. Fig. 4 (bottom row) shows the ion trajectories in the top 100 nm in the silicon sample.
--[p74]-- A much smaller interaction volume is evident in the helium ion beam case compared to the electron beam simulation. On entering the sample, helium ions are lighter than most sample nuclei, whilst much heavier than electrons, leading to weak deflection from their original direction and a low number of ion recoil events. Therefore, the ion trajectories tend not to alter significantlydhelium ions stay collimated whilst penetrating deeply into the sample before starting to disperse.

===== [p60-62] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.4.3 THREE-DIMENSIONAL TRANSFER (8块) =====
--[p61]-- As before, minimal power and maximal nitrogen dilution slow down the etch rate. The actual transfer is then carried out in a second RIE step, as illustrated in Fig. 5, Panels 3 and 4. The timing and settings depend on the intended application.
The achievable feature height for a direct etch transfer is determined by the etch rate contrast between PPA and the desired material. If this is not sufficient, a further hard-mask underlayer may be inserted between the PPA and the substrate (Fig. 6).
--[p62]-- In other words, the final depth in the substrate, attenuated by the etch rate contrast between the substrate and hard-mask material, and again attenuated by the etch rate contrast between PPA and the hard-mask material must be appropriate for the maximum patterning depth of circa 100 nm. If this is not the case, other materials or etching chemistries need to be selected.
The transfer process is carried out in multiple steps (Fig. 6). First, the PPA is thinned down with an oxygen etch (Fig.
--[p60]-- 16.4.3 THREE-DIMENSIONAL TRANSFER
Topographical 3D patterns are directly transferred into a substrate material using reactive ion etching (Fig. 5).<sup>20</sup> The transfer technique relies on a finite etch contrast, rather than an infinite one, as is ideal for a 2D pattern transfer. With a finite etch contrast, the PPA layer thins down in tandem with the substrate material, successively revealing more of the surface (Fig. 5, Panels 3 and 4).
--[p60]-- Some indications of etch rates may be taken from the study by Williams et al.<sup>44,45</sup>
The starting point for selecting the PPA layer thickness is the desired pattern depth, together with the etch rate contrast in the available RIE machine and selected etch chemistry. The typical patterning depth into PPA is limited to around 100 nm. Due to the substrate cooling effect, an additional depth allowance of 30e50 nm should be made for the thermal insulation layer.
--[p62]-- Depending on availability and suitability, the hard-mask material may be organic or inorganic.
The thickness of the layers and patterning depth need to be calculated together, again based on the etch rate contrasts of both layers. The hard-mask layer must be of appropriate thickness to allow the desired final depth to be transferred. However, it must also be appropriately thick for the transfer from the PPA layer.
--[p60]-- The key feature is an anisotropic (plasma) etch, so that features do not broaden laterally during transfer. That way, a faithful reproduction in the substrate material is achieved, amplified, or attenuated (in the vertical dimension) by the corresponding etch rate contrast. As the spectrum of possible substrate materials and available etch chemistries is very large, these need to be determined by the user.
--[p62]-- 6, Panel 2). Next, another dry etch is carried out with appropriate etch chemistry to transfer the pattern from the PPA into the hard-mask material (Fig. 6, Panels 3 and 4). Finally, RIE gases are switched once more for the final transfer into the substrate (Fig. 6, Panel 5).
--[p61]-- Recessing the entire structure preserves the top surface. This recess from the top should also include a buffer to allow some tolerance for etch rate and timing variations.
The pattern transfer is done in two steps. First, the underlying layer is thinned down with an anisotropic oxygen etch (Fig. 5, Panel 2). The settings are chosen to minimize the etch rate and increase the tolerance to timing and etch rate variations.

===== [p15-15] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.4 ELECTRIC-FIELDeINDUCED INTERACTIONS (3块) =====
--[p15]-- Beside the desired main effect, several side effects can be activated, for example, the generation of reactive water molecule ions at the tip apex.<sup>115</sup> However, these must be considered in detail.
--[p15]-- 15.2.4 ELECTRIC-FIELDeINDUCED INTERACTIONS
The most diverse method in SPL-based nanolithographic approaches utilizes electric-fieldeinduced interaction mechanisms. In summary, patterning can be achieved or assisted by applying a potential difference across the probeesample junction.
--[p15]-- As a consequence of the close proximity of a grounded nanoprobe to a biased sample, high (typically $1 0 ^ { 7 } { - } 1 0 ^ { 9 } \mathrm { V / c m } ) ^ { 3 , 1 1 }$ 1,114 nonuniform electric fields are created, which can in turn trigger a multitude of physical and chemical processes at the nanoscale.

===== [p57-58] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.4.1 HIGH-RESOLUTION ETCH TRANSFER (12块) =====
--[p57]-- Starting from the bottom of the stack, the first layer on the work piece substrate is the organic hard-mask material, for example, a fullerene-based hard-mask material<sup>47,48</sup> or if resolution is not critical, even a photoresist. This layer will be the final etch mask for the transfer into the material of the work piece.
--[p58]-- The etch time depends on the thickness and etch rate of the inorganic hard mask but is usually less critical than the previous steps.
Finally, the pattern is transferred from the organic hard mask into the substrate (Fig. 2, Panel 5). Appropriate etch chemistry needs to be selected for the substrate material. The etch timing is determined by the etch rate of the substrate material and the desired final depth.
If required, remaining organic hard-mask material may also be stripped away at the end, typically using an oxygen plasma.
--[p58]-- Depending on deposition equipment, a 3-nm evaporated silicon oxide film may be sufficient to form a continuous layer thick enough to withstand the oxygen plasma for transfer of 60-nm depth into the organic hard-mask material. Sputtered $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ on the other hand needed to be at least 5-nm thick to achieve the same. The sputtered film was observed to have a less uniform density compared to the evaporated film.
--[p57]-- 16.4.1 HIGH-RESOLUTION ETCH TRANSFER
The tip of the scanning probe lithography machine is cone shaped. As the tip penetrates deeper, the width of the hole increases. To transfer high-resolution features of similar size to the tip apex (10 nm), only the lowest part of the written pattern is useful. Typical writing depths for 10-nm-sized patterns are of the order of 5e10 nm. Correspondingly, the layers of resist are very thin compared to other lithography processes.
--[p58]-- As this layer is extremely thin, the oxygen plasma is maximally diluted with nitrogen and the power is minimized to slow down the etch rate and give the user sufficient control over the process timing.
Once the surface of the silicon oxide is exposed, a fluorocarbon etch opens the inorganic hard mask (Fig. 2, Panel 3).
--[p58]-- The transfer process is then carried out in an RIE with appropriate gases. First, the residual layer of PPA below the pattern is removed (Fig. 2, Panel 2). Best results are achieved with an oxygen plasma as etchant. Fluorine-based etch gases coat the resist surface, resulting in less uniform etching and thus higher roughness.
--[p57]-- On top of the organic hard-mask material, a thin layer of inorganic mask materia such as silicon dioxide is deposited. The material and deposition method need to be selected by availability to the user but typically an inorganic oxide would be selected. The thickness of the inorganic hard mask must be sufficient to withstand the RIE into the underlying organic hard-mask layer, while simultaneously being thin enough to allow transfer of only the high resolution part of the PPA layer.
--[p57]-- This minimal patterning depth is then enhanced using a three-layer transfer stack,<sup>46</sup> as sketched in the first panel of Fig. 2. The pattern is written into PPA, which forms the top layer. Below the PPA is a thin inorganic hard-mask material. Below this, an organic hard-mask material provides a buffer for enhancement of transferred depth. The maximization of the overall etch rate contrast between PPA and the substrate material is achieved by modulation of etch chemistries.
--[p58]-- Therefore, a 4-nm layer of silicon oxide “cuts out” roughly a $2 { \cdot } \mathrm { n m }$ slice of the pattern in PPA. The PPA thickness is calculated by adding some margin for a residual layer of PPA below the patterned depth, plus an allowance for etch timing variations, and a top layer to cut away the roughness of the top surface. In the example of a 4-nm silicon oxide film, the PPA layer of, for example, 10 nm may be used, with a patterning depth of 6e8 nm.
--[p57]-- Thus, its thickness is selected according to the required final pattern depth, as well as its etch rate contrast to the work piece material with the appropriate etch chemistry. The etch rate contrast may need to be determined for the final application. As a side note, the overall organic hard-mask height should also be high enough to provide adequate thermal insulation from the substrate material (>30e50 nm).
--[p58]-- For a $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ hard mask, good results were achieved with a $\mathrm { C H F } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { A r }$ -based RIE, again with maximal dilution and minimum power to lower the etch rate to manageable timings.
The next step is the enhancement of the aspect ratio into the organic hard-mask layer (Fig. 2, Panel 4). If the inorganic hard mask is an oxide, an oxygen-based RIE achieves very high selectivity into the underlying organic hard-mask layer.
--[p58]-- This resulted in increased line-edge roughness in the overall transferred pattern.
Finally, the top layer on the stack is PPA. Again, the layer thickness and writing depth are selected from the thickness of the underlying layer and the etch rate contrast between the materials. As an example, silicon oxide etches between two and five times as fast as PPA in a $\mathrm { C H F } _ { 3 }$ RIE, depending on settings and size of work piece.

===== [p13-13] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.2.2 Thermochemical interactions (4块) =====
--[p13]-- An interesting alternative, to pattern electroluminescent polymer poly(p-phenylene vinylene), was demonstrated by Fenwick et al.<sup>83</sup> By using a simple heated Wollaston wire probe, they were able to pattern feature sizes below 28 nm (two orders of magnitude smaller than the diameter of the probe) with speeds up to 100 mm/s.
--[p13]-- 15.2.2.2 Thermochemical interactions
As well as the heat forceeinduced polymer deformations of thermomechanical methods, thermal energy emitted by a heated nanoprobe can also be used to trigger local chemical reactions. This offers the possibility to change the functionality of a polymer surface without mechanical force interactions.
--[p13]-- Applying this method, Szoszkiewicz et al.<sup>81</sup> developed a thermally activated decomposition process, which transforms a hydrophobic tetrahydropyranyl-based copolymer into a hydrophilic dihydropyran. The creation of such hydrophilic features without corresponding topographical changes can be realized with sub-15-nm resolution at tip speeds up to 1.4 mm/s.
--[p13]-- A further method, developed by Basu et al.<sup>82</sup> used a heated nanoprobe as a spatially localized postexposure tool to cross-link flood exposed photoresist with achievable resolutions of 450e1800 nm.

===== [p19-20] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.4.6 Material removal (4块) =====
--[p20]-- Beside nanografting and electro-grafting of SAMs, field-induced and currentinduced desorption processes can also be triggered by a nanoprobe, which is in close proximity to SAMs, reviewed elsewhere.<sup>50</sup> Within both processes only a positive bias voltage causes a desorption process of the respective SAM molecules. This suggests an electric field supported interaction mechanism. For instance a positive bias will weaken the SeAu bond, based on the forced charge redistribution.
--[p19]-- Additionally, nanohole (3e10 nm) formation in Au and graphite surfaces without the presence of chemical solutions has been shown, although the mechanism is still controversial, and suggestions range between local heating,<sup>188</sup> electromigration effects,<sup>189</sup> and chemical reactions such as place-exchange mechanisms,<sup>190,191</sup> electron-assisted field ionization,<sup>115,192</sup> and electrochemical polarity-dependent meniscus-mediated etching of the carbon surface.<sup>193</sup>
--[p19]-- 15.2.4.6 Material removal
Holes and grooves are realized via the controlled etching of several semiconductor materials, such as Si and GaAs in the presence of chemical solutions.<sup>185,186</sup> Recently, platinum-catalyzed silicon etching in water without additional chemicals was presented by Yamamoto et al.<sup>187</sup> utilizing platinum deposited on the cantilever tip.
--[p20]-- If the electric field exceeds a threshold field strength, dissociation of the SeAu bond occurs. In contrast, within the current-induced desorption process, the electric field only weakens the bond, and vibrational excitations of adsorbent molecules, caused by resonant inelastic electron tunneling, induce the observable desorption processes. 50,194,195

===== [p24-24] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.3.1.1 Mix-and-match scanning probe lithography (1块) =====
--[p24]-- 15.3.1.1 Mix-and-match scanning probe lithography
In general, we have been stuck with the dilemma that high-throughput lithography methods are not able to pattern high-resolution features, and ultrahigh-resolution lithography methods require too much time for patterning of large features. The smart combination of two lithographic methods: one with high lithographic resolution and one delivering higher throughput could be a powerful approach.
Realistic lithographic patterns consist of different geometries with varying line width.<sup>205</sup>

===== [p70-73] Scanning helium ion beam lithography > 17.2.1 WORKING PRINCIPLE OF THE GAS FIELD ION SOURCE (12块) =====
--[p72]-- The higher mass gives the moving helium ions a momentum that is w300 times larger than for an electron beam, and hence a de Broglie wavelength that is w300 times smaller (see Fig. 2). The shorter the wavelength, the less diffracted the helium ion beam will become while passing through the focusing aperture in the column. Hence, smaller apertures (less than 10-mm diameter) can be used in the helium ion beam system enabling a smaller probe size compared to EBL.
--[p72]-- 1B) and it is kept in a vacuum chamber under cryogenic conditions. When a high voltage (typically w30 keV) is applied to the source, an electric field is created between the emitter and the negative extractor. The electric field is concentrated at the individual atoms of the emitter tip. Electrons from the helium atoms that drift into the ionization zones surrounding the tungsten atoms will escape due to a quantum-mechanical tunneling effect, producing positive ions by field ionization.
--[p70]-- The helium ions $( \mathrm { H e } ^ { + } )$ are accelerated down the column that contains various electrostatic optics, deflectors, and apertures used to focus and steer the ion beam onto a sample in the chamber. The source and column operate under high vacuums ranging from $1 0 ^ { - 9 }$ to 10-<sup>10</sup> Torr, in order to avoid interference from other gas particles in the generation/manipulation of the helium ion beam.
--[p72]-- The resulting beam is extremely narrow due to the atomic scale source and is ideal as a high-resolution probe. Most of the helium gas is ionized at one of the three atoms that form the trimer, resulting in sufficient beam current for lithographic applications. Typically, a beam current of 0.1e10 pA can be generated.
Some critical source parameters in a GFIS based helium ion beam system are listed in Table 1.
--[p70]-- 17.2.1 WORKING PRINCIPLE OF THE GAS FIELD ION SOURCE
A focused helium ion beam system consists of three main components: a source, a column, and a sample chamber (Fig. 1A). The ion source is a tungsten electrode at a high voltage relative to ground. Helium gas is ionized by the strong field near the tip of the source.
--[p72]-- The virtual source size is estimated to be 0.25 nm in diameter.<sup>11</sup> The source brightness is calculated to be roughly 30 times better than a Schottky electron source in an EBL system.<sup>10</sup> The very small energy spread of <1 eV of the GFIS source limits the detrimental effects of chromatic aberration on probe size.
Another contributing factor to the smaller probe size generated in HIBL is the use of heavier helium ions compared to electrons (by three orders of magnitude).
--[p70]-- The sample chamber vacuum is typically maintained at $\sim 1 0 ^ { - 7 }$ Torr. The helium ion beam can then be scanned over an area of the sample surface by octopole deflector coils in the column, either in a raster-scan to form an image from SE generation (in the same way as in a scanning electron microscope) or in a defined pattern for lithography purposes.
The ultimate probe size of an EBL system is around 1 nm and it is limited by diffraction and chromatic aberration.
--[p71 [表]]-- In comparison, the helium ion beam system has a smaller, subnanometer probe size, enabled by the extremely bright GFIS.<sup>10,11</sup> GFIS technology has been investigated and developed over many years for imaging applications.<sup>15</sup> However, it is only recently that a stable ion source with a high brightness, small virtual source size and small energy spread has been 16,17 realized, enabling the focused helium ion beam technique.
--[p72]-- Virtual source size is the dimension of the smallest circular spot that the particle beam emitted from the source would form, if it was projected back into the interior of the source.
--[p73]-- In summary, the shorter wavelength of the imaging helium ion beam along with the ultraehigh-brightness GFIS, with a small energy spread makes the helium ion beam system well-suited for producing a high quality beam that can be focused down to a sub-nm probe on the surface of a sample.
--[p72]-- These are repelled from the source, pass through the extractor plate, and are accelerated down the column in a continuous beam of helium ions.
For a GFIS, there are normally only three atoms at the very tip of the source emitter, hence, the source is called a trimer. Three ion beams are produced by these atoms, only one of which is aligned to the column optics and used to probe the specimen (see Fig. 1C).

===== [p13-13] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.2.3 Thermochemomechanical interactions (5块) =====
--[p13]-- Pires et al.<sup>85</sup> have gone one step further through the use of an organic molecular resist material,<sup>85</sup> which forms a glassy bulk state through hydrogen-bonding interactions. In general, the gradedbinding strength of strong covalent intramolecular bonds and multiple weak intermolecular H bonds enables an effective thermally activated desorption process while also allowing sufficient stability of the resist film.
--[p13]-- 15.2.2.3 Thermochemomechanical interactions
Heat (from a laser pulse) or a combined heat force stimulus (typical setup: integrated resistor and electrostatic cantilever actuation) can be used to remove covalently bound material by thermally activated processes whilst the film does not undergo significant thermal deformations or flow.
--[p13]-- Commercially available from SwissLitho AG, the t-SPL is described in Chapter 16 in more detail.
The efficiency of t-SPL also depends on the substrate thermal conductivity. Simulations of the heating efficiency versus substrate thermal conductivity were performed by Zimmermann et al.<sup>86</sup> showing that t-SPL on optically transparent substrates (glass, indium tin oxide) is more efficient than that on Si due to their lower thermal conductivity.
This method is reviewed in more detail elsewhere. 6,87
--[p13]-- However, the effectiveness of heated probes in decomposing conventional polymers is hampered by debris and pile-up effects, as well as the slow time scales of the cleavage process, which are a result of the large energetic barriers of the covalently bonded network.
--[p13]-- Coulembier et al.<sup>84</sup> circumvented these limitations via an amplification concept, where one degradation event unzips an entire chain, resulting in a clean, debris-free thermally activated decomposition and desorption process at fast time scales. By applying this concept, 50-nm lines on 100-nm pitches were realized.

===== [p58-60] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.4.2 LIFTOFF (9块) =====
--[p60]-- The first two etch steps (thinning of base layer and opening of inorganic hard mask) are identical to the high-resolution recipe (Fig. 4, Panels 2 and 3). Etching into the liftoff layer is modified to increase the isotropy and create an undercut (Fig. 4, Panel 4). This is achieved by increasing the pressure in the RIE chamber. As the undercut is achieved by RIE, it is no longer required that the developer for the liftoff layer does not attack PPA.
--[p59]-- Similarly, the developer for the liftoff layer should not dissolve PPA. PMGI is dissolved and developed in alkaline solution, for example, tetramethylammonium hydroxide. PMMA can be developed in methyl isobutyl ketone. PPA is not soluble in either of these.
As the liftoff layers are relatively soft polymers (as opposed to a hard silicon oxide), the PPA layer can be patterned all the way through, exposing the underlying liftoff layer.
--[p58]-- 16.4.2 LIFTOFF
In a research environment, the most commonly used pattern transfer technique is the liftoff process, particularly for metals. In the liftoff process, the metal is deposited on top of the patterned resist. The windows in the resist determine where the metal is to remain on the surface. In other areas, the resist layer creates a buffer to prevent direct contact of the metal to the surface. This buffer is finally washed away to undermine, or liftoff, the unwanted metal.
--[p59]-- The liftoff layer below the PPA is a suitable polymer. The polymer thickness is selected to be greater than the material to be deposited.
Polymethylglutarimide (PMGI) and PMMA have successfully been used. In general, the solvent for the PPA should not dissolve the polymer of the liftoff layer to prevent contamination, though there is a bit of tolerance. PMMA is soluble in anisole yet showed good performance as the liftoff layer.
--[p60]-- The deposition of material and liftoff are then carried out according to the standard method for the selected base layer (Fig. 4, Panels 5 and 6). Using this transfer stack, gold patterns with feature sizes down to 20 nm have been demonstrated. 49
--[p59]-- The liftoff layer is developed or opened with the appropriate solvent (Fig. 3, Panel 2). As the liquid development process is isotropic, the required undercut is created.
The material to be lifted off is deposited directly on top of the PPA (Fig. 3, Panel 3). Finally, the liftoff is carried out in the appropriate solvent of the liftoff layer (Fig. 3, Panel 4).
--[p58]-- Best liftoff results are achieved if there is an undercut in the resist layer to provide a gap (and solvent penetration) between the metal deposited at the bottom of the trench and the top of the resist.
Even though thermal scanning probe lithography creates a positive slope with its cone-shaped tip, an undercut can nevertheless be achieved. Following standard liftoff recipe methods, a bilayer of resist is used, as sketched in Panel 1 of Fig. 3. The top layer is PPA, as usual.
--[p59]-- Similar to standard undercut/liftoff procedures, the isotropic nature of the liquid development step limits the resolution and aspect ratio of structures that can be deposited. Small bridges and fingers of resist are more likely to collapse or be washed away if they are fully undermined in the first development step (Fig. 3, Panel 2).
For highest resolution, the lateral spreading of the undercut needs to be reduced.
--[p60]-- This is achieved using an anisotropic RIE tool instead of the isotropic wet etch.<sup>49</sup> As illustrated in Fig. 4, the basic layering and recipe follow the high-resolution threelayer etch transfer stack. The key difference is to substitute the organic hard-mask layer with one that can be washed away for liftoff. PMGI, PMMA, or even standard photoresist polymers are typical candidate materials for this layer.

===== [p15-17] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.4.1 Electrochemical modifications: local anodic oxidation (9块) =====
--[p17]-- More exotic methods like the direct nanowriting of conductive polymers via solid-state oxidative crosslinking, called electrochemical oxidative nanolithography, have also been demonstrated.<sup>147</sup>
--[p15]-- The water meniscus provides both essential requirements: the chemical species (oxyanions) and also the spatial confinement of the oxidation reaction.
In general, at ambient pressure and below water saturation, the close tipesample proximity induces a spontaneous capillary condensation, followed by formation of a water bridge.<sup>140</sup> The ultimate resolution achievable with this technique is determined by the meniscus size.
--[p16]-- Sigimura and Nakagiri<sup>143</sup> proposed a general reaction scheme, which describes the anodic reaction:
$$
\mathrm { \bf M } + x \mathrm { \bf H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { \bf O }  \mathrm { \bf M } \mathrm { \bf O } _ { x } + 2 x \mathrm { \bf H } ^ { + } + 2 x \mathrm { e } ^ { - }\tag{5}
$$
the reaction at the substrate surface:
$$
2 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } {  } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } + 4 \mathrm { H } ^ { + } + 4 \mathrm { e } ^ { - }\tag{6}
$$
and the cathodic reaction at the tip:
$$
2 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } + 2 \mathrm { e } ^ { - }  \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } + 2 \mathrm { O H } ^ { - }\tag{7}
$$
--[p16]-- A more detailed discussion of the molecular mechanism of field-induced formation of nanoscale menisci was undertaken by Cramer et al.<sup>140</sup> but to summarize, LAO processes can be described by
• water meniscus formation,
• field-induced activation of molecules within the water meniscus (oxyanion formation), and
• subsequent oxidation of the sample surface mediated by in situ generated ions.
--[p15]-- As found later, the oxidation growth process is rather general, and so many different materials and/or surfaces have subsequently been patterned, such as semiconductors,<sup>119,126e129</sup> metals,<sup>129e131</sup> dielectric films<sup>132,133</sup> and monolayers, such as SAMs and graphene.<sup>134,135</sup> Most of the approaches aim to create nanoelectronic demonstrators such as single-electron devices,<sup>120,136,137</sup> silicon nanowire transistors,<sup>138</sup> or field-effect transistors.<sup>128,139</sup> The key to the local chemical reaction confinement is the spontaneous and/or field-enhanced formation of a water meniscus within the nanoprobeesample gap.
--[p15]-- In general, the spatially confined, liquid-based, nanosized reaction chamber within the probeesample junction can trigger a multitude of electric-fieldeinduced electrochemical reactions. First investigations into this process were carried out by Dagata et al.<sup>125</sup> who used an ambient air STM to induce a local anodic oxidation (LAO) process on hydrogen-passivated Si substrates.
--[p16]-- The minimum theoretical width of a stable meniscus in equilibrium with the surrounding vapor, from the Kelvin equation,<sup>141</sup> is 2e4 nm, whilst Monte Carlo simulations<sup>142</sup> give a minimum of five molecular diameters, or 1.9 nm. Electric fields offer the best experimental approach to induce (critical field strength threshold to overcome the surface tension: 0.7e1.9 V/nm), control, and manipulate liquid bridges at the nanoscale.
--[p15]-- 15.2.4.1 Electrochemical modifications: local anodic oxidation
The discovery that one can utilize the water layer at ambient scanning conditions (which is usually considered to be problematic) has led to one of the simplest, most common and extensively studied lithographic technique s,<sup>116e124</sup> called probe anodization lithography.
--[p16]-- whereby the kinetic process is characterized by $h = b t ^ { \gamma }$ (h: nanostructure height; t: duration of the pulse; b and g describe the growth process).<sup>144</sup> Thus, local oxidation is a self-limiting processdthe electric-field strength decreases with increasing oxide film thickness.<sup>117</sup> Furthermore, some efforts have been made to control the size of the liquid menisci by tuning the polarity of the surrounding medium<sup>145</sup> and by the promotion of local oxidation process by diluted hydrofluoric acid.<sup>91</sup>
The understanding of the fundamental oxidation processes and the optimization of the respective reaction conditions has led to a 4-nm channel transistor<sup>138</sup> and
13-nm lattice periodicity<sup>146</sup> feature generation.

===== [p54-55] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.3.2 PATTERNING OF PPA (8块) =====
--[p54]-- Thermogravimetric analysis and differential scanning calorimetry show<sup>35</sup> that PPA decomposes at or near its glass-transition temperature of $1 4 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . Therefore, the resist does not flow during the patterning process, preserving sharp features.
--[p55]-- While PPA is stable as a solid, it is more vulnerable in solution. In particular, molecular dynamics simulations show that PPA is sensitive to acidic environments. Solvents that are acidic or form acids when aging are, therefore, less suitable for PPA preparation. Anisole dissolves PPA well without the rapid degradation seen in other solvents.
--[p54]-- 16.3.2 PATTERNING OF PPA
The standard process for thermal scanning probe lithography is topographical patterning of a resist material called PPA. PPA was originally synthesized as a self-developing resist for photolithography. It has also been used successfully in electron-beam lithography.<sup>37</sup>
The patterning mechanism into PPA is a combination of thermal decomposition of the polymer and subsequent evaporation of the monomers.
--[p55]-- After spin coating, a moderate 3-minute long soft bake is necessary to remove most of the solvent from the film, together with any monomers that may have formed during storage. Naturally, the soft bake temperature must be low enough not to trigger decomposition; 80e90 C was found to be best.
--[p55]-- Another tip-preserving feature of thermal scanning probe lithography is the cooling effect from the substrate material. In the absence of another insulating material, this results in a residual layer of PPA below the tip, preventing the abrasive shearing of the silicon tip over hard substrate material.
The decomposition of PPA is a slightly endothermal process,<sup>35</sup> which conveniently limits and controls the patterning feature sizes.
--[p54]-- The sublimation-like removal process is advantageously exploited in the guided placement of nanoparticles, where the final fixation step (heating on a hot plate) conveniently preserves the particle position relative to the substrate.<sup>38</sup>
The PPA molecule decomposes into monomers when a bond in the polymer chain is broken. No additional species are required for this reaction, so the kinetics are not limited by material transport.
--[p54]-- The fast reaction kinetics of the decomposition result in near-instantaneous evaporation. In fact, with a high-enough tip temperature, the patterning depth can be computed simply from the electrostatic deflection of the cantilever, ignoring the resist material. The low contact forces result in low shear forces and low wear during patterning, corresponding to a long tip lifetime. 39
--[p55]-- In comparison, feature geometries written into exothermally decomposing materials are more sensitive to the activation conditions and hence less controllable.<sup>40</sup>
Somewhat surprisingly, the etch rates of PPA in a reactive ion etch (RIE) are comparable to other polymeric resist materials such as polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA). It is thought that the decomposition of PPA requires physical motion of the molecule, which is suppressed below the glass-transition temperature.<sup>35</sup>

===== [p95-96] Scanning helium ion beam lithography > 17.4 CONCLUSIONS AND OUTLOOK (9块) =====
--[p95]-- The best results to date show feature sizes and densities comparable or beyond what is achievable with EBL, highlighting the potential of the technique to become an important rapid prototyping tool for nanofabrication. The demonstration of successful pattern transfer by nanoprinting using a HIBL-fabricated stamp also suggests a potential route to larger volume manufacture.
--[p95]-- The beam currents generated in the HIM are generally lower (<5 pA) than electron beam currents if a sub-nm probe size is to be maintained, which could negate any writing speed gain from an increased sensitivity. Substrate damage through defect generation as a result of collision cascades caused by the impinging ion beam is also a concern.
--[p95]-- 17.4 CONCLUSIONS AND OUTLOOK
Advances in GFIS technology over the last 10 years, most notably the commercial release of the HIM, have caused researchers to look again at ion beam lithography as an alternative to the widely used EBL technique. Key advantages of lithography with helium ions include high-resolution patterning, enabled by a sub-nm probe size, and a low proximity effect due to limited backscatter of the primary beam and the low energies of the generated SEs.
--[p95]-- The technique is also showing promise as a method for rapid characterization and prescreening of resists for EUV lithography.
Several challenges remain that could hinder progress with the technique. Although high sensitivities have been demonstrated, it is important to note that this does not immediately translate to higher throughput.
--[p95]-- Whilst required exposure doses are generally less than those that result in observable damage (amorphization, bubble formation etc.) it remains to be seen whether defect creation in the underlying substrate during HIBL has a detrimental effect on the electrical properties of devices fabricated using this approach.
--[p95]-- The nanoimprint pattern transfer route may provide a way to circumvent these problems by allowing HIBL to define the feature size whilst avoiding direct ion beam exposure of the active material from which the device will be made.
So far, standard resist processing recipes from EBL have been used and there is likely to be scope for further improvement through process optimization. Also, the systems used for HIBL to date are primarily microscopes designed for imaging.
--[p96]-- Neon FIBs are now available in commercial ion microscopes, which are also capable of exposing sub-10-nm features in HSQ resist.<sup>14</sup> Other GFIS tools with alternative ion species are being developed which may also have an impact in the field of FIB lithography in the near future.
--[p96]-- A dedicated lithography tool using GFIS technology and accurate stage movement mechanisms would lead to further improvements in terms of throughput, alignment accuracy, and stitching of write-fields. Furthermore, helium is just one of many ion species compatible with the GFIS approach.
--[p95]-- Furthermore, the greater yield of SEs results in a sensitivity gain of several orders of magnitude over EBL. This allows high etch durability resists, that may have traditionally been considered to have too low a sensitivity for EBL, to be patterned efficiently at sub-10-nm length scales. Several resist families have been investigated so far, including common EBL resists such as PMMA and HSQ, as well as highly durable fullerene derivative resists.

===== [p12-12] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.1.3 Chemically assisted methods (2块) =====
--[p12]-- 15.2.1.3 Chemically assisted methods
Modifications such as chemically assisted, force-induced methods enable further expansion of the process windows for instance the reduction of the required threshold forces for nanoplowing and indentation, with concurrent enhancement to create grooves by scratching of an oxide-covered Al surface under various etching solutions. The highest dissolution rates of Al were seen in a dilute NaOH solution.
--[p12]-- The generation of high aspect ratio features could be achieved by solventassisted indentation, first studied by Cappella and Bonaccurso.<sup>64</sup> Summarizing the technique, only a small force is required to break the topmost layer of a plasmatreated polystyrene (PS) film while the final height and depth of the patterned features were controlled by exposure to appropriate solvents.

===== [p10-10] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2 SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY CLASSIFICATION (1块) =====
--[p10]-- 15.2 SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY CLASSIFICATION
SPL methods can be classified by the primary interaction mechanism.<sup>21</sup> Shown schematically in Fig. 7, the following subsections provide a brief review of the manifold state-of-the-art SPL approaches, which differ mainly in patterning mechanism, achievable resolution, speed capability, process window, and repeatability.
In particular, focus will be placed on the specific fundamental physical/chemical interactions and their spatial confinement capabilities.

===== [p55-55] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.3.3 DIRECT EVAPORATION OF OTHER RESIST TYPES (2块) =====
--[p55]-- 16.3.3 DIRECT EVAPORATION OF OTHER RESIST TYPES
The direct evaporation of resist molecules was one of the first techniques trialled for TSPL. A micrometer-sized topographical replica of the Matterhorn was created by evaporating a small molecular resist, dubbed a “molecular glass”.<sup>41</sup>
Some redeposition and lateral displacement were observed patterning a selection of directly evaporated small molecular resists.
--[p55]-- With increasing depth and feature size, multiple passes were required to reliably carve out the desired features. While this reduces the large-area patterning fidelity and reliability, it can also be beneficial for patterning small features. The displacement and redeposition enhances the edges of a feature, reducing the line-edge roughness in subsequent transfer steps.
The difficulty of selecting small molecular resists is to find a balance between crystallization and flow of the molecules.<sup>42</sup>

===== [p35-35] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.4 CONCLUSION (4块) =====
--[p35]-- All this opens new fields in materials investigation and device prototyping, making SPL setup a versatile and budget-friendly research tool. To make it attractive for industrial applications, the issue of throughput can be addressed via mix-and-match methods, where SPL is implemented only for critical dimension patterning, or via parallelization of the writing process by creating tip arrays.
--[p35]-- This gives possibility to high-precision (nm-range) overlay alignment and consequently step-and-repeat and stitching procedures for wafer scale patterning. Since SPL can operate at ambient conditions no vacuum systems are required. Therefore SPL technology reliably not only addresses the physical sciences, but also enables life science applications together with the ability to meet the ‘on demand’ fabrication of single digit nanometer resolution features.
--[p35]-- 15.4 CONCLUSION
Here, we have made an overview of SPL methods, classified by tipematter interaction type. No other lithography method would give such a flexibility in ways of material modification. The possibility to direct modification of materials (eg, 2D semiconductors) widens the horizon of device fabrication. Closed-loop SPL systems were demonstrated, where writing and reading is done by the same tip either sequentially or simultaneously.
--[p35]-- An SPL platform based on self-actuated piezoresistive cantilevers with a built-in read-out sensor (active cantilever) is a promising candidate to develop a multitip nanopatterning system with the possibility to achieve overlay alignment.
Thus, SPL technology uncovers new possibilities for the development and realization of many novel electronic and optical devices facilitated by additive, modifying and ablative patterning processes, offering an additional cost-effective nanofabrication.

===== [p53-53] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.3 PATTERNING WITH THERMAL SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY (2块) =====
--[p53]-- 16.3 PATTERNING WITH THERMAL SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY
In general, thermal scanning probes can be used to heat up most materials in nanometer length scale locations. As TSPL operates in ambient conditions, there are no special requirements for solid materials to be processed. The probe that comes into contact with the material is a consumable, so an unsuccessful attempt at thermal processing only requires a change of probe, which is done in less than a minute.
--[p53]-- One constraint is of course the geometry of the work piece and its surface. The standard tip of SwissLitho’s TSPL system is around 700-nm tall, which limits the depth range and surface topography that can be accessed. The tip is isotropically etched from a cylinder, forming a radially symmetric tip with a diameter below 10 nm. Other thermal probes may have different or longer tip geometries.

===== [p13-13] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.2.1 Thermomechanical interactions (3块) =====
--[p13]-- By using thermomechanical local probe techniques, wherein the tip is heated by an integrated resistive heater, they can store, read back, and erase data in thin polymer films with 10- to 50-nm feature size resolution (ultrathin polymer layers above a Si substrate). Beside conventional polymers, shape memory polymers offer an interesting alternative.<sup>80</sup>
--[p13]-- 15.2.2.1 Thermomechanical interactions
In thermomechanical indentation/writing, a combination of heat (typically around 400 C) and force stimuli, induced by a nanoprobe in a spatially localized region, causes a local softening and flow of a polymeric material.
--[p13]-- However, the triggering of chemical reactions, such as for instance the decomposition of the polymer, is avoided.<sup>76</sup> This approach was taken up by IBM’s “Millipede” project<sup>77,78</sup> to realize a scanning probeebased data storage concept.

===== [p55-55] Thermal scanning probe lithography > 16.3.4 THERMOCHEMICAL REACTIONS (2块) =====
--[p55]-- 16.3.4 THERMOCHEMICAL REACTIONS
More generally, chemical processes may be activated locally using thermal probes. The success of the patterning depends on the required temperatures and reaction kinetics, as outlined previously. Various processes have been successfully trialled. Thermally activated crosslinking chemistries have been used to selectively deposit biological molecules.
--[p55]-- Chemical gradients have been created by modulating the temperature and activation rate of these crosslinking chemistries.<sup>43</sup>
Using thermal probes other than those available from SwissLitho, electrical devices have been fabricated directly from precursor materials. The organic electroluminescent molecule poly(p-phenylene vinylene) was thermally synthesized from precursor molecules.<sup>14</sup> Graphene oxide has also successfully been reduced thermally to graphene.<sup>15</sup>

===== [p11-11] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.1.2 Nanoshaving/nanografting (5块) =====
--[p11]-- Based on their selfassembly ability, SAMs offer attractive ultrathin resist layer formation properties due to their high structural order, perfect thickness homogeneity, and chemical stability.<sup>49,50</sup> In nanoshaving, the tip exerts a high local pressure at the tipemolecule contact point, resulting in high shear forces, which in turn cause a controlled displacement of adsorbed SAM molecules.
--[p11]-- In addition to nanoshaving and nanografting, further self-organization of molecular nanostructures can be triggered by SPM, for example, by mechanical perturbations on thin films made of benzylic amide rotaxanes.<sup>58</sup>
--[p11]-- The creation of sharp nanopatterns requires the immediate removal of the displaced SAM molecules and the absence of resorption processes.<sup>51e53</sup> More widespread acceptance has been gained by nanografting, also called replacement lithography, where a nanoprobe displaces the adsorbed SAM molecules and facilitates an exchange with additional thiolate molecules in solution.<sup>54e58</sup> Advantageously, the exchange process prevents diffusion effects and enables extremely high spatial resolution capabilities, down to $2 \times 4 – \mathrm { n m } ^ { 2 }$ islands (32 alkanethiol molecules) and 10-nm wide lines with a line edge roughness (LER) down to 1 nm.<sup>52,56</sup> Moreover, nanografting offers the ability to generate and repair positive and negative tone patterns,<sup>59</s
--[p11]-- 15.2.1.2 Nanoshaving/nanografting
Further improvement of force-assisted patterning, toward higher resolution capabilities, lower threshold forces, and reduction of tip wear effects, can be achieved by the integration of bottom-up approaches utilizing self-assembled monolayers (SAMs). The most popular SAMs are alkanethiol molecules on Au.
--[p11]-- up> depending upon the relative chain length between the exchange and matrix alkanethiol adsorbent. However, the creation of functional nanostructures is crucial and to date has not been demonstrated by nanografting, owing to poor dense patterning and a lack of an adequate pattern transfer step.<sup>60</sup> Therefore, exceptionally selective or hybrid, pattern transfer approaches<sup>61,62</sup> are necessary to circumvent the extremely small aspect ratios inherent in SAM resists.

===== [p18-18] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.4.4 Electrostatic nanolithography (4块) =====
--[p18]-- In addition, Jegadesan et al.<sup>173</sup> patterned poly(methacrylic acid) thin films involving lower bias voltage thresholds whilst Xie et al.<sup>174</sup> investigated charge transport within the formation of PMMA-conical structures and explained the high observed current values by a water-bridgeemediated ion conduction mechanism.
--[p18]-- 15.2.4.4 Electrostatic nanolithography
A further method to pattern raised features (lateral size: 10e500 nm, height: 1e 10 nm) on thin dielectric polymer films (PMMA, PS), triggered by an electrostatic field, was introduced by Lyuksyutov et al.<sup>170e172</sup> They assumed that within the lithographic process, no chemical reactions like cross-linking, substantial polymer degradation or ablation were activated.
--[p18]-- In contrast, the proposed model implied firstly a localized joule heating of the polymer above its glass transition temperature, based on the high breakdown current between negatively biased tip (5e50 V) and the polymer-coated conductive sample (patterning regime: 1e100 nA, for PMMA and PS the currents must exceed 5e10 nA).<sup>171</sup> Secondly, the large, nonuniform electric-field gradients polarized the softened, viscoelastic polymer and attracted it toward the tip apex to form raised features.<sup>172</sup> By raising the bias voltages above 50 V, high breakdown currents >100 nA activated a direct polymer ablation mechanism, resulting in the formation of holes and depressions.
--[p18]-- Beside the creation of raised features, Martı´n et al.<sup>175</sup> investigated a hole/groove formation mechanism within PMMA and inferred an electrochemical-based reaction mechanism in the presence of ionic transport instead of thermally based mechanisms. Further, Xie et al.<sup>176</sup> have generated raised polymer structures below a biased AFM tip under ambient conditions by the initiation of nanoscale electrical discharge and transient shock wave generation effects.

===== [p4-4] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.1 SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY (4块) =====
--[p4]-- Moreover, the nanoscale precision down to the atomic and molecular level in combination with the applicability of a wide variety of materials, while operating in various environments from ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) to atmospheric pressure, and saturated or liquid environments, enables numerous lithographic approaches.
--[p4]-- 15.1 SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY
To overcome the limitations of conventional top-down lithographic approaches, scanning proximal probe techniquesdwhich were originally developed to observe physical, chemical, or biological interactions at the nanoscale while providing additional spectroscopic capabilitiesdoffer an alternative, unconventional, and promising way for highly spatial resolved surface modification, nano-object manipulation, and nanolithographic method evolution.
--[p4]-- Throughput has previously been a significant concern, but mix-and-match process<sup>1e3</sup> and multiple tip write arrays<sup>4,5</sup> show great promise for next-generation lithography<sup>6</sup> and are reviewed here.
--[p4]-- The easiest way to induce lithographic processes is by the simple enhancement of the respective tipesample interaction forces, which are normally used for spatially confined imaging, including for instance mechanical forces or electron currents. In general, the close proximity of the tip to the sample surface opens up multiple ways to exploit extremely spatially confined, specific, and ideally selective and precisely controllable interaction mechanisms, triggered by the nanoprobe.

===== [p15-15] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.3.3 Catalytic probe nanolithography (2块) =====
--[p15]-- Firstly introduced by Mu¨ller et al.<sup>111</sup> the best resolution achieved to date is 25 nm.<sup>112</sup> Commonly, the tip activates the chemical end group of a reactive monolayer (SAM), after which the activated molecules 113 react with molecules that are present in the surrounding environment.

===== [p19-19] Tip-basednanolithography methodsand materials > 15.2.4.5 Material transfer through field evaporation (2块) =====
--[p19]-- Depending on the bias polarity and material properties, which defines the threshold value for FE of negative and positive ions, the transportation of material from the tip onto the sample surface, or vice versa, is possible.<sup>177</sup> In general, the small proximity significantly lowers the required potential for FE to a few volts, demonstrated by the formation of 5- to 10-nm metal dots on Si or on thin insulator films.<sup>177e182</sup> However, the process of material transfer between tip and sample is so far not fully understood and proposed mechanisms include large electrostatic force effects<sup>183</sup> and field-enhanced diffusion processes.<sup>184</sup>
--[p19]-- 15.2.4.5 Material transfer through field evaporation
Aside from the previous mentioned effects, the high electric fields created within the probeesample junction could cause atom ionization and ejection, known as field evaporation (FE).
